2-kings-1:1:0.summary: Moab became David’s servants bringing gifts, the subjection Moab now breaks.

2-kings-1:1:1.summary: The Greek oracle speaks of Gog, not Moab; no link.

2-kings-1:1:2.summary: Moab became servants to David, bringing gifts.

2-kings-1:1:3.summary: Edom “broke away,” a similar vassal revolt.

2-kings-1:1:5.summary: Edom broke away from Judah, a similar vassal revolt.

2-kings-1:1:6.summary: Moab named as subjected to God, a general Moab link.

2-kings-1:2:3.summary: A sick king sends to inquire, “Will I recover from this illness of mine?”

2-kings-1:2:7.summary: Elijah confronts Ahaziah’s messengers going to “Baal Fly, the god of Ekron.”

2-kings-1:2:9.summary: The messengers report the rebuke about inquiring of “Baal Fly.”

2-kings-1:2:1.summary: “Beelzebul” is linked to Baal Fly only via the Hebrew name; Saints gives a translated name.

2-kings-1:2:2.summary: “Beelzebul” relates to Baal Fly only through the underlying name.

2-kings-1:2:4.summary: Idols “were not gods,” a general critique of false gods.

2-kings-1:2:5.summary: Solomon’s worship of foreign gods, a general idolatry parallel.

2-kings-1:2:6.summary: “Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons” connects to Baal Fly only through the Hebrew name.

2-kings-1:2:8.summary: The gods of the nations could not rescue, a general idolatry theme.

2-kings-1:2:10.summary: The Saints text names Ashkelon, not Ekron, so the place link is lost.

2-kings-1:2:11.summary: Looking “through the lattice” shares only the word lattice.

2-kings-1:2:12.summary: Ahab’s battle wound shares no specific element with Ahaziah’s fall.

2-kings-1:2:13.summary: A king struck with grievous sickness as judgment, a general parallel.

2-kings-1:2:14.summary: The beloved peering through the lattice shares only the word.

2-kings-1:2:15.summary: Destruction for the unjust has no specific link.

2-kings-1:2:16.summary: Eutychus fell from an upper story, a similar accident.

2-kings-1:2:17.summary: “Beelzebul” links to Baal Fly only through the Hebrew name.

2-kings-1:2:18.summary: “Chemosh your god,” a foreign deity reference, loosely parallels the god of Ekron.

2-kings-1:2:19.summary: Jeroboam sends to “inquire … whether he will live through his illness.”

2-kings-1:3:11.summary: The angel again speaks to Elijah, who repeats the rebuke about Baal Fly.

2-kings-1:3:16.summary: Ahaziah sends to inquire of “Baal Fly, the god of Ekron.”

2-kings-1:3:1.summary: Those who guard vain things abandon mercy, a general idolatry theme.

2-kings-1:3:2.summary: God’s people exchanging Him for false gods, a general parallel.

2-kings-1:3:3.summary: An angel of the Lord says “Rise,” a shared commissioning pattern.

2-kings-1:3:4.summary: God is known “in Israel,” loosely echoing “no God in Israel.”

2-kings-1:3:5.summary: “Beelzebul” connects to Baal Fly only via the Hebrew name.

2-kings-1:3:6.summary: “An angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, Rise and go,” a close verbal echo.
2-kings-1:3:6.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-1:3:7.summary: “This is Elijah the Tishbite,” the same prophet identified.

2-kings-1:3:8.summary: “All the earth will know that there is a God in Israel.”

2-kings-1:3:9.summary: “The Lord spoke to Elijah the Tishbite, saying,” the same commission formula.

2-kings-1:3:10.summary: The Lord’s angel tells Elijah “Rise,” the same angelic messenger.

2-kings-1:3:12.summary: Someone tells Elijah “Rise and eat,” a loose echo.

2-kings-1:3:13.summary: Elijah asks God to show He is “the God of Israel,” a related theme.

2-kings-1:3:15.summary: “There is no God in all the earth except in Israel,” answering the same question.

2-kings-1:3:17.summary: The Lord sends Elijah to confront Ahab, a similar commissioning.

2-kings-1:3:18.summary: “A prophet in Israel,” loosely parallel to “no God in Israel.”

2-kings-1:4:0.summary: “You shall surely die” is the same death formula.

2-kings-1:4:1.summary: Individual responsibility for sin has no specific link.

2-kings-1:4:2.summary: The serpent’s “You shall surely not die” shares only the phrase.

2-kings-1:4:3.summary: Saul’s death foretold after consulting a medium, a loose parallel.

2-kings-1:4:4.summary: A proverb on life and death has no specific link.

2-kings-1:4:5.summary: The same sentence: “you will not come down from it, for you will surely die.”

2-kings-1:4:6.summary: Ahijah foretells death after a royal inquiry about illness, a related pattern.

2-kings-1:4:7.summary: Wilderness generation dying shares only the death formula.

2-kings-1:4:8.summary: The messengers repeat the same oracle of certain death.

2-kings-1:4:9.summary: The impious thrust away has no specific link.

2-kings-1:4:10.summary: Sirach praises Elijah, who brought “kings down … from their bed.”

2-kings-1:6:0.summary: The Greek psalm about weaknesses and gatherings has no link.

2-kings-1:6:2.summary: Saul died because he inquired through a medium and did not seek the Lord.

2-kings-1:6:3.summary: Challenge to idols to foretell the future, a general idolatry critique.

2-kings-1:7:0.summary: Asking about men’s appearance, a loose parallel to the king’s question.

2-kings-1:7:1.summary: Saul asks what she saw; the description of a cloaked man lets him recognize Samuel.

2-kings-1:8:2.summary: John wore camel’s hair “with a leather belt around his waist,” Elijah’s garb.

2-kings-1:8:1.summary: Prophets “wear a hairy skin,” the prophetic garb Elijah wore.

2-kings-1:8:3.summary: Isaiah’s sackcloth at the waist, a loose prophetic dress parallel.

2-kings-1:8:4.summary: Two witnesses clothed in sackcloth, a loose prophetic dress parallel.

2-kings-1:8:5.summary: Not soft clothing like kings’ houses, contrasting John’s rough prophet’s garb.

2-kings-1:8:6.summary: John goes “in Elijah’s spirit and power.”

2-kings-1:9:0.summary: Jesus praying on a mountain shares only the mountain.

2-kings-1:9:1.summary: Persecution of the faithful is too general to link.

2-kings-1:9:2.summary: A king sends forces to seize a prophet (Elisha), as Ahaziah sends soldiers for Elijah.

2-kings-1:9:3.summary: A king orders a prophet imprisoned, a general royal hostility parallel.

2-kings-1:9:4.summary: The taunt to “come down” loosely echoes the captain’s “Come down!”

2-kings-1:9:5.summary: Ahab sent to every nation to search for Elijah, the same royal hunt.

2-kings-1:9:6.summary: Herod seizes John, a general king-versus-prophet parallel.

2-kings-1:9:7.summary: Amaziah orders the seer away, a general prophet-versus-authority parallel.

2-kings-1:9:8.summary: Elijah goes up onto Carmel, loosely matching him on the mountaintop.

2-kings-1:9:9.summary: Soldiers mocking Jesus has no specific link.

2-kings-1:9:10.summary: The king of Israel hates the prophet Micaiah, a general hostility parallel.

2-kings-1:9:11.summary: Mockers demand “come down,” loosely echoing the captain’s command.

2-kings-1:9:12.summary: Passers-by reviling Jesus has no specific link.

2-kings-1:9:13.summary: Mocking “Prophesy to us” has no specific link.

2-kings-1:9:14.summary: Jezebel striking prophets and Obadiah hiding them “fifty” each, a loose parallel.

2-kings-1:9:15.summary: Jezebel threatens Elijah’s life, the same royal house hostile to Elijah.

2-kings-1:10:1.summary: Men walk unharmed in fire, the opposite of fire consuming the captain and his fifty; only a general fire motif.
2-kings-1:10:1.why: Contrasts God's fire protecting versus destroying.

2-kings-1:10:2.summary: Describes binding the three youths and throwing them into the furnace; the shown text does not mention the executioners being consumed.
2-kings-1:10:2.why: No shared event or wording beyond fire setting.

2-kings-1:10:3.summary: Elijah again calls for fire, and “fire from the Lord fell from heaven and consumed” to vindicate him as God's servant.
2-kings-1:10:3.why: Shows Elijah's earlier fire sign authenticating his prophetic office.

2-kings-1:10:4.summary: Fire kindled against rebels and a “flame burned up sinners” parallels judgment fire, without specific link.
2-kings-1:10:4.why: General theme of fire as divine judgment.

2-kings-1:10:5.summary: God as “a consuming fire” echoes the fire that consumed the soldiers only thematically.
2-kings-1:10:5.why: Broad theological reflection on God's consuming fire.

2-kings-1:10:6.summary: Moses stakes his commission on a sign (“By this you shall know that the Lord sent me”), as Elijah says “If I am a man of God.”
2-kings-1:10:6.why: Parallel conditional sign authenticating a prophet.

2-kings-1:10:7.summary: “Fire fell from heaven” and “consumed” the shepherds closely echoes fire coming down from heaven and consuming the men.
2-kings-1:10:7.why: Same striking image of fire falling from heaven.

2-kings-1:10:8.summary: Fire comes out and “devoureth their enemies” for the two witnesses, recalling Elijah's fire against those sent to harm him.
2-kings-1:10:8.why: Shows Elijah's fire sign echoed in Revelation's witnesses.

2-kings-1:10:9.summary: Jesus speaks of persecuting and killing prophets; the link to soldiers sent against Elijah is only general hostility to prophets.
2-kings-1:10:9.why: Broad theme of rejecting God's prophets.

2-kings-1:10:10.summary: “Fire went out from the Lord and consumed” the 250 rebels, like fire consuming the captain and his fifty.
2-kings-1:10:10.why: Parallel divine fire destroying those who oppose God's servant.

2-kings-1:10:11.summary: Micaiah stakes his prophetic authority on a conditional outcome, as Elijah says “If I am a man of God.”
2-kings-1:10:11.why: Same pattern of a prophet's word tested by outcome.

2-kings-1:10:12.summary: A parable verdict on wicked tenants shares no specific element with fire consuming soldiers.
2-kings-1:10:12.why: Only a generic idea of destruction.

2-kings-1:10:13.summary: Daniel's accusers are destroyed by lions, loosely like Elijah's opponents destroyed by fire.
2-kings-1:10:13.why: General theme of judgment on a prophet's enemies.

2-kings-1:10:14.summary: Herod executes guards after Peter's escape; no shared event, image, or wording with Elijah's fire.

2-kings-1:10:15.summary: “Do not act wickedly against My prophets” generally fits the soldiers sent against Elijah.
2-kings-1:10:15.why: Principle of God protecting His prophets.

2-kings-1:10:16.summary: Elisha's mockers are killed by bears after his curse, loosely like Elijah's opponents consumed by fire.
2-kings-1:10:16.why: Similar pattern of judgment on those who scorn a prophet.

2-kings-1:10:17.summary: Mocking God's prophets brings His anger, a general theme fitting hostility toward Elijah.
2-kings-1:10:17.why: Broad theme of contempt for prophets punished.

2-kings-1:10:18.summary: Ananias dies at Peter's word (shown text truncated), loosely like sudden death at a man of God's word.
2-kings-1:10:18.why: Parallel of sudden judgment through an apostle.

2-kings-1:10:19.summary: “Fire from the Lord” blazed and “consumed” part of the camp, echoing fire consuming the captain's company.
2-kings-1:10:19.why: Another instance of consuming fire as judgment.

2-kings-1:10:20.summary: Sirach praises Elijah as “a prophet like fire,” directly characterizing the prophet of this episode.
2-kings-1:10:20.why: Later reflection on Elijah's fiery ministry.

2-kings-1:10:21.summary: Elijah “brought down fire three times,” recalling the fire on Carmel and on the captains of fifty.
2-kings-1:10:21.why: Sirach summarizes this very fire episode.

2-kings-1:11:0.summary: Philistines test whether God's hand struck them; nothing ties this to a king sending a second captain.

2-kings-1:11:1.summary: A king heeding unjust words makes his servants lawless, loosely matching servants executing Ahaziah's order.
2-kings-1:11:1.why: General proverb on corrupt royal authority.

2-kings-1:11:2.summary: Authorities acknowledge a sign yet still try to silence God's messengers, as the king persists after the fire.
2-kings-1:11:2.why: Illustrates stubborn opposition despite clear signs.

2-kings-1:11:3.summary: Israel grumbles again the day after judgment, loosely like the king persisting after fire fell.
2-kings-1:11:3.why: Theme of persisting rebellion after judgment.

2-kings-1:11:4.summary: Saul orders his men against the Lord's priests, loosely like a king sending soldiers against a man of God.

2-kings-1:11:5.summary: Evil counsel against the lowly has no specific link to the king sending another captain.

2-kings-1:11:6.summary: An armed party sent to seize Jesus falls back before Him (truncated), loosely like soldiers sent to seize Elijah.
2-kings-1:11:6.why: Parallel of men sent to arrest God's servant.

2-kings-1:11:7.summary: Guards mock and beat Jesus; nothing corresponds to the captain's command to Elijah.

2-kings-1:11:8.summary: Herod's slaughter of infants shares only a king sending men; no real link to this episode.

2-kings-1:11:9.summary: “Fire will consume the opponents” of the Lord loosely matches the fate of the king's soldiers.
2-kings-1:11:9.why: General theme of fire against God's opponents.

2-kings-1:11:10.summary: People struck yet refusing to return parallels the king persisting after judgment only generally.
2-kings-1:11:10.why: Theme of hardened refusal after discipline.

2-kings-1:12:0.summary: The first captain's identical exchange: “If I am a man of God, fire will come down from heaven and consume you.”
2-kings-1:12:0.why: Repeated formula structuring the three-captain narrative.

2-kings-1:13:0.summary: Being “struck again” for lawlessness has no specific tie to the third captain's humble plea.

2-kings-1:13:1.summary: Pharaoh's servants will come down and bow before Moses, loosely like the captain kneeling before Elijah.
2-kings-1:13:1.why: Royal servants humbled before a prophet.

2-kings-1:13:2.summary: Souls redeemed and their name “honored” before the king echoes the plea that lives be “honored” only verbally.
2-kings-1:13:2.why: Verbal echo of lives held precious.

2-kings-1:13:3.summary: Saul says “my soul was honoured in your eyes,” the same idiom as the captain's plea that lives be “honored in your eyes.”
2-kings-1:13:3.why: Clarifies the idiom of a life held precious.

2-kings-1:13:4.summary: A general call to submit to God has no specific link to the captain's plea.

2-kings-1:13:5.summary: Former oppressors come humbly in fear, loosely like the third captain approaching Elijah.

2-kings-1:13:6.summary: Opponents made to “bow before thy feet” loosely parallel the captain kneeling before Elijah.
2-kings-1:13:6.why: Motif of adversaries bowing to God's servant.

2-kings-1:13:7.summary: A reflection on death and evil hearts has no specific link to the captain's plea.

2-kings-1:13:8.summary: God regards the humble who tremble at His words, matching the third captain's humility only generally.

2-kings-1:13:9.summary: A fool not cured by punishment loosely fits the king persisting after two judgments.

2-kings-1:13:10.summary: Insolence against the Lord contrasts with the third captain's humility, but no specific link.

2-kings-1:13:11.summary: Aaron pleads with Moses (“I beseech you, my lord”) to spare life, loosely like the captain pleading with Elijah.
2-kings-1:13:11.why: Pattern of pleading with a prophet for mercy.

2-kings-1:13:12.summary: God heeds the prayer of the lowly, generally fitting the humble captain's petition.

2-kings-1:13:13.summary: A king's request to “the man of God” for mercy after judgment parallels the captain humbly entreating the man of God.
2-kings-1:13:13.why: Similar humble appeal to a man of God.

2-kings-1:14:0.summary: Paul counting his life of no value shares only the word “life” with the plea for lives to be honored.

2-kings-1:14:1.summary: A proverb about adultery and “precious lives” has no real link to the captain's plea.

2-kings-1:14:2.summary: The death of God's holy ones is “precious” to Him, loosely echoing lives valued in one's eyes.
2-kings-1:14:2.why: Theme of life valued by God.

2-kings-1:14:3.summary: Teaching on saving or losing one's life relates only loosely to the captain seeking to save his life.
2-kings-1:14:3.why: General theme of the value of a life.

2-kings-1:14:4.summary: David says “as your soul was magnified in my eyes,” the same idiom of a life valued in another's eyes.
2-kings-1:14:4.why: Parallel idiom of sparing a life.

2-kings-1:14:5.summary: Their name “honored” before the king echoes the captain's wording only verbally.
2-kings-1:14:5.why: Verbal echo of lives held precious.

2-kings-1:14:6.summary: “My soul was honoured in your eyes” matches the captain's request that lives be “honored in your eyes.”
2-kings-1:14:6.why: Same idiom of a life held precious.

2-kings-1:14:7.summary: The price of a soul's redemption has no specific link to the captain's plea.

2-kings-1:15:0.summary: God tells His people not to dread mortals, generally like the angel's “do not be afraid of them.”
2-kings-1:15:0.why: Encouragement not to fear human threats.

2-kings-1:15:1.summary: God tells the prophet “do not fear them” though they rage, matching the angel's command to Elijah.
2-kings-1:15:1.why: Same divine reassurance to a prophet facing hostility.

2-kings-1:15:2.summary: “Do not fear them” and “rise” to speak, with God's promise of rescue, parallels Elijah's commission to go down.
2-kings-1:15:2.why: Same reassurance for a prophet confronting rulers.

2-kings-1:15:3.summary: “An angel of the Lord spoke to Elijah” earlier in the chapter, sending him to Ahaziah's messengers.
2-kings-1:15:3.why: Same angelic guidance framing the episode.

2-kings-1:15:4.summary: “Do not fear those who kill the body” generally fits the command not to fear the king's men.
2-kings-1:15:4.why: Broad teaching on fearlessness before persecutors.

2-kings-1:15:5.summary: God promises the prophet that opponents “will not prevail” because He is with him, loosely fitting Elijah's safety.
2-kings-1:15:5.why: Assurance of protection for a prophet.

2-kings-1:15:6.summary: “Whom will I fear?” expresses general trust, not the specific command to Elijah.

2-kings-1:15:7.summary: “Do not fear, Abram” is a divine reassurance like the angel's, but in an unrelated setting.

2-kings-1:15:8.summary: Elijah resolves to show himself to the hostile king Ahab, as he now goes down to face Ahaziah.
2-kings-1:15:8.why: Elijah's pattern of boldly confronting kings.

2-kings-1:15:9.summary: Moses not “fearing the king's anger” loosely parallels Elijah going unafraid to the king.
2-kings-1:15:9.why: Faith overcoming fear of a king.

2-kings-1:16:7.summary: The same oracle, nearly verbatim: “Baal Fly, the god of Ekron… you will not come down from it, for you will surely die.”
2-kings-1:16:7.why: Repetition confirming the prophetic word to the king directly.

2-kings-1:16:1.summary: Elijah delivers a “Thus says the Lord” doom oracle to Ahab, father of Ahaziah (shown text truncated).
2-kings-1:16:1.why: Elijah's judgment on the same royal house.

2-kings-1:16:2.summary: David's vow not to climb onto his bed shares only the word “bed”.

2-kings-1:16:3.summary: A “Thus says the Lord” death threat to Pharaoh resembles a prophetic death sentence on a king only generally.
2-kings-1:16:3.why: Prophetic word of death to a ruler.

2-kings-1:16:4.summary: Gehazi pursuing Naaman has no link to Elijah's oracle to Ahaziah.

2-kings-1:16:5.summary: Micaiah's prophecy against a king's return parallels a prophetic doom on a king only loosely.

2-kings-1:16:6.summary: A king's household consults a prophet about a sick child and receives a “thus says the Lord” word of death (Greek-only 12:24 section, truncated).
2-kings-1:16:6.why: Parallel of a royal inquiry about illness answered with doom.

2-kings-1:16:8.summary: Sirach says Elijah brought kings down “from their bed,” recalling Ahaziah who would not come down from his bed.
2-kings-1:16:8.why: Later summary of Elijah's word against Ahaziah.

2-kings-1:17:0.summary: Jehoram's accession follows Ahaziah's death, but the source text shown does not name him.
2-kings-1:17:0.why: Gives the succession after Ahaziah's death.

2-kings-1:17:1.summary: Records Ahaziah's two-year reign over Israel, the king whose death is reported here.
2-kings-1:17:1.why: Frames the reign that ends with this death.

2-kings-1:17:2.summary: A regnal synchronism for Joram son of Ahab; the shown source does not mention him.

2-kings-1:18:0.summary: Same closing formula: “The rest of … acts, all he did… are these not written in the” annals of the kings of Israel.
2-kings-1:18:0.why: Standard regnal formula, here for Ahaziah's father.

2-kings-1:18:1.summary: 1 Kings 14:19 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-1:18:1.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-1:18:1.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-2:1:0.summary: Enoch “was not found, for God transferred him,” the other figure taken by God without death.
2-kings-2:1:0.why: Only other OT bodily removal by God.

2-kings-2:1:1.summary: Enoch “was taken away so as not to see death,” paralleling Elijah taken up.
2-kings-2:1:1.why: NT reflection on the parallel translation.

2-kings-2:1:2.summary: God commands Elijah to anoint Elisha as prophet in his place, and Elijah calls him with his sheepskin cloak.

2-kings-2:1:3.summary: A great strong wind passes before the Lord at Horeb, a loose link to the tumult taking Elijah.

2-kings-2:1:4.summary: Explains the naming of Gilgal, the starting point here.

2-kings-2:1:5.summary: Israel camped at Gilgal after crossing the Jordan; only the place is shared.
2-kings-2:1:5.why: Locates Gilgal near Jericho and Jordan.

2-kings-2:1:6.summary: Elisha later returns to Gilgal among the sons of the prophets; shared person and place, different episode.
2-kings-2:1:6.why: Shows Gilgal as a prophetic center.

2-kings-2:1:7.summary: Elijah once asked the Lord to take his life, contrasting with God now taking him up.

2-kings-2:1:8.summary: “The days for His being taken up” echoes the language of Elijah being taken up.
2-kings-2:1:8.why: Frames Jesus’ journey like Elijah’s ascent.

2-kings-2:1:9.summary: Elijah “was taken up in a tumult, as into heaven,” the fulfillment of this verse’s announcement.

2-kings-2:1:10.summary: Obadiah fears “the Lord’s Spirit will carry you” away, showing Elijah was known to be transported by God.

2-kings-2:1:11.summary: God speaking to Job “through a whirlwind” does not match the Saints “tumult,” and the events are unrelated.

2-kings-2:1:12.summary: Jesus “was lifted up as they watched,” paralleling a master taken up before his disciple.

2-kings-2:1:13.summary: Two witnesses go “up into heaven in the cloud,” a general ascent motif.

2-kings-2:1:14.summary: Sirach recalls Elijah “taken up in a whirlwind of fire, in a chariot with fiery horses.”

2-kings-2:2:0.summary: The same exchange recurs: “Please stay here… As the Lord lives, and as you live, I will not leave you.”

2-kings-2:2:1.summary: Ruth refuses Naomi’s urging to turn back, vowing to go wherever she goes, like Elisha refusing to leave.

2-kings-2:2:2.summary: The Shunammite uses Elisha’s own oath: “As the Lord lives, and as you live, I will not leave you.”

2-kings-2:2:3.summary: Peter refuses to leave Jesus, a general theme of disciple loyalty.

2-kings-2:2:4.summary: Hannah’s “As your soul lives” shares only an oath formula.

2-kings-2:2:6.summary: Ittai, told to return, swears “As the Lord lives, and as my lord the king lives” that he will stay with David.
2-kings-2:2:6.why: Parallel oath of loyal refusal to leave.

2-kings-2:2:7.summary: Bethel as site of Jeroboam’s altar and a man of God’s oracle; shares only the place.

2-kings-2:2:8.summary: Abigail’s “as the Lord lives and as your soul lives” shares only the oath formula.

2-kings-2:2:9.summary: Jacob names the place “House of God” (Bethel), though the Saints text does not use the name Bethel.

2-kings-2:2:10.summary: Swearing “The Lord lives” shares only the oath expression.

2-kings-2:2:12.summary: Those who did not remain with the community share no specific link with Elisha staying with Elijah.
2-kings-2:2:12.why: Only an abstract idea of remaining.

2-kings-2:2:13.summary: Jeroboam placed a calf “in Bethel”; only the place is shared.

2-kings-2:3:0.summary: Elisha with “the sons of the prophets” sitting before him, the same prophetic company.
2-kings-2:3:0.why: Elisha’s later leadership of the group.

2-kings-2:3:1.summary: A woman “from among the sons of the prophets” appeals to Elisha, the same community.
2-kings-2:3:1.why: Shows the prophetic guild under Elisha.

2-kings-2:3:2.summary: “One of the sons of the prophets” appears in a separate story; only the group term is shared.

2-kings-2:3:3.summary: Elisha sends “one of the sons of the prophets” on a mission, the same company.

2-kings-2:3:4.summary: Fifty “sons of the prophets” watch Elijah and Elisha at the Jordan in the same episode.
2-kings-2:3:4.why: Same group in the same narrative.

2-kings-2:3:5.summary: “Two young men from the sons of the prophets” are mentioned in Elisha’s household, the same group.

2-kings-2:3:6.summary: Isaiah’s children as signs share nothing specific with the sons of the prophets’ question.
2-kings-2:3:6.why: Link depends on loose idea of “sons.”

2-kings-2:3:7.summary: Paul trained “at the feet of Gamaliel,” loosely like a master being over a disciple’s head.

2-kings-2:3:8.summary: The sons of the prophets recognize Elijah’s spirit resting on Elisha, continuing this episode.

2-kings-2:3:9.summary: A “chorus of prophets” in Saul’s time shares only the idea of prophetic bands.

2-kings-2:3:10.summary: An “assembly of prophets” with Samuel appointed over them parallels a prophetic band under a leader.
2-kings-2:3:10.why: Earlier prophetic guild with a head.

2-kings-2:3:12.summary: Obadiah hid a hundred prophets, showing groups of prophets existed, but no specific link.

2-kings-2:3:13.summary: Consecrated ones under God’s hands has no specific link to the prophets’ words to Elisha.

2-kings-2:4:0.summary: Identical exchange: “Please stay here… As the Lord lives, and as you live, I will not leave you.”

2-kings-2:4:1.summary: Joshua’s curse on rebuilding Jericho shares only the city.

2-kings-2:4:2.summary: Jesus passing through Jericho shares only the place name.

2-kings-2:4:3.summary: The Shunammite uses the identical oath, “As the Lord lives, and as you live, I will not leave you.”

2-kings-2:4:4.summary: Hiel the Bethelite rebuilt Jericho, sharing the place and its history only.

2-kings-2:4:5.summary: Encouragement “to remain with the Lord” shares only an abstract idea of remaining.

2-kings-2:4:6.summary: Devotion to the apostles’ teaching has no specific link to Elisha’s oath.

2-kings-2:5:1.summary: The Greek-based “Be renewed toward Me, islands” lacks the silence command the label assumes.

2-kings-2:5:2.summary: In the Saints text the earth is told to revere the Lord, not to be silent, so no link remains.
2-kings-2:5:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-2:5:3.summary: Jesus’ prayer about glory and His disciples has no specific link to the prophets’ question.

2-kings-2:5:4.summary: Jesus “was taken up from you into heaven,” a general parallel to the master being taken.

2-kings-2:5:5.summary: Jesus “was taken up” after instructing his chosen ones, a general ascent parallel.

2-kings-2:5:6.summary: Joshua succeeds Moses after his death, a general succession theme.
2-kings-2:5:6.why: Successor taking up a master’s role.

2-kings-2:5:7.summary: Jacob’s “I know, my child, I know” loosely echoes Elisha’s “I too know it.”

2-kings-2:5:8.summary: “A time to be silent” loosely relates to Elisha’s “Be silent.”

2-kings-2:5:9.summary: Jesus “parted from them and was carried up into heaven,” a general ascent parallel.

2-kings-2:5:10.summary: Paul’s defense before Festus shares nothing specific with this verse.

2-kings-2:6:0.summary: Identical exchange: “Please stay here… As the Lord lives, and as you live, I will not leave you.”

2-kings-2:6:1.summary: The Jordan where Israel crossed with the ark; only the river is shared in the shown text.

2-kings-2:7:0.summary: Prophets hidden “fifty to a cave” share only the number fifty and prophetic company.

2-kings-2:7:1.summary: The sons of the prophets later send “fifty men” who search for Elijah, the same group in the same episode.

2-kings-2:7:2.summary: Obadiah hid prophets “fifty to a cave,” sharing only the number and prophetic group.

2-kings-2:8:0.summary: Elijah threw “his sheepskin cloak” over Elisha, the same garment used here.

2-kings-2:8:1.summary: Moses’ sea is “split” and Israel crosses “on dry ground,” the model for this water-parting.
2-kings-2:8:1.why: Elijah’s miracle echoes the Exodus crossing.

2-kings-2:8:3.summary: Elisha strikes the water with Elijah’s sheepskin and it splits “to this side and that,” repeating this miracle.

2-kings-2:8:4.summary: The psalm asks why the sea fled and the Jordan “withdrew backward,” celebrating water parting before God.
2-kings-2:8:4.why: Poetic memory of the Jordan parting.

2-kings-2:8:5.summary: Israel crossed the Red Sea “as through dry land,” a general parallel to crossing on barren ground.
2-kings-2:8:5.why: NT recollection of a similar crossing.

2-kings-2:8:6.summary: The Lord will strike waters so people may pass, a general water-crossing image.

2-kings-2:8:7.summary: Elijah covers his face with “his sheepskin cloak,” the same garment.

2-kings-2:8:8.summary: The Euphrates’ water is dried up to prepare a way, a general water-drying image.

2-kings-2:9:0.summary: God takes “of the Spirit that is upon you” and puts it on others, like Elisha seeking a share of Elijah’s spirit.
2-kings-2:9:0.why: Precedent for transferring a leader’s spirit.

2-kings-2:9:2.summary: Jesus must go away for the Advocate to come, loosely like a departing master leaving the Spirit.

2-kings-2:9:3.summary: Paul’s farewell before departure, entrusting his charge to others; shown text gives only a general parallel.
2-kings-2:9:3.why: Farewell of a leader to successors.

2-kings-2:9:4.summary: The Lord took “some of the Spirit that was upon him” and put it on the seventy elders.
2-kings-2:9:4.why: Spirit shared from a leader to others.

2-kings-2:9:5.summary: The Lord shielding Jerusalem’s residents shares nothing specific with Elisha’s request.

2-kings-2:9:6.summary: Disciples will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes, a general parallel to the departing master’s spirit.

2-kings-2:9:7.summary: Believers receive the Holy Spirit through laid hands, only a broad Spirit-transfer theme.

2-kings-2:9:8.summary: “Double honor” for elders echoes the idea of a double portion only verbally.
2-kings-2:9:8.why: Double share for a worthy leader.

2-kings-2:9:9.summary: “I will repay you double” to prisoners has no real link beyond the word double.

2-kings-2:9:10.summary: The colophon ending David’s hymns has no connection to this request.

2-kings-2:9:11.summary: Jesus, leaving the world, prays for those He leaves behind; truncated text gives only a general farewell parallel.

2-kings-2:9:12.summary: Solomon asks God for wisdom to lead, a general parallel of requesting a gift for a task.

2-kings-2:9:13.summary: Jesus promises power from on high, then parts from them; shown text gives a general departure-and-endowment parallel.

2-kings-2:9:14.summary: Believers will do “greater works” because Jesus goes to the Father, loosely like a double portion.
2-kings-2:9:14.why: Greater works after the master departs.

2-kings-2:9:15.summary: Joshua “was filled with a spirit of understanding” because Moses laid hands on him, a successor receiving spirit.

2-kings-2:9:16.summary: Solomon asks for a hearing heart to judge, a general request for an endowment.

2-kings-2:9:17.summary: Elisha’s deathbed scene shares the person and the “Israel’s chariot” cry, but not this request.

2-kings-2:9:18.summary: “Earnestly desire the greater gifts” loosely relates to seeking a greater spiritual portion.

2-kings-2:9:19.summary: A prayer for the king’s judgment has no specific link to Elisha’s request.

2-kings-2:9:20.summary: Moses is to lay hands on Joshua and “put of your glory upon him,” transferring authority to a successor.

2-kings-2:9:21.summary: David’s prayer for Solomon’s heart lacks any specific link to the double-portion request.

2-kings-2:9:22.summary: Sirach says “Elisha was filled with his spirit,” recalling the granted request.
2-kings-2:9:22.why: Later witness the request was fulfilled.

2-kings-2:10:0.summary: Faith-filled asking in prayer is not linked to Elijah’s condition of seeing him taken up.

2-kings-2:10:1.summary: “Ask, and you will receive” has no specific link to this conditional promise.

2-kings-2:10:3.summary: Jesus “was lifted up as they watched,” disciples seeing the ascent, a general parallel.
2-kings-2:10:3.why: Disciples witnessing the master taken up.

2-kings-2:11:0.summary: God makes His ministers “a burning fire” and clouds His ascent, loosely like fiery heavenly agents.

2-kings-2:11:1.summary: The mountain was full of horses and “a chariot of fire” around Elisha, the same heavenly host image.

2-kings-2:11:2.summary: Angels as ministering spirits has no specific tie to the chariot of fire in the texts shown.

2-kings-2:11:3.summary: “God’s chariot is ten-thousandfold” shares only the divine chariot image.

2-kings-2:11:4.summary: Ezekiel’s vision of “a sweeping wind” with fire and living creatures shares only fiery theophany imagery.

2-kings-2:11:5.summary: Cherubim and wheels form a heavenly vehicle, a general parallel to the chariot of fire.

2-kings-2:11:6.summary: Bringing the servant “Rising” has no link to Elijah’s ascent.

2-kings-2:11:7.summary: The Lord mounting His horses for salvation shares only the divine horses image.

2-kings-2:11:8.summary: Jesus “was taken up into heaven,” a general ascension parallel.

2-kings-2:11:9.summary: Enoch “was not found, for God transferred him,” the other person taken by God without death.

2-kings-2:11:10.summary: The narrative opens with the Lord about “to take Elijah up in a tumult, as into heaven,” identical wording.

2-kings-2:11:11.summary: Four chariots with colored horses are heavenly agents, a general chariot-and-horses image.

2-kings-2:11:12.summary: Mattathias recalls that Elijah “was taken up into heaven.”

2-kings-2:12:1.summary: “No one has ascended into heaven” except the Son of Man stands in tension with Elijah’s ascent.

2-kings-2:12:2.summary: Groaning to be clothed over in the tent has no specific link to Elisha’s cry and torn clothes.

2-kings-2:12:3.summary: Hezekiah praying to the Lord has no connection to Elisha’s cry.

2-kings-2:12:4.summary: “Who went up to heaven and came down?” loosely touches the ascent theme.

2-kings-2:12:5.summary: Job “tore his garments” in grief, sharing the mourning gesture.

2-kings-2:12:6.summary: Christ “ascended on high” and gave gifts, a general ascent-and-gift parallel.

2-kings-2:12:7.summary: Isaiah’s message to Hezekiah about Sennacherib is unrelated to Elijah’s departure.

2-kings-2:12:8.summary: The witnesses “went up into heaven” as enemies watched, a general ascent parallel.

2-kings-2:12:9.summary: The righteous man “was taken” from injustice, a loose removal theme.

2-kings-2:12:10.summary: Jesus “parted from them and was carried up into heaven,” a general parallel.

2-kings-2:12:11.summary: Angels departing into heaven after the nativity announcement has no real link.

2-kings-2:12:12.summary: Jesus “was taken up into heaven,” a general ascension parallel.

2-kings-2:12:13.summary: Devout men lament Stephen, sharing only the theme of mourning a departed man of God.

2-kings-2:12:14.summary: Jesus was lifted up “as they watched,” and was hidden from sight, like Elisha seeing him no more.

2-kings-2:12:15.summary: Longing for a heavenly dwelling has no specific link to this scene.

2-kings-2:12:16.summary: Hezekiah’s plea about Rapsakes has no connection to Elijah’s ascent.

2-kings-2:12:17.summary: God granting Paul those sailing with him is unrelated.

2-kings-2:12:18.summary: Rescue through clean hands has no link to “Israel’s chariot” or the ascent in the Saints text.

2-kings-2:12:19.summary: A city razed by the impious has no link to this verse.

2-kings-2:12:20.summary: Wisdom outweighing ten rulers is at most an inferred link to the prophet as Israel’s defense.

2-kings-2:12:21.summary: “Wisdom is better than weapons of war” links only by interpreting the prophet as Israel’s chariot.

2-kings-2:13:1.summary: Elijah’s “sheepskin” struck the Jordan earlier; Elisha now takes up that same garment.

2-kings-2:13:2.summary: Solomon’s ship at the sea’s shore shares only the idea of a shore or edge.

2-kings-2:13:3.summary: Sirach: “Elijah was covered by a whirlwind, and Elisha was filled with his spirit,” recalling this succession.

2-kings-2:14:0.summary: Believers will do the master’s works after He goes, loosely like Elisha repeating Elijah’s miracle.

2-kings-2:14:1.summary: Enemies taunt “Where is your God?”, verbally like Elisha’s “Where is the God of Elijah?” but in mockery.
2-kings-2:14:1.why: Same question in a different sense.

2-kings-2:14:2.summary: “Where is their God?” shares the question form only.

2-kings-2:14:3.summary: Peter attributes a miracle not to himself but to the God of the fathers, a loose parallel.

2-kings-2:14:4.summary: Joshua succeeds Moses, is told to “cross the Jordan,” and God says “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you.”
2-kings-2:14:4.why: Successor crossing the Jordan as sign.

2-kings-2:14:5.summary: The exalted Christ pours out the Spirit, a general parallel of a departed master’s spirit at work.

2-kings-2:14:6.summary: “Where is their God?” shares the question form only.

2-kings-2:14:7.summary: The Lord confirms the disciples’ word through signs, a general parallel to God confirming Elisha.

2-kings-2:14:8.summary: Thirsting for the living God has no specific link to Elisha’s question.

2-kings-2:14:10.summary: Gideon asks “Where are all His wonders” the fathers recounted, loosely like asking for the former God’s power.

2-kings-2:14:11.summary: Elijah’s God answers by fire at Carmel, background to invoking “the God of Elijah.”
2-kings-2:14:11.why: Shows the God of Elijah acting.

2-kings-2:15:0.summary: “The Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you” shares the resting-spirit wording.

2-kings-2:15:1.summary: Power comes when the Holy Spirit comes upon the disciples, a general parallel.

2-kings-2:15:2.summary: The Advocate’s coming and the disciples’ witness loosely parallel the spirit recognized on Elisha.
2-kings-2:15:2.why: Spirit given after the master departs.

2-kings-2:15:3.summary: The same “sons of the prophets” stood opposite them at the Jordan in this episode.

2-kings-2:15:4.summary: The men of the city next address Elisha as lord, the following scene in the same place.

2-kings-2:15:5.summary: “The Spirit of God will rest upon him” matches the spirit coming “to rest upon” Elisha.

2-kings-2:15:6.summary: God exalts Joshua at the Jordan so all may know “as I was with Moses, so I will be with you.”

2-kings-2:15:7.summary: “When the Spirit rested upon them, they prophesied,” the Spirit taken from Moses resting on others.
2-kings-2:15:7.why: Spirit resting on others from a leader.

2-kings-2:15:8.summary: Putting Moses’ glory on Joshua so Israel obeys him loosely parallels the prophets recognizing Elisha.

2-kings-2:15:9.summary: After the Jordan crossing Israel “feared him as they had Moses,” as the prophets now bow to Elisha.

2-kings-2:15:10.summary: “My spirit that is upon you” remaining on offspring loosely parallels a spirit passing on.

2-kings-2:15:11.summary: The woman “bowed to the ground” before Elisha, sharing only the gesture.

2-kings-2:15:12.summary: The sons of the prophets dwell before Elisha and seek his leave, showing him as their head.

2-kings-2:15:13.summary: A woman “from among the sons of the prophets” appeals to Elisha as leader.

2-kings-2:15:14.summary: Christ’s power resting on Paul in weakness has no specific link here.

2-kings-2:16:1.summary: “The Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away,” just as the prophets fear a spirit of the Lord lifted Elijah.
2-kings-2:16:1.why: Spirit physically carrying a prophet away.

2-kings-2:16:2.summary: “A spirit lifted me and brought me” elsewhere, the same idea of a spirit transporting a prophet.

2-kings-2:16:3.summary: Ezekiel is set “upon a very high mountain” in a vision; the shown text lacks the spirit lifting him.

2-kings-2:16:4.summary: “The spirit raised me and took me up,” a prophet carried by the spirit.

2-kings-2:16:5.summary: A man “caught up as far as the third heaven” shares a general catching-up theme.

2-kings-2:16:6.summary: “A spirit lifted me between earth and heaven and brought me” to Jerusalem, a prophet carried away.

2-kings-2:17:0.summary: Elisha fixed his gaze “until shame,” echoing the phrase “until he was ashamed.”

2-kings-2:17:1.summary: A friend yields because of “shameless insistence,” like Elisha yielding to pressure.

2-kings-2:17:2.summary: Ahimaaz presses Joab until told “Run,” a similar giving way to insistence.

2-kings-2:17:3.summary: Enoch “was not found, because God took him away,” as the searchers “did not find” Elijah.
2-kings-2:17:3.why: Taken by God, not found by men.

2-kings-2:17:4.summary: Zeal without knowledge loosely describes the prophets’ futile search.

2-kings-2:19:0.summary: God promises none “unfruitful or barren in your land,” the blessing this bereaved land lacks.

2-kings-2:19:1.summary: “Blessed are you in the city… blessed are the offspring” sets the covenant blessing this city lacks.

2-kings-2:19:2.summary: God multiplies “the offspring of your womb” and land’s produce, the blessing missing here.

2-kings-2:19:3.summary: “Cursed are the offspring of your womb, and the produce of your land” matches the city’s barrenness generally.

2-kings-2:19:4.summary: Egypt’s waters become blood, a general picture of bad water as judgment.

2-kings-2:19:5.summary: Hiel rebuilt Jericho at the cost of his firstborn and youngest son, the curse behind the land’s loss of offspring.

2-kings-2:19:6.summary: At Marah the water could not be drunk “because it was bitter,” another bad water God heals.

2-kings-2:19:7.summary: Aaron addressing Moses as “my lord” shares only a title.

2-kings-2:19:8.summary: Obadiah calling Elijah “my lord” shares only a title.

2-kings-2:19:9.summary: Joshua cursed Jericho’s rebuilder “at the cost of his firstborn,” source of the city’s loss of offspring.

2-kings-2:19:10.summary: “A childless womb” as judgment loosely matches a land bereaved of offspring.

2-kings-2:19:11.summary: Jericho placed under the ban, background to the city’s condition.

2-kings-2:19:12.summary: Honor for elders has no link to Jericho’s bad waters.

2-kings-2:19:13.summary: Obadiah hiding prophets has no link to this verse.

2-kings-2:20:0.summary: The Saints text of Zephaniah lacks any salt, so nothing links it to Elisha’s salt jar.

2-kings-2:20:1.summary: Abimelech “sowed it with salt” to curse a city, contrasting Elisha’s salt that heals.

2-kings-2:20:2.summary: Marsh outlets “given over to salt” are not healed, contrasting salt used to heal here.

2-kings-2:21:1.summary: Elisha puts flour in the cauldron and “there was no longer anything harmful,” another healing by a simple substance.

2-kings-2:21:2.summary: “The salt of the covenant” in offerings gives background on salt’s sacred use.

2-kings-2:21:3.summary: Elisha throws wood into the water and the iron floats, another miracle by casting something in.

2-kings-2:21:4.summary: River-side leaves “for the healing,” and “no accursed thing” any more, a general healing-waters theme.

2-kings-2:21:5.summary: “Death shall be no more” loosely echoes “No longer will death” come from the waters.

2-kings-2:21:6.summary: Jesus heals with mud, a loose parallel of healing through a humble material.

2-kings-2:21:7.summary: Saying about salt losing saltiness shares only the word salt.

2-kings-2:21:8.summary: Blessing on the persecuted has no link to healing the waters.

2-kings-2:21:9.summary: God using foolish means to save is at most an interpretive link; shown text is truncated.

2-kings-2:21:10.summary: Water reaching “the water of the outlet” will “heal the waters” so that everything lives.

2-kings-2:21:11.summary: God turns “outlets of waters” to thirst and brine, then makes them fruitful so people multiply.
2-kings-2:21:11.why: God reversing barren waters and land.

2-kings-2:23:0.summary: Israel was “mocking His prophets” until the Lord’s anger rose, like the children mocking Elisha.

2-kings-2:23:1.summary: Job is laughed at by the least, a general picture of being mocked by inferiors.
2-kings-2:23:1.why: Mocking by the young or lowly.

2-kings-2:23:2.summary: They “speak against me” whenever Job rises; the shown text does not name children.

2-kings-2:23:4.summary: Ishmael “playing” with Isaac carries no mockery in the Saints wording.

2-kings-2:23:5.summary: Lips speaking “in arrogance and contempt” against the righteous generally parallel the taunting.

2-kings-2:23:6.summary: Amos warns against seeking Bethel, sharing only the place.

2-kings-2:23:7.summary: “Lawless sons” of a sinful nation is a general indictment, not linked to this event.

2-kings-2:23:8.summary: “The child will collide with the elder” loosely fits children insulting the prophet.

2-kings-2:23:9.summary: Mockers taunt Jesus to “come down from the cross,” a general taunting parallel.

2-kings-2:23:10.summary: Sons gathering wood for idol worship has no specific link.

2-kings-2:23:11.summary: Soldiers mock Jesus and strike His head, a general parallel of mocking God’s servant.

2-kings-2:23:12.summary: Senselessness bound in a young person’s heart loosely explains the children’s behavior.

2-kings-2:23:13.summary: Israel’s king cast off has no link to the mocking at Bethel.

2-kings-2:23:14.summary: Opponents rejoice and gather against the psalmist, a general mockery theme.

2-kings-2:23:15.summary: The Saints wording about a young man with a devout person has no link to this mocking.

2-kings-2:23:16.summary: The faithful “experienced mockery,” a general parallel.

2-kings-2:23:17.summary: “You entered Bethel and acted lawlessly,” Bethel as a place of sin.

2-kings-2:23:18.summary: Children who “let loose your tongue” in mockery are rebuked, a general parallel.

2-kings-2:23:19.summary: Warning not to go up to “the house of On” (Bethel), sharing only the place.

2-kings-2:23:20.summary: Persecution of the Spirit-born has no specific link to this event.

2-kings-2:23:21.summary: Job is made the taunt-song of dishonored sons; a general mockery theme in truncated text.

2-kings-2:23:22.summary: Jeroboam set a golden heifer in Bethel, background to the city’s hostility.

2-kings-2:23:23.summary: Amos is told never to prophesy at Bethel, showing Bethel’s hostility to prophets.

2-kings-2:23:24.summary: The calf of “the house of On” (Bethel) recalls the city’s idolatry only.

2-kings-2:23:25.summary: Advice to remove anger in youth has no link to this event.

2-kings-2:23:26.summary: Judgment on “Bethel’s altars” shares only the place.

2-kings-2:23:27.summary: Elijah was “taken up,” possibly mocked by the children’s “Go up”; the link is inferred.

2-kings-2:24:0.summary: Paul pronounces judgment and Elymas is struck blind at once, a general prophetic-curse parallel.

2-kings-2:24:1.summary: Amos pronounces judgment on his opponent’s children, a general parallel.

2-kings-2:24:2.summary: Ananias falls dead at Peter’s word and great fear follows, a general sudden-judgment parallel.

2-kings-2:24:3.summary: God will meet them “like a bear” and “tear open,” sharing the bear-tearing image.

2-kings-2:24:4.summary: Peter announces Sapphira’s death for testing the Spirit, a general sudden-judgment parallel.

2-kings-2:24:5.summary: The fig tree Jesus cursed has withered, a general curse-fulfilled parallel.

2-kings-2:24:6.summary: “Like a bear bereaved of her cubs” shares only the dangerous-bear image.

2-kings-2:24:7.summary: False prophets made a byword curse has no specific tie to Elisha’s curse.

2-kings-2:24:8.summary: Jeremiah pronounces death on Hananiah, a general prophetic death-sentence parallel.

2-kings-2:24:9.summary: “Elisha will put to death” those spared, foreshadowing his judging role generally.

2-kings-2:24:10.summary: For not heeding the Lord’s voice, “a lion found him and struck him,” a wild beast executing prophetic judgment.
2-kings-2:24:10.why: Animal judgment after a prophet’s word.

2-kings-2:24:11.summary: Fire consumes those who disrespect “a man of God,” as Elijah declared.
2-kings-2:24:11.why: Deadly judgment on those scorning a prophet.

2-kings-2:24:12.summary: Jesus’ curse on the fig tree is a general curse parallel.

2-kings-2:24:13.summary: Covenant curses for disobedience give broad background, not this event.

2-kings-2:24:14.summary: Fathers’ sins repaid on children is not specifically linked here.

2-kings-2:24:15.summary: “A lion met him on the road and killed him,” a wild beast executing judgment tied to a prophet.

2-kings-2:24:16.summary: Nehemiah “cursed them,” sharing only the act of cursing.

2-kings-2:24:17.summary: Peter pronounces “May your silver perish with you,” a general apostolic curse parallel.

2-kings-2:24:18.summary: “The curse of Jotham” came upon Shechem’s men, a general fulfilled-curse parallel.

2-kings-2:24:19.summary: The Saints text speaks of “a shielding of heart,” lacking the curse the label assumes.

2-kings-2:24:20.summary: “Cursed be Canaan” shares only the act of cursing.

2-kings-2:24:21.summary: Jotham’s conditional curse of consuming fire is a general curse parallel.

2-kings-2:24:22.summary: The Saints text has a lion and wolf, no bear, and concerns tyranny, not this judgment.

2-kings-2:24:23.summary: The Saints text of Proverbs lacks any bear, so the link disappears.

2-kings-2:24:24.summary: Readiness to punish disobedience is not specifically connected.

2-kings-2:25:1.summary: Mount Carmel, where Elijah confronted the prophets, shares only the place Elisha now visits.

2-kings-2:25:2.summary: Elijah went up onto Carmel to pray, sharing the place only.

2-kings-2:2:11.summary: 1 Samuel 17:55 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-2:2:11.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-2:2:11.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-2:23:3.summary: Proverbs 22:6 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-2:23:3.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-2:23:3.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-3:1:0.summary: Ahaziah’s death per Elijah’s word sets up the succession, but the shown text lacks Jehoram’s accession.

2-kings-3:1:1.summary: Ahaziah son of Ahab began in Jehoshaphat’s seventeenth year, the predecessor in the same synchronism.

2-kings-3:1:2.summary: Joram son of Ahab king of Israel, the same king, is used to date Judah’s Joram.

2-kings-3:2:0.summary: Jehu’s ruse about Ahab serving Baal relates to Ahab’s Baal worship generally.

2-kings-3:2:1.summary: Jehu brought out and burned “Baal’s pillar,” the same pillar partly removed by Jehoram.
2-kings-3:2:1.why: Completes the removal of Baal’s pillars.

2-kings-3:2:2.summary: Ahab sold to do evil as Jezebel turned him aside, the parents Jehoram is compared to.
2-kings-3:2:2.why: Shows the parents’ standard of evil.

2-kings-3:2:3.summary: The command to shatter pagan pillars loosely relates to removing Baal’s pillars.

2-kings-3:2:4.summary: Manasseh “did much evil in the Lord’s eyes,” a shared evaluation formula only.

2-kings-3:2:5.summary: Doing evil before the Lord in Jeroboam’s ways is a shared formula only.

2-kings-3:2:6.summary: Jezebel’s scheme against Naboth illustrates his mother’s wickedness generally.

2-kings-3:2:7.summary: Ahab “sold in vain to do evil,” the father whose evil Jehoram did not fully match.

2-kings-3:2:8.summary: Jehu cites “Jezebel your mother” to Joram, the same mother named in the comparison.

2-kings-3:2:9.summary: Jezebel’s burial as a king’s daughter concerns his mother but not his reign.

2-kings-3:2:10.summary: Ahab served Baal and set up an altar for Baal, the father’s Baal worship Jehoram partly undid.

2-kings-3:2:11.summary: Saul’s rebuke shares only the phrase “do evil before the Lord.”

2-kings-3:2:12.summary: The king seeking Elisha’s head is likely Jehoram, “son of a murderer,” but is unnamed here.

2-kings-3:2:13.summary: Amon did evil “as his father” had done, a contrasting evaluation formula.

2-kings-3:3:1.summary: Same formula: did not turn away from the sins of “Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.”
2-kings-3:3:1.why: Shows the standard verdict on Israel's kings.

2-kings-3:3:4.summary: Repeats the formula of not turning from the sins of “Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.”
2-kings-3:3:4.why: Places Jehoram in the line of northern kings judged alike.

2-kings-3:3:7.summary: Same formula about the sins of “Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.”
2-kings-3:3:7.why: Shows the recurring verdict on northern kings.

2-kings-3:3:9.summary: Baasha too “walked in the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat,” who “caused Israel to sin.”
2-kings-3:3:9.why: Earlier example of the same dynastic sin.

2-kings-3:3:11.summary: Same formula: did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, “who caused Israel to sin.”
2-kings-3:3:11.why: Shows the verdict repeated across reigns.

2-kings-3:3:12.summary: Nearly identical wording: followed Jeroboam's sins and “did not turn away from them.”
2-kings-3:3:12.why: Close verbal parallel in a later reign.

2-kings-3:3:14.summary: Jehu's purge of Baal worshippers relates to removing Baal while Jeroboam's sin persisted; shown text covers only the Baal festival.
2-kings-3:3:14.why: Background on Baal versus calf worship in Israel.

2-kings-3:3:2.summary: Jeroboam himself “did not turn from his evil,” the original sin later kings clung to.
2-kings-3:3:2.why: Shows the source of the sin named here.

2-kings-3:3:3.summary: Narrates Jeroboam's golden heifers at Bethel and Dan, the “sin” of Jeroboam that Jehoram kept.
2-kings-3:3:3.why: Explains what “the sin of Jeroboam” was.

2-kings-3:3:5.summary: Israel “did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam's house, who caused Israel to sin.”
2-kings-3:3:5.why: Same formula applied to the people.

2-kings-3:3:8.summary: The Israelites walked in Jeroboam's sin and “did not turn away from it,” same wording.
2-kings-3:3:8.why: Shows the national result of the kings' sin.

2-kings-3:3:10.summary: Nadab walked in his father's sins “by which he caused Israel to sin.”

2-kings-3:3:13.summary: Ahab, Jehoram's father, walked in “the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat” and added Baal worship.
2-kings-3:3:13.why: Contrasts father's Baalism with son's partial reform.

2-kings-3:3:15.summary: Paul on God destroying worldly wisdom has no link to Jehoram's clinging to Jeroboam's sin.

2-kings-3:4:0.summary: David made Moab his servants “bringing gifts,” the origin of Moab's tribute to Israel.

2-kings-3:4:1.summary: Isaac's great flocks share only the theme of wealth in sheep.

2-kings-3:4:2.summary: Psalm portrays Moab as subjected to God; Mesha is a subject king paying tribute.

2-kings-3:4:3.summary: Job's large flock numbers share only the theme of livestock wealth.

2-kings-3:4:4.summary: Uzziah's many herds and love of farming loosely parallel Mesha as a sheep-breeding king.

2-kings-3:4:5.summary: “Moab is the basin of My hope… foreigners were subjected,” a general picture of Moab's subjection.

2-kings-3:4:6.summary: Chronicles parallel: Moab “became servants to David, bringing gifts,” the root of Moab's tribute.

2-kings-3:4:7.summary: Job's thousands of sheep share only the theme of vast flocks.

2-kings-3:4:8.summary: The Greek-based Isaiah 16:1 speaks of “creeping creatures,” not sending lambs as tribute; the link is lost.
2-kings-3:4:8.why: The tribute-of-lambs link does not carry.

2-kings-3:4:9.summary: Abram rich in livestock shares only a general theme of herd wealth.
2-kings-3:4:9.why: Loose parallel of wealth in flocks.

2-kings-3:5:1.summary: In the same era Edom “broke away” from Judah, a parallel vassal revolt.
2-kings-3:5:1.why: Shows vassal revolts against Israel and Judah.

2-kings-3:5:2.summary: Edom “broke away from Judah” and Lomna “rebelled,” parallel vassal revolts of the period.
2-kings-3:5:2.why: Shows a pattern of vassal rebellion.

2-kings-3:6:0.summary: Saul “mustered” the people for war; only the act of mustering is shared.
2-kings-3:6:0.why: General parallel of a king mustering troops.

2-kings-3:6:1.summary: Israel's men “mustered” for battle; only the act of mustering is shared.
2-kings-3:6:1.why: General parallel of mustering for war.

2-kings-3:6:2.summary: Israel “mustered” against Syria; shares only the mustering for battle.
2-kings-3:6:2.why: General parallel of mustering for war.

2-kings-3:6:3.summary: David's census shares only the word “muster”; it is a sinful census, not a campaign.

2-kings-3:7:1.summary: Jehoshaphat answers Ahab with the same pledge: “As I am, so are you,” my people with you.
2-kings-3:7:1.why: Shows Jehoshaphat's repeated alliance with Ahab's house.

2-kings-3:7:2.summary: Athaliah's massacre of the royal offspring has no direct link to this war alliance.

2-kings-3:7:3.summary: Ahaziah of Judah followed Ahab's house, a later result of the Judah-Israel alliance.

2-kings-3:7:4.summary: Joram of Judah married Ahab's daughter, part of the same Judah-Israel alliance.
2-kings-3:7:4.why: Background on the alliance between houses.

2-kings-3:7:5.summary: Jehoshaphat earlier fought alongside the king of Israel and was nearly killed.
2-kings-3:7:5.why: Shows the risks of his earlier joint campaign.

2-kings-3:7:6.summary: Jehoshaphat's earlier joint battle with Israel's king, where he was surrounded and cried out.
2-kings-3:7:6.why: Shows a prior alliance that endangered him.

2-kings-3:7:7.summary: Jehu rebukes Jehoshaphat: “do you help a sinner?” for allying with Ahab's house.
2-kings-3:7:7.why: Prophetic judgment on this kind of alliance.

2-kings-3:8:0.summary: Israel went by “the road” around “the land of Edom”; only the route near Edom is shared.

2-kings-3:8:1.summary: Malachi on God's love for Jacob and Esau's wilderness desolation shares only Edom and wilderness.

2-kings-3:9:0.summary: The Greek-based text reads “no king in Syria,” so the expected note about Edom's king does not carry.
2-kings-3:9:0.why: The Edom link is lost in this reading.

2-kings-3:9:1.summary: Pharaoh's servants and Moses leaving in anger share no real link to the waterless march.

2-kings-3:9:2.summary: “There was no water for the congregation” echoes “no water for the camp.”

2-kings-3:9:3.summary: Only the phrase “at his feet” is shared; Barak's muster has no link to the water shortage.

2-kings-3:9:4.summary: “Water of affliction” for Micaiah in prison has no link to this water shortage.

2-kings-3:9:5.summary: At Rephidim “there was no water there for the people,” a similar wilderness shortage.

2-kings-3:9:6.summary: Israel travelled “three days in the wilderness without finding water,” like the seven-day march.

2-kings-3:9:7.summary: Near Edom the people complain there is “no bread or water,” a similar wilderness lack.

2-kings-3:9:8.summary: “There was no water for the people to drink” at Rephidim, similar shortage.

2-kings-3:9:9.summary: Fear of dying in the wilderness with “our livestock,” as the camp and livestock lack water.
2-kings-3:9:9.why: Shared concern for people and animals.

2-kings-3:10:0.summary: The king of Israel's court says “this calamity is from the Lord,” the same attitude Jehoram shows.
2-kings-3:10:0.why: Shows Jehoram's habit of blaming the Lord.

2-kings-3:10:1.summary: People seek God only when struck and speak falsely; loosely fits a king turning to the Lord in crisis.

2-kings-3:10:2.summary: In famine people speak evil and look up to heaven; loosely parallels blaming God in distress.
2-kings-3:10:2.why: General theme of blame in distress.

2-kings-3:10:3.summary: Exhausted sons “full of the Lord's anger” share no specific link with the kings' complaint.

2-kings-3:10:4.summary: “A man's foolishness ruins his ways, but in his heart he blames God,” apt for Jehoram's complaint.
2-kings-3:10:4.why: Proverb that interprets the king's reaction.

2-kings-3:10:5.summary: Cain's despair over his guilt has no specific link to the king's complaint.

2-kings-3:11:2.summary: Jehoram clings to Jeroboam's sin, contrasting with Jehoshaphat seeking a prophet of the Lord.
2-kings-3:11:2.why: Highlights the two kings' different piety.

2-kings-3:11:3.summary: Failing to “seek according to judgment” brought trouble; loosely relates to seeking the Lord properly.
2-kings-3:11:3.why: General theme of seeking God rightly.

2-kings-3:11:4.summary: The Lord reveals His plans to “His servants the prophets,” the reason to seek a prophet.

2-kings-3:11:5.summary: David “inquired” of God before battle, as Jehoshaphat seeks to “inquire of the Lord” before war.
2-kings-3:11:5.why: Model of inquiring of God before battle.

2-kings-3:11:6.summary: “There is no prophet any longer” contrasts with Elisha being found present.
2-kings-3:11:6.why: Shows the value of a present prophet.

2-kings-3:11:7.summary: David again “inquired of God” about battle, as Jehoshaphat wishes to do.
2-kings-3:11:7.why: Model of inquiring of God before battle.

2-kings-3:11:8.summary: Elisha's movements to Carmel and Samaria and Jehoram's accession set up this scene.

2-kings-3:11:9.summary: Jesus “poured water” to wash feet, a servant act like Elisha's pouring water on Elijah's hands.

2-kings-3:11:10.summary: Israel “inquired of the Lord” through a priest before battle, as Jehoshaphat wishes to inquire.

2-kings-3:11:11.summary: Timothy served Paul “as a child with a father,” like Elisha's service to Elijah.

2-kings-3:11:12.summary: The leaders “did not inquire of the Lord,” contrasting with Jehoshaphat's insistence on inquiring.
2-kings-3:11:12.why: Shows the danger of not inquiring.

2-kings-3:11:13.summary: Israel “inquired of the Lord” whether to go to battle, the same practice Jehoshaphat seeks.

2-kings-3:11:14.summary: Jesus as Teacher washing feet loosely echoes Elisha's servant role toward Elijah.
2-kings-3:11:14.why: Image of service to a master.

2-kings-3:11:15.summary: Israel “inquired of God” who should lead in battle, as Jehoshaphat seeks guidance.

2-kings-3:11:16.summary: Joshua, “Moses' attendant,” succeeds his master, as Elisha the attendant succeeds Elijah.

2-kings-3:11:17.summary: Washing saints' feet as service shares only a general servant image.

2-kings-3:11:18.summary: Israel's vow against Gibeah involves no inquiring of the Lord or prophet.

2-kings-3:11:19.summary: Saul “inquired through the spirit medium” instead of the Lord, contrasting with seeking a true prophet.

2-kings-3:11:20.summary: Water brought to wash guests' feet shares only a general service image.

2-kings-3:11:21.summary: Leaders as “the one who serves” loosely relates to Elisha's humble service.

2-kings-3:12:0.summary: Elisha speaks “Thus says the Lord” and heals waters, showing the Lord's word is with him.

2-kings-3:12:1.summary: Elisha acts “in the name of the Lord” and returns via Carmel to Samaria, near the kings' route.

2-kings-3:12:2.summary: Oppressors' sons coming to Zion has no specific link to kings visiting Elisha.

2-kings-3:12:3.summary: Samuel recognized as the Lord's prophet with none of his words failing, like Jehoshaphat's trust in Elisha.
2-kings-3:12:3.why: General theme of a recognized prophet.

2-kings-3:12:4.summary: Opponents bowing at the church's feet has no specific link to this scene.

2-kings-3:12:5.summary: “The spirit of Elijah has come to rest upon Elisha,” grounding Jehoshaphat's confidence in him.
2-kings-3:12:5.why: Shows why Elisha carries the Lord's word.

2-kings-3:12:6.summary: A king's crisis leads to Elisha, “that there is a prophet in Israel,” and a great man comes to him.
2-kings-3:12:6.why: Parallel of leaders coming to Elisha.

2-kings-3:12:7.summary: Kings bowing to Zion is an eschatological image, not linked to kings visiting a prophet.

2-kings-3:12:8.summary: Naaman returns to Elisha and stands before him; only the motif of a ruler coming to Elisha is shared.

2-kings-3:13:0.summary: Ahab's four hundred court prophets are the “father's prophets” Elisha tells Jehoram to consult.

2-kings-3:13:1.summary: The prophets eating at Jezebel's table are the prophets of Jehoram's parents.
2-kings-3:13:1.why: Identifies the prophets Elisha refers to.

2-kings-3:13:2.summary: “Where are their gods… Let them arise and help you,” the same taunt as “Go to your father's prophets.”
2-kings-3:13:2.why: Shows the ironic challenge in Elisha's words.

2-kings-3:13:3.summary: The king repeats his complaint that the Lord called “the three kings” to give them into Moab's hand.

2-kings-3:13:4.summary: Ahab's prophets had a “lying spirit,” showing why Elisha dismisses the father's prophets.
2-kings-3:13:4.why: Shows the unreliability of Ahab's prophets.

2-kings-3:13:5.summary: Ahab's prophets prophesied before the kings of Israel and Judah, the prophets Elisha rejects.
2-kings-3:13:5.why: Earlier scene with Ahab's prophets and Jehoshaphat.

2-kings-3:13:6.summary: “What portion does a believer have with an unbeliever?” loosely echoes “What have I to do with you?”
2-kings-3:13:6.why: General theme of separation from the ungodly.

2-kings-3:13:7.summary: Hosea's call to return to the Lord who heals has no specific link to Elisha's rebuff.

2-kings-3:13:8.summary: Knowing no one according to the flesh has no specific link here.

2-kings-3:13:9.summary: Calling on wisdom too late and not being heard loosely parallels Jehoram seeking help only in crisis.

2-kings-3:13:10.summary: “Where are your gods… Will they rise and save you in the time of your affliction?” parallels Elisha's taunt.
2-kings-3:13:10.why: Same ironic challenge to idolaters in crisis.

2-kings-3:13:11.summary: An idolater who comes to the prophet and whether the Lord should answer him parallels Jehoram coming to Elisha.
2-kings-3:13:11.why: Shows the problem of idolaters consulting a prophet.

2-kings-3:13:12.summary: “What have we to do with Thee” shares the idiom of Elisha's “What have I to do with you?”

2-kings-3:13:13.summary: Returning “to her people and her gods” shares only the idea of going back to one's gods.
2-kings-3:13:13.why: Loose overlap of returning to other gods.

2-kings-3:13:14.summary: “Go and cry to the gods which you have chosen… let them save you,” same rebuff as Elisha's.
2-kings-3:13:14.why: Close parallel of a divine rebuff to idolaters.

2-kings-3:13:15.summary: “What is this to Me and to you” shares the idiom of Elisha's reply.

2-kings-3:14:10.summary: Elijah's identical oath: “As the Lord of hosts lives, before whom I stand.”

2-kings-3:14:0.summary: Elisha repeats “As the Lord lives, before whom I stand,” the same oath.

2-kings-3:14:2.summary: Elijah's hostile encounter with Ahab loosely parallels Elisha's coldness toward Ahab's son.

2-kings-3:14:3.summary: Daniel's interpretation and rebuke of Belshazzar shares only a prophet confronting a king.

2-kings-3:14:4.summary: The wicked are held in contempt but “he honors those who fear the Lord,” as Elisha treats Jehoram and Jehoshaphat.
2-kings-3:14:4.why: Explains Elisha's differing regard for the kings.

2-kings-3:14:5.summary: Ahijah receives Jeroboam's wife with harsh words; a prophet's hostility to an evil royal house.
2-kings-3:14:5.why: General parallel of prophet versus sinful dynasty.

2-kings-3:14:6.summary: Jeremiah made strong “against all Judah's kings”; general picture of a prophet unafraid of kings.

2-kings-3:14:7.summary: Jesus does “not look at people's outward status,” while Elisha shows regard for Jehoshaphat for his piety.
2-kings-3:14:7.why: Loose contrast on regard for persons.

2-kings-3:14:8.summary: Samuel refuses to return with rejected Saul; a prophet's coolness to a rejected king.

2-kings-3:14:9.summary: Jehoshaphat “sought the Lord” and removed idols, explaining Elisha's regard for him.

2-kings-3:14:11.summary: “Good things have been found in you,” said of Jehoshaphat, explains Elisha's regard.

2-kings-3:15:0.summary: David's playing the kinyra affected the spirit upon Saul, as music precedes the Lord's hand on Elisha.

2-kings-3:15:1.summary: Being filled in the Spirit with psalms and melody loosely relates music and the Spirit.
2-kings-3:15:1.why: General link of music and Spirit.

2-kings-3:15:3.summary: “The Lord's hand came upon me,” same expression for prophetic inspiration.
2-kings-3:15:3.why: Shows the idiom of prophetic seizure.

2-kings-3:15:4.summary: “The Lord's hand was upon Elijah,” same expression used of Elisha's master.
2-kings-3:15:4.why: Shows the idiom of prophetic empowerment.

2-kings-3:15:5.summary: “The Lord's hand came upon me” as Ezekiel prophesies before elders.

2-kings-3:15:6.summary: Asaph's sons “uttered inspired words with kinyrai,” linking stringed music and prophecy.
2-kings-3:15:6.why: Shows music as a vehicle of prophecy.

2-kings-3:15:7.summary: “The Lord's hand came strongly upon me,” same idiom of inspiration.

2-kings-3:15:8.summary: “The Lord's hand was with them” shares the phrase but concerns the church's growth.
2-kings-3:15:8.why: Verbal echo in a different setting.

2-kings-3:15:10.summary: “The Lord's hand came upon me, and He said,” same prelude to a divine word.

2-kings-3:16:0.summary: The camp formation list has no link to digging pits in the torrent bed.

2-kings-3:16:1.summary: Elisha has empty vessels prepared for God to fill, as pits are dug for water to fill.
2-kings-3:16:1.why: Pattern of preparing for Elisha's miracle.

2-kings-3:17:0.summary: God makes “waterless land outlets of waters,” a general theme of water in dry places.
2-kings-3:17:0.why: General theme of God providing water.

2-kings-3:17:1.summary: God promises springs and rivers for the thirsty in the wilderness, general water provision.
2-kings-3:17:1.why: General theme of God providing water.

2-kings-3:17:2.summary: “I gave water in the wilderness… to give drink,” a general picture of miraculous water.
2-kings-3:17:2.why: General theme of God providing water.

2-kings-3:17:3.summary: Water flows from a rock and “My people will drink,” recalling wilderness provision.

2-kings-3:17:4.summary: The Greek-based Psalm speaks of a valley of weeping and blessings, not springs; the water link is lost.
2-kings-3:17:4.why: The water image does not carry.

2-kings-3:17:5.summary: Water comes from the rock “and My people shall drink,” a miraculous water supply for a thirsty camp.

2-kings-3:17:6.summary: Water from the rock for “the congregation and their livestock to drink,” like “you… and your livestock.”
2-kings-3:17:6.why: Close parallel of water for people and animals.

2-kings-3:17:7.summary: Elijah's miracle of fire consuming water in the trench is a different sign at a sacrifice.

2-kings-3:18:0.summary: “No word from God will be powerless,” general theme of God's ease in doing wonders.

2-kings-3:18:1.summary: The Greek-based text asks whether anything can be “hidden” from God, not whether it is too hard.
2-kings-3:18:1.why: The “easy for the Lord” link is lost.
2-kings-3:18:1.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-3:18:2.summary: The Greek-based wording “Nothing can be hidden from Thee” does not carry the “nothing too hard” link.
2-kings-3:18:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-3:18:3.summary: “It is easy” for the shadow to move echoes the “light thing” idea of a sign.
2-kings-3:18:3.why: Verbal echo about an easy sign.

2-kings-3:18:4.summary: God able to do “far more abundantly than all we ask” loosely fits the added promise of victory.
2-kings-3:18:4.why: General theme of abundant divine power.

2-kings-3:18:5.summary: The Greek-based text says “It is a great thing,” so the “light thing” echo does not carry.

2-kings-3:18:6.summary: “All things are possible with God,” a general theme of divine ease.

2-kings-3:18:7.summary: “Is it a small thing” echoes the idiom but concerns Judah's sins.

2-kings-3:18:8.summary: A prophet tells Israel's king “I am giving it into your hands,” a similar promise of victory.

2-kings-3:18:9.summary: Isaiah assures a king against invading kings; a general prophetic assurance in war.

2-kings-3:18:10.summary: God gives more than was asked, as water is followed by victory over Moab.
2-kings-3:18:10.why: General theme of God giving beyond the request.

2-kings-3:18:11.summary: The man of God says “I will give this great force into your hand” to Israel's king.

2-kings-3:18:12.summary: “Is it a small thing” echoes the idiom of a light matter, in a different setting.

2-kings-3:18:13.summary: “It was not enough” about Ahab's sins shares only an idiom of degree.

2-kings-3:19:0.summary: Deuteronomy forbids cutting down fruit trees in siege, while Elisha orders felling “every good tree.”

2-kings-3:19:2.summary: “You shall strike Midian” is a general divine promise of victory.

2-kings-3:19:3.summary: “You will strike these foreigners,” a general divine promise of victory.

2-kings-3:19:4.summary: Elisha again promises “you shall strike Syria,” a parallel oracle of victory from the same prophet.

2-kings-3:19:5.summary: Balaam foretells a man from Israel who “shall crush Moab's leaders.”

2-kings-3:19:6.summary: Total destruction of Amalek loosely parallels the sweeping devastation ordered against Moab.

2-kings-3:20:0.summary: The lamb offered “in the morning” is the morning sacrifice during which the water came.
2-kings-3:20:0.why: Explains the time-marker of the miracle.

2-kings-3:20:1.summary: Elijah's prayer at sacrifice, answered by a sign; the shown text lacks the sacrifice-time detail.
2-kings-3:20:1.why: Parallel of a sign at a sacrifice.

2-kings-3:20:2.summary: God “made waters descend like rivers,” general miraculous water provision.

2-kings-3:20:3.summary: “Waters flowed, and torrents were flooded,” loosely echoing the flooding torrent bed.

2-kings-3:20:4.summary: Gabriel came “at the hour of the evening sacrifice,” a divine act at a sacrifice time.
2-kings-3:20:4.why: Pattern of divine action at sacrifice hour.

2-kings-3:20:5.summary: “Water burst out in the wilderness and a ravine in a thirsty land,” general water miracle imagery.
2-kings-3:20:5.why: General image of water in dry land.

2-kings-3:21:0.summary: The Greek-based text speaks of a “bent man” boasting, so the girding-armor link is lost.
2-kings-3:21:0.why: The belt or armor link does not carry.

2-kings-3:21:1.summary: Fastening truth around the waist shares only the belt image, not Moab's muster.

2-kings-3:23:0.summary: Elisha's blinding of the Syrians is another divine deception of enemies, but a different event.
2-kings-3:23:0.why: General theme of enemies misled by God.

2-kings-3:23:1.summary: Sisera's household imagines him “dividing spoils,” a premature assumption of victory like Moab's.
2-kings-3:23:1.why: Parallel of enemies counting spoil too soon.

2-kings-3:23:2.summary: The enemy boasts “I will divide the spoil,” just before destruction, like Moab's rush to the spoils.

2-kings-3:23:3.summary: The Lord made Syria misread a sound and assume kings had come against them, a divinely caused misjudgment.

2-kings-3:23:4.summary: Assyria's boast of seizing the world loosely parallels Moab's greedy confidence.

2-kings-3:23:5.summary: Jehoshaphat's people plunder many spoils; the shown text lacks the enemies' mutual slaughter.

2-kings-3:24:0.summary: “Sudden destruction” comes on the confident, loosely matching Moab's surprise in Israel's camp.

2-kings-3:24:1.summary: Benjamin flees and is cut down; a general pursuit-and-slaughter parallel.

2-kings-3:24:2.summary: Israel turns and strikes Ai's men until none escape; a general rout parallel.

2-kings-3:25:0.summary: Jeremiah laments Moab and “Kiradas,” but this Saints reading of the source does not name the city.

2-kings-3:25:1.summary: Wailing over Moab and “Kiradas”; the source as shown does not name the city.

2-kings-3:25:2.summary: Moab will wail for “Deseth's residents”; a general lament over Moab's devastation.

2-kings-3:25:4.summary: Lament for Moab mentioning a “wall,” loosely linked to Moab's demolished wall.

2-kings-3:25:5.summary: Wells “stopped up” by enemies parallel blocking every spring, in a different setting.
2-kings-3:25:5.why: Shared image of stopping water sources.

2-kings-3:25:6.summary: “The wall of Moab's country will perish,” a general prophecy of Moab's ruin.

2-kings-3:25:7.summary: Israel was once told not to fight Moab, contrasting with this devastation.

2-kings-3:25:8.summary: Wells “stopped up and filled with earth,” similar to blocking springs and filling plots.
2-kings-3:25:8.why: Shared image of ruining water sources.

2-kings-3:25:9.summary: Hezekiah “blocked the waters of the springs,” the same tactic in a defensive setting.
2-kings-3:25:9.why: Shows blocking springs as a war tactic.

2-kings-3:25:10.summary: Deuteronomy forbids destroying fruit trees in siege, yet Israel “brought down every good tree.”

2-kings-3:25:11.summary: Abimelech “demolished the city, and sowed it with salt,” a parallel of ruining conquered land.

2-kings-3:25:12.summary: David's harsh defeat of Moab is an earlier campaign, not this event.

2-kings-3:25:13.summary: God desolating “fortified cities” is a general picture of conquest.

2-kings-3:26:0.summary: Amos condemns Moab for burning the bones of “Idumea's king,” showing Moab-Edom hostility.
2-kings-3:26:0.why: Background of Moab's hostility to Edom.

2-kings-3:26:1.summary: Names “the king of Edom” in the allied campaign, the king Moab tried to break through to.
2-kings-3:26:1.why: Identifies the Edomite king in the coalition.

2-kings-3:27:0.summary: “Shall I give my firstborn offspring for impieties?” recalls the sacrifice of a firstborn.

2-kings-3:27:1.summary: The nations “burn their sons and their daughters with fire unto their gods,” the practice Mesha performs.
2-kings-3:27:1.why: Shows child sacrifice as a pagan abomination.

2-kings-3:27:2.summary: Jephthah vows to offer a person “as a whole burnt offering,” a parallel human offering in war.
2-kings-3:27:2.why: Parallel human offering tied to battle.

2-kings-3:27:3.summary: Israel “sacrificed” sons and daughters to idols, the same practice as Mesha's.

2-kings-3:27:4.summary: Amos condemns Moab's burning of Edom's king's bones; only Moabite atrocity by fire is shared.

2-kings-3:27:5.summary: “They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons,” the same pagan practice.

2-kings-3:27:6.summary: Saul is ready to put his son Jonathan to death during war; loosely parallels a king sacrificing his son.
2-kings-3:27:6.why: Loose parallel of king and son in war.
