2-kings-3:27:7.summary: Jephthah “fulfilled the vow,” offering his daughter, a parallel sacrifice of one's own child.

2-kings-3:27:8.summary: Abraham offered a ram “instead of Isaac his son,” contrasting with Mesha's actual son sacrifice.
2-kings-3:27:8.why: Contrast of spared versus sacrificed son.

2-kings-3:27:9.summary: “Offer him there for a whole burnt offering,” the same terms used of a son, but God stopped it.
2-kings-3:27:9.why: Contrast of Abraham's test with Mesha's act.

2-kings-3:27:10.summary: A prophet's promise of victory over Syria has no specific link to Mesha's sacrifice or Israel's withdrawal.

2-kings-3:27:11.summary: A victory oracle against Syria has no specific link to this verse.

2-kings-3:27:12.summary: The king of Israel returns home “confounded and dispirited,” loosely like Israel withdrawing to its land.

2-kings-4:1:0.summary: A debtor to be “sold, with his wife and children,” like the lender taking the widow's sons.
2-kings-4:1:0.why: Shows the practice of debt slavery.

2-kings-4:1:1.summary: “The sons of the prophets” come to Elisha, the same community the widow belongs to.
2-kings-4:1:1.why: Shows Elisha's ties to the prophetic guild.

2-kings-4:1:2.summary: The Lord delights in “those who fear Him,” loosely fitting the husband who “feared the Lord.”
2-kings-4:1:2.why: General theme of God's care for the God-fearing.

2-kings-4:1:3.summary: Debtors were “forcing our sons and daughters into slavery,” the same crisis the widow faces.

2-kings-4:1:4.summary: The law limits debt slavery for a brother “and his children,” the situation threatening the widow's sons.

2-kings-4:1:5.summary: The Lord's mercy “toward those who fear Him,” a general theme fitting the God-fearing husband.
2-kings-4:1:5.why: General theme of mercy to the God-fearing.

2-kings-4:1:6.summary: A debtor thrown into prison until he repaid shows harsh debt collection.

2-kings-4:1:7.summary: Mercy toward those who fear Him and “children's children,” loosely fitting the widow's sons.
2-kings-4:1:7.why: General promise to families of the God-fearing.

2-kings-4:1:8.summary: A general teaching on mercy and judgment has no specific link to the widow's plight.

2-kings-4:1:9.summary: The parable's warning to forgive has no specific link to this verse.

2-kings-4:1:10.summary: The man who “fears the Lord” will have a powerful seed, loosely fitting the God-fearer's sons.

2-kings-4:1:11.summary: “It will be good for those who fear God” offers only a general theme.

2-kings-4:1:12.summary: Elisha cares for “the sons of the prophets” in famine, the same community as the widow.
2-kings-4:1:12.why: Shows Elisha's provision for the prophets' guild.

2-kings-4:1:13.summary: “Everyone in debt” gathered to David; a general picture of debtors seeking a protector.

2-kings-4:1:14.summary: Paul's address to “those who fear God” shares only a common phrase.
2-kings-4:1:14.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-4:1:15.summary: A pledge to release “the demand of every hand” in the seventh year relates loosely to debt relief.

2-kings-4:1:16.summary: Those who fear God's name will be released “from bonds,” loosely fitting the God-fearer's family.

2-kings-4:1:17.summary: “Fear God and keep His commandments” shares only a general phrase.

2-kings-4:1:18.summary: “The sons of the prophets” at Jericho come to Elisha, the widow's community.
2-kings-4:1:18.why: Shows Elisha's ties to the prophetic guild.

2-kings-4:1:19.summary: Obadiah “feared the Lord greatly,” matching the description, though no link to this man is stated.
2-kings-4:1:19.why: Another God-fearer serving in Ahab's time.

2-kings-4:1:20.summary: A Hebrew “sold to you” must be freed after six years, the law governing debt slavery.
2-kings-4:1:20.why: Legal background to the creditor's claim.

2-kings-4:1:21.summary: A heavenly hymn about fearing the Lord has no specific link here.

2-kings-4:1:22.summary: “Now I know that you fear God” shares only a general phrase.

2-kings-4:1:23.summary: A sold person has “a right of redemption” by kin, loosely fitting the widow's need for rescue.

2-kings-4:1:24.summary: The Lord remembers “those who feared the Lord,” a general theme fitting the God-fearing husband.

2-kings-4:1:25.summary: A call for all who fear God to praise Him has no specific link here.

2-kings-4:1:26.summary: Anania “feared God more than many,” sharing only the description of a God-fearer.

2-kings-4:1:27.summary: The Lord blessed “those who fear the Lord,” a general theme only.

2-kings-4:1:28.summary: Mentions “the sons of the prophets,” the same group, in an unrelated episode.

2-kings-4:2:0.summary: A poor widow tells Elijah she has only “a little oil,” before a miracle of oil, closely parallel.

2-kings-4:2:1.summary: God chose “those poor in the world,” a general theme fitting the destitute widow.
2-kings-4:2:1.why: General theme of God's care for the poor.

2-kings-4:2:2.summary: Elijah asks Elisha, “Ask what I should do for you,” echoing “What should I do for you?”

2-kings-4:2:3.summary: Jesus tests Philip about scarce provisions before a multiplication; loosely parallel.
2-kings-4:2:3.why: Parallel of scarcity before a miracle.

2-kings-4:2:4.summary: “How many loaves do you have?” asks what is on hand before multiplying it, like Elisha's question.
2-kings-4:2:4.why: Parallel question before a multiplication miracle.

2-kings-4:2:5.summary: Peter gives “what I have” though lacking silver, loosely about little becoming much.

2-kings-4:2:6.summary: A woman cries to the king, who answers “From where could I save you?” unlike Elisha's “What should I do for you?”
2-kings-4:2:6.why: Contrasts the helpless king with the prophet.

2-kings-4:2:7.summary: “Having nothing, and yet possessing everything” loosely fits the widow's poverty and provision.
2-kings-4:2:7.why: General paradox of poverty and riches.

2-kings-4:3:0.summary: “Fill the jars with water” before a miracle, like gathering vessels to be miraculously filled.
2-kings-4:3:0.why: Parallel of vessels filled by a miracle.

2-kings-4:3:1.summary: “Ask, and you will receive” loosely fits asking for many vessels.
2-kings-4:3:1.why: General theme of asking and receiving.

2-kings-4:3:2.summary: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it,” general image of God filling what is opened.

2-kings-4:3:3.summary: Elisha has pits dug to be filled by God, as he has empty vessels gathered to be filled.
2-kings-4:3:3.why: Same pattern of preparing for Elisha's miracle.

2-kings-4:3:4.summary: The king's limited striking limited the victory, as the number of vessels limits the oil.
2-kings-4:3:4.why: Shows blessing limited by human response.

2-kings-4:4:0.summary: Jesus multiplies a few loaves to feed many, a general parallel of multiplied provision.

2-kings-4:4:1.summary: “Enter your inner room, shut your door” echoes shutting the door, but for prayer.

2-kings-4:4:2.summary: Jesus multiplies five loaves and two fish, a general multiplication parallel.

2-kings-4:4:3.summary: Peter “put everyone outside” before a miracle, loosely parallel to the private setting.

2-kings-4:4:4.summary: Elijah takes the child to a private room for a miracle for a widow; loosely parallel.
2-kings-4:4:4.why: Pattern of private miracles for widows.

2-kings-4:4:5.summary: Elisha “shut the door behind the two of them,” the same private act before a miracle.

2-kings-4:4:6.summary: Jars are filled, then drawn out and taken, like pouring into vessels and taking each full one.

2-kings-4:4:7.summary: God able to do “far more abundantly than all we ask,” a general theme of abundance.

2-kings-4:4:8.summary: Jesus “put them all outside” before raising a child, loosely like the closed-door miracle.

2-kings-4:4:9.summary: Jesus distributes loaves “as much as they wanted,” a general abundance parallel.

2-kings-4:4:10.summary: “Enter your inner rooms, shut your door” shares wording but concerns hiding from wrath.
2-kings-4:4:10.why: Verbal echo in a different setting.

2-kings-4:5:0.summary: Noah and Abraham obeyed by faith, loosely like the widow doing as instructed.

2-kings-4:5:1.summary: Naaman “went away” angry rather than obeying, contrasting with the widow who “did so.”

2-kings-4:5:2.summary: Blessed is she who believed the Lord's word would be fulfilled, loosely fitting the widow's trust.

2-kings-4:5:3.summary: The widow “went and acted,” and the flask of oil did not diminish, closely parallel.

2-kings-4:6:0.summary: Baskets “full” after the feeding, a general parallel of miraculous abundance.

2-kings-4:6:1.summary: Victory limited to three strikes, as the oil stopped when vessels ran out.
2-kings-4:6:1.why: Shows blessing measured by human response.

2-kings-4:6:2.summary: Power going out to heal the crowd has no specific link to the oil stopping.

2-kings-4:6:3.summary: Elisha's food multiplication “according to the word of the Lord,” a parallel miracle.

2-kings-4:6:4.summary: Solomon's prayer posture at the altar has no link to the oil miracle.

2-kings-4:6:5.summary: Manna ceased when no longer needed, loosely like the oil stopping.

2-kings-4:6:6.summary: Baskets “full” of leftovers, a general abundance parallel.

2-kings-4:6:7.summary: “The flask of oil will not diminish, until” rain comes, a parallel oil miracle with a set limit.

2-kings-4:6:8.summary: Few mighty works because of unbelief loosely relates to limits on miraculous provision.
2-kings-4:6:8.why: General theme of response limiting miracles.

2-kings-4:6:9.summary: Gathering leftovers after a feeding is a general abundance parallel.

2-kings-4:6:10.summary: “According to your faith,” loosely like provision matching the vessels prepared.
2-kings-4:6:10.why: General theme of faith measuring blessing.

2-kings-4:7:0.summary: Working so as not to burden others loosely fits living on the oil and paying debts.

2-kings-4:7:1.summary: A general list of virtues has no specific link to selling oil and paying debt.

2-kings-4:7:2.summary: Not repaying evil for evil has no real link to paying a creditor.

2-kings-4:7:3.summary: Shares only the title “the man of God,” used here of Shemaiah.

2-kings-4:7:4.summary: “The sinner borrows and will not repay,” loosely relating to repaying the debt.

2-kings-4:7:5.summary: Walking properly and having “need of no one” loosely fits the family's new independence.

2-kings-4:7:6.summary: Paul worked so as not to burden others, a general theme of honest living.

2-kings-4:8:0.summary: Lists “Shunem” in Issachar's borders, locating the town Elisha passed through.

2-kings-4:8:1.summary: Elisha keeps coming, turns aside to the upper room, and calls “this Shunammite woman.”

2-kings-4:8:2.summary: The Greek-based “long-lived are not wise” does not carry a link to a “prominent” woman.

2-kings-4:8:3.summary: Abishag “the Shunammite” comes from the same town of Shunem.

2-kings-4:8:4.summary: Job was “of noble standing,” loosely matching the prominent, wealthy woman.
2-kings-4:8:4.why: General parallel of a prominent person.

2-kings-4:8:5.summary: The disciples “urged Him strongly” to stay and eat, like the woman pressing Elisha to eat.

2-kings-4:8:6.summary: Lot “urged them greatly; and they turned aside to him” and they ate, close to this verse.

2-kings-4:8:7.summary: Wealthy Barzillai supported the king, loosely like the wealthy woman supporting Elisha.

2-kings-4:8:8.summary: An old man offers lodging to travelers, a general hospitality parallel.

2-kings-4:8:9.summary: The seductress's persuasion shares only the idea of pressing someone; no real link.

2-kings-4:8:10.summary: “Great before the Lord” of John the Baptist shares only the word “great.”

2-kings-4:8:11.summary: Lydia “urged us… come into my house and stay” and prevailed, like the woman pressing Elisha.
2-kings-4:8:11.why: Parallel of insistent hospitality to God's messenger.

2-kings-4:8:12.summary: Continues the Shunammite family's story with her son, but does not involve Elisha's visits.
2-kings-4:8:12.why: Shows what came of her hospitality.

2-kings-4:8:13.summary: Philistines camp at “Soman,” the Greek form of Shunem; the place name is not obvious in this reading.
2-kings-4:8:13.why: Locates the town in a later battle.

2-kings-4:8:14.summary: The master tells his slave to “compel people to come in,” loosely like the woman pressing Elisha.

2-kings-4:9:0.summary: “Behold, I know that you are a man of God,” said by a woman hosting Elijah.
2-kings-4:9:0.why: Parallel recognition by a hosting woman.

2-kings-4:9:2.summary: Elisha is called “the man of God” in the preceding episode, the same title used here.

2-kings-4:9:3.summary: “Hospitable… devout” loosely fits the hospitable woman and the holy man.
2-kings-4:9:3.why: General virtues of hospitality and holiness.

2-kings-4:9:4.summary: Conduct “devoutly and justly and blamelessly” observed by others, loosely like Elisha's evident holiness.

2-kings-4:9:5.summary: Others “see your good works,” loosely fitting how the woman perceived Elisha's holiness.

2-kings-4:9:6.summary: A widow addresses Elijah as “man of God,” sharing the title in a different mood.

2-kings-4:9:7.summary: Advice to wives on submission has no specific link to the woman's words to her husband.

2-kings-4:9:8.summary: Moses is called “the man of God,” sharing only the title.

2-kings-4:9:9.summary: “The holy prophets” shares only the idea of a holy prophet.

2-kings-4:9:10.summary: “A man of God came… by the Lord's word,” sharing only the title.

2-kings-4:9:11.summary: Prophets spoke from God, a general description of prophetic holiness.

2-kings-4:9:12.summary: “O man of God” shares only the title.

2-kings-4:10:0.summary: “Pursue hospitality,” a general command fitting the woman's provision.

2-kings-4:10:1.summary: “Whoever receives a prophet… will receive a prophet's reward,” as the woman is later rewarded with a son.
2-kings-4:10:1.why: Shows the reward for hosting a prophet.

2-kings-4:10:2.summary: Service to the least is service to Christ, a general theme of kindness.

2-kings-4:10:3.summary: A general exhortation to love and good works has no specific link here.

2-kings-4:10:4.summary: “Be hospitable,” a general command fitting her hospitality.

2-kings-4:10:5.summary: Hospitality to strangers who prove to be heaven's messengers loosely fits hosting a holy man.

2-kings-4:10:6.summary: Reward for giving even a cup of water to Christ's own; general reward for hospitality.

2-kings-4:10:7.summary: Women “served them out of their own belongings,” like the wealthy woman providing for Elisha.
2-kings-4:10:7.why: Parallel of women supporting God's messengers.

2-kings-4:10:8.summary: “The devout made wise plans” shares only a general idea of planning good.

2-kings-4:10:9.summary: Elijah stayed in an “upper room” with his bed at a woman's home, like Elisha's upstairs room.

2-kings-4:12:0.summary: Gehazi, Elisha's attendant, later presents this same woman to the king.
2-kings-4:12:0.why: Shows Gehazi and the woman later.

2-kings-4:12:1.summary: Gehazi is sent to the same woman's dead child with Elisha's staff.
2-kings-4:12:1.why: Continues Gehazi's role in her story.

2-kings-4:12:2.summary: Elijah had a “young attendant,” paralleling Elisha's attendant only in role.

2-kings-4:12:3.summary: Gehazi, “Elisha's attendant,” appears in the Naaman episode.

2-kings-4:12:4.summary: Elisha himself served Elijah, pouring water on his hands, as Gehazi now serves Elisha.

2-kings-4:12:5.summary: John as an “assistant” to apostles parallels a prophet's attendant only loosely.

2-kings-4:12:6.summary: Elijah sends his “young attendant” on an errand, like Elisha sending Gehazi.

2-kings-4:13:0.summary: Paul prays for mercy on Onesiphorus who often refreshed him, like Elisha seeking to repay her care.
2-kings-4:13:0.why: Theme of repaying care for God's servant.

2-kings-4:13:1.summary: God will not forget love shown “by serving the saints,” loosely fitting the woman's care.

2-kings-4:13:2.summary: Paul thanks the giver and promises God will meet their need, loosely like Elisha's offer.

2-kings-4:13:3.summary: “Godliness with contentment,” loosely fitting her reply that she lives among her own people.

2-kings-4:13:4.summary: Honoring those who labor in the Lord loosely relates to her care for Elisha.

2-kings-4:13:5.summary: Mary “labored much” shares only a general theme of service.

2-kings-4:13:6.summary: “Content with what you have” loosely fits her declining any favor.

2-kings-4:13:7.summary: Phoebe, a patron, should be helped “in whatever matter she may need,” like Elisha's offer to his patron.
2-kings-4:13:7.why: Parallel of repaying a patron's support.

2-kings-4:13:8.summary: “Settle in the land” loosely fits her contentment dwelling among her people.

2-kings-4:13:9.summary: Receiving a prophet brings “a prophet's reward,” the principle behind Elisha's offer.
2-kings-4:13:9.why: Shows reward for hosting a prophet.

2-kings-4:13:10.summary: Amasa's appointment as “commander of the army” shares only the title.

2-kings-4:13:11.summary: The same woman later appeals “to the king” for her house and fields, and he helps her.
2-kings-4:13:11.why: Later fulfillment of the offered royal help.

2-kings-4:13:12.summary: Abram's division of spoils has no specific link to this offer of help.

2-kings-4:13:13.summary: Elisha later warns the same woman of famine, continuing his care for her.
2-kings-4:13:13.why: Shows Elisha's continued concern for her.

2-kings-4:13:14.summary: Messengers stay in a house that receives them, a general theme of hosting God's servants.
2-kings-4:13:14.why: General theme of hospitality to messengers.

2-kings-4:13:15.summary: Barzillai declines the king's offer to prefer his own home, like her “I am living among my own people.”

2-kings-4:13:16.summary: A message to an army “commander” shares only the title.

2-kings-4:13:17.summary: Elisha's recent oracle for the kings shows his standing with royalty, but is not referenced here.

2-kings-4:13:18.summary: Joab's killing of two army commanders shares only the title.

2-kings-5:7:4.summary: God strikes and heals; general echo of God’s power over life.

2-kings-5:7:5.summary: Lying in wait to catch someone, loosely like suspecting a pretext.

2-kings-5:7:12.summary: A king tears his garments on receiving a foreign power’s message; loose parallel.

2-kings-5:7:13.summary: Apostles tear their garments; shared gesture only.

2-kings-5:8:0.summary: “Is it because there is no God in Israel” parallels letting Naaman know “there is a prophet in Israel”.

2-kings-5:8:2.summary: Mourning by tearing garments for Abner is unrelated.

2-kings-5:8:3.summary: A woman recognizes Elijah as a true man of God; loose recognition theme.

2-kings-5:8:4.summary: Elijah prays that the people “know” he is the Lord’s servant, like Elisha’s aim that Naaman know there is a prophet.

2-kings-5:8:7.summary: The king’s tearing of his garments is the event Elisha responds to here.

2-kings-5:9:3.summary: A jailer comes to Paul seeking salvation; loose parallel of a seeker.

2-kings-5:9:4.summary: Elisha in his house with a visitor at the door; place overlap only.

2-kings-5:10:2.summary: “You washed yourselves clean” is a spiritual washing; general theme.

2-kings-5:10:13.summary: Seven circuits before God acts at Jericho; loose obedience-sevenfold parallel.

2-kings-5:10:14.summary: Moses’ hand becomes white “as snow” and is “restored” to its flesh colour, matching flesh restored from leprosy.

2-kings-5:10:15.summary: Another Elisha instruction preceding a miracle; general parallel.

2-kings-5:10:16.summary: Elisha heals waters; another healing with water by the same prophet.

2-kings-5:11:0.summary: God’s ways are not human ways, as Naaman’s expectation clashes with the prophet’s method.

2-kings-5:11:1.summary: The Greek about wronging the innocent has no link to Naaman’s anger.

2-kings-5:11:2.summary: “Do not be prudent in your own estimation”; general warning against Naaman’s presumption.

2-kings-5:11:3.summary: Demand for signs and wonders loosely parallels Naaman expecting a showy cure.

2-kings-5:11:4.summary: Worldly wisdom is folly with God; general theme.

2-kings-5:11:5.summary: Receiving those sent is not specifically linked to Naaman’s anger at a messenger.

2-kings-5:11:6.summary: The self-exalting are humbled; general theme of Naaman’s pride.

2-kings-5:11:7.summary: Disciples “went back” offended; loose parallel of walking away.

2-kings-5:11:8.summary: Seeking signs or wisdom versus God’s “foolishness”; general theme.

2-kings-5:13:4.summary: “Father, father” to Elisha; shared address only.

2-kings-5:16:4.summary: A man of God refuses a king's offered reward (“half your house”), much as Elisha refuses Naaman's gift.

2-kings-5:17:2.summary: Leaving Gentile “idolatry” loosely matches Naaman's vow to sacrifice no longer to other gods.

2-kings-5:19:7.summary: Jesus says “go in peace” to a healed woman, echoing Elisha's farewell to the healed Naaman.

2-kings-5:19:8.summary: New wine and old wineskins bears no shared element with Elisha's farewell.

2-kings-5:19:9.summary: Jesus withholding teaching the disciples cannot bear has no specific link to Elisha's farewell.

2-kings-5:19:10.summary: Milk for the immature does not connect with Elisha's “Go in peace” to Naaman.

2-kings-6:16:1.summary: “Do not fear, for I am with you,” and enemies will perish, matching Elisha's reassurance.

2-kings-6:16:2.summary: “He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” echoes “more … than those with them.”

2-kings-6:16:3.summary: Hezekiah says “more are with us than with him,” nearly identical to Elisha's words.
2-kings-6:16:3.why: Same reassurance before an enemy army.

2-kings-6:16:4.summary: “Do not fear … I am with you … I have many people,” echoing Elisha's assurance.

2-kings-6:16:5.summary: “Among many they were with me” loosely echoes unseen allies.

2-kings-6:16:6.summary: Moses tells the people to take courage and see God's salvation from a pursuing army.

2-kings-6:16:7.summary: Enemy counsel fails “because the Lord God is with us,” matching Elisha's confidence.

2-kings-6:16:8.summary: “Even if an army draws up against me, my heart will not fear,” fitting the encircling army.

2-kings-6:16:9.summary: Jesus could have “twelve legions of angels,” unseen heavenly forces like Elisha's host.

2-kings-6:16:10.summary: “Surrounding me, they surrounded me,” yet the Lord's name repels them, like the encircling army.
2-kings-6:16:10.why: Encircled but defended by the Lord.

2-kings-6:16:11.summary: Not frightened by opponents, a general parallel.

2-kings-6:16:12.summary: “The Lord of powers is with us,” the heavenly hosts behind Elisha's assurance.

2-kings-6:16:13.summary: “Do not fear its fear,” a general call to fearlessness.

2-kings-6:16:14.summary: The Lord's eyes range the earth to strengthen the faithful, a general parallel.

2-kings-6:16:15.summary: “The Lord of powers is with us,” the hosts that outnumber the enemy.

2-kings-6:16:16.summary: “I will not fear tens of thousands … who attack me all around,” like the encircling Syrians.
2-kings-6:16:16.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-6:16:17.summary: Trusting the Lord rather than fleeing, a loose parallel.

2-kings-6:16:18.summary: “Do not be alarmed” at the empty tomb shares only a reassurance formula.

2-kings-6:17:0.summary: “God’s chariot is ten-thousandfold,” the heavenly chariots seen around Elisha.

2-kings-6:17:1.summary: An angel of the Lord “will encamp around” those who fear him, as fiery chariots surround Elisha.

2-kings-6:17:2.summary: Visionary chariots and horses between mountains loosely echo the heavenly horses on the mountain.

2-kings-6:17:3.summary: Angels are ministering spirits sent for the heirs of salvation, as the fiery host protects Elisha.

2-kings-6:17:4.summary: “To open their eyes” is spiritual, loosely echoing the attendant's opened eyes.

2-kings-6:17:6.summary: “To open blind people’s eyes” echoes the opening of eyes, in a different sense.

2-kings-6:17:7.summary: Twelve legions of angels available to Jesus parallel the unseen army around Elisha.

2-kings-6:17:8.summary: “Uncover my eyes” to see God's wonders matches Elisha's prayer to open eyes.

2-kings-6:17:9.summary: Heavenly armies on horses loosely echo the horses on the mountain.

2-kings-6:17:10.summary: God commands angels to guard his own, as the fiery host guards Elisha.

2-kings-6:17:11.summary: Visionary horses among mountains loosely echo heavenly horses on the mountain.

2-kings-6:17:12.summary: “Eyes of your heart enlightened” to know spiritual realities echoes opened eyes.

2-kings-6:17:13.summary: Heaven opened with a warrior on a horse, loosely echoing heavenly cavalry.

2-kings-6:17:14.summary: Elisha again prays “open their eyes so they may see,” repeating the formula and outcome.
2-kings-6:17:14.why: Paired prayers for opened and closed eyes.

2-kings-6:17:15.summary: God rides the clouds and winds, a general image of divine chariotry.

2-kings-6:17:16.summary: Fiery creatures and wheels loosely echo the “chariot of fire.”

2-kings-6:17:17.summary: God answers the one who calls and is with him in affliction, general parallel to Elisha's prayer.

2-kings-6:17:18.summary: A righteous person's prayer is powerful, exemplified by Elijah; general parallel to Elisha's prayer.

2-kings-6:17:19.summary: Christ who opens and shuts is about doors, not opened eyes.

2-kings-6:17:20.summary: A great divine manifestation overwhelms a hostile intruder, loosely like heavenly forces around Elisha.

2-kings-6:17:21.summary: Heavenly horsemen seen in the air parallel the visible fiery horses around Elisha.

2-kings-6:17:22.summary: Heavenly men on horses appear to protect the Jews, like the fiery horsemen guarding Elisha.

2-kings-6:18:0.summary: An opponent is struck blind by the Lord's hand and needs leading, like the Syrians led blind.

2-kings-6:18:1.summary: Attackers at Lot's door are “struck … with blindness,” the same miracle against hostile men.

2-kings-6:18:2.summary: God blinding eyes is spiritual hardening, a loose parallel.

2-kings-6:18:3.summary: Those who see becoming blind is spiritual, a loose echo.

2-kings-6:18:4.summary: The crafty grope at noon as at night, like confused blinded soldiers.

2-kings-6:18:5.summary: The Lord smites with blindness, the same divine judgment, here a covenant curse.

2-kings-6:18:6.summary: God will strike the enemies' horses with blindness and bewilderment, like Syria's army struck.

2-kings-6:18:7.summary: Israel's hardening is spiritual and unrelated to Syrians' blindness.

2-kings-6:18:8.summary: “Struck with blindness, like those at the righteous man’s doors,” the same miracle type.

2-kings-6:19:0.summary: Jesus' call to follow him shares only the word “follow.”

2-kings-6:19:3.summary: Hushai's misleading but technically true words loosely parallel Elisha's ruse.

2-kings-6:19:4.summary: Eyes held from recognizing loosely parallels the blinded Syrians failing to recognize Elisha.

2-kings-6:20:0.summary: Elisha's identical prayer “open … eyes … that he may see” and “behold” revelation.

2-kings-6:20:1.summary: The rich man lifting his eyes in Hades shares only seeing.

2-kings-6:20:2.summary: “Their eyes were opened and they recognized,” a parallel divine opening of eyes.

2-kings-6:20:3.summary: An army suddenly sees it is trapped, loosely like Syrians finding themselves in Samaria.

2-kings-6:21:0.summary: Naaman's servants address him with respect, perhaps “father” in other texts; the shown text lacks it.

2-kings-6:21:1.summary: The Syrian king calls himself Elisha's “son,” paralleling the king's “father.”

2-kings-6:21:2.summary: “Father, father!” addressed to a prophet, as Israel's king calls Elisha “father.”

2-kings-6:21:3.summary: Sending an enemy away unharmed earns the Lord's reward, the issue the king raises.
2-kings-6:21:3.why: Sparing an enemy in one's power.

2-kings-6:21:4.summary: Disciples ask to destroy foes and are rebuked, as the king asks to strike and is refused.

2-kings-6:21:5.summary: David's men urge him to strike the enemy delivered into his hands, like the king's question.
2-kings-6:21:5.why: Temptation to kill a captive enemy.

2-kings-6:21:6.summary: Joash king of Israel calls Elisha “Father, father!”, the same title.

2-kings-6:21:7.summary: “Lord, shall we strike with a sword?” closely mirrors “Shall I indeed strike them?”
2-kings-6:21:7.why: Request to strike, met with restraint.

2-kings-6:21:8.summary: Abishai offers to strike the enemy delivered into David's hands, which David refuses.
2-kings-6:21:8.why: Restraint toward enemy in one's power.

2-kings-6:22:0.summary: Taken “with my sword and bow” echoes the phrase but in an unrelated context.

2-kings-6:22:1.summary: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him … thirsty, give him a drink,” as Elisha commands for the Syrians.
2-kings-6:22:1.why: Feeding enemies, conquering evil with good.

2-kings-6:22:2.summary: A prophet stops Israel enslaving captives, who are then fed and returned (truncated), like Elisha's command.

2-kings-6:22:3.summary: The law of war allows killing males of a besieged city (truncated), contrasting Elisha's mercy.

2-kings-6:22:4.summary: God will shatter “bow, sword and war,” loosely like Elisha's peaceable solution.

2-kings-6:22:5.summary: Victory “not by your sword or by your bow,” as these captives were not taken by sword and bow.

2-kings-6:22:6.summary: “Love your enemies,” the principle in feeding the Syrian captives.

2-kings-6:22:7.summary: God saves “not … by bow, sword,” as Syria's army was captured by God, not by Israel's sword and bow.

2-kings-6:22:8.summary: Not trusting “my bow” and “sword,” loosely echoing captives not taken by sword and bow.

2-kings-6:23:0.summary: “Lightly equipped Syrians” raided Israel, the same raiding bands that now stop coming.

2-kings-6:23:1.summary: “Lightly equipped raiders” including Syria, the same kind of raiding bands later.
2-kings-6:23:1.why: Raiding bands as a recurring threat.

2-kings-6:23:2.summary: Begins the Syrian campaign that this verse concludes.

2-kings-6:23:3.summary: A Samaritan shows mercy to a stranger (truncated), loosely like kindness to enemies.

2-kings-6:23:4.summary: “Love your enemies, do good,” as Israel feeds and releases its enemies.

2-kings-6:23:5.summary: Going beyond greeting only brothers, loosely like kindness to foes.

2-kings-6:23:6.summary: Captives are fed, clothed and sent home to their brethren, closely like the Syrians fed and sent away.

2-kings-6:23:7.summary: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if thirsty, give him drink,” exactly as done here.
2-kings-6:23:7.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-6:23:8.summary: Saul acknowledges David repaid evil with good by sparing him, as Israel spares the Syrians.

2-kings-6:24:0.summary: “The son of Ader gathered all his force, went up, and besieged Samaria,” nearly identical wording.

2-kings-6:24:1.summary: The covenant curse of siege on Israel's cities loosely frames Samaria's siege.

2-kings-6:24:2.summary: The king of Syria's earlier war against Israel's king.

2-kings-6:24:3.summary: A great king surrounds a small city with siegeworks, a general siege image.

2-kings-6:24:4.summary: Samaria besieged again, by Assyria, a later siege of the same city.

2-kings-6:24:5.summary: Babylon's siege of Jerusalem is a parallel siege of a capital.

2-kings-6:24:6.summary: Assyria besieges Samaria, the same city later.

2-kings-6:25:0.summary: False prophets deny famine will come (truncated), a loose parallel to siege famine.

2-kings-6:25:1.summary: Famine grows severe in a besieged city with no bread, like Samaria under siege.

2-kings-6:25:2.summary: The mothers eating their sons shows the extremity of this same Samaria famine.

2-kings-6:25:3.summary: “The pain of famine” in the city, general parallel.

2-kings-6:25:4.summary: A besieged city given over by sword and famine, general parallel.

2-kings-6:25:5.summary: The lepers note “the famine is in the city,” the same Samaria siege famine.

2-kings-6:25:6.summary: Dung used in food preparation and bread by weight during siege, like the dung prices in Samaria.

2-kings-6:25:7.summary: “The famine was severe in Samaria,” an earlier famine in the same city.

2-kings-6:25:8.summary: Famine grows severe in besieged Jerusalem with no loaves, a parallel siege famine.

2-kings-6:25:9.summary: The covenant curse of bread by weight and hunger is fulfilled in Samaria's famine.

2-kings-6:26:0.summary: A woman cries out to the king “Help, O king!”, like “Save me, lord king!”

2-kings-6:26:1.summary: “To whom will you flee for help” in disaster, general parallel.

2-kings-6:26:2.summary: A widow pleads with a judge for justice, loosely like the woman appealing to the king.

2-kings-6:26:3.summary: A mob's “help!” against Paul shares only the cry.

2-kings-6:27:0.summary: The psalm prefers trusting the Lord over man and rulers; the king’s helplessness only loosely illustrates that maxim.
2-kings-6:27:0.why: Frames the king’s admission of helplessness theologically.

2-kings-6:27:1.summary: The psalm credits deliverance to the Lord being among His people; only a general theme of rescue from enemies.
2-kings-6:27:1.why: General contrast of divine versus human rescue.

2-kings-6:27:2.summary: The psalm warns against trusting “rulers” who “have no salvation”; the king openly confesses he cannot save the woman.
2-kings-6:27:2.why: The king embodies a ruler without salvation.

2-kings-6:27:3.summary: Unless the Lord guards a city the watchman is vain; loosely fits besieged Samaria but no specific link.
2-kings-6:27:3.why: Broad theme of the Lord as the city’s only guard.

2-kings-6:27:4.summary: Jeremiah curses hope placed in a human; the king’s refusal only loosely echoes the futility of human help.
2-kings-6:27:4.why: General warning against relying on human aid.

2-kings-6:27:5.summary: The psalm calls the people to hope in God as “helper”; only a general theme of where help comes from.
2-kings-6:27:5.why: Points to God as the true helper.

2-kings-6:27:6.summary: “Human salvation is vain” matches the king’s confession that he has no means to save the starving woman.
2-kings-6:27:6.why: Crisp statement of the futility the king voices.

2-kings-6:27:7.summary: Isaiah’s vision of the exalted mountain of the Lord has no connection to the famine plea or the king’s reply.

2-kings-6:28:0.summary: Same scene formula: “The king said to her, What troubles you?” followed by a woman’s petition to the king.
2-kings-6:28:0.why: Parallel royal-petition scenes with a woman’s grievance.
2-kings-6:28:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-6:28:1.summary: Only the idiomatic question “What is wrong” is shared; the contexts are unrelated.

2-kings-6:28:2.summary: The covenant curse “you shall eat the flesh of your sons” is grimly realized in the mothers’ agreement to eat their sons.
2-kings-6:28:2.why: Shows the siege horror as fulfilled covenant curse.

2-kings-6:28:3.summary: Women “boiled their children” for food in a siege, the same atrocity the women of Samaria describe.
2-kings-6:28:3.why: Closest parallel of mothers eating children in famine.

2-kings-6:28:4.summary: Days when the barren are called blessed loosely recall mothers’ suffering in siege; no specific shared detail.
2-kings-6:28:4.why: Echoes the anguish of mothers in judgment.

2-kings-6:28:5.summary: Ezekiel threatens that “fathers will eat children” in the besieged city, matching parents eating sons in Samaria.
2-kings-6:28:5.why: Prophetic threat of siege cannibalism realized here.

2-kings-6:28:6.summary: “What happened to you” in a city under threat echoes the king’s question, but the link is mostly idiomatic.

2-kings-6:28:7.summary: The psalm’s poetic question to the sea shares only the idiom “What is it with you”.

2-kings-6:28:8.summary: Isaiah’s image of a woman failing to have mercy on her child is tragically realized by the mothers in the siege.
2-kings-6:28:8.why: Contrasts failed maternal mercy with God’s unfailing love.

2-kings-6:28:9.summary: Shares the question “What is the matter” addressed to a distressed woman; contexts otherwise unrelated.
2-kings-6:28:9.why: Similar address to a woman in distress.

2-kings-6:28:11.summary: “What is wrong, Hagar?” is addressed to a mother over her child, a loose verbal and situational echo.

2-kings-6:28:12.summary: Famine so severe that people eat their own flesh and turn on each other loosely parallels the siege horror.

2-kings-6:28:13.summary: Woe to mothers nursing in days of great affliction loosely echoes the plight of mothers in besieged Samaria.
2-kings-6:28:13.why: General theme of mothers suffering in calamity.

2-kings-6:29:0.summary: “You shall eat the flesh of your sons” is precisely what the woman reports doing in the siege.
2-kings-6:29:0.why: Shows covenant curse fulfilled in Samaria.

2-kings-6:29:1.summary: Eating “the flesh of your sons” in siege “straitness” caused by an enemy matches the woman’s confession.

2-kings-6:29:2.summary: A mother eating her child “secretly” in siege distress parallels the women eating sons, one son being hidden.

2-kings-6:29:3.summary: Two women dispute over a son before a king; Solomon’s mother pleads for life, while Samaria’s mothers consume their sons.
2-kings-6:29:3.why: Striking contrast of two royal judgment scenes.

2-kings-6:29:4.summary: A mother comforting her child shares only the motherhood image; no link to the siege narrative.

2-kings-6:29:5.summary: A woman failing to have mercy on her offspring is tragically enacted, set against God’s promise not to forget.
2-kings-6:29:5.why: Contrasts maternal failure with divine faithfulness.

2-kings-6:30:0.summary: A king of Israel “tore his tunic” and wore “sackcloth” on his body, matching the king’s hidden sackcloth.
2-kings-6:30:0.why: Parallel royal mourning gestures in the same dynasty.

2-kings-6:30:1.summary: Isaiah critiques sackcloth fasting without justice; loosely questions the king’s outward sackcloth.
2-kings-6:30:1.why: Raises the question of sincere repentance.

2-kings-6:30:2.summary: “When King Hezekiah heard, he tore his garments, put on sackcloth” mirrors the king’s reaction on hearing.
2-kings-6:30:2.why: Contrasts two kings’ responses to crisis.

2-kings-6:31:0.summary: Uses the same oath formula “May the Lord do these things to me, and add”.

2-kings-6:31:1.summary: Jezebel swears “May the god do thus to me and add more” to kill Elijah, as the king swears to behead Elisha.
2-kings-6:31:1.why: Royal oath against a prophet’s life in the same house.

2-kings-6:31:2.summary: A king of Israel says he “hates” the prophet Micaiah; loosely parallels royal hostility to a prophet.
2-kings-6:31:2.why: Pattern of Israel’s kings opposing prophets.
2-kings-6:31:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-6:31:3.summary: Caiaphas’s counsel that one man die for the nation has no specific link to the king’s oath against Elisha.

2-kings-6:31:4.summary: Eli uses the oath formula “May God do these things to you, and add these things”.

2-kings-6:31:5.summary: Rulers strike and imprison Jeremiah; only the general theme of officials persecuting a prophet.

2-kings-6:31:6.summary: David swears “May God do so to David, and more besides” before planned killing.
2-kings-6:31:6.why: Same oath formula with lethal intent.

2-kings-6:31:7.summary: Abner swears “May God do these things to Abner, and add these things” with “this very day”.

2-kings-6:31:8.summary: Ahab blames Elijah as Israel’s troubler, as the king blames Elisha; shared pattern of a king blaming a prophet.
2-kings-6:31:8.why: King blames prophet for national distress.

2-kings-6:31:9.summary: Officials demand “Let that man be killed” regarding Jeremiah during a siege; general parallel of seeking a prophet’s death.
2-kings-6:31:9.why: Prophet’s life threatened in besieged city.

2-kings-6:31:10.summary: Conspirators bind themselves under an oath to kill Paul; loosely parallels an oath to kill God’s messenger.
2-kings-6:31:10.why: Sworn intent to kill a servant of God.

2-kings-6:31:11.summary: Solomon swears “May God do thus to me and add more” to put Adonijah to death.

2-kings-6:31:12.summary: David swears “May God do these things to me, and add these things” concerning that day.

2-kings-6:31:13.summary: David uses “may God do so to me, and more besides” in an oath.

2-kings-6:31:14.summary: Saul swears “May God do so to me and add still more” that Jonathan must die “today”.
2-kings-6:31:14.why: Rash royal death oath, same formula.

2-kings-6:32:0.summary: “I was sitting in the house, and Judah’s elders were sitting before me” mirrors Elisha sitting with the elders.
2-kings-6:32:0.why: Same image of elders seated with a prophet.

2-kings-6:32:1.summary: Elders came and “sat before” the prophet; a general echo of elders consulting a prophet.
2-kings-6:32:1.why: Shared scene of elders with prophet.

2-kings-6:32:2.summary: Elders of Israel came and sat before the prophet; similar setting, different occasion.
2-kings-6:32:2.why: Shared scene of elders with prophet.

2-kings-6:32:3.summary: Jezebel striking the Lord’s prophets may explain “son of a murderer”, but the shown text names no link.
2-kings-6:32:3.why: Background to the murderous royal house.

2-kings-6:32:4.summary: The plot to kill Naboth is plausible background for “son of a murderer”, but no shared wording or name.
2-kings-6:32:4.why: Background to the murderous royal house.

2-kings-6:32:5.summary: Jezebel killing the Lord’s prophets may lie behind “son of a murderer”; only indirectly connected.
2-kings-6:32:5.why: Background to royal hostility to prophets.

2-kings-6:32:6.summary: Naboth’s judicial murder plausibly underlies “son of a murderer”, though the shown texts do not tie them.
2-kings-6:32:6.why: Background to the murderous royal house.

2-kings-6:32:7.summary: People “sit before” the prophet; only the general scene of hearers seated before a prophet.

2-kings-6:32:8.summary: Jesus calls a murderous ruler “that fox”, loosely like Elisha’s scornful “son of a murderer”.
2-kings-6:32:8.why: Prophetic boldness toward a hostile ruler.

2-kings-6:32:9.summary: Elisha reports kings’ private words, the same supernatural knowledge he shows in foreseeing the king’s messenger.

2-kings-6:32:10.summary: Ahijah knows of the visitor before she enters and instructs his attendant, like Elisha foreseeing the messenger.
2-kings-6:32:10.why: Prophet’s foreknowledge of an approaching visitor.

2-kings-6:32:11.summary: “Did not my heart go with you” shows Elisha perceiving unseen events, as he perceives the king’s plot.
2-kings-6:32:11.why: Elisha’s prophetic insight into hidden actions.

2-kings-6:33:0.summary: Job’s wife urges giving up under suffering; loosely parallels the despairing “Why should I wait for the Lord?”

2-kings-6:33:1.summary: In famine the hungry “speak evil of the ruler”; loosely parallels famine-driven bitterness toward God.

2-kings-6:33:2.summary: The fragment about holding fast to truth and peace has no evident link to the messenger’s despair.

2-kings-6:33:3.summary: People under plagues blaspheme God instead of repenting; loosely like blaming the Lord for calamity.
2-kings-6:33:3.why: Calamity provoking rebellion rather than repentance.

2-kings-6:33:4.summary: Paul on Satan’s designs has no specific connection to the king’s despairing words.

2-kings-6:33:5.summary: “Wait for the Lord” is urged twice, directly countering “Why should I wait for the Lord any longer?”
2-kings-6:33:5.why: Direct verbal contrast to the despairing question.

2-kings-6:33:6.summary: Those in darkness are told to trust the Lord’s name; general contrast to giving up on the Lord.

2-kings-6:33:7.summary: “Those who wait for the Lord will inherit the land” directly answers the refusal to wait for the Lord.
2-kings-6:33:7.why: Promise for those who keep waiting.

2-kings-6:33:8.summary: The accuser predicts affliction will make Job curse God; loosely like calamity provoking rejection of the Lord.

2-kings-6:33:9.summary: The call to pray always and not lose heart loosely contrasts the king’s impatience with the Lord.

2-kings-6:33:10.summary: Loss is expected to make Job curse God; general theme of calamity turning someone against the Lord.

2-kings-6:33:11.summary: Hungry Israel’s murmuring is “against God”; loosely parallels famine-driven complaint against the Lord.

2-kings-6:33:12.summary: A man “blames God” for ruin; loosely fits “this calamity is from the Lord” spoken in resentment.

2-kings-6:33:13.summary: Saul, unanswered by the Lord, turns elsewhere; loosely parallels a king abandoning patience with the Lord.
2-kings-6:33:13.why: King giving up on the Lord.

2-kings-6:33:14.summary: Paul’s instruction to forgive a penitent has no specific link to the king’s despair.

2-kings-6:33:15.summary: Cain’s complaint about his guilt shares only a vague note of despair.

2-kings-6:33:16.summary: The Greek reads “Submit to the Lord and beseech Him”, a general contrast to giving up on the Lord.

2-kings-6:33:17.summary: “If he delays, wait for him” loosely counters the impatience of “Why should I wait”.

2-kings-6:33:18.summary: “Submit to God, my soul” offers a general contrast to impatience; the Greek lacks explicit “wait”.

2-kings-6:33:19.summary: Both attribute calamity to the Lord, but Job blesses God where the king despairs.

2-kings-6:33:20.summary: “I will wait for God, who turned His face away” directly contrasts refusing to wait for the Lord in calamity.
2-kings-6:33:20.why: Faithful waiting even when God seems hidden.

2-kings-6:33:21.summary: Judas’s remorse and suicide have no specific link to the messenger’s words.

2-kings-6:33:22.summary: “The Lord is good to those who wait for Him” directly answers the question of waiting for the Lord.
2-kings-6:33:22.why: Counters despair with the goodness of waiting.

2-kings-6:33:23.summary: Saul’s death by his own sword is unrelated to the despairing question in Samaria.

2-kings-6:33:24.summary: Israel’s stubborn love of strangers is unrelated to the king’s despair over famine.

2-kings-6:33:25.summary: “How shall we live?” expresses despair under judgment, loosely like the hopelessness in Samaria.

2-kings-6:8:1.summary: Proverbs 20:18 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-6:8:1.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-6:8:1.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-7:1:13.summary: The narrator repeats Elisha’s prophecy of flour and barley for a shekel at Samaria’s gate as fulfilled.
2-kings-7:1:13.why: Records the exact fulfilment of the prophecy.

2-kings-7:1:0.summary: “Tomorrow the Lord will do wonders” parallels a next-day promise of divine action, in an unrelated setting.

2-kings-7:1:1.summary: God promises the hungry bread by morning; loosely like the promise of food tomorrow.
2-kings-7:1:1.why: Divine provision of food for the hungry.

2-kings-7:1:2.summary: Only the prophetic formula “hear the Lord’s word” is shared.

2-kings-7:1:3.summary: “Tomorrow… you will have deliverance” to a besieged city parallels a next-day rescue announcement.
2-kings-7:1:3.why: Announced next-day deliverance of a besieged city.

2-kings-7:1:4.summary: Moses announces the salvation God will accomplish; a general theme of announced deliverance.

2-kings-7:1:5.summary: God sets a time, “Tomorrow the Lord will do this”, and it happens next day; similar timed-prophecy pattern.

2-kings-7:1:6.summary: God helps His city “toward morning”; loosely fits overnight deliverance of besieged Samaria.

2-kings-7:1:7.summary: “Tomorrow this sign shall be” shares the timed announcement pattern only.

2-kings-7:1:8.summary: Shares only the prophetic opener “Hear the Lord’s word”.

2-kings-7:1:9.summary: Famine prices in Samaria (a donkey’s head for fifty shekels) set up the reversal to cheap flour and barley.

2-kings-7:1:10.summary: Both price measures of wheat and barley for a coin, though Revelation signals scarcity where Elisha promises plenty.
2-kings-7:1:10.why: Distinctive grain-price formula, used in reverse.

2-kings-7:1:11.summary: Barley loaves brought to Elisha feed people; only a general link of Elisha and food provision.

2-kings-7:1:12.summary: Barley loaves in the feeding miracle share only the word barley.

2-kings-7:1:14.summary: Elisha’s promise answers the immediately preceding despair: “Why should I wait for the Lord any longer?”
2-kings-7:1:14.why: Immediate narrative setting of the promise.

2-kings-7:1:15.summary: Shares only the formula “Hear the Lord’s word”.

2-kings-7:1:16.summary: Micaiah’s “Hear the Lord’s word” to a king of Israel shares the formula only.

2-kings-7:2:0.summary: “The floodgates of heaven were opened” uses the same image the officer mocks.

2-kings-7:2:1.summary: Sarah’s inward doubt meets “Is any word impossible with God?”, like the officer’s doubt of the Lord’s word.
2-kings-7:2:1.why: Doubting the possibility of God’s promise.

2-kings-7:2:2.summary: God promises to “open heaven’s floodgates” to pour out blessing, the very abundance the officer deems impossible.
2-kings-7:2:2.why: Floodgates as image of divine provision.

2-kings-7:2:3.summary: Human unfaithfulness cannot nullify God’s faithfulness; a general theme for the officer’s unbelief.

2-kings-7:2:4.summary: Israel tested God; general theme of distrusting God’s power.

2-kings-7:2:5.summary: God remains faithful despite human unfaithfulness; general theme only.

2-kings-7:2:6.summary: A master “leans on my arm”, the same idiom describing the king’s officer as royal aide.

2-kings-7:2:7.summary: “If you do not believe” warns a royal house; loosely like the officer’s unbelief toward the prophet.

2-kings-7:2:8.summary: “Trust in His prophet, and you will prosper” contrasts the officer who doubts Elisha and loses the benefit.

2-kings-7:2:9.summary: Moses doubts God can feed the people; God replies “whether My word shall overtake you”, as with the officer’s doubt.
2-kings-7:2:9.why: Classic doubt that God can supply food.

2-kings-7:2:10.summary: “Surely God cannot… give bread” parallels the officer’s “surely this word cannot come true”.
2-kings-7:2:10.why: Same sceptical question about food provision.

2-kings-7:2:11.summary: Unbelief bars entry to promised rest; loosely like the officer barred from eating.

2-kings-7:2:12.summary: Moses may “behold with your eyes” the land but not enter, as the officer will see but not eat.
2-kings-7:2:12.why: Seeing the blessing without sharing it.

2-kings-7:3:0.summary: The law requires a leper to dwell apart outside the camp, explaining why the lepers sit outside the gate.

2-kings-7:3:1.summary: Everyone with leprosy is sent outside the camp, the reason the four lepers are outside Samaria.

2-kings-7:3:3.summary: “Why are we sitting?” is nearly the lepers’ own question in a context of besieged cities.

2-kings-7:3:5.summary: The shown text about Gehazi recounting Elisha’s deeds does not mention leprosy or the four men.
2-kings-7:3:5.why: No link in the shown text.

2-kings-7:3:6.summary: Miriam is set outside the camp for leprosy-related shame; general background on exclusion.

2-kings-7:3:7.summary: Naaman is afflicted with leprosy; only the shared condition of leprosy.

2-kings-7:4:0.summary: Out in the field is death and in the city famine; the same deadly dilemma the lepers weigh.

2-kings-7:4:1.summary: Esther risks the king’s presence “even if I must perish”; loose parallel of a desperate gamble.

2-kings-7:4:2.summary: The starving son reasons and resolves to go; loosely like the lepers’ hunger-driven reasoning.

2-kings-7:4:3.summary: “We must certainly die” is a general statement on mortality, not the lepers’ dilemma.

2-kings-7:4:4.summary: “Who knows… so that we do not perish” shares the uncertain hope of survival.
2-kings-7:4:4.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-7:4:5.summary: “Why are we sitting? …let us enter the fortified cities” echoes the lepers’ deliberation about entering the city.

2-kings-7:4:6.summary: Hebrews on dying once and judgment has no specific link.

2-kings-7:4:7.summary: Jeremiah is accused of deserting to the besiegers; loose parallel of going over to the enemy.

2-kings-7:4:8.summary: Men come over to David amid foreign armies; only a loose theme of crossing to the other side.

2-kings-7:5:0.summary: Enemies who come out will flee; loosely anticipates the deserted Syrian camp.

2-kings-7:5:1.summary: A law on firstborn livestock has no link to the lepers entering the camp.

2-kings-7:5:2.summary: Ezekiel’s sign of going out in the evening is unrelated beyond the time of day.

2-kings-7:5:3.summary: A ruler escaping through a wall shares no specific element with the empty camp.

2-kings-7:5:4.summary: Terror bereaving enemies is a general theme of God-sent panic.

2-kings-7:5:5.summary: David’s slaughter of Amalekites shares no specific element with the empty Syrian camp.

2-kings-7:5:6.summary: Few routing many because the Lord gave them up; loosely like four lepers finding an army gone.

2-kings-7:5:7.summary: A rule on valuing a poor man’s vow is unrelated.

2-kings-7:6:0.summary: A sound in the trees signals the Lord going out to strike the enemy, like the Lord’s sound routing Syria.
2-kings-7:6:0.why: God fights through a supernatural sound.

2-kings-7:6:1.summary: Egypt’s horses and chariots as military help loosely match Syria’s fear of hired Egyptian kings.

2-kings-7:6:2.summary: Egyptian chariots and horses supplied to “the Hittite kings” matches the feared alliance of Hittite and Egyptian kings.
2-kings-7:6:2.why: Shows why Hittites and Egypt meant chariot armies.

2-kings-7:6:3.summary: “The sound of chariots of many horses running to war” echoes the phantom sound, in a different vision.
2-kings-7:6:3.why: Similar sound of a chariot army.

2-kings-7:6:4.summary: Trust in Egypt for horses and riders; general theme of Egyptian cavalry.

2-kings-7:6:5.summary: Kings hiding in terror at the end shares only a general fear motif.

2-kings-7:6:6.summary: “His fear is in his ears” fits terror induced by sound, though Job speaks generally of the wicked.

2-kings-7:6:7.summary: Moab misreads a sight, assumes the kings struck each other, and rushes to spoils; another God-caused misperception in war.

2-kings-7:6:8.summary: An Egyptian king with vast chariot forces attacks; only the general picture of Egyptian chariotry.

2-kings-7:6:9.summary: “They cowered in fear where there was no fear” describes the Syrians fleeing a phantom army.

2-kings-7:6:10.summary: The sound of cherubim’s wings shares only the idea of a heard sound.

2-kings-7:6:11.summary: God makes an enemy king “hear a report and return”, as He made Syria hear sounds and abandon the siege.
2-kings-7:6:11.why: God lifts a siege through a report.

2-kings-7:6:12.summary: Jeremiah’s rename of Pashhur has no link to the Syrians’ panic.

2-kings-7:7:0.summary: Hostile kings gather, are shaken, and seized with trembling before God’s city, like Syria’s sudden flight.
2-kings-7:7:0.why: Enemy kings panic before God’s city.

2-kings-7:7:1.summary: “Flees when no one pursues” exactly describes the Syrians fleeing a nonexistent army.

2-kings-7:7:2.summary: A king’s heart is in God’s hand; general theme of God directing rulers.

2-kings-7:7:3.summary: Cities of refuge share only the word “flee”.

2-kings-7:7:4.summary: Those relying on chariots and horses fall; general theme fitting the abandoned horses.

2-kings-7:7:5.summary: Job’s curse of pains and famine on the wicked has no specific link to the flight.

2-kings-7:7:6.summary: “A horse is false for salvation” loosely fits the Syrians abandoning horses to flee.

2-kings-7:7:7.summary: People cast away valuables in that day; loosely like abandoning possessions in flight.

2-kings-7:7:8.summary: The horseman will not save his life and the warrior flees naked, as the Syrians flee abandoning horses.
2-kings-7:7:8.why: Prophetic picture of army in panic flight.

2-kings-7:7:9.summary: Fleeing for refuge to God’s promise shares only the word “fled”.

2-kings-7:7:10.summary: Destruction on Moab’s cities has no specific link to Syria’s flight.

2-kings-7:7:11.summary: Saving oneself like a gazelle from a snare loosely fits fleeing for one’s life.

2-kings-7:7:12.summary: Flee without going back for belongings; loosely like abandoning tents and animals.

2-kings-7:7:13.summary: Dividing spoils after kings flee; general theme, obscure in the Greek.

2-kings-7:8:0.summary: Achan took silver, gold, and a garment from spoil and hid them in his tent, like the lepers.

2-kings-7:8:1.summary: Treasure found and hidden shares the act of hiding, nothing more specific.

2-kings-7:8:2.summary: A servant hides silver in the ground; only the act of hiding silver.

2-kings-7:8:3.summary: Men with hidden stores of food bargaining for life share no specific link.

2-kings-7:8:4.summary: Gehazi takes goods and stashes them in a house, paralleling the lepers taking and hiding loot.

2-kings-7:9:0.summary: “One bringing good news” of salvation echoes the lepers’ “day of good news” to be reported.

2-kings-7:9:1.summary: Looking to others’ interests loosely fits the lepers’ decision to share the news.

2-kings-7:9:2.summary: The Greek about comforting Jerusalem for a journey lacks a link to good news here.

2-kings-7:9:3.summary: The Lord’s routing of Syria is the content of the good news the lepers now resolve to report.
2-kings-7:9:3.why: Immediate narrative cause of the good news.

2-kings-7:9:4.summary: “You shall recognize your sin when evils overtake you” loosely matches fear of punishment for silence.

2-kings-7:9:5.summary: “One bringing good news and announcing peace” fits the lepers bringing news of deliverance.

2-kings-7:9:6.summary: The same four lepers: “One said to his neighbor”, continuing their earlier deliberation.

2-kings-7:9:7.summary: Rebuke for enjoying one’s own house while God’s lies waste; loosely like enjoying spoil while others starve.

2-kings-7:9:8.summary: The righteous rising after falling has no specific link.

2-kings-7:9:9.summary: Gehazi took silver and garments and was struck with leprosy; contrasts lepers who stop hoarding.

2-kings-7:9:10.summary: “Good news of great joy… for all the people” shares the good-news idea in a different context.

2-kings-7:10:0.summary: The parable’s doorkeeper shares only the gatekeeper idea.

2-kings-7:10:1.summary: The watchman guarding a city has no specific link to the lepers’ report.

2-kings-7:10:3.summary: The gatekeepers relay the lepers’ report into the king’s house, the next step of the same event.

2-kings-7:10:4.summary: A watchman calls out at the gate about a runner with news; similar gate-report scene.
2-kings-7:10:4.why: News delivered at a city gate.

2-kings-7:12:0.summary: Joshua’s ambush behind the city to draw defenders out is the tactic the king suspects Syria of using.

2-kings-7:12:1.summary: The famine in besieged Samaria explains the king’s remark that Syria knows “we are hungry”.

2-kings-7:13:0.summary: Attendants give their master sensible counsel; general parallel of a servant’s advice.

2-kings-7:13:1.summary: Death by sword outside and famine inside; general background of the city’s plight.

2-kings-7:13:2.summary: Like the lepers, the attendant reasons that those sent risk nothing since all are perishing anyway.

2-kings-7:13:3.summary: The earlier despair of the king’s side forms general background; no specific shared element.

2-kings-7:13:4.summary: Famine is worse than the sword; general theme of the people “failing”.

2-kings-7:15:0.summary: Paul counting gains as loss is unrelated to the Syrians’ discarded gear.

2-kings-7:15:1.summary: Casting away impieties shares only the verb “cast away”.

2-kings-7:15:2.summary: Royal drinking vessels have no link to the strewn equipment.

2-kings-7:15:3.summary: “To whom will you flee… where will you leave your glory” loosely fits fleeing and leaving possessions.

2-kings-7:15:4.summary: People renounce silver and gold in that day; loose image of discarding valuables.

2-kings-7:15:5.summary: Life is worth more than possessions; loosely fits throwing away gear to escape.

2-kings-7:15:6.summary: “Whatever a person has, he will pay for his life” fits soldiers discarding everything to survive.
2-kings-7:15:6.why: Giving up all to save life.

2-kings-7:15:7.summary: Hanging dependents on Eliakim has no link to the road strewn with gear.

2-kings-7:15:8.summary: Casting out silver and gold in panic loosely mirrors throwing away equipment.

2-kings-7:15:9.summary: Laying aside every weight to run loosely images the Syrians shedding gear to flee.

2-kings-7:15:10.summary: Fleeing without stopping for belongings loosely matches the fleeing Syrians.

2-kings-7:16:1.summary: Even the lame take spoil after an enemy fails; loosely like starving Samaria plundering the camp.

2-kings-7:16:2.summary: Spoils gathered like locusts; general image of plundering.

2-kings-7:16:3.summary: Christ’s words never pass away; general theme of the word fulfilled.

2-kings-7:16:4.summary: “Having spoken, shall He not act?” fits fulfilment “according to the word of the Lord” generally.

2-kings-7:16:5.summary: Afflicters are handed over and defeated; only a general theme of oppressors undone.

2-kings-7:16:6.summary: God establishes His servant’s words; general theme of prophecy confirmed.

2-kings-7:16:7.summary: Enemies flee before the Lord and Judah plunders tents and much spoil, as Samaria plunders Syria’s camp.
2-kings-7:16:7.why: Parallel divine rout followed by plunder.

2-kings-7:16:8.summary: The wicked’s silver passes to the righteous; loose theme of wealth transferred.

2-kings-7:16:9.summary: Dividing spoils is a general shared idea, obscure in the Greek.

2-kings-7:16:10.summary: Jehoshaphat’s people plunder abundant spoils after the Lord routs the enemy, as Samaria plunders Syria’s camp.

2-kings-7:16:11.summary: Israel returns from pursuit and tramples the fleeing enemy’s camps, like the plundering of Syria’s camp.

2-kings-7:17:0.summary: The officer’s death fulfills Elisha’s word spoken “when the messenger came down”, the messenger of this scene.
2-kings-7:17:0.why: Links fulfilment to the original encounter.

2-kings-7:17:2.summary: Jezebel is “trampled” in a judgment death; shared verb and theme of prophesied death.

2-kings-7:17:3.summary: Trampling the Son of God is a metaphor unrelated to the officer’s death.

2-kings-7:17:4.summary: Moab trampled like a threshing floor shares only the trampling image.

2-kings-7:17:5.summary: Benjamin trampled in battle is unrelated.

2-kings-7:17:6.summary: The one who mocks “Where is the Lord your God?” becomes a trampling place, loosely like the scoffing officer.

2-kings-7:18:0.summary: “Is any word impossible with God?” with a promise at a set time loosely fits the timed prophecy fulfilled.
2-kings-7:18:0.why: God’s word fulfilled at the set time.

2-kings-7:18:2.summary: The king’s visit after his messenger is the setting where the prophecy was spoken; indirect link.

2-kings-7:20:0.summary: Moses’ unbelief bars him from entering the land; loosely like unbelief barring the officer from eating.

2-kings-7:20:1.summary: They could not enter because of unbelief; general theme fitting the officer.

2-kings-7:20:2.summary: “If you do not believe” loosely warns of consequences of unbelief.

2-kings-7:20:3.summary: Wrath falls as one might fill his belly; loosely like death just as food arrives.
2-kings-7:20:3.why: Judgment at the point of plenty.

2-kings-7:20:4.summary: One trusting in man “will not see when good things come”; loosely like the officer who misses the plenty.
2-kings-7:20:4.why: Missing the blessing through misplaced trust.

2-kings-7:20:5.summary: “Trust in His prophet, and you will prosper” contrasts the officer who doubted and died.

2-kings-7:3:4.summary: Jeremiah 27:13 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-7:3:4.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-7:3:4.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-8:1:1.summary: “He called a famine upon the land” matches “the Lord has called famine upon the land” nearly verbatim.
2-kings-8:1:1.why: Same idiom of God summoning famine.

2-kings-8:1:2.summary: The Greek has God bringing a “sword” upon the land, so the famine link the label assumes is absent.

2-kings-8:1:3.summary: A famine drives a family to sojourn in a foreign land, as Elisha sends the woman’s household abroad.

2-kings-8:1:4.summary: This is the Shunammite’s son whose growth and later death precede his revival referenced here.

2-kings-8:1:5.summary: “There was a famine in the land” and Abram goes abroad “to stay there”, like the woman’s sojourn.

2-kings-8:1:6.summary: God afflicts with scarcity of bread; general theme of famine as divine act.

2-kings-8:1:7.summary: A prophet announces drought for years; general parallel of prophetically announced famine.

2-kings-8:1:8.summary: Severe famine in Samaria under Elijah; general famine background.

2-kings-8:1:9.summary: “Seven years of famine” revealed by God beforehand matches Elisha’s announced seven-year famine.

2-kings-8:1:10.summary: Great famine in Elijah’s days; general theme of prophetic-era famine.

2-kings-8:1:11.summary: A multi-year famine sent for a cause; general famine parallel.

2-kings-8:1:12.summary: A prophet foretells a great famine, allowing preparation; loose parallel.

2-kings-8:1:13.summary: “There was a famine in the land” and Isaac goes to the Philistines’ king, like the woman’s sojourn among foreigners.

2-kings-8:1:14.summary: Years of famine offered as judgment; general theme only.

2-kings-8:1:15.summary: Days of vengeance in Luke has no specific link to this famine.

2-kings-8:1:16.summary: Fruitful land made barren for wickedness; general theme of God-sent barrenness.

2-kings-8:1:17.summary: End-time famines in various places share only the generic word famine.

2-kings-8:1:18.summary: “We have come to live as strangers… because the famine has become severe” matches sojourning to escape famine.

2-kings-8:1:19.summary: God reveals what He is about to do; general theme of famine foretold.

2-kings-8:1:20.summary: The repeated dream shows God will hasten to act; general theme of certain famine.

2-kings-8:1:21.summary: Covenant curse of failed harvests; general famine theme.

2-kings-8:1:22.summary: Heaven like iron and barren land; general theme of drought judgment.

2-kings-8:1:23.summary: God “summoning a sword” loosely parallels God calling famine, but the calamity differs.

2-kings-8:1:24.summary: Bronze heaven and dust for rain; general drought curse.

2-kings-8:2:0.summary: Providing for one’s household loosely fits the woman taking her household to safety.

2-kings-8:2:1.summary: David escapes “to the foreigners’ land” with households, as the woman lives “in the land of the foreigners”.

2-kings-8:2:2.summary: Lists “the five satrapies of the foreigners”, identifying the region, but no narrative link.

2-kings-8:3:0.summary: The same woman once said she needed no “matter for the king”; now she must appeal to the king.
2-kings-8:3:0.why: Shows the reversal in her circumstances.

2-kings-8:3:2.summary: Rulers are to vindicate the needy; general theme for her appeal.

2-kings-8:3:3.summary: A widow persistently appeals for justice; general parallel of a woman seeking redress.
2-kings-8:3:3.why: Woman seeking justice from a ruler.

2-kings-8:3:4.summary: Another woman “cried to” the king of Israel; he could not help her, whereas this woman is helped.
2-kings-8:3:4.why: Two women’s appeals to the king.

2-kings-8:3:5.summary: A woman appeals to the king for help; general royal-petition scene.

2-kings-8:3:6.summary: Rulers failing to judge the poor’s case; general theme of justice for the lowly.

2-kings-8:4:0.summary: Gehazi, “Elisha’s attendant”, the same man now recounting Elisha’s deeds (judged on shown text).

2-kings-8:4:1.summary: The floating axe head is one of the “great things Elisha has done” Gehazi could recount.

2-kings-8:4:2.summary: The lepers’ report at the gate has no evident link to the king’s talk with Gehazi.

2-kings-8:4:3.summary: The cursing of the jeering youths is among the great things Elisha did.

2-kings-8:4:4.summary: A ruler summons Paul to hear about faith; loosely like a king asking to hear of a prophet’s works.

2-kings-8:4:5.summary: The king who once sought Elisha’s head now asks about his great deeds; indirect link.

2-kings-8:4:6.summary: Elisha’s warnings to the king of Israel about Syria are among his great deeds.

2-kings-8:4:7.summary: The four lepers are not connected to Gehazi or the king’s inquiry in the shown text.

2-kings-8:4:8.summary: Elisha parting the Jordan with Elijah’s cloak is one of his great deeds.

2-kings-8:4:9.summary: The healed blind man’s retort shares no specific element.

2-kings-8:4:10.summary: Herod wanted to see a sign; loosely like a king curious about miracles.

2-kings-8:4:11.summary: Elisha’s prophecy of cheap flour is a recent great thing the king would know.

2-kings-8:4:12.summary: Fulfilment of Elisha’s food prophecy and the officer’s death are among his great things (shown portion).

2-kings-8:4:13.summary: Herod asks who this is about whom he hears such things; loose royal curiosity parallel.

2-kings-8:4:14.summary: Herod’s inquiry about the Child shares no specific element.

2-kings-8:4:15.summary: Elisha’s prophecy to the kings about the torrent bed is one of his great deeds.

2-kings-8:4:16.summary: Naaman’s cleansing “according to the word of Elisha” is a great deed Gehazi witnessed.

2-kings-8:4:17.summary: Elisha’s blinding and leading of the Syrians to Samaria is among his great deeds (shown portion).

2-kings-8:4:18.summary: The multiplied oil is one of the great things Elisha did.

2-kings-8:4:19.summary: Healing Jericho’s waters “according to the word Elisha spoke” is among his deeds.

2-kings-8:4:20.summary: Elisha’s promise of a son to the Shunammite begins the story Gehazi is recounting.

2-kings-8:4:21.summary: Gehazi and the Shunammite woman appear together, the same pair now before the king.

2-kings-8:5:1.summary: God’s detailed providence loosely explains the timely arrival of the woman.

2-kings-8:5:2.summary: Ruth “by chance” comes to Boaz’s field; loosely like the woman arriving just as she is spoken of.

2-kings-8:5:3.summary: Only the address “lord king” is shared.

2-kings-8:5:4.summary: The Greek proverb about the Lord’s righteous works and the impious has no link to the scene.

2-kings-8:5:5.summary: A providential reversal at court loosely parallels well-timed royal favor.

2-kings-8:5:6.summary: A divinely arranged meeting on the road loosely parallels the timely encounter (shown portion).

2-kings-8:5:7.summary: Another woman cried to the king in vain; contrasts with this woman’s successful plea.
2-kings-8:5:7.why: Two women crying to the king.

2-kings-8:5:8.summary: Haman’s gallows plot has no specific link.

2-kings-8:5:9.summary: “If God is for us” is too general to link specifically.

2-kings-8:5:10.summary: A praise psalm shares only the word “King”.

2-kings-8:5:11.summary: “Time and encounter” loosely relates to the coincidental timing here.

2-kings-8:5:12.summary: Elisha’s fame reaching kings loosely relates to the king hearing his deeds.

2-kings-8:6:0.summary: The Greek proverb on righteous deeds over sacrifice has no link to the restoration.

2-kings-8:6:1.summary: The king’s heart in God’s hand loosely explains the king’s favorable ruling.

2-kings-8:6:2.summary: David says “I will restore to you all the land”, a king restoring property, as here.

2-kings-8:6:3.summary: Eunuchs at Jezebel’s window share only the word eunuch.

2-kings-8:6:4.summary: A list of David’s officials has no specific link.

2-kings-8:6:5.summary: The law to “restore” lost property to its owner loosely parallels restoring her belongings.

2-kings-8:6:6.summary: Potiphar as Pharaoh’s eunuch shares only the word eunuch.

2-kings-8:6:7.summary: A territorial demand to “restore” land shares only the verb.

2-kings-8:7:1.summary: “The son of Ader, king of Syria” is the same king who besieged Samaria.

2-kings-8:7:0.summary: An earlier Ader seizes Damascus; only the name and city, not the same king.

2-kings-8:7:2.summary: “The son of Ader” besieging Samaria is the same Syrian royal title.

2-kings-8:7:3.summary: Prophets bow to Elisha; general recognition of Elisha’s status.

2-kings-8:7:4.summary: Shares only the title “man of God”.

2-kings-8:7:5.summary: Abram’s pursuit near Damascus shares only the place name.

2-kings-8:7:6.summary: A report that someone “has come here” to enemy territory; loose verbal parallel.
2-kings-8:7:6.why: Report of arrival in enemy city.

2-kings-8:7:7.summary: “The son of Ader… king of Syria, who lived in Damascus” names the same royal line and city.

2-kings-8:7:8.summary: “Have come here too” is incidental wording in an unrelated scene.

2-kings-8:7:9.summary: Syrian dealings with Israel involving Damascus; only the place link.

2-kings-8:7:10.summary: A man of God comes to a foreign shrine city; general parallel.

2-kings-8:7:11.summary: A king summons the “man of God”; loose link without the illness in the shown text.
2-kings-8:7:11.why: King’s dealing with a man of God.

2-kings-8:7:12.summary: Syrian courtiers know Elisha; loosely explains Syria’s report of his arrival.

2-kings-8:7:13.summary: Damascus as head of Aram; only the place.

2-kings-8:8:1.summary: God commands Hazael’s anointing as king of Syria; the same Hazael sent here.

2-kings-8:8:2.summary: Saul asks what gift to bring the man of God, like the gift sent with Hazael.
2-kings-8:8:2.why: Custom of gifts for a man of God.

2-kings-8:8:3.summary: A question about who is saved has no link to the king’s inquiry.

2-kings-8:8:4.summary: A Syrian king sends a man with lavish gifts toward Israel for healing, as with Hazael.
2-kings-8:8:4.why: Syrian king seeking healing via Israel.

2-kings-8:8:5.summary: A king sends a messenger with gifts to the man of God asking whether the sick one will live through illness.
2-kings-8:8:5.why: Close parallel royal inquiry about recovery.

2-kings-8:8:6.summary: Hazael’s sword is foretold as judgment on Israel; the same Hazael.

2-kings-8:8:7.summary: A sick king inquires of a foreign god and is told he will die; here a foreign king inquires of the Lord.

2-kings-8:8:8.summary: Kings seek to “inquire of the Lord” through Elisha, as the Syrian king does.
2-kings-8:8:8.why: Elisha as the Lord’s oracle for kings.

2-kings-8:8:9.summary: “What must I do to be saved?” concerns salvation, not physical recovery.

2-kings-8:9:0.summary: Paul on voluntary good deeds is unrelated.

2-kings-8:9:1.summary: “Your son David” is a deferential self-designation, loosely like “Your son, the son of Ader”.

2-kings-8:9:2.summary: A Syrian king sends lavish gifts with an envoy toward Israel’s prophet for healing, like Hazael’s load.

2-kings-8:9:3.summary: Naaman’s attendants on the prophet’s word; loose link to a Syrian envoy and Elisha.

2-kings-8:9:4.summary: The command to anoint Hazael king of Syria identifies the envoy standing before Elisha.

2-kings-8:9:5.summary: A king calls Elisha “father”; loosely like a king calling himself Elisha’s son.

2-kings-8:9:6.summary: “I am your slave and your son” is a submissive formula like “Your son… sent me”.

2-kings-8:9:7.summary: A king calls the ill Elisha “Father”; loose parallel of royal reverence and illness.

2-kings-8:10:0.summary: A sick king’s inquiry answered “you will surely die” uses the same verdict as Elisha’s.
2-kings-8:10:0.why: Same oracle of death to a sick king.

2-kings-8:10:1.summary: Shares only the formula “The Lord showed me”.

2-kings-8:10:2.summary: Shares only the formula “The Lord showed me”.

2-kings-8:10:3.summary: Speaking what the Lord “had shown me” shares the revelation formula.

2-kings-8:10:4.summary: Elijah tells a sick king “you will surely die” after an inquiry, as Elisha foresees here.
2-kings-8:10:4.why: Same death oracle on a royal inquiry.

2-kings-8:10:5.summary: The Lord reveals His plans to the prophets; general theme behind “the Lord has shown me”.

2-kings-8:10:6.summary: “The word the Lord showed me” shares the revelation formula addressed to a king.

2-kings-8:10:7.summary: “God has shown you” shares the idea of divine disclosure only.

2-kings-8:10:8.summary: Seeing the river of life shares only the verb “showed”.

2-kings-8:10:10.summary: Micaiah gives a king a favorable-sounding answer while doom awaits, like Elisha’s two-sided reply.

2-kings-8:10:11.summary: Shares only the formula “The Lord showed me”.

2-kings-8:10:12.summary: Shares only the formula “The Lord showed me”.

2-kings-8:10:13.summary: “Will surely be put to death” shares only the emphatic death formula.

2-kings-8:10:14.summary: Shares only the formula “The Lord showed me”.

2-kings-8:10:15.summary: “You shall surely die” shares the emphatic death formula only.

2-kings-8:11:0.summary: Jesus weeps over the city foreseeing its destruction, as Elisha weeps foreseeing Hazael’s ravages.

2-kings-8:11:1.summary: Call to lament with tears; general theme of weeping over disaster.

2-kings-8:11:2.summary: Tears over lawlessness; general theme of godly weeping.

2-kings-8:11:3.summary: Paul’s great sorrow for his people; general theme of grief for Israel.

2-kings-8:11:4.summary: The prophet’s anguish at hearing a cry of war loosely parallels Elisha’s grief over coming war.

2-kings-8:11:5.summary: Joseph’s weeping at reunion shares only the act of weeping.

2-kings-8:11:6.summary: Paul admonishing with tears is unrelated beyond tears.

2-kings-8:11:7.summary: Tears day and night because the people are crushed; general prophetic grief.

2-kings-8:11:8.summary: “Jesus wept” shares the image of a man of God weeping.

2-kings-8:11:9.summary: Paul serving with tears amid plots shares only tears.

2-kings-8:11:10.summary: Paul’s tears over enemies of the cross share only weeping.

2-kings-8:11:11.summary: “Pressed him until he was ashamed” matches the distinctive idiom of a fixed gaze “until shame”.

2-kings-8:11:12.summary: The prophet’s secret weeping for the crushed flock; general grief theme.

2-kings-8:11:13.summary: Jeremiah longs to weep for “the wounded of the daughter of My people”, as Elisha weeps for Israel’s slain.
2-kings-8:11:13.why: Prophet weeping over his people’s slaughter.

2-kings-8:12:0.summary: Samaria’s “nursing infants will be dashed” and “pregnant women… ripped open”, the same atrocities Elisha foresees.

2-kings-8:12:1.summary: “They will dash her infants to the ground” echoes the war atrocity Elisha foretells.

2-kings-8:12:2.summary: Menahem “ripped open the pregnant women”, the same atrocity foreseen of Hazael.

2-kings-8:12:4.summary: Hazael king of Syria attacks Gath and threatens Jerusalem, fulfilling his foreseen aggression.
