2-kings-8:12:5.summary: “They will dash their children” echoes the foretold dashing of infants.

2-kings-8:12:6.summary: Ammon “ripped open the pregnant women of the Gileadites”, the same atrocity language.

2-kings-8:12:7.summary: The king of Syria destroyed Israel’s troops, leaving them like dust, fulfilling the foreseen slaughter.

2-kings-8:12:8.summary: “Hazael struck them throughout Israel’s territory”, directly fulfilling Elisha’s foreboding.

2-kings-8:12:9.summary: Walled places vanish and a mother is dashed upon children; partial verbal overlap.

2-kings-8:12:10.summary: Attackers with no pity on young men or children; general atrocity theme.

2-kings-8:12:11.summary: Damascus sawed “pregnant women… in Gilead”, and fire is sent on “Hazael’s house”; names Hazael’s atrocities.

2-kings-8:12:12.summary: The Shunammite’s complaint to Elisha has no link to Hazael’s atrocities.

2-kings-8:12:13.summary: Seizing infants and dashing them against the rock shares the atrocity image in a different context.

2-kings-8:12:14.summary: Obadiah hiding prophets from Jezebel is unrelated to Hazael’s future evils.

2-kings-8:13:0.summary: Goliath’s “Am I like a dog” uses a dog self-reference, but defiantly rather than humbly.

2-kings-8:13:2.summary: “Who am I, your servant… a dead dog like me” is the same self-abasing formula Hazael uses.

2-kings-8:13:3.summary: People planning evil on their beds is not specifically linked.

2-kings-8:13:4.summary: “The Lord has shown me” appears in Elisha’s prior answer about the king’s death, continuing the revelation.

2-kings-8:13:5.summary: Rescue from the dog’s hand shares only the word dog.

2-kings-8:13:6.summary: Holy things to dogs shares only the word dog.

2-kings-8:13:7.summary: Dogs surrounding the sufferer shares only the word dog.

2-kings-8:13:8.summary: The heart is deep and unknowable; loosely fits Hazael’s denial of the evil within him.

2-kings-8:13:9.summary: Mute, greedy dogs as faithless watchmen share only the dog image.

2-kings-8:13:10.summary: “Watch out for the dogs” shares only the word dog.

2-kings-8:13:11.summary: Peter protests he will never do what is foretold; loosely like Hazael’s disclaimer.

2-kings-8:13:12.summary: Dogs and murderers outside the city share only the word dogs.

2-kings-8:14:1.summary: Judas seeks an opportunity to betray; loosely like Hazael’s deceit toward his master.

2-kings-8:14:2.summary: A servant returns to his master and answers evasively, loosely like Hazael’s partial report.

2-kings-8:15:1.summary: Micah speaks of evildoers plotting on their beds; Hazael’s smothering with the “machma” shares no bed imagery or person in these texts.
2-kings-8:15:1.why: Only a loose idea of scheming evil.

2-kings-8:15:2.summary: Zimri strikes the king, puts him to death and “reigned in his place,” the same regicide-and-succession pattern as Hazael.
2-kings-8:15:2.why: Shows the recurring pattern of usurpation by murder.

2-kings-8:15:3.summary: The psalm describes devising lawlessness upon a bed; nothing in Hazael’s act is linked beyond general wickedness.

2-kings-8:15:4.summary: Jeroboam is designated future king by the prophet Ahijah, loosely like Elisha’s prediction of Hazael; shown text is truncated.
2-kings-8:15:4.why: Prophetic designation of a usurping king.

2-kings-8:15:5.summary: Phakee strikes his king, puts him to death, and “became king in his place,” matching Hazael’s usurpation formula.
2-kings-8:15:5.why: Another instance of regicide and seizure of the throne.

2-kings-8:15:6.summary: Samuel anoints David as future king; only a general parallel to a prophetically designated successor.
2-kings-8:15:6.why: Contrasts a godly anointing with Hazael’s murderous accession.

2-kings-8:15:7.summary: The proverb “From the lawless comes wrongdoing” fits Hazael’s crime only generally.

2-kings-8:15:8.summary: The Lord commands Elijah to “Anoint Hazael as king of Syria,” the commission fulfilled when Hazael becomes king.
2-kings-8:15:8.why: Shows Hazael’s reign was foretold by God.

2-kings-8:15:9.summary: Hoshea conspires, strikes Phakee, puts him to death and “became king in his place,” the same usurpation formula.

2-kings-8:15:10.summary: Jehu kills King Joram, another violent end of a king, but no shared wording or succession formula is shown.

2-kings-8:15:11.summary: Baasha “put him to death” and reigned, the same pattern of killing the king and taking the throne.

2-kings-8:15:12.summary: Zimri’s death by fire is a royal death but differs from Hazael’s smothering of his master.
2-kings-8:15:12.why: Only general theme of violent royal deaths.

2-kings-8:15:13.summary: David refuses to “bring my hand against the Lord’s anointed,” contrasting with Hazael killing his own king.

2-kings-8:15:14.summary: Isaiah’s woe on afflicters and rejecters has no specific link to Hazael’s murder of the king.

2-kings-8:15:15.summary: Sellum conspires, kills the king and becomes king “in his place,” then is struck by Manaem: repeated regicide formula.
2-kings-8:15:15.why: Shows the cycle of assassination and usurpation.

2-kings-8:15:16.summary: David will not put Saul to death though given opportunity, unlike Hazael who kills his master.

2-kings-8:16:0.summary: The Saints text shows only Ahaziah dying by Elijah’s word; the synchronism of the two Jorams assumed by the label is absent.
2-kings-8:16:0.why: Greek-based wording lacks the dating link.

2-kings-8:16:1.summary: Records the accession of Jehoram son of Ahab, the Israelite king whose fifth year dates Joram of Judah’s reign.
2-kings-8:16:1.why: Clarifies the synchronized reigns of the two Jorams.

2-kings-8:16:2.summary: Jehoshaphat dies and “Joram his son reigned in his place,” the same Joram son of Jehoshaphat.
2-kings-8:16:2.why: Gives the succession from Jehoshaphat to Joram.

2-kings-8:18:11.summary: Ahaziah, Joram’s son by Athaliah, also “walked in the way of Ahab’s house” and did evil before the Lord.
2-kings-8:18:11.why: Shows the Ahab influence continuing to the next generation.

2-kings-8:18:0.summary: Names Athaliah, daughter of Omri’s house, the Ahab-family wife of Joram who mothered Ahaziah.

2-kings-8:18:1.summary: Sons of God taking wives from daughters of men has no specific link to Joram marrying Ahab’s daughter.

2-kings-8:18:2.summary: Elijah’s letter accuses Joram of walking “in the ways of Israel’s kings” as “Ahab’s house” did.
2-kings-8:18:2.why: Chronicles’ parallel judgment on the same king.

2-kings-8:18:3.summary: Jehoshaphat formed “a marriage alliance with Ahab’s house,” explaining how Ahab’s daughter became Joram’s wife.
2-kings-8:18:3.why: Explains the origin of the fatal marriage.

2-kings-8:18:4.summary: Solomon’s foreign wives turned his heart after other gods, a general parallel to a wife leading a king astray.

2-kings-8:18:5.summary: Jerusalem will be measured by “the weight of Ahab’s house,” showing Ahab’s house as a byword for judgment.
2-kings-8:18:5.why: Later consequence of following Ahab’s ways.

2-kings-8:18:6.summary: Jehu is commissioned to destroy “the house of Ahab,” the house whose way Joram followed.
2-kings-8:18:6.why: Shows the judgment on Ahab’s house.

2-kings-8:18:7.summary: Manasseh made groves “as Ahab king of Israel had done,” another Judean king imitating Ahab.
2-kings-8:18:7.why: Ahab as the model of apostasy.

2-kings-8:18:8.summary: Jehoram of Israel did evil before the Lord, the contemporary Israelite king whose way Joram followed.
2-kings-8:18:8.why: Describes the kings of Israel of that time.

2-kings-8:18:9.summary: Ahab did evil “as Jezebel his wife turned him aside,” a parallel of a wife leading a king to evil.

2-kings-8:18:10.summary: The law forbids intermarriage because it will “turn your son away,” loosely fitting Joram’s marriage to Ahab’s daughter.

2-kings-8:18:12.summary: Ahaziah of Israel “did evil before the Lord and walked in the way of Ahab,” the same formula applied to Joram.
2-kings-8:18:12.why: Defines what walking in Ahab’s way meant.

2-kings-8:18:13.summary: Jehoshaphat is rebuked for helping one hated by the Lord, the alliance that led to this marriage.
2-kings-8:18:13.why: Prophetic warning about the Ahab alliance.

2-kings-8:18:14.summary: Nehemiah forbids giving daughters to foreigners, citing Solomon turned aside by foreign women.

2-kings-8:18:16.summary: Micah condemns those keeping “all the works of Achaab’s house,” using Ahab’s house as a byword.
2-kings-8:18:16.why: Ahab’s house as a pattern of sin.

2-kings-8:19:0.summary: The Lord preserves part of the kingdom so that “My servant David may have a place before Me always”; the Greek lacks “lamp.”

2-kings-8:19:1.summary: God’s promise to raise David’s seed and establish his throne “for ever” underlies sparing Judah for David’s sake.

2-kings-8:19:2.summary: Jesus receives “the throne of His father David” forever, a later fulfilment of the Davidic promise.

2-kings-8:19:3.summary: God refuses to erase Ephraim despite anger, a general parallel of mercy restraining destruction.

2-kings-8:19:4.summary: God shields Jerusalem “because of David My servant,” the same motive for not destroying Judah.

2-kings-8:19:5.summary: God promises not to withdraw His mercy from David’s son, the covenant basis for sparing Judah.

2-kings-8:19:6.summary: The Emmanuel sign shown contains no reference to David, a lamp, or sparing Judah.
2-kings-8:19:6.why: No specific link in the shown text.

2-kings-8:19:8.summary: David is called “Israel’s lamp,” the same image as the lamp promised to David and his sons.

2-kings-8:19:9.summary: “For David’s sake” the Lord kept a remnant and preserved Jerusalem, the same reason Judah is spared.
2-kings-8:19:9.why: Parallel statement of the Davidic preservation.

2-kings-8:19:11.summary: God shields Jerusalem “for the sake of David My servant,” the same motive as in the source.

2-kings-8:20:0.summary: The Greek reading says “no king in Syria,” losing the Hebrew note on Edom’s lack of a king that the label assumes.
2-kings-8:20:0.why: Greek wording does not carry the Edom link.

2-kings-8:20:1.summary: The king of Edom marches with Judah and Israel, showing Edom under Judah before its revolt.

2-kings-8:20:2.summary: “Edom has remained broken away from beneath Judah’s hand,” the continuation of the same revolt.
2-kings-8:20:2.why: Completes the account of Edom’s revolt.

2-kings-8:20:3.summary: Moab’s king sacrificing his son has no link to Edom breaking away from Judah.

2-kings-8:20:4.summary: David garrisoned Idumea and “all the Idumeans became the king’s servants,” the subjection Edom now throws off.
2-kings-8:20:4.why: Shows the origin of Edom’s subjection.

2-kings-8:20:5.summary: Isaac foretells Esau will serve his brother but “loosen his yoke from your neck,” fulfilled in Edom’s revolt.

2-kings-8:21:0.summary: “All Israel fled, each to his tent” echoes the people fleeing “to their dwellings,” but the events differ.
2-kings-8:21:0.why: Stock phrase for a routed army.

2-kings-8:22:0.summary: Libnah given to Aaron’s sons is the same town as “Lobena,” which broke away from Judah.
2-kings-8:22:0.why: Identifies the priestly city that revolted.

2-kings-8:22:1.summary: The Assyrian king fights against “Lomna,” the same town Libnah, here again in Judah’s orbit.
2-kings-8:22:1.why: Later history of the same town.

2-kings-8:22:2.summary: Isaac’s word that Esau would “loosen his yoke” from his brother is fulfilled as Edom remains free of Judah.

2-kings-8:23:0.summary: Jotham’s regnal summary uses the same formula: “the rest … and everything he did—are these not written.”

2-kings-8:23:1.summary: Solomon’s closing formula “The rest … all he did … are these not written” matches Joram’s.

2-kings-8:23:2.summary: Chronicles gives the fuller account of Joram’s reign: high places, Elijah’s letter, and judgment (shown text truncated).
2-kings-8:23:2.why: Supplies the ‘rest of the acts’ of Joram.

2-kings-8:23:3.summary: Rehoboam’s summary uses the same “rest of … acts and all he did … not written” formula for a king of Judah.

2-kings-8:23:4.summary: Asa’s closing formula “The rest of Asa’s acts … are these not written” parallels Joram’s.

2-kings-8:23:5.summary: Azariah’s summary repeats “the rest … and all that he did … written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.”

2-kings-8:24:1.summary: Jehoshaphat buried “in David’s city” and “His son Joram reigned in his place” uses the same formula at Joram’s accession.
2-kings-8:24:1.why: Frames the beginning of Joram’s reign.

2-kings-8:24:5.summary: The genealogy lists “Joram his son, Ahaziah his son,” the same succession.
2-kings-8:24:5.why: Places the succession in David’s line.

2-kings-8:24:8.summary: David “lay down with his fathers and was buried in the City of David,” the same burial formula.

2-kings-8:24:0.summary: Ahaziah son of Joram appears visiting Joram of Israel, the same person but a later event.

2-kings-8:24:2.summary: Raiders took Joram’s sons so that “no son remained to him except Ahaziah,” explaining Ahaziah’s succession.

2-kings-8:24:3.summary: Joash of Israel capturing Amaziah has no link to Joram’s burial or Ahaziah’s accession.

2-kings-8:24:6.summary: Rehoboam “slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the City of David,” same formula.

2-kings-8:24:7.summary: Solomon slept with his fathers, was buried in the City of David, and his son reigned in his place.

2-kings-8:25:2.summary: Chronicles records Joram’s death and that “Ahaziah son of Joram king of Judah reigned,” the same accession.

2-kings-8:25:1.summary: The parallel synchronism of Joram son of Ahab with Judah’s king frames the dating of Ahaziah’s accession.

2-kings-8:26:1.summary: Athaliah, Ahaziah’s mother named here, later cries “Conspiracy!” and is executed (shown text truncated).

2-kings-8:26:2.summary: Ahaziah king of Judah rides out with Joram to meet Jehu, leading to his death (shown text truncated).
2-kings-8:26:2.why: Tells how Ahaziah’s one-year reign ended.

2-kings-8:26:3.summary: “Athaliah, Ahaziah’s mother” destroys the royal offspring after his death.
2-kings-8:26:3.why: Shows the aftermath of Ahaziah’s death.

2-kings-8:26:4.summary: Chronicles parallels Ahaziah’s war with Joram against Hazael and his downfall through Jehu.

2-kings-8:27:1.summary: Paul warns against being “unequally yoked,” a general application to Judah’s alliance with Ahab’s house.

2-kings-8:27:2.summary: A woman whose heart is nets is not tied in these texts to Ahab’s house or Ahaziah’s evil.

2-kings-8:27:3.summary: His father Joram also “walked in the way … as the house of Ahab had done” and did evil, nearly identical wording.
2-kings-8:27:3.why: Shows father and son followed Ahab’s way.

2-kings-8:28:1.summary: Jehoshaphat is rebuked for helping a sinner, as Ahaziah now joins Joram of Israel in war.
2-kings-8:28:1.why: Warning against alliances with Ahab’s house.

2-kings-8:28:2.summary: Israel and Judah’s kings again go up together to Remmath-gilead, the same battlefield against Syria.
2-kings-8:28:2.why: Earlier joint campaign at the same site.

2-kings-8:28:3.summary: Joram returns to Jezreel for wounds from fighting “Hazael king of Syria,” the same battle.

2-kings-8:28:4.summary: Ahab entices Jehoshaphat to Ramoth in Galaaditis, an earlier Israel–Judah campaign at the same city.
2-kings-8:28:4.why: Earlier pattern of joint war at Ramoth.

2-kings-8:28:5.summary: Joram of Israel enlists Jehoshaphat for war against Moab, a similar alliance but different enemy and place.

2-kings-8:28:6.summary: Israel’s king seeks to take Remmath-gilead “from the hand of the king of Syria,” the same contested city.

2-kings-8:28:7.summary: Jehoshaphat is endangered in the earlier Ramoth battle, only generally like this campaign.

2-kings-8:28:8.summary: Mentions “Hazael’s sword” and Jehu, foreshadowing the war with Hazael, but not this battle specifically.

2-kings-8:28:9.summary: Remath-gilead appears only as a district in Solomon’s administration.

2-kings-8:28:10.summary: Ramoth in Gilead is listed as a Gadite city of refuge, the same place only.

2-kings-8:28:11.summary: Elisha foresees Hazael’s cruelty against Israel’s sons, now beginning in his war with Joram.

2-kings-8:28:12.summary: Hazael’s seizing of the Syrian throne makes him the king Joram now fights.

2-kings-8:29:0.summary: Repeats Joram being treated in Jezreel for wounds from Hazael and Ahaziah going down to see him.

2-kings-8:29:2.summary: The immediately preceding verse tells of Joram being struck at Remmoth-gilead by the Syrians.
2-kings-8:29:2.why: Gives the cause of Joram’s wounds.

2-kings-8:29:3.summary: Ahab was also wounded fighting Syria at Ramoth-gilead; now his son Joram is wounded there too.
2-kings-8:29:3.why: Father and son wounded at the same battlefield.

2-kings-8:19:10.summary: Jeremiah 33:25–26 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-8:19:10.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-8:19:10.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-8:24:4.summary: 1 Kings 14:20 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-8:24:4.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-8:24:4.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-9:1:1.summary: Elisha tells Gehazi “Fasten your belt, take my staff in your hand,” the same commissioning formula.
2-kings-9:1:1.why: Elisha’s typical charge to a messenger.

2-kings-9:1:0.summary: Samuel takes “the flask of oil” and anoints Saul as ruler, matching the flask of oil for Jehu.
2-kings-9:1:0.why: Prophet anointing a king with a flask.

2-kings-9:1:2.summary: Gives the setting: Israel’s war at Remmoth-gilead and Joram wounded in Jezreel.
2-kings-9:1:2.why: Explains why the prophet goes there.

2-kings-9:1:3.summary: God tells Samuel, “Fill your horn with oil and come,” sending a prophet to anoint a replacement king.
2-kings-9:1:3.why: Prophet sent with oil to anoint a new king.

2-kings-9:1:4.summary: Zadok anoints Solomon with the horn of oil, a general royal anointing parallel.

2-kings-9:1:5.summary: Peter’s “gird up the loins of your mind” only echoes the call to fasten one’s belt metaphorically.

2-kings-9:1:6.summary: Moses’ call to hear the ordinances has no link to Elisha sending a prophet with oil.

2-kings-9:1:7.summary: “Let your loins be girded” echoes readiness for a task only generally.

2-kings-9:1:8.summary: Shows the “sons of the prophets” associated with Elisha, but no link to this mission.

2-kings-9:1:9.summary: Remmath-gilead appears as the target of an earlier campaign, only the same place.

2-kings-9:1:10.summary: A son of the prophets acting by the Lord’s word against Ahab’s house is a loose parallel.

2-kings-9:1:11.summary: Ahab was lured to fall at Remmath-gilead; now Ahab’s house meets its end from the same place.
2-kings-9:1:11.why: Ironic link of place and judgment.

2-kings-9:1:12.summary: The sons of the prophets with Elisha appear, but in an unrelated building episode.

2-kings-9:1:13.summary: Elijah “bound up his waist” and ran to Jezreel, a loose echo of girding for a mission.

2-kings-9:1:14.summary: “Gird your waist, rise and tell them” echoes a prophetic commission only generally.

2-kings-9:1:15.summary: Baal-peor’s judgment has no specific link to Elisha’s instruction.

2-kings-9:1:16.summary: A widow of the sons of the prophets appeals to Elisha; only the prophetic guild is shared.

2-kings-9:2:1.summary: Same full name “Jehu son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi,” who conspires against Joram.
2-kings-9:2:1.why: Identifies Jehu and his next act.

2-kings-9:2:2.summary: Jehu comes out to his fellow officers after the secret anointing, continuing the scene.
2-kings-9:2:2.why: Shows the aftermath of the private meeting.

2-kings-9:2:3.summary: God commands Elijah, “Anoint Jehu son of Nimshi as king over Israel,” the commission now carried out.

2-kings-9:2:4.summary: Micaiah’s “inner chamber within an inner chamber” matches the distinctive “chamber within a chamber.”
2-kings-9:2:4.why: Same unusual phrase for a hidden room.

2-kings-9:2:5.summary: The son of Ader flees “into the inner chamber,” sharing only the idea of an inner room.

2-kings-9:2:6.summary: Names “Jehu son of Nimshi,” the same man, driving furiously toward Jezreel.
2-kings-9:2:6.why: Same person later in the story.

2-kings-9:3:0.summary: “Anoint Jehu son of Nimshi as king over Israel” is the command this anointing fulfils.
2-kings-9:3:0.why: Shows fulfilment of God’s word to Elijah.

2-kings-9:3:1.summary: God tells Samuel to anoint a man “as ruler over My people Israel,” a general anointing parallel.

2-kings-9:3:2.summary: Samuel fears Saul will kill him over a secret anointing, loosely like the instruction to flee.
2-kings-9:3:2.why: Danger of anointing a rival king.

2-kings-9:3:3.summary: “He humbles this one and raises that one” expresses God’s control of rulers generally.

2-kings-9:3:4.summary: Moses “poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron’s head, anointed him,” the same rite of pouring oil on the head.

2-kings-9:3:5.summary: Elisha reveals Hazael will reign over Syria, a parallel prophetic designation of a king.

2-kings-9:3:6.summary: God gives the earth to whomever He chooses, a general statement of divine appointment.

2-kings-9:3:7.summary: The angel’s command to “flee to Egypt” shares only the verb flee.

2-kings-9:3:8.summary: Nebuchadnezzar’s troubled dream has no connection to Jehu’s anointing.

2-kings-9:3:9.summary: Authority “given you from above” relates only generally to God appointing kings.

2-kings-9:3:10.summary: Calls “Jehu son of Namessi, the Lord’s anointed,” confirming the anointing commanded here.
2-kings-9:3:10.why: Confirms Jehu as the Lord’s anointed.

2-kings-9:3:12.summary: “Take the anointing oil, pour it on his head, and anoint him” closely matches the instruction.

2-kings-9:3:14.summary: “The Lord anointed you king over Israel” matches the proclamation for Jehu.

2-kings-9:3:15.summary: Samuel anoints David with the horn of oil “among his brothers,” a prophet anointing a replacement king.
2-kings-9:3:15.why: Parallel prophetic anointing of a new king.

2-kings-9:3:16.summary: “The Lord sent me to anoint you king over Israel” echoes “I have anointed you king over Israel.”

2-kings-9:3:17.summary: “Through me kings reign” states generally that rule comes from divine wisdom.

2-kings-9:3:18.summary: Being sent as sheep among wolves has no specific link to anointing Jehu and fleeing.

2-kings-9:3:19.summary: Elijah “anointed kings for retribution,” recalling the commission to anoint Jehu to punish Ahab’s house.

2-kings-9:5:0.summary: Ehud’s “I have a secret word for you, O king” closely echoes “I have a word for you, commander.”
2-kings-9:5:0.why: Similar private message before a coup.

2-kings-9:6:1.summary: Elisha’s instruction to pour oil and say “I have anointed you king over Israel” is carried out here.

2-kings-9:6:2.summary: Jehu is called “the Lord’s anointed” against Ahab’s house, referring to this anointing.

2-kings-9:6:5.summary: The Lord of heaven has authority over all and does what He wills, generally relevant to appointing kings.

2-kings-9:6:6.summary: “I was appointed king by Him” relates generally to a king appointed by God.

2-kings-9:6:7.summary: The shown half-verse about goings-out and settings lacks the idea of God raising kings.

2-kings-9:6:8.summary: God “transfers kings and appoints them,” a general statement fitting Jehu’s anointing.

2-kings-9:6:9.summary: Nebuchadnezzar’s humiliation and loss of kingdom has no specific link to Jehu’s anointing.

2-kings-9:6:10.summary: “Anoint him king over Israel” describes Solomon’s anointing in the same terms.

2-kings-9:6:11.summary: Solomon calls Israel “Thy people,” echoing “the Lord’s people” only generally.

2-kings-9:6:12.summary: Cyrus is God’s “anointed” instrument against kings, a general parallel to Jehu.
2-kings-9:6:12.why: God anointing an agent of judgment.

2-kings-9:6:13.summary: God “made you leader over My people Israel” yet the king sinned, foreshadowing Jehu’s later failures.

2-kings-9:6:14.summary: A private report to a tribune has no meaningful link to Jehu’s anointing.

2-kings-9:6:15.summary: The Lord set Solomon “on Israel’s throne” to do judgment, a general royal appointment parallel.

2-kings-9:7:0.summary: Jezebel arranges Naboth’s death, one of her bloody crimes, though not against prophets.
2-kings-9:7:0.why: Example of Jezebel’s shedding of blood.

2-kings-9:7:1.summary: God “avenges the blood of His sons,” matching the charge to avenge the blood of His slaves.
2-kings-9:7:1.why: God as avenger of His servants’ blood.

2-kings-9:7:2.summary: “Jezebel was striking the Lord’s prophets,” the very bloodshed Jehu is to avenge.

2-kings-9:7:3.summary: “In the day of vengeance I will repay” expresses divine retribution generally.

2-kings-9:7:4.summary: Elijah’s oracle to “destroy from Ahab every male” is the sentence Jehu is now commissioned to execute.

2-kings-9:7:5.summary: Jehu has Jezebel thrown down and eaten, fulfilling the vengeance on her (shown text truncated).

2-kings-9:7:6.summary: Jezebel turned Ahab to evil, explaining her role but not the prophets’ blood.

2-kings-9:7:7.summary: “The God of vengeance is the Lord” against those who killed His people, a general theme.

2-kings-9:7:8.summary: “Vengeance belongs to Me; I will repay” expresses the general principle behind Jehu’s commission.

2-kings-9:7:9.summary: Martyrs ask God to “avenge our blood,” the same plea answered for the slain prophets.

2-kings-9:7:10.summary: “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay” gives the general principle of God’s vengeance.

2-kings-9:7:11.summary: God “avenged the blood of His slaves from her hand,” closely echoing avenging His slaves’ blood at Jezebel’s hand.

2-kings-9:7:12.summary: Jesus speaks of righteous blood, including murdered prophets, coming upon the guilty; general theme.

2-kings-9:7:13.summary: Prophets rejoice because God judged their case against the harlot city, a general vengeance theme.

2-kings-9:7:14.summary: God brings justice for His chosen ones who cry to Him, a general theme of vindication.

2-kings-9:7:15.summary: The ruler as “an avenger who brings wrath” on evildoers fits Jehu’s role only generally.

2-kings-9:8:0.summary: David vows to leave none “who urinates against a wall,” the same idiom for every male.

2-kings-9:8:1.summary: The Greek reading speaks of servants “weakened … exhausted,” lacking the “confined and abandoned” phrase the label assumes.
2-kings-9:8:1.why: Greek wording drops the shared idiom.

2-kings-9:8:2.summary: Israel is “hemmed in … and abandoned,” partly echoing “confined and abandoned,” in a different context.

2-kings-9:8:3.summary: Jehu strikes all who remained of Ahab in Samaria, fulfilling this sentence.

2-kings-9:8:5.summary: The same judgment, “destroy from Jeroboam’s house every male who urinates against a wall,” was pronounced on Jeroboam.

2-kings-9:9:3.summary: Baasha’s house is made “like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat,” the precedent invoked for Ahab.
2-kings-9:9:3.why: Explains the comparison to Baasha’s house.

2-kings-9:9:0.summary: Baasha destroyed Jeroboam’s house according to Ahijah’s word, the fate cited as the pattern.

2-kings-9:9:2.summary: The prophecy to destroy Jeroboam’s house and leave its dead to dogs and birds is the model for Ahab’s house.
2-kings-9:9:2.why: Shows the precedent for Ahab’s fate.

2-kings-9:9:4.summary: Zimri strikes down “all Baasha’s house” by the Lord’s word, the fate cited for Ahab’s house.

2-kings-9:10:0.summary: Elijah’s word that “The dogs will devour her at Jezreel’s outer wall” is repeated here.

2-kings-9:10:2.summary: Elisha’s instruction “open the door and flee” is exactly what the young prophet does.

2-kings-9:10:3.summary: Jehoiakim’s dishonourable “donkey’s burial” parallels Jezebel lying unburied only in theme.

2-kings-9:10:4.summary: Ehud escapes after delivering his secret word, loosely like the prophet’s flight.
2-kings-9:10:4.why: Messenger’s escape after a fateful act.

2-kings-9:11:0.summary: Prophets are classed with “every person raging,” loosely like calling the prophet “deranged.”

2-kings-9:11:1.summary: Hosea speaks of “the deranged prophet,” the same scornful label the officers use.

2-kings-9:11:2.summary: Festus calls Paul “mad,” a later example of God’s messenger dismissed as insane.

2-kings-9:11:3.summary: Jesus is said to be “mad,” another messenger of God scorned as insane.

2-kings-9:11:4.summary: The Saints text lacks any “Is there peace?” greeting; only a meeting is described.
2-kings-9:11:4.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

2-kings-9:11:5.summary: Joram’s “Is there peace, Jehu?” repeats the question that runs through this narrative.
2-kings-9:11:5.why: Recurring question of peace in Jehu’s coup.

2-kings-9:11:6.summary: The rider asks Jehu, “Is there peace?” continuing the motif.

2-kings-9:11:7.summary: Joram sends a rider to ask “Is there peace?” in the same narrative.

2-kings-9:11:8.summary: Jesus’ family say “He is out of His mind,” a general parallel of a messenger thought mad.

2-kings-9:11:9.summary: “Is there peace with you?” uses the same stock greeting in an unrelated scene.

2-kings-9:11:10.summary: Paul being “beside ourselves” for God loosely relates to prophets seen as deranged.

2-kings-9:11:11.summary: Truth taken away and minds turned from understanding has no specific link to the deranged-prophet remark.

2-kings-9:11:12.summary: Apostles “foolish for Christ’s sake” loosely parallels prophets dismissed as fools.

2-kings-9:11:13.summary: Paul is called a “babbler,” akin to dismissing the prophet’s “idle chatter.”

2-kings-9:13:0.summary: At Solomon’s anointing “He sounded the horn” and people acclaimed the king, as with Jehu.

2-kings-9:13:1.summary: “Sound the horn and say, ‘Long live King Solomon!’” parallels the horn and “Jehu has become king!”

2-kings-9:13:2.summary: Crowds spread their garments before Jesus, as the officers placed their garments beneath Jehu.
2-kings-9:13:2.why: Garments spread to honour a king.

2-kings-9:13:3.summary: Trumpets and “the sound of a horn trumpet” acclaim the Lord as King, a general echo.

2-kings-9:13:4.summary: At the horn’s sound people are to say “King Absalom has begun to reign,” a usurper’s acclamation like Jehu’s.
2-kings-9:13:4.why: Horn signals a rival king’s proclamation.

2-kings-9:13:5.summary: God ascends “with the sound of a trumpet” as King, a general acclamation image.

2-kings-9:13:6.summary: Garments are placed and spread on the road for Jesus, echoing garments laid beneath Jehu as king.
2-kings-9:13:6.why: Garments spread to honour a king.

2-kings-9:14:1.summary: Israel’s claim to Remmath-gilead from Syria’s king provides background to guarding it against Hazael.

2-kings-9:14:2.summary: Jezebel taunts Jehu as “Zimri, murderer of his master,” naming the conspiracy begun here.
2-kings-9:14:2.why: Shows how Jehu’s conspiracy was viewed.

2-kings-9:14:3.summary: Jehu admits, “I conspired against my master and killed him,” referring to this conspiracy against Joram.
2-kings-9:14:3.why: Jehu’s own account of the plot.

2-kings-9:14:4.summary: Baasha strikes King Nadab while Israel besieges a city, a general parallel of a military coup.

2-kings-9:14:5.summary: Introduces Hazael, the Syrian king Israel was guarding against, and his own seizure of power (truncated).

2-kings-9:14:6.summary: Hoshea “formed a conspiracy” against his king, a similar act but a different event.

2-kings-9:14:7.summary: An army commander is made king in the camp after a conspiracy, as Jehu, commander at Ramoth, is acclaimed.
2-kings-9:14:7.why: Parallel military coup from the camp.

2-kings-9:14:8.summary: Jehu son of Hanani is a different Jehu, a prophet, not the conspirator son of Nimshi.

2-kings-9:14:9.summary: Zimri “conspired against him,” a parallel act of conspiracy by a military officer.

2-kings-9:15:1.summary: Joram returned to Jezrael to be healed of wounds from fighting Hazael king of Syria, the same report.
2-kings-9:15:1.why: Chronicles parallel of the same situation.

2-kings-9:15:2.summary: David left none alive so they could “not report” him, loosely like Jehu’s order that none escape to report.

2-kings-9:16:1.summary: Chronicles parallels Joram’s healing in Jezrael and Ahaziah going down to see him, then meeting Jehu.

2-kings-9:17:0.summary: Elders ask Samuel, “Do you enter in peace?” a similar anxious question about an arrival.
2-kings-9:17:0.why: Fearful greeting of an approaching figure.

2-kings-9:17:1.summary: A watcher reports approaching riders, a general watchman-scene parallel.

2-kings-9:17:2.summary: A watchman goes up on the gate roof and sees a man approaching while the king waits, a closely similar scene.
2-kings-9:17:2.why: Parallel watchman scene reporting to a king.

2-kings-9:17:3.summary: Blind, mute dogs that doze have no specific link to Jezreel’s lookout spotting Jehu.
2-kings-9:17:3.why: No real connection in shown text.

2-kings-9:17:4.summary: Greeting a house with “Peace” relates only loosely to Joram’s question “Is there peace?”

2-kings-9:17:5.summary: The king of Israel sends “two horse riders” to see, similar to sending a rider to investigate.

2-kings-9:17:6.summary: A second horse rider asks, “Is there peace?” continuing the same scene.

2-kings-9:17:7.summary: Paul’s farewell warning to elders shares nothing specific with the lookout scene in the shown text.

2-kings-9:17:8.summary: Ezekiel’s watchman who sees the sword coming is a general watchman image (shown text truncated).

2-kings-9:17:10.summary: Adonijah’s claim that the kingdom was his has no link to the Jezreel lookout.

2-kings-9:17:11.summary: Guards set on Jerusalem’s walls are a general watchman image.

2-kings-9:17:12.summary: A watchman raises his eyes, sees people coming on the road, and reports to the king, as in Jezreel.

2-kings-9:17:13.summary: A watchman asked to “guard the battlements” is only a general watch image.

2-kings-9:18:0.summary: Joram asks “Is there peace, Jehu?” and Jehu answers “What peace?” continuing the same exchange.

2-kings-9:18:2.summary: The wicked “do not know the way of peace,” loosely relating to Jehu’s denial of peace.

2-kings-9:18:3.summary: “The way of peace they did not know” echoes the peace theme only generally.

2-kings-9:18:4.summary: The Greek reading says “no rejoicing for the ungodly,” losing the “no peace” wording the label assumes.
2-kings-9:18:4.why: Greek wording lacks the peace link.
2-kings-9:18:4.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-9:18:5.summary: God has “removed My peace from this people,” loosely matching Jehu’s refusal of peace.

2-kings-9:20:0.summary: The watchman recognizes Ahimaaz by his running, as the lookout recognizes Jehu by his driving.
2-kings-9:20:0.why: Identifying a man by his manner of movement.

2-kings-9:20:1.summary: Jehu in his chariot shows his zeal, matching his driving temperament only generally.

2-kings-9:20:2.summary: Foretells Jehu’s sword against the guilty, background to his headlong approach.

2-kings-9:20:3.summary: A smith blowing coals has no link to Jehu’s driving.

2-kings-9:20:4.summary: Doing things with all your strength has no specific tie to Jehu’s furious driving.

2-kings-9:20:5.summary: God bringing nations down in fury has no specific link to Jehu’s driving.

2-kings-9:20:6.summary: The swift Chaldean nation has no specific link to Jehu’s deranged driving.

2-kings-9:20:7.summary: A king going out in strong anger in Daniel has no specific link to Jehu.

2-kings-9:21:0.summary: Joram goes out with Ahaziah to Jehu, the parallel noting Ahaziah’s downfall came from God.

2-kings-9:21:1.summary: Naboth the Jezreelite’s vineyard by Ahab’s palace is the very “portion of Naboth” where they meet Jehu.
2-kings-9:21:1.why: Recalls the crime tied to this place.

2-kings-9:21:3.summary: Micah’s noise of chariots at Lachish shares only the word chariots.

2-kings-9:21:4.summary: Moses sending messengers to Edom has no link to Joram going out to Jehu.

2-kings-9:21:5.summary: Ahab takes Naboth’s vineyard and Elijah pronounces judgment, explaining the significance of meeting there.
2-kings-9:21:5.why: Shows the crime about to be avenged.

2-kings-9:21:6.summary: Ahab asking who will engage in battle shares no wording or event with yoking a chariot.

2-kings-9:22:0.summary: Nineveh is a prostitute and “mistress of potions,” pairing harlotry and sorcery as Jehu does of Jezebel.
2-kings-9:22:0.why: Same pairing of harlotry and sorcery.

2-kings-9:22:1.summary: Ahab’s house “caused prostitution,” the same spiritual-harlotry charge Jehu makes against Jezebel.
2-kings-9:22:1.why: Ahab’s house as source of harlotry.

2-kings-9:22:2.summary: Ahab marries Jezebel and serves Baal, the idolatry behind “the prostitutions of Jezebel.”

2-kings-9:22:3.summary: Jezebel kills the Lord’s prophets, another of her crimes but not her prostitutions or sorceries.

2-kings-9:22:5.summary: Babylon deceived nations “by thy sorcery,” a general echo of sorcery charges.
2-kings-9:22:5.why: Sorcery as mark of wicked power.

2-kings-9:22:6.summary: Peace is offered to the near and far but the unjust cannot rest, loosely linked to “What peace?”

2-kings-9:22:7.summary: “The woman Jezebel” leads into sexual immorality and idolatry, drawing on Jezebel’s prostitutions.
2-kings-9:22:7.why: Jezebel as a type in Revelation.

2-kings-9:22:8.summary: Jezebel threatens Elijah’s life, showing her character but not her harlotries or sorceries.

2-kings-9:22:9.summary: Babylon’s sexual immorality with kings is a general harlotry image.

2-kings-9:22:10.summary: Jezebel’s forged letter against Naboth shows her wickedness, not her prostitutions or sorceries.

2-kings-9:22:11.summary: Babylon “the mother of prostitutes” echoes the harlot image only generally.

2-kings-9:22:12.summary: Hundreds of Baal and grove prophets “eat at Jezebel’s table,” showing the idolatry she sponsored.

2-kings-9:22:13.summary: The rider’s “Is there peace?” and Jehu’s “What have you to do with peace?” lead into this exchange.

2-kings-9:23:0.summary: Athaliah cries “Conspiracy!” as Joram cries “Deceit,” both royals realizing a coup too late.

2-kings-9:23:1.summary: Athaliah cries “You are attacking!” when overthrown, a general parallel to Joram’s cry.

2-kings-9:24:0.summary: Ahab was struck by an arrow and told his charioteer to “Turn your hands”; his son Joram turns his hands and is shot.
2-kings-9:24:0.why: Father and son both slain by arrows.

2-kings-9:24:1.summary: No wisdom or counsel with the impious has no specific link to Jehu shooting Joram.

2-kings-9:24:2.summary: The wicked are wounded by a bow and “an arrow pass through his body,” matching the arrow through Joram’s heart.
2-kings-9:24:2.why: Wisdom image of the wicked’s end.

2-kings-9:24:3.summary: God seizing those who forget Him with “no rescuer” fits Joram’s fate only generally.

2-kings-9:24:4.summary: Sudden destruction when they say “Peace and security” loosely fits Joram’s question of peace before death.

2-kings-9:24:5.summary: The ungodly will not prolong his days, a general principle applied to Joram.

2-kings-9:25:0.summary: Elijah’s oracle against Ahab over Naboth’s blood is the very oracle Jehu recalls.

2-kings-9:25:1.summary: Isaiah’s vision against Babylon shares only the idea of a prophetic pronouncement.

2-kings-9:25:2.summary: Continues Elijah’s oracle against Ahab’s house and Ahab’s repentance, which delayed the judgment to his son (truncated).
2-kings-9:25:2.why: Explains why Joram bears the judgment.

2-kings-9:25:3.summary: Nahum’s oracle on Nineveh shares only the word “oracle.”

2-kings-9:25:4.summary: Jesus’ light burden shares no wording with the source’s “oracle.”

2-kings-9:25:5.summary: Jeremiah’s wordplay on “the Lord’s burden” does not match the source’s “oracle” wording.
2-kings-9:25:5.why: English-label link lost in this reading.

2-kings-9:25:6.summary: Malachi’s heading “A pronouncement” is only a generic prophetic formula.

2-kings-9:26:1.summary: The law that sons shall not die for fathers contrasts with Joram dying for Ahab’s guilt.
2-kings-9:26:1.why: Raises the question of inherited judgment.

2-kings-9:26:2.summary: God repays “the sins of fathers upon children,” loosely fitting Ahab’s judgment on his son.

2-kings-9:26:3.summary: Amaziah spares the sons per the law that each dies for his own sin, contrasting with this judgment.

2-kings-9:26:4.summary: A righteous son does not bear his father’s injustice, a general contrast with Joram’s fate.

2-kings-9:26:5.summary: Joash is killed “because of the blood of the son” of Jehoiada, another king slain to avenge innocent blood.

2-kings-9:26:6.summary: God repays “the sins of fathers upon children,” loosely fitting the judgment on Ahab’s son.

2-kings-9:27:0.summary: Lists “Magedon” and “Jeblaam,” the Megiddo and Ibleam where Ahaziah was struck and died.

2-kings-9:27:1.summary: Megiddo is listed among Manasseh’s towns, the same place only.

2-kings-9:27:2.summary: Chronicles gives a differing account of Ahaziah being caught and killed by Jehu.

2-kings-9:27:3.summary: Megiddo appears in Solomon’s district list, the same place only.

2-kings-9:27:4.summary: Josiah also dies at Mageddo and is carried to Jerusalem for burial in David’s city.
2-kings-9:27:4.why: Another Judean king dying at Megiddo.

2-kings-9:27:5.summary: “Come out from their midst and be separated” loosely applies to Ahaziah’s fatal association with Ahab’s house.
2-kings-9:27:5.why: Danger of association with the wicked.

2-kings-9:27:6.summary: Kings fought “by Megiddo’s water,” the same place in another battle.

2-kings-9:27:7.summary: The Saints text transliterates “Baithaggan,” so the garden link to Ahab’s vegetable garden is not carried.
2-kings-9:27:7.why: Greek-based reading loses the garden link.

2-kings-9:27:8.summary: Ahaziah went down to Jezreel to see the wounded Joram, explaining why he was there to flee.

2-kings-9:27:9.summary: “Separate yourselves … lest you perish with them” loosely applies to Ahaziah perishing with Ahab’s house.

2-kings-9:27:10.summary: Walking with fools brings harm, a general lesson from Ahaziah’s alliance.

2-kings-9:28:1.summary: Josiah’s servants bring him by chariot to Jerusalem for burial, closely parallel to Ahaziah’s burial.

2-kings-9:28:0.summary: Josiah is carried dead to Jerusalem and “buried … in David’s city,” matching Ahaziah’s return and burial.

2-kings-9:28:2.summary: Amaziah, killed away from Jerusalem, is carried back and buried “in David’s city.”
2-kings-9:28:2.why: Parallel return and burial of a slain king.

2-kings-9:28:3.summary: Joash, struck down by conspirators, is buried “in the city of David,” the same burial formula.

2-kings-9:28:4.summary: Josiah burning priests’ bones and returning to Jerusalem has no link to Ahaziah’s burial.

2-kings-9:28:5.summary: Amaziah is carried and buried “with his fathers in David’s city,” the same pattern.

2-kings-9:29:0.summary: Describes the death of Ahaziah’s father Joram, only background to Ahaziah’s accession.

2-kings-9:29:2.summary: Gives another synchronism of Judah’s king with Joram son of Ahab, relevant to dating Ahaziah’s reign.

2-kings-9:29:3.summary: Chronicles records Ahaziah son of Joram becoming king of Judah.

2-kings-9:30:0.summary: “Paint your eyes with antimony” and adorn yourself, the same cosmetic image, here futile.

2-kings-9:30:1.summary: The harlot sisters “painted your eyes with antimony and adorned yourself,” closely matching Jezebel.

2-kings-9:30:2.summary: Ezekiel’s mourning instructions about hair and footwear do not connect to Jezebel’s adornment.

2-kings-9:30:3.summary: The Lord removes women’s ornaments in judgment, a general parallel to Jezebel’s doomed adornment (truncated).

2-kings-9:30:4.summary: Women should adorn with modesty, not braids and gold, a general contrast to Jezebel’s adornment.

2-kings-9:30:5.summary: Adornment should not be outward braiding and gold, contrasting generally with Jezebel.

2-kings-9:30:6.summary: Jezebel’s defiant threat to Elijah shows the same proud character facing Jehu.

2-kings-9:32:0.summary: Two royal eunuchs turn against their sovereign, loosely like the two eunuchs who betray Jezebel.

2-kings-9:32:1.summary: Winning over Herod’s chamberlain shares only a court official, not the event.

2-kings-9:32:2.summary: “Had the Lord not been among us” does not echo Jehu’s “Who are you?” in this reading.

2-kings-9:32:3.summary: Rehoboam fortifying cities with shields has no link to Jehu calling from below the window.

2-kings-9:32:4.summary: Amasai declares allegiance to David, loosely like servants siding with Jehu.
2-kings-9:32:4.why: Choosing sides with a rising king.

2-kings-9:32:5.summary: The seven eunuchs of Artaxerxes share only the word eunuch.

2-kings-9:32:6.summary: Moses’ “Whoever is for the Lord, come to me!” loosely echoes Jehu’s call for supporters.

2-kings-9:32:7.summary: Trust in the Lord as helper has no specific link to Jehu’s call to the eunuchs.

2-kings-9:32:8.summary: Esther following a eunuch’s instructions shares only the word eunuch.

2-kings-9:33:0.summary: The female enemy “will become a trampling place,” loosely paralleling Jezebel trampled.

2-kings-9:33:1.summary: Trampling the Son of God is a spiritual metaphor unrelated to Jezebel’s death.

2-kings-9:33:2.summary: The righteous “will trample the lawless,” a general image of the wicked trampled.

2-kings-9:33:3.summary: Recalls Jezebel’s plot against Naboth, the crime now repaid, but not her death.

2-kings-9:33:4.summary: God promises to repay Naboth’s blood, loosely tied to Jezebel’s blood spattering.

2-kings-9:33:5.summary: Moab trampled like a threshing floor, a general image of trampling in judgment.

2-kings-9:33:6.summary: “The people trampled him … and he died” shares the death by trampling, in an unrelated event.

2-kings-9:33:7.summary: The Lord treading the winepress for Judah is a general trampling image.

2-kings-9:33:8.summary: Tasteless salt trampled underfoot shares only the verb trample.

2-kings-9:34:0.summary: Jezebel is “daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians,” explaining Jehu’s “she is a king’s daughter.”

2-kings-9:34:1.summary: Jezebel turned Ahab to evil, explaining why she is called cursed, but no shared wording.

2-kings-9:34:2.summary: The “cursed” sent into eternal fire share only the word cursed.

2-kings-9:34:3.summary: The Greek reading leaves a name “as a surfeit,” not a curse, so the cursed-woman link is lost.
2-kings-9:34:3.why: Greek wording lacks the curse link.

2-kings-9:34:4.summary: The king and Haman drink while the city is troubled, loosely like Jehu eating after a killing.

2-kings-9:34:5.summary: “The name of the impious is extinguished,” a general principle fitting Jezebel’s end.

2-kings-9:34:6.summary: Elijah tells Ahab to “eat and drink,” sharing only the phrase.

2-kings-9:34:7.summary: Amos’s luxurious feasters on ivory beds have no specific link to Jehu’s meal.

2-kings-9:35:0.summary: The tyrant is denied honourable burial and thrown out like an abhorred corpse, generally like Jezebel.

2-kings-9:35:1.summary: Destruction for the unjust is a general principle fitting Jezebel’s end.

2-kings-9:35:2.summary: Jehoiakim’s carcass will be thrown out unburied, a parallel royal disgrace.

2-kings-9:35:3.summary: Having “no burial” is called worse than stillbirth, generally relevant to Jezebel.

2-kings-9:35:4.summary: Jehoiakim receives a “donkey’s burial,” a parallel shameful end for royalty.

2-kings-9:35:5.summary: Herod is struck and eaten by worms, another proud ruler’s gruesome end.

2-kings-9:36:1.summary: Aaron obeying Moses’ directions shares no specific link with the fulfilment of Elijah’s prophecy.

2-kings-9:36:2.summary: Naming the child through Nathan shares only the idea of speaking through a prophet.

2-kings-9:36:3.summary: “According to the word of the Lord … which He spoke through His servant Jonah” uses the same fulfilment formula.

2-kings-9:37:0.summary: Both describe unburied corpses left on the earth’s “surface”, but the Greek reads “example” rather than “dung”, so the verbal link is lost.
2-kings-9:37:0.why: Shows the recurring curse of bodies left unburied.

2-kings-9:37:1.summary: Unburied dead become “an example upon the earth’s surface”; shares the image of exposed corpses but not the “dung” wording.
2-kings-9:37:1.why: Places Jezebel’s fate within prophetic curses of non-burial.

2-kings-9:37:2.summary: The defeated enemies “became like dung for the earth”, the same image as Jezebel’s carcass “like dung on the surface of the field”.
2-kings-9:37:2.why: Shows a stock image for the shameful end of God’s enemies.

2-kings-9:37:3.summary: A Judean king is denied burial, “swept up” and “thrown beyond Jerusalem’s gate”, paralleling a royal corpse cast out without burial.
2-kings-9:37:3.why: Another royal figure condemned to a dishonored, unburied end.

2-kings-9:37:4.summary: Mentions a man who “has no burial” as a misfortune; only a general link to Jezebel’s lack of burial.
2-kings-9:37:4.why: Illustrates how lack of burial was viewed as calamity.

2-kings-9:37:5.summary: The dead lie as “an example on the surface of your land’s plain”; similar exposed-corpse image, but Greek lacks “dung”.
2-kings-9:37:5.why: Echoes the field-exposure image in judgment oracles.

2-kings-9:37:6.summary: The slain “will certainly not be buried; they will be dung upon the earth’s face”, closely matching Jezebel’s fate.
2-kings-9:37:6.why: Same idiom of corpses as dung on the ground.

2-kings-9:37:7.summary: Describes officials reporting the scroll to the king in Elishama’s house; nothing about corpses, burial, or Jezebel.

2-kings-9:37:8.summary: Shown text describes slain nations in the pit around tombs; only a general theme of the shamed dead (truncated range).
2-kings-9:37:8.why: Broad picture of disgraced dead powers.

2-kings-9:37:9.summary: Unlike kings resting in honor, this ruler is “thrown into the mountains like an abhorred dead man”, denied honorable burial.
2-kings-9:37:9.why: Parallel image of a wicked ruler’s corpse cast out.

2-kings-9:3:11.summary: Daniel 4:35 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-9:3:11.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-9:3:11.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-9:3:13.summary: Daniel 5:18 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-9:3:13.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-9:3:13.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-9:6:3.summary: Daniel 5:20–21 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-9:6:3.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-9:6:3.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-9:6:4.summary: 1 Kings 14:7 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-9:6:4.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-9:6:4.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-9:17:9.summary: 1 Samuel 17:22 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-9:17:9.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-9:17:9.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-10:1:0.summary: A prophecy against the high places of Samaria shares only the place name.

2-kings-10:1:1.summary: Gideon also had “seventy sons,” a numeric echo without shown narrative link.

2-kings-10:1:2.summary: Jair's thirty-two sons share only the motif of a ruler's many sons.

2-kings-10:1:3.summary: Jehu kills Ahaziah of Judah in Samaria, part of the same purge of Ahab's house.

2-kings-10:1:4.summary: The prophet in Samaria for Naaman shares only the city name.

2-kings-10:1:5.summary: Omri's founding of Samaria gives background to the capital where Ahab's sons lived.
2-kings-10:1:5.why: Background on the city of Samaria.

2-kings-10:1:6.summary: Ahab succeeds Omri, buried in Samaria; background to Ahab's dynasty in Samaria.

2-kings-10:1:7.summary: Abdon's sons riding seventy donkeys shares only the number seventy.

2-kings-10:1:8.summary: A law appointing judges has no specific link to Jehu's letter to Samaria's rulers.

2-kings-10:1:9.summary: Jezebel writes a letter to a city's elders to arrange a murder, as Jehu writes to Samaria's elders about Ahab's sons.
2-kings-10:1:9.why: Ironic parallel: letters to elders bring Ahab's house its reckoning.

2-kings-10:2:0.summary: Same epistolary formula “Now, when this letter reaches you” in a letter to the king of Israel.

2-kings-10:3:0.summary: Supporters of Saul's surviving son fight David's men (truncated), loosely like the call to “fight for your master's house.”
2-kings-10:3:0.why: Example of fighting for a fallen king's house.

2-kings-10:3:1.summary: Law on setting a ruler “from among your brethren” relates only generally to choosing a king among Ahab's sons.
2-kings-10:3:1.why: General principle of choosing a king.

2-kings-10:3:2.summary: Saul is made king at Gilgal; only the general act of installing a king is shared.

2-kings-10:3:3.summary: Abner sets Saul's son Ish-bosheth on the throne after the king's fall, exactly what Jehu dares Samaria's leaders to do.
2-kings-10:3:3.why: Precedent for propping up a fallen dynasty's heir.

2-kings-10:3:4.summary: Adonijah is proclaimed to “sit on my throne” by supporters; only the motif of placing a son on a throne.
2-kings-10:3:4.why: Contested succession to a father's throne.

2-kings-10:3:5.summary: Rehoboam musters warriors “to fight Israel's house” to restore his kingdom, loosely like fighting for a master's house.

2-kings-10:3:6.summary: Samuel presents the chosen king with “no one like him,” loosely like choosing the best of the master's sons.

2-kings-10:3:7.summary: Jesus' attendants would “be fighting” if His kingdom were worldly, a loose contrast to fighting for a royal house.

2-kings-10:4:0.summary: Jehu shoots Joram king of Israel, one of “the two kings” who could not stand before him.
2-kings-10:4:0.why: Shows the first king Jehu defeated.

2-kings-10:4:1.summary: Jehu strikes Ahaziah king of Judah, the second of “the two kings” the leaders fear.
2-kings-10:4:1.why: Shows the second king Jehu killed.

2-kings-10:4:2.summary: “What shepherd can stand before Me?” echoes “How shall we stand?” only in phrasing.
2-kings-10:4:2.why: Rhetorical question of who can stand.

2-kings-10:4:3.summary: A king weighing whether he can meet a stronger foe loosely mirrors the leaders' calculation against Jehu.
2-kings-10:4:3.why: Prudent assessment of strength before conflict.

2-kings-10:4:4.summary: “Who will stand before His anger?” parallels “How shall we stand?” rhetorically, about God not Jehu.
2-kings-10:4:4.why: Rhetorical question of standing before overwhelming power.

2-kings-10:4:5.summary: A vineyard oracle about hostility and burning has no specific link to fear of Jehu.

2-kings-10:5:0.summary: Israel's king tells a stronger king “I am yours, and so is everything of mine,” like the leaders' total submission to Jehu.
2-kings-10:5:0.why: Parallel formula of submission to a superior power.

2-kings-10:5:1.summary: Ben-Hadad's servants come in submission as “your servant” seeking life, loosely like Samaria's leaders yielding.
2-kings-10:5:1.why: Defeated party submits to the victor.

2-kings-10:5:2.summary: Elders send envoys to say “We are your servants,” as Samaria's elders tell Jehu “We are your attendants.”
2-kings-10:5:2.why: Same pattern of elders offering submission.

2-kings-10:5:3.summary: Hezekiah sends word “whatever you impose on me, I will bear,” like “Everything you tell us, we will do.”

2-kings-10:5:4.summary: The Gibeonites declare “We are your servants” to a conquering leader.

2-kings-10:5:5.summary: Fearful Gibeonites say “Do to us as pleases you and seems best to you,” echoing “what is good in your eyes.”
2-kings-10:5:5.why: Fear-driven surrender in closely similar words.

2-kings-10:5:6.summary: Nations must submit to Babylon's yoke or perish, a general theme of submission to power.
2-kings-10:5:6.why: General theme of yielding to a conqueror.

2-kings-10:5:8.summary: Serving and following Jesus shares only the idea of service, not this political submission.

2-kings-10:6:0.summary: Of the figure “Jezebel” God says “I will kill her children with death,” recalling the slaughter of Ahab's house.
2-kings-10:6:0.why: Revelation reuses the fate of Jezebel's house.

2-kings-10:6:1.summary: Fathers' sins repaid on children generally explains judgment on Ahab's sons.
2-kings-10:6:1.why: Principle behind judgment on a dynasty.

2-kings-10:6:2.summary: A wicked man's sons losing his goods relates only generally to Ahab's sons' fate.
2-kings-10:6:2.why: General theme of judgment reaching descendants.

2-kings-10:6:3.summary: “Whoever is not against you is for you” shares only a for/against phrase with Jehu's ultimatum.

2-kings-10:6:4.summary: “Whoever is not with Me is against Me” shares only the loyalty idea, not the event.

2-kings-10:6:5.summary: Jezebel's letter has a city's elders kill Naboth and they comply, as Jehu's letter makes Samaria's leaders kill Ahab's sons.
2-kings-10:6:5.why: Ironic reversal: letters to elders now destroy Ahab's house.

2-kings-10:6:6.summary: Leaders made a public example for idolatry has no specific link to Jehu's order.

2-kings-10:6:7.summary: Jehu calls on those in Jezebel's palace to side with him, loosely like his loyalty test to Samaria's leaders.
2-kings-10:6:7.why: Jehu enlists insiders against Ahab's house.

2-kings-10:6:8.summary: Achar's sons die with him, loosely like a father's house destroyed for his sin.

2-kings-10:6:9.summary: Children slaughtered “because of your father's sins” generally fits the killing of Ahab's sons.
2-kings-10:6:9.why: Theme of a dynasty cut off for its father's sins.

2-kings-10:7:0.summary: Elijah's oracle to “destroy from Ahab every male” is fulfilled in the slaughter of Ahab's seventy sons.

2-kings-10:7:1.summary: Athaliah destroys all royal offspring, another royal massacre, but a different house and event.

2-kings-10:7:2.summary: John's head is brought to a ruler on a platter, loosely like heads sent in baskets to Jehu.
2-kings-10:7:2.why: Shared grim image of severed heads delivered.

2-kings-10:7:3.summary: Abimelech kills Jerubbaal's sons, “seventy men,” for power, closely paralleling the slaughter of Ahab's seventy sons (truncated).
2-kings-10:7:3.why: Parallel massacre of a ruler's seventy sons.

2-kings-10:7:4.summary: Jehu asks “who struck all these?” about the seventy heads, the direct sequel.

2-kings-10:7:5.summary: Joram kills all his brothers with the sword, a different dynastic purge.

2-kings-10:8:0.summary: A messenger reports deaths to a king, only a general reporting motif.

2-kings-10:8:1.summary: Elders report Naboth's death to Jezebel after her letter, loosely mirroring the report of heads to Jehu.

2-kings-10:8:2.summary: John's head is brought and handed over, loosely like reporting the arrival of the princes' heads.

2-kings-10:8:3.summary: Law forbids leaving a body exposed overnight, contrasting with heads piled at the gate until morning.

2-kings-10:9:1.summary: Samuel asks the people to judge his conduct, loosely like Jehu addressing the people about guilt.
2-kings-10:9:1.why: Leader appeals to the people's judgment.

2-kings-10:9:2.summary: God invites the people to “judge My case,” loosely like Jehu's appeal to the people's verdict.

2-kings-10:9:3.summary: God will “avenge Jezreel's blood upon Jehu's house,” reflecting on the bloodshed Jehu acknowledges here.
2-kings-10:9:3.why: Later prophetic verdict on Jehu's killings.

2-kings-10:10:0.summary: God defers the harm on Ahab's house to “his son's days,” the word now being fulfilled.
2-kings-10:10:0.why: Explains why judgment falls on Ahab's sons.

2-kings-10:10:1.summary: Elijah's “Thus says the Lord” against Ahab is the word Jehu says will not fall to the ground.

2-kings-10:10:2.summary: Jehu is commissioned to “destroy the house of Ahab,” the Lord's word he now claims is fulfilled.

2-kings-10:10:4.summary: Same fulfillment formula: “the word of the Lord that He spoke through His slave Elijah.”
2-kings-10:10:4.why: Repeated fulfillment formula in Jehu's story.

2-kings-10:10:5.summary: God's words through the prophets “overtook your fathers,” a general statement of prophetic fulfillment.
2-kings-10:10:5.why: Principle that prophetic words come true.

2-kings-10:10:6.summary: God “will not turn back or change His mind,” generally supporting the certainty of His word.

2-kings-10:10:7.summary: “None of his words fell to the ground” uses the same idiom for a prophet's word being fulfilled.
2-kings-10:10:7.why: Explains the idiom of words not falling.

2-kings-10:10:8.summary: Survivors “will know whose word will endure,” a general theme of God's word proving true.

2-kings-10:10:9.summary: Jesus' words “will certainly not pass away,” a broad parallel to the reliability of God's word.
2-kings-10:10:9.why: General theme of enduring divine word.

2-kings-10:11:0.summary: The wicked man's house “will not be preserved,” generally fitting the extinction of Ahab's house.
2-kings-10:11:0.why: General fate of a wicked house.
2-kings-10:11:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-10:11:1.summary: Ahab's four hundred court prophets give background to “his priests” killed, though not the same group explicitly.

2-kings-10:11:2.summary: A proverb on keeping company with fools has no specific link to killing Ahab's acquaintances.

2-kings-10:11:3.summary: The beast and false prophet thrown into fire share no specific element with Jehu's purge.

2-kings-10:11:4.summary: God will destroy every male from Jeroboam's house (Greek-only 12:24m), the same dynastic judgment now on Ahab's house.
2-kings-10:11:4.why: Pattern of a dynasty wiped out by prophetic word.

2-kings-10:11:5.summary: God will destroy a tyrant's “remnant and offspring,” echoing “no remnant” only generally.
2-kings-10:11:5.why: Theme of a dynasty left without remnant.

2-kings-10:11:6.summary: “Left no survivor” in a conquest account echoes “left him no remnant” only as formula.

2-kings-10:11:7.summary: Josiah slaughters priests of the high places, loosely like Jehu killing Ahab's priests.
2-kings-10:11:7.why: Another reform purge of illegitimate priests.

2-kings-10:11:8.summary: Prophets who “eat at Jezebel's table” illustrate the religious retinue of Ahab's house.

2-kings-10:11:9.summary: Zimri, on taking the throne, “struck down all Baasha's house,” a parallel dynastic purge.
2-kings-10:11:9.why: Recurring pattern of exterminating a prior dynasty.

2-kings-10:11:10.summary: A curse that a man's children be destroyed and name erased generally fits Ahab's fate.
2-kings-10:11:10.why: Theme of a line cut off.

2-kings-10:11:11.summary: God will avenge “Jezreel's blood upon Jehu's house,” the bloodshed carried out here in Jezreel.
2-kings-10:11:11.why: Later verdict on Jehu's Jezreel massacre.

2-kings-10:11:12.summary: Baasha “left Jeroboam no breath… according to the Lord's word,” paralleling Jehu leaving no remnant per Elijah's word.
2-kings-10:11:12.why: Parallel prophetic fulfillment against a dynasty.

2-kings-10:11:13.summary: Elijah declares Ahab's house will be like Jeroboam's and Baasha's, the judgment fulfilled here.

2-kings-10:11:14.summary: A psalm line about the crooked led away with evildoers has no specific link.

2-kings-10:11:15.summary: Elijah orders Baal's prophets seized, “Let none of them be spared,” loosely like Jehu killing Ahab's priests.

2-kings-10:11:16.summary: Enemies cut down “until none of them was left alive,” a formulaic echo of total destruction.

2-kings-10:11:17.summary: The devil cast into the lake of fire has no specific link to Jehu's purge.

2-kings-10:13:0.summary: Ahaziah king of Judah “went down to see Joram” at Jezreel, explaining why his brothers come down to visit.
2-kings-10:13:0.why: Background on the Judahite royal visit.

2-kings-10:13:1.summary: Records Ahaziah's accession in Judah; background on the king whose brothers Jehu meets.

2-kings-10:13:2.summary: Says only Ahaziah remained of Joram's sons, which bears on, and seems to sit awkwardly with, “Ahaziah's brothers.”
2-kings-10:13:2.why: Raises the question of who these brothers were.

2-kings-10:13:3.summary: Joram and Ahaziah ride out to meet Jehu and are struck (truncated), the events these brothers have not heard of.
2-kings-10:13:3.why: The immediately preceding killings of the two kings.

2-kings-10:14:0.summary: Athaliah destroys the royal offspring after her sons' deaths, a related but separate massacre.
2-kings-10:14:0.why: Aftermath of the purge on Judah's royal line.

2-kings-10:14:1.summary: Chronicles parallel: Jehu found “Ahaziah's brethren” and killed them while taking vengeance on Ahab's house.
2-kings-10:14:1.why: Parallel account of the same killing.

2-kings-10:14:2.summary: Judah's king married Ahab's daughter, explaining the tie that drew Judah's royals into Ahab's fate.

2-kings-10:14:3.summary: The earlier slaughter of Ahab's seventy sons, a separate killing in the same purge.

2-kings-10:14:4.summary: Jehu struck all of Ahab's house and “left him no remnant,” matching “He left not one of them.”
2-kings-10:14:4.why: Same campaign and formula of total destruction.

2-kings-10:14:5.summary: Athaliah destroys Judah's royal offspring after her son's death, a related later massacre.

2-kings-10:14:6.summary: “Take them alive” is the same order given here, “Seize them alive.”
2-kings-10:14:6.why: Same military command to capture alive.

2-kings-10:15:0.summary: “Jonadab son of Rechab” and his faithful sons are named, the same man Jehu meets.
2-kings-10:15:0.why: Shows Jonadab's lasting legacy of faithfulness.

2-kings-10:15:1.summary: “He has given his hand” as a pledge echoes Jonadab giving his hand, but in a different context.
2-kings-10:15:1.why: Gesture of the hand as covenant pledge.

2-kings-10:15:2.summary: Names the Kinaians as father of “Rechab's house,” the family of Jonadab son of Rechab.

2-kings-10:15:3.summary: “They gave their hand in pledge” echoes Jonadab giving his hand, but in an unrelated setting.
2-kings-10:15:3.why: Hand-giving as a gesture of pledge.

2-kings-10:15:4.summary: Paul's reciprocal appeal “Become as I am… I too became as you are” loosely echoes Jehu's mutual-heart question.

2-kings-10:15:5.summary: David meets newcomers: “If you have come unto me in peace, may my heart be… inclined toward you,” a loyalty test like Jehu's.
2-kings-10:15:5.why: Parallel test of a newcomer's heart before alliance.

2-kings-10:15:6.summary: Jacob blesses Pharaoh on meeting, loosely like Jehu blessing Jonadab.

2-kings-10:15:7.summary: Kings ride out in chariots “to meet Jehu,” a hostile meeting unlike Jonadab's friendly one.

2-kings-10:15:8.summary: Jehu meets travellers on the road and asks who they are, just before meeting Jonadab.
2-kings-10:15:8.why: Adjacent roadside encounter with opposite outcome.

2-kings-10:15:9.summary: The Rechabites obey “Jonadab son of Rechab, our father,” the same Jonadab who joins Jehu (truncated).

2-kings-10:15:10.summary: Jesus questions Peter's love, loosely like Jehu questioning Jonadab's loyalty.

2-kings-10:15:11.summary: Jacob blesses Pharaoh, only a general blessing at an encounter.

2-kings-10:15:12.summary: The apostles “gave… their right hands in fellowship,” a similar hand-pledge of partnership.
2-kings-10:15:12.why: Hand given as sign of alliance.

2-kings-10:15:13.summary: The eunuch invites Philip “to come up and sit with him,” loosely like Jehu bringing Jonadab up onto his chariot.
2-kings-10:15:13.why: Shared image of inviting someone up beside oneself.

2-kings-10:15:14.summary: Laban blessing his family and departing shares only the word “blessed.”

2-kings-10:16:0.summary: Elijah says “I have been most zealous for the Lord Almighty,” the same zeal Jehu claims for the Lord Sabaoth.
2-kings-10:16:0.why: Jehu echoes Elijah's zeal against Baal.

2-kings-10:16:1.summary: Hypocrites pray “so that people may see them,” loosely like Jehu's “see me being zealous.”

2-kings-10:16:2.summary: Jehu “did not take care to walk in the law… with his whole heart,” qualifying his boasted zeal.
2-kings-10:16:2.why: Shows the limits of Jehu's zeal.

2-kings-10:16:3.summary: “Zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” generally fits Jehu's flawed zeal.
2-kings-10:16:3.why: Warns that zeal can be misdirected.

2-kings-10:16:4.summary: Balaam's altars and offerings share nothing specific with Jehu's invitation.

2-kings-10:16:5.summary: People hearing but not doing God's words has no specific link to Jehu's zeal.

2-kings-10:16:6.summary: Elijah repeats “I have been most zealous for the Lord Almighty,” language Jehu now applies to himself.

2-kings-10:16:7.summary: Balaam's oracle introduction shares no specific element with Jehu's boast.

2-kings-10:16:8.summary: “Let your neighbor praise you, and not your mouth” loosely critiques Jehu's self-display.

2-kings-10:16:9.summary: Jehu's commission to destroy Ahab's house and avenge the prophets is the zeal he now displays.
2-kings-10:16:9.why: The divine mandate behind his zeal.

2-kings-10:16:10.summary: Hypocrites sound a trumpet “so that people may glorify them,” loosely like Jehu's showy zeal.

2-kings-10:16:11.summary: Elijah is told “whoever is spared from Hazael's sword, Jehu will put to death,” foretelling Jehu's zealous purge.

2-kings-10:17:0.summary: “You shall destroy from Ahab's house every one,” the commission fulfilled as Jehu strikes all Ahab's remnant.

2-kings-10:17:1.summary: Chronicles notes Jehu “took vengeance on Ahab's house,” the same purge.
2-kings-10:17:1.why: Chronicler's view of the same purge.

2-kings-10:17:3.summary: Jehu acts “according to the word of the Lord” spoken against Ahab, as again in Samaria.

2-kings-10:17:4.summary: Jehu strikes “all who remained in Ahab's house” per Elijah's word, the Jezreel counterpart to the Samaria purge.
2-kings-10:17:4.why: Parallel purge with the same fulfillment formula.

2-kings-10:17:5.summary: A curse that a man's sons become orphans and another take his office loosely fits Ahab's end.
2-kings-10:17:5.why: Theme of a wicked house cut off.

2-kings-10:17:6.summary: “Neither root nor branch will remain” of the lawless, a general image of total destruction.

2-kings-10:18:0.summary: Ahab “served Baal and bowed down to him,” the worship Jehu cites in his ruse.

2-kings-10:18:1.summary: Mentions “the pillars of Baal that his father had made,” background on Ahab's Baal cult.
2-kings-10:18:1.why: Background on Baal worship in Ahab's house.

2-kings-10:18:2.summary: A call to think on true and honorable things has no link to Jehu's ruse.

2-kings-10:18:3.summary: Elijah's slaughter of Baal's prophets foreshadows Jehu's coming purge but not this deceptive speech.

2-kings-10:18:4.summary: Rejecting “Let us do evil things so that good things may come” bears loosely on Jehu's deceit.
2-kings-10:18:4.why: Raises the ethics of deception for a good end.

2-kings-10:18:5.summary: Elijah gathers Baal's prophets at Carmel; loosely related to Jehu's assembly plan.

2-kings-10:18:6.summary: “Uttering deceit” before the Lord loosely bears on Jehu's deceptive claim.

2-kings-10:18:7.summary: Elijah alone against Baal's many prophets gives background to Baal's following in Israel.

2-kings-10:19:0.summary: The king gathers all the prophets, about four hundred, a general royal summons of prophets.

2-kings-10:19:1.summary: Elijah summons all Baal's prophets to Carmel for a sacrifice that ends in their slaughter, as Jehu summons them now.
2-kings-10:19:1.why: Parallel summons of Baal's servants to their doom.

2-kings-10:19:2.summary: The serpent's “cunning” deceit loosely parallels Jehu's trickery.

2-kings-10:19:3.summary: Paul denies acting “in deceit”; only an incidental word link to Jehu's trickery.

2-kings-10:19:4.summary: Jehu's preceding claim to serve Baal “much,” the opening of the same ruse.

2-kings-10:19:5.summary: Paul ironically speaks of catching by “deceit,” a loose verbal link to Jehu's trickery.

2-kings-10:19:6.summary: Ministers disguising themselves loosely parallels Jehu posing as a Baal worshipper.

2-kings-10:19:7.summary: Preparing a net before a friend's face loosely fits Jehu's trap.

2-kings-10:19:8.summary: Paul renounces “walking in cunning,” contrasting with Jehu's trickery.

2-kings-10:19:9.summary: Elisha's mention of “your father's prophets” refers to Ahab's prophets, loosely linking to Baal's prophets here.

2-kings-10:19:10.summary: “Uttering deceit” before the Lord loosely bears on Jehu acting with trickery.

2-kings-10:20:0.summary: “Consecrate a fast; proclaim a service” uses the same consecrate-and-proclaim formula for a sacred assembly.
2-kings-10:20:0.why: Shows the liturgical formula Jehu exploits.

2-kings-10:20:1.summary: Aaron “proclaimed” a feast at an idol's altar, like the proclaimed festival for Baal.
2-kings-10:20:1.why: Parallel proclamation of an idolatrous feast.

2-kings-10:20:2.summary: Ahab gathers Baal's prophets at Carmel, a related but different assembly.

2-kings-10:20:3.summary: Jezebel's elders “proclaimed a fast” as a pretext for killing Naboth, as Jehu proclaims a festival as a deadly pretext.
2-kings-10:20:3.why: Ironic mirror: a sham religious assembly used to kill.

2-kings-10:21:0.summary: Ahab built an altar for Baal in a house in Samaria, the Baal's house now filled with worshippers.
2-kings-10:21:0.why: Origin of the temple in this scene.

2-kings-10:21:1.summary: People enter “Baal's house,” tear it down, and kill Baal's priest, a parallel purge in Judah.
2-kings-10:21:1.why: Parallel destruction of Baal's house and priest.

2-kings-10:21:2.summary: Forces gathered to Harmagedon for judgment loosely parallel Baal's servants gathered for slaughter.

2-kings-10:21:3.summary: God gathers the nations into a valley for judgment, a loose parallel to gathering Baal's servants.

2-kings-10:21:4.summary: Nations assemble for judgment as the “winepress is full,” loosely like Baal's house filled before slaughter.
2-kings-10:21:4.why: Image of the wicked gathered for judgment.

2-kings-10:21:5.summary: Dagon's house is “full of men and women” just before its destruction, like Baal's house filled before the slaughter.
2-kings-10:21:5.why: Parallel image of a crowded pagan temple doomed.

2-kings-10:22:0.summary: A guest lacking a wedding garment is singled out, loosely like vestments distinguishing Baal's servants.

2-kings-10:22:1.summary: Holy robes for Aaron illustrate priestly vestments only generally.

2-kings-10:23:0.summary: Angels gather out the lawless from the kingdom, loosely like separating Baal's servants for judgment.
2-kings-10:23:0.why: Separation of the wicked for judgment.

2-kings-10:23:1.summary: Separating sheep from goats loosely parallels ensuring only Baal's servants remain.

2-kings-10:23:2.summary: Gathering darnel to burn apart from wheat loosely parallels isolating Baal's servants.

2-kings-10:24:0.summary: Ben-Hadad's men plead for life before Israel's king; the shown (truncated) text lacks the “life for his life” penalty.
2-kings-10:24:0.why: Possible echo of a life-for-life penalty.
2-kings-10:24:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-10:25:0.summary: Blood repaid to those who shed prophets' blood loosely fits judgment on Baal's servants.

2-kings-10:25:1.summary: Elijah orders Baal's prophets seized and slaughtered, “Let none of them be spared,” like “Let no man come out.”

2-kings-10:25:2.summary: Melting in the furnace of God's wrath shares no specific element with the sword slaughter.

2-kings-10:25:3.summary: Executioners are told to go in and “strike,” sparing none, beginning in the house, much like Jehu's order.
2-kings-10:25:3.why: Parallel command for merciless judgment in a sanctuary.

2-kings-10:25:4.summary: The law requiring death for enticers to other gods (truncated) gives a general rationale for the purge.

2-kings-10:25:5.summary: Levites go through the camp with swords killing idolaters, a parallel armed purge of idolatry.
2-kings-10:25:5.why: Precedent for killing idolaters by command.

2-kings-10:26:0.summary: Building “standing stones” shows pillar worship generally, not Baal's pillar specifically.

2-kings-10:26:1.summary: Joram removed “the pillars of Baal that his father had made,” the same Baal pillar cult now burned.

2-kings-10:26:2.summary: Nations' gods “put… into the fire” loosely parallels burning Baal's pillar.

2-kings-10:26:3.summary: David's men take abandoned Philistine gods; the shown text does not mention burning.

2-kings-10:27:0.summary: The Greek-based text says the offender's house will be “dealt with,” lacking the latrine/dunghill image the link assumes.
2-kings-10:27:0.why: Shared image absent in this wording.

2-kings-10:27:1.summary: Here the penalty is a public example and confiscation, not a house turned to a dunghill, so the link fails.
2-kings-10:27:1.why: Shared image absent in this wording.

2-kings-10:27:2.summary: The decree says the house will be “confiscated,” not made a refuse heap, so no real echo.
2-kings-10:27:2.why: Shared image absent in this wording.

2-kings-10:27:3.summary: Ahab set up Baal's altar in the house he built in Samaria, the house now torn down.

2-kings-10:27:4.summary: Hezekiah “shattered all the pillars” and removed idolatrous shrines, a parallel reform.
2-kings-10:27:4.why: Parallel destruction of pillars by a reforming king.

2-kings-10:27:5.summary: The law commands “pull down their altars, and break their pillars,” which Jehu carries out.
2-kings-10:27:5.why: Shows the command behind the action.

2-kings-10:27:6.summary: Josiah “pulled down” cultic houses and defiled high places (truncated), a parallel purge.
2-kings-10:27:6.why: Parallel reform with desecration of cult sites.

2-kings-10:27:7.summary: God threatens to “lay waste your pillars,” a general judgment on pillar worship.

2-kings-10:27:8.summary: Josiah “pulled down… the altars of the Baals” (truncated), a parallel destruction of Baal worship.

2-kings-10:27:9.summary: The law to burn idols fits the burning of the pillar more than tearing down the house.

2-kings-10:29:3.summary: Same regnal formula: “He did not turn away from… the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.”
2-kings-10:29:3.why: Shows the recurring verdict on Israel's kings.

2-kings-10:29:6.summary: Repeats the formula “did not turn away from every sin of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.”
