2-kings-10:29:7.summary: Same formula “did not turn away from any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat.”

2-kings-10:29:11.summary: Same formula “did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.”

2-kings-10:29:13.summary: Same formula “did not turn away from any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat.”

2-kings-10:29:15.summary: Jehu's son “followed the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat… he did not turn away from them.”
2-kings-10:29:15.why: Same failing continued in Jehu's dynasty.

2-kings-10:29:20.summary: Same formula “did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.”

2-kings-10:29:0.summary: Jeroboam made “two golden heifers” and placed them “in Bethel” and “in Dan,” the very sins Jehu kept.
2-kings-10:29:0.why: Origin of the golden heifers cult.

2-kings-10:29:1.summary: Jeroboam “did not turn from his evil,” and this “became a sin for Jeroboam's house.”
2-kings-10:29:1.why: Defines the sin of Jeroboam Jehu continued.

2-kings-10:29:4.summary: Herodias' request for John's head has no link to Jehu's continuance of the calf cult.

2-kings-10:29:5.summary: Hosea condemns Samaria's devotion to “the calf of the house of On,” the calf cult Jehu kept.
2-kings-10:29:5.why: Prophetic judgment on the same calf worship.

2-kings-10:29:8.summary: Abimelech protests being brought into “a great sin,” loosely like a leader causing his people to sin.
2-kings-10:29:8.why: Theme of sin brought on a kingdom.

2-kings-10:29:9.summary: Aaron's cast calf with “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up,” the model for Jeroboam's heifers.
2-kings-10:29:9.why: Links the calves to the original golden calf sin.

2-kings-10:29:10.summary: Peter's hypocrisy carries others along, loosely like a leader who causes others to sin.

2-kings-10:29:12.summary: “The Israelites walked in every sin Jeroboam committed; they did not turn away from it.”
2-kings-10:29:12.why: Shows the national consequence of the same sin.

2-kings-10:29:14.summary: Moses rebukes Aaron for bringing “so great a sin” on the people through the calf, like Jeroboam who caused Israel to sin.
2-kings-10:29:14.why: Leader's calf worship causing national sin.

2-kings-10:29:16.summary: Warning against causing a brother to stumble toward idol food loosely parallels causing Israel to sin.
2-kings-10:29:16.why: Responsibility for leading others into sin.

2-kings-10:29:17.summary: Israel “continued to sin” with cast images and calves, the persistent calf cult Jehu did not remove.
2-kings-10:29:17.why: Prophetic view of the ongoing calf worship.

2-kings-10:29:18.summary: Eli's sons cause the people not to serve God, a general theme of leaders leading people astray.

2-kings-10:29:19.summary: “Rub away your calf, Samaria!”—the calf “leading people astray,” the same calf cult.

2-kings-10:30:0.summary: Jehoahaz succeeds Jehu, the first of the promised generations on Israel's throne.
2-kings-10:30:0.why: Shows the promise beginning to be fulfilled.

2-kings-10:30:1.summary: “Jehoahaz son of Jehu became king in Samaria,” fulfilling the dynastic promise.
2-kings-10:30:1.why: First generation of Jehu's sons reigns.

2-kings-10:30:2.summary: Jeroboam son of Joash, Jehu's great-grandson, reigns in Samaria, continuing the promised line.

2-kings-10:30:3.summary: Joash son of Jehoahaz reigns over Israel, the second generation of Jehu's sons.

2-kings-10:30:4.summary: God deferred harm on Ahab's house to “his son's days,” which Jehu carried out.
2-kings-10:30:4.why: The judgment Jehu executed on Ahab's house.

2-kings-10:30:5.summary: Elijah's oracle that Ahab's house will be like Jeroboam's and Baasha's, the judgment Jehu completed.

2-kings-10:30:6.summary: God will “avenge Jezreel's blood upon Jehu's house,” a later counterweight to the reward promised here.
2-kings-10:30:6.why: Shows the limit and end of Jehu's dynasty.

2-kings-10:30:7.summary: Saul fails to complete a mission of destruction (truncated), contrasting with Jehu doing all God intended.

2-kings-10:30:8.summary: God gives Nebuchadnezzar Egypt as “wages” for his service against Tyre, as Jehu is rewarded for executing judgment.
2-kings-10:30:8.why: God rewarding an agent of His judgment.

2-kings-10:30:9.summary: Ahab is condemned for letting a doomed man go, contrasting with Jehu's complete execution of judgment.
2-kings-10:30:9.why: Contrasts failure and completion of God's sentence.

2-kings-10:31:0.summary: Immediately preceding verse: Jehu “did not turn away from following the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat.”

2-kings-10:31:4.summary: Joram “clung to the sin of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin; he did not turn away from it.”
2-kings-10:31:4.why: Same verdict on Ahab's son and on Jehu.

2-kings-10:31:1.summary: “With every guard keep your heart” generally relates to Jehu's lack of wholehearted care.

2-kings-10:31:2.summary: Paying attention so as not to drift away loosely fits Jehu not taking care.

2-kings-10:31:3.summary: They “were unwilling to walk in His law,” closely matching Jehu not taking care “to walk in the law.”
2-kings-10:31:3.why: Same failure to walk in God's law.

2-kings-10:31:5.summary: God requires Israel “to walk in all His ways… with all your heart,” the standard Jehu failed.
2-kings-10:31:5.why: Defines the wholehearted obedience Jehu lacked.

2-kings-10:31:6.summary: An oath “to walk in the law of God” shares covenant wording but no specific link to Jehu.

2-kings-10:31:7.summary: “Guard your souls diligently” since God showed no likeness loosely relates to Jehu's tolerance of the calves.

2-kings-10:31:8.summary: God's promise to cause His people to walk in His ordinances is only a general theme.

2-kings-10:31:10.summary: Confession of not following God's law is a general parallel to Jehu's failure.
2-kings-10:31:10.why: Theme of failing to follow the law.

2-kings-10:31:11.summary: Command to “walk in all the way” the Lord commanded is general covenant language.

2-kings-10:31:12.summary: Keeping God's words to set one's way right is a general theme of careful obedience.

2-kings-10:31:13.summary: A throne promise conditioned on sons who “guard their way, walking in My law,” the condition Jehu neglected.

2-kings-10:31:14.summary: “I will guard my ways” is a general resolve to avoid sin.

2-kings-10:31:15.summary: “Take heed” not to make a graven likeness relates generally to Jehu tolerating the calves.

2-kings-10:31:16.summary: The throne is promised if sons walk before God “with all their heart,” the wholehearted standard Jehu missed.
2-kings-10:31:16.why: Dynastic promise tied to wholehearted obedience.

2-kings-10:31:17.summary: “Watch lest anyone fall short” is a general warning, not specific to Jehu.

2-kings-10:32:0.summary: Elijah is told of “Hazael's sword” as God's instrument against Israel, now being fulfilled.

2-kings-10:32:1.summary: Elisha weeps foreseeing “all the evils” Hazael will do to Israel, which begin here.

2-kings-10:32:2.summary: Joash recovers towns taken by Hazael's son, reversing Hazael's conquests.

2-kings-10:32:3.summary: “Hazael afflicted Israel all Jehoahaz's days,” continuing the attacks begun under Jehu.

2-kings-10:32:4.summary: Jeroboam II restores Israel's boundary by Jonah's word, a later reversal of territorial losses.

2-kings-10:33:1.summary: “From Aroer, which is upon the bank of the torrent Arnon… unto… Gilead,” the same region Hazael took.

2-kings-10:33:3.summary: Lists Aroer “on the bank of the Arnon torrent,” Gilead, and Bashan, the same Transjordan lands.
2-kings-10:33:3.why: Defines the territory lost to Hazael.

2-kings-10:33:4.summary: Moses gives Aroer by the Arnon, Gilead, and Bashan to Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh, the tribes named here.
2-kings-10:33:4.why: Original allotment of the lands lost.

2-kings-10:33:0.summary: Amos condemns Damascus for atrocities in Gilead and sends fire on “Hazael's house.”
2-kings-10:33:0.why: Prophetic judgment on Hazael's Gilead campaigns.

2-kings-10:33:2.summary: Moses gives Gad, Reuben, and half-Manasseh the lands of Sihon and Og, including Aroer (truncated).
2-kings-10:33:2.why: Origin of the tribes' Transjordan territory.

2-kings-10:34:1.summary: Same formula for Jehu's son: “The rest of… deeds… and his mighty acts—are these not written” in the chronicles.

2-kings-10:34:2.summary: Same closing formula “The rest of… acts, all he did… are these not written,” for Solomon.

2-kings-10:34:3.summary: Same closing formula “The rest of… acts and all he did… are these not written,” for Rehoboam.

2-kings-10:35:0.summary: Describes the reign of Jehoahaz, the son who succeeds Jehu here.
2-kings-10:35:0.why: Shows the weakened kingdom Jehoahaz inherited.

2-kings-10:35:1.summary: “Sleep with your fathers” and a son raised after, a general succession formula in a different promise.

2-kings-10:35:2.summary: Same burial formula: “David lay down with his fathers and was buried.”

2-kings-10:35:3.summary: “Lies down with his fathers” appears in a different context about succession danger.

2-kings-10:35:4.summary: Same formula: slept with his fathers, was buried, and “his son reigned in his place.”

2-kings-10:5:7.summary: Jeremiah 27:17 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-10:5:7.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-10:5:7.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-10:29:2.summary: 1 Kings 14:16 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-10:29:2.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-10:29:2.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-10:31:9.summary: 1 Kings 14:16 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-10:31:9.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.

2-kings-12:10:0.summary: People putting money into the temple treasury; general giving parallel.

2-kings-12:10:2.summary: The rich putting gifts into the treasury; general giving.

2-kings-12:10:7.summary: “Doorpost guards” named in Josiah’s purge; same office, different task.

2-kings-12:10:8.summary: List of gatekeepers of the second rank; general office background.

2-kings-12:10:10.summary: “The three doorpost guards” taken captive; same office, different event.

2-kings-12:11:0.summary: Lists priests and a scribe as officials; general pairing of offices.

2-kings-12:11:2.summary: Scribe and priests sent as officials; general office pairing.

2-kings-12:11:3.summary: Silver put into bags; loose parallel to binding up silver.

2-kings-12:11:4.summary: Officials list with scribe and priests; general offices.

2-kings-12:11:5.summary: Josiah sends the scribe to the high priest to seal the silver “brought into the Lord’s house.”

2-kings-12:12:1.summary: Josiah’s silver given to workers “to the carpenters, builders,” repeating this procedure.

2-kings-12:12:2.summary: Silver handed to those appointed and on to craftsmen and builders for repairs.

2-kings-12:13:1.summary: The temple adorned with beautiful stones shares only stones.

2-kings-12:13:2.summary: Silver given to stonecutters and for timber for the temple; general building parallel.

2-kings-12:13:3.summary: God’s house built with selected stones and timber; general construction.

2-kings-12:13:4.summary: Stones and timber prepared for Solomon’s house; general construction.

2-kings-12:14:1.summary: Solomon’s gold “nails, bowls” and doors for the Lord’s house, the very items not made now.

2-kings-12:14:2.summary: Silver trumpets made for Israel; shares the item trumpets.

2-kings-12:14:3.summary: Silver dish and bowl gifts; general sacred vessels.

2-kings-12:14:4.summary: Gold and silver vessels returned from Babylon; general vessels.

2-kings-12:16:1.summary: A steward accused of wasting possessions contrasts the trustworthy workers.

2-kings-12:16:3.summary: Stewards must be found faithful; general stewardship theme.

2-kings-12:16:5.summary: In Josiah’s repairs “the men were faithful in their work,” matching the trustworthy workers here.

2-kings-12:16:6.summary: The faithful and prudent slave; general faithful service.

2-kings-12:16:7.summary: A trustworthy man given charge; general trustworthiness.

2-kings-12:17:0.summary: Sin and guilt offerings “shall belong unto the priest,” the basis for this rule.

2-kings-12:17:1.summary: Trespass offering valued in silver and given to the priest (shown text truncated).

2-kings-12:17:2.summary: Procedure for a sin offering; general background only.

2-kings-12:17:3.summary: Procedure for a sin offering; general background only.

2-kings-12:17:4.summary: Priests who “eat My people’s sins”; loose link to priests profiting from sin offerings.

2-kings-12:17:5.summary: Repayment for an offence “shall be the priest’s,” matching trespass silver belonging to priests.

2-kings-12:17:6.summary: Every guilt and sin offering is given to Aaron and his sons.

2-kings-12:17:7.summary: Holy portions given to the priests forever; general priestly provision.

2-kings-12:18:0.summary: Chronicles’ account of Syria’s army coming against Judah and Jerusalem under Joash.

2-kings-12:18:1.summary: Jesus “set His face to go to Jerusalem”; shared idiom, unrelated event.

2-kings-12:18:2.summary: Shimei’s trip to Gath shares only the place name.

2-kings-12:18:3.summary: Setting faces toward Egypt shares only the idiom.

2-kings-12:18:4.summary: Elisha foresees Hazael’s cruelty to Israel and his seizing Syria’s throne (shown text truncated).

2-kings-12:18:5.summary: David going to the king of Gath shares only the place name.

2-kings-12:18:6.summary: Jesus’ “face was set toward Jerusalem”; shared idiom only.

2-kings-12:18:7.summary: Benjaminites driving out inhabitants of Geth; place name only.

2-kings-12:18:8.summary: David took Geth from the foreigners; same city, different era.

2-kings-12:18:9.summary: Prophecy of “Hazael’s sword” punishing Israel, which his campaigns fulfil.

2-kings-12:19:0.summary: Asa sends temple and palace treasury silver and gold to the king of Syria, as Joash does.
2-kings-12:19:0.why: Same pattern of buying off Syria.

2-kings-12:19:2.summary: Ahaz takes silver and gold from the treasuries of “the Lord’s house and the king’s house” as gifts.

2-kings-12:19:3.summary: Asa sends treasuries of the Lord’s house and king’s house to Syria’s king.

2-kings-12:19:4.summary: All treasures of “the Lord’s house and the king’s house” taken by Egypt’s king.

2-kings-12:19:5.summary: Joash earlier gathered silver of the holy things for the Lord’s house, now given away.

2-kings-12:20:1.summary: Identical closing formula citing “the book of the daily records for the kings of Judah.”

2-kings-12:20:0.summary: Same regnal formula: rest of the acts written in the annals of Judah’s kings.

2-kings-12:20:3.summary: Same closing formula for Solomon’s acts.

2-kings-12:21:0.summary: Amaziah executes the servants who struck down his father Joash.

2-kings-12:21:2.summary: David’s citadel in this wording carries no “Mallo” name, so the place link is lost.

2-kings-12:21:3.summary: “House of Maallon” resembles the “house of Mallo” name, though in Shechem.

2-kings-12:21:4.summary: Solomon’s citadel and enclosure carry no “Mallo” in this wording.

2-kings-12:21:5.summary: Amaziah, Joash’s son, is also killed by conspirators; general pattern.

2-kings-12:21:6.summary: Amon’s “servants attacked him and struck him in his house,” a parallel assassination.

2-kings-12:22:1.summary: Amaziah son of Joash becomes king, continuing the succession named here.

2-kings-13:1:0.summary: Joash being shown as king’s son; only background to the Joash named here.

2-kings-13:1:1.summary: Joash’s accession at seven, the start of the reign used to date Jehoahaz.

2-kings-13:1:2.summary: Ahaziah, father of Joash named here, and his reign.

2-kings-13:1:3.summary: Jehu dies and “Jehoahaz his son became king,” the accession dated here.

2-kings-13:2:2.summary: Jehu likewise “did not turn away from” Jeroboam’s sins, the same formula.
2-kings-13:2:2.why: Father and son share the sin.

2-kings-13:2:4.summary: Identical verdict for Joash of Israel: did evil, did not turn from Jeroboam’s sins.

2-kings-13:2:0.summary: Jeroboam’s golden heifers at Bethel and Dan, the sin referred to (shown text truncated).

2-kings-13:2:3.summary: Ephraim following worthless things; general apostasy theme.

2-kings-13:3:0.summary: Hazael and his son “the son of Ader,” and Israel’s later recovery of towns.

2-kings-13:3:1.summary: Prophecy of Hazael’s sword against Israel, fulfilled here.

2-kings-13:3:2.summary: “The Lord was greatly angered against Israel” and delivered them into enemies’ hands, the same formula.

2-kings-13:3:3.summary: Hazael king of Syria campaigning toward Jerusalem; same oppressor.

2-kings-13:3:4.summary: “Hazael afflicted Israel all Jehoahaz’s days,” restating this oppression.

2-kings-13:3:5.summary: The Lord “greatly angered against Israel” sold them to enemies; same formula (shown text truncated).

2-kings-13:3:6.summary: The Lord angered sold Israel to a king of Syria; same formula and enemy nation.

2-kings-13:3:8.summary: Covenant curse of defeat before enemies; general theme.

2-kings-13:3:9.summary: God is a consuming fire; general divine wrath.

2-kings-13:3:10.summary: Falling before enemies as covenant punishment; general theme.

2-kings-13:3:11.summary: Warning that idolatry provokes God to anger; general theme.

2-kings-13:3:12.summary: A foreign nation as the rod of God’s anger; general theme.

2-kings-13:4:0.summary: “The Lord saw Israel’s humiliation,” a parallel statement of God seeing Israel’s affliction.

2-kings-13:4:1.summary: “I have surely seen the affliction of My people,” the same divine response.

2-kings-13:4:2.summary: Israel sought God when struck; general pattern.

2-kings-13:4:3.summary: “Cry out to Me and I will answer”; general prayer promise.

2-kings-13:4:4.summary: The Lord saved them from affliction; general theme.

2-kings-13:4:5.summary: “Call on Me in the day of affliction”; general prayer promise.

2-kings-13:4:6.summary: God grew weary over Israel’s distress after their plea; general pattern.

2-kings-13:4:7.summary: God heard the child’s voice; general divine hearing.

2-kings-13:4:8.summary: Moses prays for the people; general intercession.

2-kings-13:4:9.summary: “I have seen the oppression”; general divine seeing of oppression.

2-kings-13:4:10.summary: Idolaters cry “Rise and save us” in calamity; loose contrast.

2-kings-13:4:11.summary: “Hazael afflicted Israel all Jehoahaz’s days,” the affliction prayed about.

2-kings-13:4:12.summary: Israel cried to the Lord because of Midian; general Judges pattern.

2-kings-13:4:13.summary: “God saw my humiliation”; general divine seeing.

2-kings-13:4:14.summary: Manasseh’s prayer and how He listened; general answered prayer.

2-kings-13:4:15.summary: Afflicted Manasseh “sought the face of the Lord” and “He listened to him,” closely matching.

2-kings-13:4:16.summary: “He saw when they were afflicted”; general recurring pattern.

2-kings-13:4:17.summary: Israel cries to the Lord confessing sin; general Judges pattern.

2-kings-13:4:18.summary: Remembering the Lord in affliction; general theme.

2-kings-13:5:5.summary: Men who have been saved ascend Zion; general salvation theme.

2-kings-13:5:7.summary: David was before Saul “as in former days”; shared phrase only.

2-kings-13:5:8.summary: Law of the accidental slayer; no link.

2-kings-13:5:9.summary: Birth of a Savior in David’s city shares only the idea of saving.

2-kings-13:5:10.summary: David leading Israel “formerly”; incidental overlap only.

2-kings-13:6:0.summary: Ahab made the grove, which still “stood in Samaria.”

2-kings-13:6:2.summary: Omri walked in Jeroboam’s sins “by which he caused Israel to sin,” the same formula.

2-kings-13:6:3.summary: Josiah burns vessels made for the grove; general grove theme in Judah.

2-kings-13:6:4.summary: Israel made two heifers and groves, the sins named here, leading to exile.

2-kings-13:6:5.summary: Israel walked in Jeroboam’s sins and “did not turn away from it” until exile.

2-kings-13:6:6.summary: Hezekiah destroys the groves; general contrast in Judah.

2-kings-13:6:7.summary: Jehu “did not turn away from” Jeroboam’s sins; same formula for Jehoahaz’s father.

2-kings-13:6:8.summary: Israel forsook God for foreign gods; general apostasy.

2-kings-13:6:9.summary: Command to cut down sacred groves; general background.

2-kings-13:6:10.summary: Abijam walked in his father’s sins; general formula.

2-kings-13:7:0.summary: Both concern Syrian (Damascus) brutality against Israel's people, but the Greek “sawed the pregnant women” lacks the threshing/dust image the link assumes.
2-kings-13:7:0.why: Shows Syria's cruelty toward Israel in this era.

2-kings-13:7:1.summary: Hazael's striking of Israel throughout its territory explains how Jehoahaz's forces were reduced to a remnant.
2-kings-13:7:1.why: Shows the beginning of the Syrian oppression.

2-kings-13:7:2.summary: Isaiah's swords put into the earth and bows like brushwood concern a conqueror from the east, not Syria's crushing of Israel; no dust wording here.
2-kings-13:7:2.why: No real link in the Greek text.

2-kings-13:7:3.summary: Both picture Israel's army reduced to helplessness before an enemy, Saul's men hiding in caves; only a general parallel.
2-kings-13:7:3.why: Loose parallel of Israel's military weakness.

2-kings-13:7:4.summary: Joel's “Valley of Judgment” and the Lord's day have no specific tie to Syria trampling Jehoahaz's army.

2-kings-13:7:5.summary: The Assyrian taunt about Judah lacking riders for two thousand horses loosely echoes Israel's depleted horsemen and chariots.
2-kings-13:7:5.why: Loose image of a kingdom stripped of cavalry.

2-kings-13:7:6.summary: Both use the image of enemies made “like dust”; Isaiah reverses it, with Israel threshing its foes.
2-kings-13:7:6.why: Shared crushing image, reversed in direction.

2-kings-13:7:7.summary: Elisha foresaw the evils Hazael would do to Israel, killing its chosen men; the depleted army fulfills that prophecy.

2-kings-13:7:8.summary: Israel's small force facing Syria “like two flocks of goats” while Syria filled the land parallels Israel's meager army against Syria.
2-kings-13:7:8.why: Earlier picture of Israel outnumbered by Syria.

2-kings-13:7:9.summary: Israel disarmed by the foreigners under Saul loosely parallels an army left powerless by an oppressor.
2-kings-13:7:9.why: General theme of an oppressed, weakened army.

2-kings-13:7:10.summary: Saul's army dwindled to about six hundred men, a loose parallel to Jehoahaz's reduced forces.
2-kings-13:7:10.why: General parallel of a shrunken army.

2-kings-13:7:11.summary: The psalm's grinding foes “like dust” and smoothing them like mud in streets echoes being made “like dust for trampling.”
2-kings-13:7:11.why: Shared image of enemies trampled to dust.

2-kings-13:7:12.summary: Ahab's muster of troops against Syria offers a numerical contrast with Jehoahaz's tiny remaining army.
2-kings-13:7:12.why: Contrasts Israel's earlier strength against Syria.

2-kings-13:8:0.summary: Rehoboam's burial formula resembles regnal closing formulas but not the “rest of the deeds” wording of the source.

2-kings-13:8:1.summary: Same regnal formula: “the rest of” the king's acts and all he did, “are these not written” in the royal annals.
2-kings-13:8:1.why: Shows the standard citation of royal records.

2-kings-13:8:3.summary: Solomon's heart turned by foreign wives has no connection to the closing notice of Jehoahaz's reign.

2-kings-13:8:4.summary: Jehu's closing formula about his deeds and power ends with Jehoahaz his son becoming king, the same dynasty and formula.
2-kings-13:8:4.why: Links Jehoahaz's reign to his father's record.

2-kings-13:9:0.summary: Names “Joash son of Jehoahaz son of Jehu,” the son who succeeded Jehoahaz.
2-kings-13:9:0.why: Identifies Jehoahaz's successor in later events.

2-kings-13:9:2.summary: Joash, who became king here, later “lay down with his fathers” in Samaria with the same formula.
2-kings-13:9:2.why: Completes the reign of Jehoahaz's son.

2-kings-13:9:3.summary: Ahijah's oracle against Jeroboam's house is unrelated to Jehoahaz's burial and Joash's succession.

2-kings-13:9:4.summary: Jehu “lay down with his fathers” and was buried in Samaria with Jehoahaz succeeding, the same formula one generation earlier.

2-kings-13:11:1.summary: Same formula: the king clung to “the sin of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin” and did not turn away.
2-kings-13:11:1.why: Shows the recurring verdict on Israel's kings.

2-kings-13:11:2.summary: Jehu likewise “did not turn away” from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, naming the golden heifers.

2-kings-13:11:3.summary: Under Jehoahaz too, they did not turn from Jeroboam's sins but “walked in them,” nearly identical wording.
2-kings-13:11:3.why: Shows continuity of sin across the dynasty.

2-kings-13:12:0.summary: Describes Jeroboam II's boundary restoration, not Joash's deeds or his war with Amaziah.

2-kings-13:12:1.summary: Recounts Joash's war with Amaziah king of Judah, the mighty acts the source cites.
2-kings-13:12:1.why: Gives the story behind the summary.

2-kings-13:12:3.summary: Narrates Joash's dealings with the dying Elisha and his promised victories over Syria, part of his recorded deeds.
2-kings-13:12:3.why: Details Joash's mighty acts against Syria.

2-kings-13:13:0.summary: Shares only the burial formula “lay down with his fathers,” applied to David.

2-kings-13:13:1.summary: The promise of a successor after David sleeps with his fathers echoes the succession idea only generally.

2-kings-13:13:2.summary: Concerns Jeroboam son of Nebat receiving ten tribes, a different Jeroboam from Joash's successor.

2-kings-13:13:3.summary: Shares only the idiom of a king lying down with his fathers.

2-kings-13:13:4.summary: Gives the reign summary and death of the same Jeroboam who took Joash's throne.

2-kings-13:14:1.summary: Epaphroditus' sickness and longing shares only the idea of illness.

2-kings-13:14:2.summary: Hezekiah sick to the point of death with a prophet present loosely parallels a deathbed scene involving king and prophet, roles reversed.

2-kings-13:14:3.summary: Joseph visits his ailing father Jacob, as Joash visits the dying Elisha whom he calls “Father.”
2-kings-13:14:3.why: Similar deathbed visit and blessing setting.

2-kings-13:14:4.summary: Lazarus being ill shares only the theme of sickness.

2-kings-13:14:5.summary: Herod's fearful respect for John has no specific tie to Joash weeping over Elisha.

2-kings-13:14:6.summary: The righteous man perishing unnoticed relates only generally to a holy prophet's death.
2-kings-13:14:6.why: General theme of the righteous dying.

2-kings-13:14:7.summary: David falling asleep after serving his generation is only a general death notice.

2-kings-13:14:8.summary: God seeking a man to stand before Him for the land has no specific link to Elisha's illness.

2-kings-13:14:9.summary: A city razed by the mouths of the impious has no connection to this scene.

2-kings-13:14:10.summary: Lament that “the holy one is gone” loosely fits grief at losing a holy prophet.
2-kings-13:14:10.why: General lament over loss of the godly.

2-kings-13:14:11.summary: Noah, Daniel and Job saving only themselves has no tie to Elisha's death.

2-kings-13:14:12.summary: The king of Israel earlier addressed Elisha as “father,” the same title Joash uses here.
2-kings-13:14:12.why: Shows the kings' regard for Elisha as father.

2-kings-13:14:13.summary: “The prophets—surely they will not live forever?” touches the mortality of prophets generally.

2-kings-13:16:0.summary: Bows and the strengthening hand of the Mighty One loosely parallel Elisha's hands strengthening the king's on the bow.
2-kings-13:16:0.why: Image of God strengthening hands on the bow.

2-kings-13:16:1.summary: God training hands for battle loosely fits the prophet guiding the king's hands on the bow.
2-kings-13:16:1.why: General theme of God-given war skill.

2-kings-13:16:2.summary: Elisha puts “his hands on his hands” on the child, the same distinctive gesture he uses with Joash.

2-kings-13:17:0.summary: Syria came up to Aphek against Israel, the same place where Elisha promises Joash victory over Syria.
2-kings-13:17:0.why: Recalls an earlier Israelite victory at Aphek.

2-kings-13:17:1.summary: Elisha commanding a symbolic action (bathing seven times) requiring obedience loosely parallels the arrow sign.

2-kings-13:17:2.summary: Paul on the word of the cross shares only the idea of deliverance or salvation.

2-kings-13:17:3.summary: Removing Lazarus' stone shares only a command to act before a miracle.

2-kings-13:17:4.summary: Moses' staff used to perform signs loosely parallels the bow and arrow as a prophetic sign.
2-kings-13:17:4.why: Object as instrument of God's sign.

2-kings-13:17:5.summary: “What is this in your hand?” has no specific connection to the arrow of deliverance.

2-kings-13:17:6.summary: Gideon is assured that the enemy camp is delivered into his hand, a general parallel to the promised victory over Syria.
2-kings-13:17:6.why: Divine assurance of victory before battle.

2-kings-13:17:7.summary: Servants obeying Jesus at Cana shares only obedience to a command.

2-kings-13:17:8.summary: A divine signal for David to attack, with the Lord going out before him, loosely parallels a sign of victory in battle.

2-kings-13:17:9.summary: Aphek appears as a battle site, but this is the Philistine war, not Syria.

2-kings-13:18:0.summary: The oil “stopped” when vessels ran out, as the victory is limited when the king stopped striking; a loose pattern.

2-kings-13:18:1.summary: Isaiah's prophetic sign-act foretells military outcome, a general parallel to the striking of the ground.

2-kings-13:18:2.summary: Ezekiel's symbolic action with hair foretelling judgment is a general parallel of prophetic sign-acts.

2-kings-13:18:3.summary: Ezekiel enacts the siege on a brick, another symbolic act foreshadowing military events.

2-kings-13:18:4.summary: Ezekiel acts out captivity as a sign, a general parallel to enacted prophecy.

2-kings-13:18:5.summary: Moses' raised hands decide Israel's success against Amalek, as Joash's strikes determine the extent of victory.

2-kings-13:19:1.summary: Elisha's promise of a son to the Shunammite has no tie to the incomplete striking.

2-kings-13:19:2.summary: Moses' distress at Korah's rebellion shares only a prophet's displeasure.

2-kings-13:19:3.summary: Jesus could do few mighty works there, loosely like victory limited by the king's half-hearted response.
2-kings-13:19:3.why: Divine power limited by human response.

2-kings-13:19:4.summary: Shares only the title “man of God.”

2-kings-13:19:5.summary: Jesus grieving at hardness of hearts loosely parallels the man of God grieved at the king's limited response.

2-kings-13:19:6.summary: Jesus' indignance at the disciples blocking children has no specific link.

2-kings-13:19:7.summary: Elisha advising the king of Israel about Syria shows the same prophetic role against Syria, but a different episode.

2-kings-13:19:8.summary: Moses angry with Aaron's sons over the sin offering has no specific connection.

2-kings-13:19:9.summary: Elijah calling down fire on captains shares only the title “man of God.”

2-kings-13:20:0.summary: The Lord sends “lightly equipped raiders” of Moab and others, the same term used for Moab's raids here.
2-kings-13:20:0.why: Same kind of raiding bands, later against Judah.

2-kings-13:20:1.summary: Moab's breaking faith and war with Israel give general background for Moabite hostility.

2-kings-13:20:2.summary: “Lightly equipped” Syrian raiders entering Israel's land share the term, though from Syria, not Moab.
2-kings-13:20:2.why: Shows the raiding pattern of the period.

2-kings-13:20:3.summary: Moab breaking faith with Israel after Ahab's death explains why Moabite raiders came.

2-kings-13:20:4.summary: Stephen's burial shares only the act of burying a holy man.

2-kings-13:20:5.summary: Jehoiada buried with honor for his service is a general parallel to Elisha's burial.

2-kings-13:20:6.summary: Israel's war against Moab shows ongoing conflict but not these raids.

2-kings-13:20:7.summary: Midianite raiders coming up each sowing season loosely parallels seasonal raids “when the year came round.”

2-kings-13:20:8.summary: The Lord strengthening Moab against Israel is a general theme of Moabite oppression.

2-kings-13:20:9.summary: “Lightly equipped troops” no longer “came into the land of Israel” closely echoes the raiders who “came into the land.”
2-kings-13:20:9.why: Contrasts earlier peace with renewed raids.

2-kings-13:21:0.summary: Healing through cloths that touched Paul loosely parallels life through touching Elisha's bones.
2-kings-13:21:0.why: Power through contact with a holy man.

2-kings-13:21:1.summary: Elisha raising the Shunammite's child shows his power over death, here continuing even after his own death.
2-kings-13:21:1.why: Elisha's life-giving power across life and death.

2-kings-13:21:2.summary: Those in the tombs coming out to life is a general resurrection parallel.

2-kings-13:21:3.summary: Dry bones made to live loosely parallels a dead man revived by touching bones; shown text only.

2-kings-13:21:4.summary: The dead hearing and living is a general resurrection theme.

2-kings-13:21:5.summary: Healing through Peter's shadow parallels power conveyed through contact with a holy man.
2-kings-13:21:5.why: Power through proximity to God's servant.

2-kings-13:21:6.summary: Bodies raised from opened tombs loosely parallels a dead man coming to life in a grave.

2-kings-13:21:7.summary: “The dead will rise, those in the tombs will be awakened” states the hope this miracle prefigures.

2-kings-13:21:8.summary: Life enters the dead witnesses and they “stood upon their feet,” echoing the man who came to life and “stood on his feet.”

2-kings-13:21:9.summary: Lazarus coming out of the tomb is a general parallel of a dead man restored.

2-kings-13:22:0.summary: Elisha's foretelling of “all the evils” Hazael would do to Israel is fulfilled in Hazael afflicting Israel all Jehoahaz's days.
2-kings-13:22:0.why: Shows prophecy fulfilled in Hazael's oppression.

2-kings-13:22:1.summary: God handing His people to nations, so “their enemies afflicted them,” states the general pattern behind Hazael's affliction.
2-kings-13:22:1.why: Theological pattern of oppression for sin.

2-kings-13:23:0.summary: God “remembered His covenant for ever,” the same ground on which He spares Israel here.
2-kings-13:23:0.why: Grounds God's mercy in His enduring covenant.

2-kings-13:23:1.summary: The Lord had not spoken of blotting out Israel and saved them, echoing His unwillingness to destroy them.
2-kings-13:23:1.why: Shows the same mercy continuing under Jeroboam.

2-kings-13:23:2.summary: God will “pity us” and grant mercy to Abraham and truth to Jacob as sworn to the fathers, matching covenant-based pity here.
2-kings-13:23:2.why: Same covenant mercy to the patriarchs.

2-kings-13:23:4.summary: God described as compassionate and merciful states the attribute shown, but without the covenant specifics.

2-kings-13:23:5.summary: God's promise of countless seed and land to Abram is part of the covenant, but not explicitly named as such.

2-kings-13:23:6.summary: Later the Lord did “cast them from His presence” in Judah's case, the very thing He refrains from here.
2-kings-13:23:6.why: Contrasts mercy now with eventual judgment.

2-kings-13:23:7.summary: Eventually the Lord “removed them from His presence,” reversing the forbearance shown in this verse.
2-kings-13:23:7.why: Shows the patience that finally ended.

2-kings-13:23:8.summary: Solomon asks God to “look upon” his supplication, sharing only the idea of God looking toward His people.

2-kings-13:23:9.summary: God sets His covenant with Abraham, the covenant explicitly cited as the reason for mercy.

2-kings-13:23:10.summary: Moses appeals to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the Lord relents from destroying His people, the same covenant-based reprieve.
2-kings-13:23:10.why: Precedent for sparing Israel for the patriarchs' sake.

2-kings-13:23:11.summary: The Lord proclaimed “compassionate and merciful” describes the character shown, but generally.

2-kings-13:23:12.summary: God returning to “have mercy on them” after judgment is a general parallel.

2-kings-13:23:13.summary: Eternal destruction “from the presence of the Lord” contrasts loosely with Israel not being cast from His presence.

2-kings-13:23:14.summary: The One who humbled will have compassion, a general theme of mercy after affliction.

2-kings-13:23:15.summary: In compassion God “didst not make an end of them or abandon them” and keeps covenant and mercy, matching this verse closely.
2-kings-13:23:15.why: Same covenant mercy that refuses to destroy.

2-kings-13:23:16.summary: The Lord is moved for His servants when He sees them weakened and failing under assault, as Israel was under Hazael.
2-kings-13:23:16.why: God's pity for an exhausted people.

2-kings-13:23:17.summary: The everlasting covenant with Abraham and his seed is the covenant God honors here.
2-kings-13:23:17.why: Defines the covenant behind the mercy.

2-kings-13:23:18.summary: Showing mercy to the fathers and remembering His covenant sworn to Abraham matches the basis of mercy here.
2-kings-13:23:18.why: Same covenant mercy fulfilled in Christ.

2-kings-13:23:19.summary: God waiting to pity and have mercy is a general parallel to His pity here.

2-kings-13:23:20.summary: Banishment to eternal fire has no specific link to God's forbearance with Israel.

2-kings-13:23:21.summary: The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob sees His people's affliction and acts, as He looks toward afflicted Israel here.

2-kings-13:23:22.summary: “Do not cast me away from Thy face” echoes the Lord not casting Israel from His presence.
2-kings-13:23:22.why: Same idea of being cast from God's presence.

2-kings-13:23:23.summary: God helped Israel, remembering mercy as spoken to Abraham, the same covenant mercy toward Israel.
2-kings-13:23:23.why: Covenant mercy to Israel for Abraham's sake.

2-kings-13:23:24.summary: God will remember His covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham, the three patriarchs named here.
2-kings-13:23:24.why: Promise that covenant memory brings mercy.

2-kings-13:23:25.summary: “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy” speaks of God's sovereign mercy generally.

2-kings-13:23:26.summary: God limiting man's days to 120 years has no connection to covenant mercy on Israel.

2-kings-13:23:27.summary: The Lord grew weary over Israel's distress, a general parallel to His pity here.

2-kings-13:24:0.summary: God bringing justice for His chosen ones has no specific link to Hazael's death and succession.

2-kings-13:24:1.summary: The rod of sinners not remaining on the righteous loosely fits the end of Hazael's oppression.

2-kings-13:25:1.summary: Hazael struck Israel throughout its territory, the losses Joash now recovers.

2-kings-13:25:2.summary: Jeroboam's restoration of Israel's boundary continues the recovery begun by Joash, but is a later event.
2-kings-13:25:2.why: Further restoration under the next king.

2-kings-13:2:1.summary: 1 Kings 14:16 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-13:2:1.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-13:2:1.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-13:8:2.summary: 1 Kings 14:19–20 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-13:8:2.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-13:8:2.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-14:1:0.summary: Records the accession of Joash son of Jehoahaz, the king whose second year dates Amaziah's reign.

2-kings-14:1:1.summary: Chronicles' parallel opening of Amaziah's reign as king in Jerusalem.

2-kings-14:1:2.summary: Names Joash king of Israel and his fight with Amaziah king of Judah, the two kings of this synchronism.
2-kings-14:1:2.why: Shows the two kings' later conflict.

2-kings-14:1:3.summary: Amasias appears in Judah's royal genealogy as the son in the line of kings.

2-kings-14:3:1.summary: Nations renouncing their fathers' idols has no link to Amaziah following his father.

2-kings-14:3:2.summary: Abijam's heart was not whole “like the heart of David his father,” the same comparison with David.
2-kings-14:3:2.why: Same measure of kings against David.

2-kings-14:3:3.summary: Ransom from futile ancestral conduct has no specific tie to Amaziah's mixed record.

2-kings-14:3:4.summary: Warnings not to be like the fathers share only the idea of following fathers' ways.

2-kings-14:3:5.summary: Amaziah's worship of Edom's gods shows how he fell short of David.

2-kings-14:3:6.summary: Solomon's heart was not whole “as was the heart of David his father,” the same Davidic standard.

2-kings-14:3:7.summary: Joash did what was upright before the Lord, the father whose example Amaziah followed.

2-kings-14:3:8.summary: Joash's turn after Jehoiada's death shows the flawed side of the father Amaziah imitated.

2-kings-14:3:9.summary: Joash “did what was right before the Lord,” the same verdict given to his son.

2-kings-14:4:1.summary: Ahaz “sacrificed and burned incense at the high places,” the same practice in the same wording.

2-kings-14:4:2.summary: Identical formula: “Only he did not remove the high places; the people still sacrificed and burned incense.”

2-kings-14:4:3.summary: The same formula about not removing the high places, applied to Jotham.

2-kings-14:5:0.summary: Joash's slaves conspired and struck him down, the very servants Amaziah now executes.

2-kings-14:5:1.summary: Blood shed is atoned only by the blood of the one who shed it, the legal principle behind punishing the assassins.

2-kings-14:5:3.summary: The law that one who strikes and kills shall be put to death underlies Amaziah's execution of the killers.

2-kings-14:5:4.summary: “Whoever sheds the blood of man” states the general principle of retribution for murder.

2-kings-14:6:1.summary: “The son will not receive his father's injustice” restates the law Amaziah obeyed.
2-kings-14:6:1.why: Prophetic restatement of the same law.

2-kings-14:6:2.summary: “The soul that sins will die” expresses individual responsibility as in the quoted law.

2-kings-14:6:3.summary: “Each will die in his own sin” closely echoes “each shall die only for his own sins.”
2-kings-14:6:3.why: Close verbal echo of the law.

2-kings-14:7:0.summary: David struck Idumea at Gaimale, the same place where Amaziah strikes Edom.

2-kings-14:7:1.summary: A list of Judean towns (“Jakareel”) does not carry the name Kathoel given to the captured Rock.
2-kings-14:7:1.why: Link depends on a name absent here.

2-kings-14:7:2.summary: Idumea struck in the Valley of Salts, the same battle site against Edom.

2-kings-14:7:3.summary: The shown psalm verse speaks of God rejecting and pitying, with no Edom or valley reference.

2-kings-14:7:5.summary: Isaiah's “deserted rock” refers to Mount Zion, not the Edomite Rock Amaziah captured.

2-kings-14:7:6.summary: Edom broke away from Judah's hand under Joram, the revolt Amaziah's campaign seeks to reverse.

2-kings-14:8:1.summary: Abner's challenge to Joab leads to civil war between Israel and Judah, a loose parallel to Amaziah's challenge.

2-kings-14:8:2.summary: Amaziah and the king of Israel “faced one another” at Baithsamys, the outcome of this challenge.

2-kings-14:8:3.summary: A fool's rash mouth calling upon death loosely fits Amaziah's reckless challenge.

2-kings-14:8:5.summary: Doing evil with insolence loosely matches Amaziah's proud provocation.

2-kings-14:8:6.summary: Faction and battle leading to want loosely warns against such a challenge.
2-kings-14:8:6.why: Wisdom on the cost of strife.

2-kings-14:8:7.summary: “Do not rush quickly into battle” is general counsel against Amaziah's hasty challenge.

2-kings-14:9:0.summary: Jotham's fable of trees and the bramble is the closest parallel to Joash's thornbush-and-cedar fable.
2-kings-14:9:0.why: Same plant-fable form of political rebuke.

2-kings-14:9:1.summary: Manasseh taken in bonds has no thorn or fable link in the Greek text shown.

2-kings-14:9:3.summary: Thorns in Israel's dwellings is an incidental word overlap only.

2-kings-14:9:4.summary: Amaziah's Edom victory and dismissal of Ephraim's troops provide context for the conflict, not the fable itself.

2-kings-14:9:5.summary: Ezekiel's hearers call his words a parable, a general link to the parable form.

2-kings-14:9:6.summary: Thorns in a drunkard's hand in the Greek has no real tie to the thornbush fable.

2-kings-14:9:7.summary: Solomon spoke of trees “from the cedar in Lebanon” to hyssop, sharing only the cedar of Lebanon.

2-kings-14:9:8.summary: Job's nurture from youth has no connection to this fable.

2-kings-14:9:9.summary: Thorny trees growing in ruined Edom is only an incidental word overlap.

2-kings-14:9:10.summary: Nathan's parable to David is another rebuke of a king by story, a general genre parallel.
2-kings-14:9:10.why: Parable used to rebuke a king.

2-kings-14:9:11.summary: Israelites hiding in caves and rocks has no thornbush in the Greek text.

2-kings-14:9:12.summary: A lily among thorns shares only the thorn image.

2-kings-14:10:0.summary: Uzziah grew strong and “his heart was lifted up to destruction,” the same pride after success.
2-kings-14:10:0.why: Same pattern of pride before a fall.

2-kings-14:10:1.summary: Warning against becoming “lifted up in heart,” the phrase used of Amaziah's pride.

2-kings-14:10:2.summary: Hezekiah's heart was lifted up and wrath came upon him and Judah, as Amaziah's pride brings Judah down with him.
2-kings-14:10:2.why: Pride bringing ruin on king and Judah.

2-kings-14:10:3.summary: Not seeking enmity in vain loosely matches “Why contend in your wickedness?”

2-kings-14:10:4.summary: Glory in turning from strife while fools entangle themselves loosely fits the warning to stay home.

2-kings-14:10:5.summary: Insolence leads to ruin and evil-mindedness “before a fall,” the principle behind “You will fall” to proud Amaziah.
2-kings-14:10:5.why: States the proverb Amaziah's story illustrates.

2-kings-14:10:6.summary: A quick-tempered man prepares battles, loosely matching Amaziah's provocation.

2-kings-14:10:7.summary: Moses offering Pharaoh a time for prayer does not carry the “glory” wording of the source in the Greek.
2-kings-14:10:7.why: No real link in Greek wording.

2-kings-14:10:8.summary: Faction and battle leading to want is general counsel against needless conflict.
2-kings-14:10:8.why: Wisdom on the cost of strife.

2-kings-14:10:9.summary: “Do not rush quickly into battle” loosely echoes Joash's warning to Amaziah.

2-kings-14:10:10.summary: God bringing Gog against Israel has no specific tie to Joash's warning.

2-kings-14:10:11.summary: Necho warns Josiah not to make war lest he be destroyed, a close parallel of a foreign king warning a Judean king away from battle.
2-kings-14:10:11.why: Similar unheeded warning leading to defeat.

2-kings-14:10:12.summary: A list of Gog's allies has no connection to this warning.

2-kings-14:10:13.summary: “God opposes the proud” states the general principle behind Amaziah's lifted-up heart and fall.

2-kings-14:10:14.summary: Belshazzar's failure to honor God despite a God-given kingdom is a general example of royal pride.

2-kings-14:10:15.summary: The Greek “if he draws back” lacks the puffed-up pride the link presumes.
2-kings-14:10:15.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

2-kings-14:10:16.summary: Meddling in another's dispute is like grasping a dog's tail, loosely fitting needless contention.

2-kings-14:10:17.summary: Prophecy against Gog of Magog has no link to Amaziah's pride.

2-kings-14:10:18.summary: A king weighing whether he can win before going to war loosely matches the counsel Amaziah ignored.
2-kings-14:10:18.why: Wisdom of counting the cost of war.

2-kings-14:10:19.summary: “Let no strong man boast in his strength” loosely applies to Amaziah's boasting after victory.

2-kings-14:10:20.summary: The lowly boasting in exaltation has no specific link to Amaziah.

2-kings-14:10:21.summary: Amaziah's victory over Edom, the success Joash says has lifted up his heart (“You have indeed struck Idumea”).
2-kings-14:10:21.why: Identifies the victory behind his pride.

2-kings-14:11:0.summary: “Thessamys” in Naphtali's town list is not Baithsamys in Judah where the battle occurred.

2-kings-14:11:1.summary: Beth-shemesh, where the ark returned, is the same Judean town Baithsamys where the kings met.

2-kings-14:11:3.summary: Bethsamys appears among Judah's Levitical cities, the same town where the battle was fought.

2-kings-14:11:4.summary: “City of the Sun” on Judah's boundary renders Beth-shemesh's meaning, but the name Baithsamys is not visible here.
2-kings-14:11:4.why: Locates the site, link not obvious.

2-kings-14:11:5.summary: Amaziah refuses the prophet's counsel, matching “Amaziah did not listen” and foreshadowing his defeat.
2-kings-14:11:5.why: Shows Amaziah's pattern of not listening.

2-kings-14:12:1.summary: Israel “stumbled” and “each fled to his dwelling,” the same rout formula.
2-kings-14:12:1.why: Same wording for a defeated army.

2-kings-14:12:0.summary: “All Israel fled, each to his tent” uses the same formula for a defeated army scattering.

2-kings-14:12:2.summary: “Each man to his own city” after defeat partly echoes each man fleeing to his dwelling.

2-kings-14:13:0.summary: Mentions the Ephraim Gate of Jerusalem, one end of the wall Joash tore down.

2-kings-14:13:1.summary: Mentions the Gate of Corners, the other end of the demolished stretch of wall.

2-kings-14:13:2.summary: Names the Corner Gate in a promise of rebuilding Jerusalem.
2-kings-14:13:2.why: Links the breached gate to future restoration.

2-kings-14:13:3.summary: Names the Ephraim Gate on Nehemiah's rebuilt wall.
2-kings-14:13:3.why: Locates the gate on the wall.

2-kings-14:13:4.summary: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” loosely fits proud Amaziah's capture.
2-kings-14:13:4.why: General principle of humbling the proud.

2-kings-14:13:5.summary: Humbling every insolent person is a general theme matching Amaziah's humiliation.

2-kings-14:13:6.summary: Insolence before ruin applies generally to Amaziah's capture.

2-kings-14:13:7.summary: Zedekiah seized and brought to his conqueror parallels a Judean king captured, but a different event.

2-kings-14:13:8.summary: God taking kingdoms from kings is a general theme of royal humiliation.

2-kings-14:13:10.summary: Jehoiakim bound and taken by Nebuchadnezzar is another Judean king captured, a different event.

2-kings-14:13:11.summary: Manasseh seized in bonds is another captured Judean king, only a general parallel.

2-kings-14:13:12.summary: The arrogant humbled on the Lord's day is a general theme.

2-kings-14:13:13.summary: “Insolence brings a man low” states the principle behind Amaziah's downfall.

2-kings-14:13:14.summary: Jehoiachin taken with temple vessels loosely parallels capture of the king and plunder.
2-kings-14:13:14.why: Later capture and plunder of Jerusalem.

2-kings-14:14:0.summary: Solomon placed silver, gold and utensils in the treasuries of the Lord's house, the treasures later plundered.

2-kings-14:14:1.summary: Shishak took the treasures of “the Lord's house and the king's house,” the same twofold plunder.
2-kings-14:14:1.why: Earlier plundering of the same treasuries.

2-kings-14:14:2.summary: The Babylonians taking gold and silver bowls is a later, general parallel to plundering temple vessels.

2-kings-14:14:3.summary: Nebuchadnezzar brought out the treasures of the Lord's house and the king's house, the same plunder pattern.

2-kings-14:14:4.summary: Joash of Judah gave away gold from the treasuries of the Lord's house and king's house, depleting the same treasures.
2-kings-14:14:4.why: Same treasuries emptied a generation earlier.

2-kings-14:14:5.summary: The Assyrian offer of horses shows no hostage or “mixed unions” wording in the Greek text.
2-kings-14:14:5.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

2-kings-14:14:6.summary: Asa took silver and gold from the treasuries of the king's house to send away, the same treasury depletion.

2-kings-14:15:0.summary: Jehu's closing formula about his acts, power and engagements “are these not written” in Israel's records, the same formula.
2-kings-14:15:0.why: Standard regnal citation for Israel's kings.

2-kings-14:16:0.summary: Shares only the idiom of a king lying down with his fathers.

2-kings-14:16:1.summary: Hosea prophesied in the days of “Jeroboam son of Joash,” the son who became king here.
2-kings-14:16:1.why: Dates Hosea to this king's reign.

2-kings-14:16:2.summary: Amos confronted Jeroboam king of Israel, Joash's successor.
2-kings-14:16:2.why: Shows prophetic opposition to the new king.

2-kings-14:16:3.summary: Sleeping with one's fathers and a son succeeding is a general succession pattern.

2-kings-14:16:4.summary: Amos dates his words to the days of “Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel.”
2-kings-14:16:4.why: Dates Amos to this king's reign.

2-kings-14:16:6.summary: Jehoahaz lay down with his fathers, was buried in Samaria and Joash succeeded, the same formula one generation earlier.

2-kings-14:17:1.summary: Joash son of Jehoahaz's sixteen-year reign frames the fifteen years Amaziah outlived him.

2-kings-14:17:2.summary: Jeroboam began in Amaziah's fifteenth year, consistent with Amaziah's years after Joash's death.

2-kings-14:17:3.summary: Amaziah's accession in Joash's second year and twenty-nine-year reign frame this chronological note.

2-kings-14:18:0.summary: Same Judean regnal formula: the rest of the king's acts “are these not written” in the annals of the kings of Judah.

2-kings-14:18:1.summary: The rest of Solomon's acts and all he did, “are these not written,” the same closing formula.

2-kings-14:18:2.summary: Joash's closing formula, mentioning his acts with Amaziah, uses the same wording.

2-kings-14:18:3.summary: Jehoahaz's closing formula uses the same “rest of … deeds, all that he did” wording.

2-kings-14:19:2.summary: Hoshea “formed a conspiracy” and killed Pekah, the same phrase for a different king in Israel.

2-kings-14:19:0.summary: Joshua besieging Lachish names the same town, but in an unrelated event.

2-kings-14:19:1.summary: The Assyrian king at Lachish names the same town in a different event.

2-kings-14:19:3.summary: Sellum's conspiracy and killing of the king parallels royal assassination in Israel generally.

2-kings-14:19:4.summary: Pekah's conspiracy against the king is a general parallel of regicide.

2-kings-14:19:5.summary: The king of Lachish is named, sharing only the town.

2-kings-14:19:6.summary: Amon's servants “conspired against him and put the king to death,” another Judean king killed by conspiracy.
2-kings-14:19:6.why: Same fate befalls a later Judean king.

2-kings-14:19:8.summary: The Assyrian force sent from Lachish shares only the town.

2-kings-14:19:9.summary: Manaem striking Sellum and putting him to death is a general parallel of regicide.

2-kings-14:19:10.summary: Amaziah's father Joash was also slain by a conspiracy, so father and son meet the same end.

2-kings-14:19:11.summary: Micah addresses the inhabitant of Lachish, sharing only the town.

2-kings-14:20:0.summary: Ahaziah's body was carried by chariot to Jerusalem and buried in the city of David, closely paralleling Amaziah's burial.
2-kings-14:20:0.why: Similar return of a slain king for burial.

2-kings-14:20:1.summary: Manasseh was buried in his house's garden rather than in David's city, a loose contrast.

2-kings-14:20:2.summary: Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the City of David, the same burial formula.
2-kings-14:20:2.why: Standard royal burial in David's city.

2-kings-14:20:3.summary: David himself was buried in the City of David, the place where Amaziah is buried with his fathers.
2-kings-14:20:3.why: Origin of the royal burial site.

2-kings-14:20:4.summary: Uzziah was buried in the field of the kings' burial because of leprosy, a loose contrast.

2-kings-14:20:5.summary: Joram was “buried with his fathers in the city of David,” the same formula.

2-kings-14:20:6.summary: Jehoram was buried in David's city but not in the kings' tombs, a loose contrast with honored burial.

2-kings-14:20:7.summary: Amaziah's father Joash, also assassinated, was buried “with his fathers in the city of David.”
2-kings-14:20:7.why: Father and son buried alike after murder.

2-kings-14:21:0.summary: Names Azariah king of Judah in a later synchronism, the son crowned here.
2-kings-14:21:0.why: Shows the length of Azariah's reign.

2-kings-14:21:1.summary: Genealogy lists Amasias followed by “Azariah his son.”
2-kings-14:21:1.why: Places Azariah in the royal line.

2-kings-14:21:2.summary: After Amon's assassination the people of the land made his son king, the same pattern as Azariah's enthronement.
2-kings-14:21:2.why: People installing the heir after regicide.

2-kings-14:21:3.summary: Uzziah, another name for Azariah, appears in Jesus' genealogy.
2-kings-14:21:3.why: Places this king in Christ's lineage.

2-kings-14:22:0.summary: Ailath, the town Azariah restored to Judah, is later lost to Syria and Edom.

2-kings-14:22:1.summary: Elath near Ezion-geber in Edom, the same port Azariah rebuilt.
2-kings-14:22:1.why: Solomon's earlier use of the port.

2-kings-14:22:2.summary: Ailon by Ezion-geber on the Arabah road is the same place as Ailoth.

2-kings-14:22:3.summary: Solomon went to coastal Ailath in Idumea, the same port town.
2-kings-14:22:3.why: Earlier Judean control of the port.

2-kings-14:23:0.summary: The Lord saved Israel through “Jeroboam son of Joash,” the king whose reign begins here.
2-kings-14:23:0.why: Shows God's purpose in his reign.

2-kings-14:23:1.summary: Amos prophesies against Jeroboam king of Israel and his house.

2-kings-14:23:2.summary: Hosea prophesied in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash.
2-kings-14:23:2.why: Dates Hosea's ministry to this reign.

2-kings-14:23:3.summary: Amos dates his words to the days of Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel.
2-kings-14:23:3.why: Dates Amos' ministry to this reign.

2-kings-14:24:2.summary: Same verdict: he did evil and followed “the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.”

2-kings-14:24:1.summary: Shares the phrase “doing evil before the Lord,” but concerns Israel's sin in the wilderness.

2-kings-14:24:3.summary: They “did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam's house, who caused Israel to sin,” the same verdict.

2-kings-14:24:4.summary: Jeroboam son of Nebat's golden heifers at Bethel and Dan are the sins later kings did not turn from.
2-kings-14:24:4.why: Explains what “the sins of Jeroboam” were.

2-kings-14:24:5.summary: Er being evil before the Lord shares only a generic phrase.

2-kings-14:24:6.summary: Ahab sold himself “to do evil before the Lord,” a common phrase for an Israelite king.

2-kings-14:24:7.summary: Exchanging glory for a calf's likeness loosely recalls the calf worship behind Jeroboam's sin.

2-kings-14:24:8.summary: Manasseh “did much evil in the Lord's eyes,” a general phrase for a different king.

2-kings-14:25:0.summary: Names the “Sea of Arabah,” the Salt Sea, the southern limit of Jeroboam's restored boundary.

2-kings-14:25:2.summary: Jesus cites “Jonah the prophet,” the same Jonah whose word Jeroboam's expansion fulfilled.
2-kings-14:25:2.why: Connects the historical Jonah to Christ's sign.

2-kings-14:25:3.summary: Zebulun's boundary passes “toward Gebere,” possibly Jonah's hometown Gethchober, but the name form differs.

2-kings-14:25:4.summary: Solomon's Israel stretched “from the entrance of Hamath,” the same northern limit Jeroboam restored.
2-kings-14:25:4.why: Shows the boundary restored to Solomon's extent.

2-kings-14:25:5.summary: The spies went “as one enters Ephaath,” the same northern entrance of Hamath, though spelled differently.
2-kings-14:25:5.why: Ancient northern limit of the promised land.

2-kings-14:25:6.summary: Ezekiel's ideal boundaries mention Hamath and the eastern sea, a general boundary parallel.

2-kings-14:25:7.summary: The promised northern border runs “toward the entrance into Hamath,” the limit Jeroboam reached.

2-kings-14:25:8.summary: Joash's recovery of Israel's towns began the restoration that Jeroboam extended.

2-kings-14:25:9.summary: The Salt Sea is the Sea of the Arabah, but the link requires that identification.

2-kings-14:25:10.summary: Jesus refers to “the sign of Jonah,” the same prophet named here.

2-kings-14:25:11.summary: Hazael's striking throughout Israel's territory is the loss reversed by Jeroboam's boundary restoration.
2-kings-14:25:11.why: Shows what was lost and regained.

2-kings-14:25:12.summary: Amos foretells Israel crushed so it cannot enter Emath, reversing the Hamath boundary Jeroboam regained.

2-kings-14:26:0.summary: The Lord “saw them weakened, and failing” and was moved for His servants, as He saw Israel's humiliation here.
2-kings-14:26:0.why: Same divine pity for a helpless people.

2-kings-14:26:1.summary: “I have surely seen the affliction of My people” matches the Lord seeing Israel's bitter humiliation.

2-kings-14:26:3.summary: The Lord grew weary over Israel's distress, a general parallel to His compassion here.

2-kings-14:26:4.summary: The Lord Himself saving His people from affliction is a general theme of rescue.
2-kings-14:26:4.why: God's personal rescue of His people.

2-kings-14:26:5.summary: “I have seen the oppression” parallels the Lord seeing Israel's bitter humiliation before delivering them.

2-kings-14:26:6.summary: “He saw when they were afflicted” and changed His purpose in mercy, the same pattern as here.

2-kings-14:26:7.summary: “Confined and abandoned in Israel” echoes “hemmed in … and abandoned,” but in a judgment oracle, not pity.

2-kings-14:26:8.summary: The Greek oracle against Jeroboam's house lacks the “hemmed in … abandoned” phrasing the link assumes.
2-kings-14:26:8.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

2-kings-14:27:1.summary: “The Lord gave Israel deliverance” from Syria, the same saving action continued through Jeroboam.
2-kings-14:27:1.why: God delivering Israel despite its sin.

2-kings-14:27:2.summary: Erasure from the book of the living shares only the idea of blotting out.

2-kings-14:27:3.summary: The Lord gave deliverance through Naaman, a general parallel of God saving through a human agent.
2-kings-14:27:3.why: God saving through a chosen leader.

2-kings-14:27:4.summary: “I will blot out their name from under heaven” is the threat the Lord had not spoken against Israel here.
2-kings-14:27:4.why: Recalls the averted threat of destruction.

2-kings-14:27:5.summary: Not erasing the conqueror's name from the book of life loosely parallels Israel not being blotted out.
2-kings-14:27:5.why: General theme of not being blotted out.

2-kings-14:27:6.summary: Hosea announces no more mercy for Israel's house, loosely contrasting with mercy shown here.

2-kings-14:27:7.summary: “The Lord shall blot out his name from under heaven” uses the same idiom of destruction.

2-kings-14:27:8.summary: “God has not rejected His people” loosely parallels the Lord's refusal to blot out Israel.

2-kings-14:27:9.summary: God saving according to His mercy rather than works is a general parallel to saving undeserving Israel.

2-kings-14:27:10.summary: “Blot out the name of Amalek from under heaven” shares the idiom but applies it to Amalek.

2-kings-14:27:11.summary: Blotting out of God's book shares only the idea of being blotted out.

2-kings-14:28:0.summary: Damascus seized by an adversary of Solomon shows its loss from Israel's control, only background.

2-kings-14:28:1.summary: David garrisoned Syria near Damascus, the earlier Israelite control that Jeroboam restored.

2-kings-14:28:2.summary: David placed a garrison around Damascus, the territory Jeroboam is said to have restored.

2-kings-14:28:3.summary: Solomon prevailed over Aimath Soba and built cities in Emath, the Hamath Jeroboam restored.

2-kings-14:29:0.summary: Zechariah son of Jeroboam became king, the successor of the Jeroboam who died here.

2-kings-14:8:4.summary: Proverbs 20:18 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-14:8:4.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-14:8:4.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-14:15:1.summary: 1 Kings 14:19–20 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-14:15:1.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-14:15:1.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-15:1:0.summary: Azariah king of Judah dates Sellum's reign in his thirty-ninth year, the same king.

2-kings-15:1:1.summary: Chronicles' parallel opening for Uzziah (Azariah), king at sixteen, doing right like his father Amaziah.
2-kings-15:1:1.why: Parallel account of the same reign.

2-kings-15:1:3.summary: The people made Uzziah, aged sixteen, king in place of his father Amaziah, the same accession.

2-kings-15:1:4.summary: Synchronism with Azariah king of Judah dating Jeroboam's son's reign.

2-kings-15:1:5.summary: Jeroboam's accession and Amaziah's final years frame the synchronism for Azariah's accession.

2-kings-15:1:6.summary: Names Jotham son of Azariah king of Judah, continuing Azariah's line.

2-kings-15:3:0.summary: Amaziah “did what was right in the Lord's eyes … in accordance with everything his father” did, the same formula.
2-kings-15:3:0.why: Same verdict passed from father to son.

2-kings-15:3:2.summary: Joash did what was upright, yet the high places remained, the same qualified verdict.
2-kings-15:3:2.why: Recurring qualified verdict on Judah's kings.

2-kings-15:4:1.summary: Identical formula about not removing the high places, applied to Jotham.

2-kings-15:4:6.summary: Asa “did not remove the high places,” the same qualification of a good king.

2-kings-15:4:0.summary: Hezekiah “removed the high places,” the reform Azariah failed to make.
2-kings-15:4:0.why: Shows the reform finally carried out.

2-kings-15:4:2.summary: Jehoshaphat removed the high places and groves from Judah, unlike Azariah.

2-kings-15:4:3.summary: Josiah cleansed Judah of the high places, the reform left undone here.

2-kings-15:4:4.summary: Hezekiah removed the high places and centralized incense at one altar, contrasting with incense burned at high places here.

2-kings-15:4:5.summary: Jehoshaphat did what was right in the Lord's eyes; the shown verse lacks the high-places qualification.

2-kings-15:4:7.summary: “The high places were not removed, and the people were still sacrificing and burning incense,” the same formula.

2-kings-15:5:0.summary: The leper “shall dwell apart,” explaining why the leprous king lived in a separate house.

2-kings-15:5:1.summary: Miriam set apart outside the camp for leprosy loosely parallels the king's separation.

2-kings-15:5:2.summary: Judgment given to “the king's son” loosely fits Jotham judging the people for his father.

2-kings-15:5:3.summary: Miriam struck “leprous as snow” by the Lord parallels the Lord touching the king with leprosy.

2-kings-15:5:4.summary: Gehazi is afflicted with leprosy for life as divine judgment, as the king was leprous until death.

2-kings-15:5:6.summary: David administering judgment for his people loosely parallels Jotham judging the people.

2-kings-15:5:7.summary: David's curse on Joab's house mentions leprosy only incidentally.

2-kings-15:5:8.summary: Absalom seeking to judge the people's cases shares only the theme of administering judgment.

2-kings-15:5:9.summary: The law on the affliction of leprosy gives general background to the king's condition.

2-kings-15:5:10.summary: Lepers kept outside the city loosely parallel the king's separation.

2-kings-15:5:11.summary: God not honoring the powerful has no specific connection to the king's leprosy.

2-kings-15:5:12.summary: Solomon asks for a heart to judge God's people, loosely like Jotham judging the people.

2-kings-15:5:13.summary: Solomon's judgment shows a king carrying out justice, a general parallel.

2-kings-15:6:0.summary: Amaziah's closing formula, “the rest of … deeds … are these not written” in Judah's chronicles, matches exactly.

2-kings-15:6:1.summary: Chronicles details Uzziah's (Azariah's) victories and building works, the deeds summarized here.
2-kings-15:6:1.why: Fills in the deeds this verse omits.

2-kings-15:7:1.summary: Isaiah's vision dates to “the year that King Oziah died,” the death of Azariah recorded here.
2-kings-15:7:1.why: Links the king's death to Isaiah's call.

2-kings-15:8:0.summary: Jeroboam's death and Azariah's accession frame the synchronism dating Zechariah's reign.

2-kings-15:8:1.summary: Jeroboam became king after Joash, the father Zechariah succeeded.

2-kings-15:8:2.summary: Azariah's accession anchors the synchronism in his thirty-eighth year.
2-kings-15:8:2.why: Identifies the Judean king of the synchronism.

2-kings-15:9:0.summary: He did evil and did not turn from “the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin,” the same formula.

2-kings-15:9:2.summary: Jehu, Zechariah's ancestor, “did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat,” the same formula.

2-kings-15:9:3.summary: Joash, Zechariah's grandfather, did evil and did not turn from Jeroboam's sins, matching “as his fathers had done.”

2-kings-15:9:4.summary: Jehu did not turn from Jeroboam's sins, the golden heifers, the same sin continued by his descendant.

2-kings-15:10:4.summary: Sellum son of Jabis is himself struck down and killed by Manaem a month later.

2-kings-15:10:0.summary: Jezebel calls Jehu a murderer of his master, a general parallel of regicide.

2-kings-15:10:1.summary: Jehu's killing of Joram founded the dynasty that ends with Zechariah's assassination.
2-kings-15:10:1.why: Start of the dynasty that ends here.

2-kings-15:10:2.summary: Baasha killing his predecessor and reigning is a general regicide parallel.

2-kings-15:10:3.summary: Zimri “conspired against him … struck him, put him to death, and reigned in his place,” the same usurpation formula.

2-kings-15:10:5.summary: Hoshea conspired, struck Pekah, put him to death and became king in his place, the same formula.

2-kings-15:10:6.summary: Pekah conspired, struck the king, put him to death and became king in his place, the same formula.

2-kings-15:10:7.summary: “I will rise against Jeroboam's house with a sword” is fulfilled when Jeroboam's son is struck down.

2-kings-15:10:8.summary: God would avenge Jezreel upon Jehu's house, fulfilled in the killing of Zechariah, Jehu's last descendant to reign.

2-kings-15:11:0.summary: Jeroboam's closing formula cites the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel, as for his son.

2-kings-15:12:1.summary: Zechariah says God’s words to the prophets overtook the fathers; only the general idea of God’s word coming true is shared.
2-kings-15:12:1.why: General principle of the prophetic word fulfilled.

2-kings-15:12:2.summary: Joash dies and Jeroboam “sat on his throne,” one of Jehu’s descendants whose reigns fulfil the promise of four generations.
2-kings-15:12:2.why: Traces the Jehu dynasty the promise covered.

2-kings-15:12:3.summary: John notes Scripture being fulfilled at the cross; only the general idea of a spoken word coming to pass links them.

2-kings-15:12:4.summary: Jesus says His words will not pass away; shares only the general reliability of the divine word.

2-kings-15:12:5.summary: Soldiers casting lots fulfil a Scripture; the link is only the generic fulfillment idea.

2-kings-15:12:6.summary: Joash son of Jehoahaz becomes king over Israel, another generation of Jehu’s line on the throne.
2-kings-15:12:6.why: Documents a generation in the promised dynasty.

2-kings-15:12:7.summary: Peter says Scripture had to be fulfilled about Judas; only the general fulfillment idea is shared.

2-kings-15:12:8.summary: Records Jeroboam’s death, a Jehu descendant, but the shown text names Azariah, not Zechariah, as successor.
2-kings-15:12:8.why: Background on the dynasty’s third generation.

2-kings-15:12:9.summary: Jehu carries out the Lord’s oracle against Ahab’s house; related Jehu narrative but not the promise of four generations.
2-kings-15:12:9.why: Shows Jehu as agent of fulfilled prophecy.

2-kings-15:12:10.summary: “The Scripture cannot be broken” shares only the general theme of God’s word standing.

2-kings-15:12:11.summary: Jehoahaz son of Jehu becomes king in Samaria, the first generation of the promised succession.

2-kings-15:12:12.summary: “Having spoken, shall He not act?” states the principle that God carries out His word.

2-kings-15:12:13.summary: “It is the word of the Lord that He spoke” closes Jezebel’s death with the same fulfillment formula used in the Jehu story.
2-kings-15:12:13.why: Same fulfillment pattern in Jehu’s career.

2-kings-15:12:14.summary: Jehu declares nothing of the Lord’s word will fall to the ground; the Lord “has done all that He spoke.”
2-kings-15:12:14.why: Jehu’s own testimony to fulfilled prophecy.

2-kings-15:13:0.summary: Azariah king of Judah, whose regnal years date Sellum’s accession, begins his reign here.

2-kings-15:13:1.summary: Men of bloodshed will not live out half their days; loosely fits Sellum’s one-month reign after murder.
2-kings-15:13:1.why: Moral lens on a short violent reign.

2-kings-15:13:2.summary: Matthew lists Uzziah, but the shown text never equates him with Azariah named in the source.
2-kings-15:13:2.why: Places the Judean king in Christ’s genealogy.

2-kings-15:13:3.summary: Omri’s founding of Samaria (Semeron) explains the capital where Sellum reigned; only the place is shared.

2-kings-15:13:4.summary: Zimri “reigned seven days,” a parallel usurper whose reign is likewise measured in days.

2-kings-15:13:5.summary: Unjust wealth vomited up has no link to Sellum’s accession or reign.

2-kings-15:13:6.summary: A man charged with murder will not be secure; only a loose fit for an assassin’s brief reign.

2-kings-15:13:7.summary: Zechariah’s accession in Azariah’s thirty-eighth year directly precedes Sellum’s in the thirty-ninth.

2-kings-15:13:8.summary: The Greek-based proverb speaks of disputes arising from sins, not many rulers, so the expected link is absent.
2-kings-15:13:8.why: Greek wording drops the rulers theme.

2-kings-15:14:0.summary: The child dies as the woman enters Sarira; no shared name or event with Manaem going up from Tharsila.
2-kings-15:14:0.why: Place link not carried in this text.

2-kings-15:14:1.summary: Omri “went up” to besiege Tirzah in a coup; similar usurper pattern, but the place names differ from Tharsila.

2-kings-15:14:2.summary: Baasha’s accession in Tirzah shares no name or event with the shown text of Manaem’s coup.

2-kings-15:14:3.summary: Zimri conspires against and replaces Elah; a general pattern of assassination of Israel’s kings.

2-kings-15:14:4.summary: Baasha returning to Tirzah has no link to Manaem killing Sellum.

2-kings-15:14:5.summary: Zimri’s seven-day reign parallels short usurper reigns, but the source verse is about Manaem’s coup, not reign length.

2-kings-15:15:1.summary: The “rest of … acts … written in the Book” formula, but for Rehoboam and the annals of Judah.

2-kings-15:15:2.summary: Same concluding formula citing the annals of the kings of Israel, applied to Ahab.

2-kings-15:15:3.summary: Near-identical closing formula for Zechariah, the king Sellum killed: “written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.”

2-kings-15:16:0.summary: Elisha foresees Hazael will “tear open their pregnant women,” the same atrocity Manaem commits.

2-kings-15:16:1.summary: Solomon’s peaceful rule beyond the River contains no shared place name with Thersa in this text.

2-kings-15:16:2.summary: Hosea foretells Samaria’s “pregnant women will be ripped open,” echoing Manaem’s brutality.
2-kings-15:16:2.why: Prophetic echo of the same atrocity.

2-kings-15:16:3.summary: Ammon is condemned because “they ripped open the pregnant women,” the same crime.
2-kings-15:16:3.why: Shows how God judges this atrocity.

2-kings-15:19:0.summary: Amaziah has the kingdom “firmly in his hand”; only loosely echoes Phul’s hand being with Manaem.
2-kings-15:19:0.why: Partial verbal echo on securing rule.

2-kings-15:19:1.summary: “Phaloch king of Assour” is Phul, named alongside Thaglathphalnasar in the deportation of the Transjordan tribes.

2-kings-15:19:2.summary: Hezekiah strips gilded doors to pay the Assyrian king; a later instance of tribute to Assyria.

2-kings-15:19:3.summary: Cursed is one who hopes in a human; general warning applicable to buying Assyria’s support.
2-kings-15:19:3.why: Moral lens on trusting foreign power.

2-kings-15:19:4.summary: Ephraim “went up to the Assyrians … loved gifts,” matching Manaem’s silver paid to Assyria’s king.

2-kings-15:19:5.summary: Hoshea becomes tributary to Assyria; a later instance of an Israelite king paying an Assyrian king.

2-kings-15:19:6.summary: Joash sends temple gold to Hazael to make him withdraw; similar buying-off of a foreign king.
2-kings-15:19:6.why: Parallel pattern of paying off invaders.

2-kings-15:19:7.summary: Ahaz sends silver and gold as gifts to the Assyrian king; a similar payment for support.

2-kings-15:19:8.summary: The oracle on Zebulun, Naphtali and Galilee has no link to Phul or Manaem’s payment in the shown text.

2-kings-15:19:9.summary: Ephraim carried to the Assyrians “as guest-gifts for King Jarim”; loosely recalls gifts to Assyria.
2-kings-15:19:9.why: Prophetic irony on gifts to Assyria.

2-kings-15:19:10.summary: “Ephraim went to the Assyrians” seeking help that could not heal, mirroring Manaem buying Phul’s support.
2-kings-15:19:10.why: Hosea’s verdict on seeking Assyrian aid.

2-kings-15:20:0.summary: Boaz is “a man mighty in strength,” sharing only the phrase, not any event.

2-kings-15:20:1.summary: Hoshea pays manaa to Assyria’s king; a later tribute, not Manaem’s levy.

2-kings-15:20:2.summary: Joakim “assessed the land” to raise silver for Pharaoh, a close parallel to Manaem levying silver from Israel for Assyria.
2-kings-15:20:2.why: Same method of funding foreign tribute.

2-kings-15:20:3.summary: Thaglathphellasar later comes and deports Israel; shows Assyria did return despite this withdrawal.

2-kings-15:20:4.summary: Job’s great wealth has no link to Manaem’s levy on Israel’s wealthy men.

2-kings-15:20:5.summary: Barzillai being wealthy shares only the idea of rich men, not the tribute.
