2-kings-15:20:6.summary: Hezekiah pays silver to the Assyrian king to make him “withdraw,” parallel to Assyria leaving after Manaem’s payment; range truncated.

2-kings-15:23:0.summary: Nadab also reigned over Israel two years; shares only reign length.

2-kings-15:23:1.summary: Elah reigned two years; shares only the length of reign.

2-kings-15:23:2.summary: The fall of the ungodly is a generic proverb with no tie to Phakeias.

2-kings-15:23:3.summary: Ahaziah became king over Israel in Samaria with a synchronism and reigned two years; same formula, different king.

2-kings-15:23:4.summary: Amon of Judah reigned two years; only reign length is shared.

2-kings-15:24:0.summary: Identical verdict on Zechariah: did evil and did not turn from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat.

2-kings-15:25:0.summary: Phakee son of Romelia, king of Israel, kills 120,000 in Judah; same usurper.

2-kings-15:25:1.summary: Sellum “conspired against him, struck him, and put him to death,” the same coup formula.

2-kings-15:25:2.summary: Zimri, a cavalry commander, “conspired against him,” paralleling an officer’s coup against his king.

2-kings-15:25:3.summary: Jehu, an army commander, “conspired against Joram,” another officer’s coup.

2-kings-15:25:4.summary: A word for the commander Jehu; relates only to the general idea of army officers seizing power.

2-kings-15:27:8.summary: Phakee son of Romelias is sent with Raasson against Judah.

2-kings-15:27:0.summary: Phakee son of Romelias, king of Israel, joins Raasson against Jerusalem.

2-kings-15:27:1.summary: Phakeias son of Manaem, whom Phakee killed and replaced, began in Azariah’s fiftieth year.

2-kings-15:27:2.summary: The “two smoking firebrand logs” refer to the kings of Aram and Israel, but the shown verse names neither.

2-kings-15:27:3.summary: Same accession formula dated by Azariah for Zechariah; a different king.

2-kings-15:27:4.summary: “The head of Somoron Romelias’s son” names Phakee as Samaria’s ruler.

2-kings-15:27:5.summary: Sellum’s accession formula dated by Azariah; a different king.

2-kings-15:27:6.summary: Phakee son of Romelia, king of Israel, kills 120,000 Judeans.

2-kings-15:27:7.summary: Azariah reigned fifty-two years, so Phakee’s accession falls in Azariah’s last year.

2-kings-15:28:0.summary: Jehoahaz “did evil … followed the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat”; same verdict formula.

2-kings-15:28:2.summary: Manaem’s verdict is word-for-word identical: did not turn from any of the sins of Jeroboam.

2-kings-15:28:3.summary: Zechariah did evil and did not turn from Jeroboam’s sins; same formula.

2-kings-15:28:1.summary: “They did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam’s house, who caused Israel to sin.”

2-kings-15:28:4.summary: Manasseh “did evil in the Lord’s eyes,” but with the nations’ abominations, not Jeroboam’s sins.

2-kings-15:29:3.summary: Ahaz appeals to Thaglathphellasar king of the Assyrians against Israel’s king.

2-kings-15:29:0.summary: Thaglathphalnasar deports Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh, a parallel record of his deportations.
2-kings-15:29:0.why: Chronicles’ account of the same campaign.

2-kings-15:29:2.summary: Ben-Hadad strikes “Ain … Abelmaa … the land of Naphtali,” the same northern towns.

2-kings-15:29:4.summary: Kedesh in Galilee in Naphtali; shares Galilee and Naphtali, though the source lists “Kenez.”

2-kings-15:29:5.summary: “Abel and Beth-maacah,” the town the source calls Abelbaithamaacha.

2-kings-15:29:6.summary: Jabin reigned in Hazor; the source spells it “Asor,” so the place link is only implied.

2-kings-15:29:7.summary: “Ion, Dan, Abelmain, and all Naphtali’s” districts parallel the towns taken by Assyria.

2-kings-15:29:8.summary: Kedesh and Hazor in Naphtali’s allotment; spellings differ from the source’s Kenez and Asor.

2-kings-15:29:9.summary: Jabin king of Hazor; only the place (Asor in the source) is shared.

2-kings-15:29:10.summary: Thaglathphalnasar king of Assour deported Beera of Reuben.

2-kings-15:29:11.summary: Deuteronomy threatens scattering among the nations; the deportation is a partial fulfilment.

2-kings-15:29:12.summary: Gilead given to Machir; only the region is shared.

2-kings-15:29:13.summary: Reuben and Gad saw the land of Gilead; place only.

2-kings-15:29:14.summary: “Israel was deported from its land to the Assyrians,” completing the deportation begun here.

2-kings-15:29:15.summary: God will desolate the land before enemies; general covenant curse.

2-kings-15:29:16.summary: Gileadites ravaged by Ammon; only Gilead is shared.

2-kings-15:29:17.summary: Moses gives Gilead to Machir; region only.

2-kings-15:29:18.summary: Joshua captures Hazor; place only, spelled Asor in the source.

2-kings-15:29:19.summary: Isaiah addresses the “land of Naphtali … Galilee of the nations” with hope of light, the region Assyria just took.
2-kings-15:29:19.why: Prophetic hope for the devastated north.

2-kings-15:29:20.summary: Thaglath-phellasar king of Assour comes against Ahaz; same Assyrian king.

2-kings-15:29:21.summary: Solomon gives Hiram twenty cities in Galilee; region only.

2-kings-15:29:22.summary: Perishing among the nations in enemies’ land; general exile curse.

2-kings-15:29:23.summary: The Lord shaves with the razor of “the king of the Assyrians”; general image of Assyrian judgment.

2-kings-15:29:25.summary: Damascus brutalized Gilead; only Gilead is shared.

2-kings-15:29:26.summary: A land deserted and overturned by foreigners; general image of invasion.

2-kings-15:29:27.summary: Matthew quotes “land of Naphtali … Galilee of the nations,” the region Assyria conquered, via Isaiah.
2-kings-15:29:27.why: Shows the region’s later hope in Christ.

2-kings-15:29:28.summary: “The king of Hazor” in Joshua’s list; place only.

2-kings-15:29:29.summary: Warning of perishing from the land and scattering among nations; general covenant threat.

2-kings-15:29:30.summary: Ephraim’s boundary reaches Janoka, similar to Janoch, though not clearly the same town.

2-kings-15:29:31.summary: Defeat and scattering among kingdoms; general covenant curse.

2-kings-15:30:5.summary: Phakee himself had “conspired against him … put him to death and became king in his place”; now the same befalls him.
2-kings-15:30:5.why: The usurper meets the usurper’s fate.

2-kings-15:30:8.summary: Ahaz’s accession is dated to the seventeenth year of Phakee son of Romelias.

2-kings-15:30:9.summary: Jotham son of Azariah, by whose years Hoshea’s coup is dated, begins his reign in Phakee’s second year.

2-kings-15:30:1.summary: Ahaz sends to Assyria’s king for help; related period but not Hoshea’s coup.

2-kings-15:30:2.summary: Phakee son of Romelia, king of Israel, strikes Judah; same king later overthrown.

2-kings-15:30:3.summary: “Samaria cast off her king” loosely fits the repeated overthrow of Israel’s kings.

2-kings-15:30:4.summary: Phakee son of Romelias with Raasson attacks Jerusalem; range truncated.

2-kings-15:30:6.summary: Sellum “conspired against him, struck him, and put him to death … became king in his place”; same coup formula.

2-kings-15:30:7.summary: Isaiah names “Romelias’s son,” Phakee, as a king the people wanted.

2-kings-15:30:10.summary: “Israel’s king was cast off”; general prophetic judgment on Israel’s kingship.
2-kings-15:30:10.why: Loose fit for the king’s fall.

2-kings-15:30:11.summary: “We have no king”; general commentary on failing kingship.

2-kings-15:32:8.summary: Phakee son of Romelias, in whose second year Jotham began, becomes king of Israel.

2-kings-15:32:0.summary: Genealogy lists “Azariah his son, Joathan his son,” the same father and son.

2-kings-15:32:2.summary: Azariah son of Amaziah, Jotham’s father, becomes king of Judah.

2-kings-15:32:3.summary: “Uzziah begot Jotham” places Jotham in Matthew’s genealogy of Christ.

2-kings-15:32:4.summary: Phakeias’s accession formula, dated by Azariah; same series, different king.

2-kings-15:32:5.summary: Manaem’s accession dated by Azariah; same series, different king.

2-kings-15:32:6.summary: Sellum’s accession dated by Azariah; same series, different king.

2-kings-15:32:7.summary: Azariah, Jotham’s father, is made king at sixteen in place of Amaziah.

2-kings-15:32:9.summary: Chronicles’ parallel account of Jotham’s reign: twenty-five years old, sixteen years, mother Jerousa daughter of Sadok; range truncated.

2-kings-15:34:1.summary: “He did what was right in the Lord’s eyes, in accordance with everything his father … had done,” said of Azariah.
2-kings-15:34:1.why: Same verdict for father and son.

2-kings-15:34:0.summary: Uzziah (Ozias) “did what was right … according to everything his father” did; same formula for the father named in the source.

2-kings-15:35:3.summary: Identical clause: “Only he did not remove the high places; the people still sacrificed and burned incense.”
2-kings-15:35:3.why: Same reservation for father and son.

2-kings-15:35:0.summary: The king enters through the “Inner Gate”; the Greek-based wording does not match the upper gate Jotham built.

2-kings-15:35:1.summary: “Yet the high places were not removed, and the people were still sacrificing and burning incense.”

2-kings-15:35:2.summary: Hezekiah is said to have removed the high places; a later contrast, though voiced in the Assyrian taunt.
2-kings-15:35:2.why: Shows when high places were removed.

2-kings-15:35:5.summary: Hezekiah “removed the high places,” the reform Jotham failed to make.

2-kings-15:36:0.summary: Azariah’s closing formula matches, and his son Jotham “became king in his place.”

2-kings-15:37:0.summary: “Raasson king of Aram and Phakee son of Romelias” go up against Jerusalem; same coalition.
2-kings-15:37:0.why: Isaiah’s account of the same threat.

2-kings-15:37:2.summary: God as turmoil to Ephraim and a goad to Judah; general judgment on both kingdoms.

2-kings-15:37:3.summary: The Lord is “sending” Nebuchadnezzar; shares only the idea of God sending a foreign king.

2-kings-15:37:4.summary: “I am beginning to bring harm” echoes the Lord beginning to send enemies, but concerns a later judgment.

2-kings-15:37:5.summary: “In those days the Lord began cutting down within Israel” uses the same opening and idea of God beginning judgment through Syria.
2-kings-15:37:5.why: Same formula of God using Syria.

2-kings-15:37:6.summary: Assyria as the rod God sends against a lawless nation; general theme of God sending enemies.

2-kings-15:37:7.summary: “When these things begin to happen” shares only the verb, not the event.

2-kings-15:37:8.summary: Phakee son of Romelia kills 120,000 in Judah because they abandoned the Lord.
2-kings-15:37:8.why: Shows the result of this sending.

2-kings-15:37:9.summary: God “sent upon them” wrath and affliction; generic image of divine sending.

2-kings-15:37:10.summary: God will “begin” judgment on Eli’s house; only the verb is shared.

2-kings-15:37:11.summary: God sending fishermen and hunters; only the verb “sending” is shared.

2-kings-15:37:12.summary: Hezekiah’s illness and recovery has no link to Raasson and Phakee; range truncated.

2-kings-15:37:13.summary: Enemies “whom the Lord shall send against you”; covenant curse behind the attack.

2-kings-15:37:14.summary: Aram’s head is Damascus and Ephraim will cease; part of Isaiah’s oracle on the coalition, though no kings named here.

2-kings-15:38:0.summary: Seeking a virgin to warm David shares only the word “lie,” not burial with the fathers.

2-kings-15:38:1.summary: Rehoboam “slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the City of David”; same formula, different king.

2-kings-15:38:2.summary: Ahaz, Jotham’s successor, begins his reign at twenty.

2-kings-15:38:4.summary: “Jotham begot Ahaz” confirms the succession in Matthew’s genealogy.

2-kings-15:38:5.summary: David sleeping with his fathers and his seed raised up; the dynastic promise behind each succession.

2-kings-15:38:6.summary: “Ahaz his son” in the Davidic genealogy follows Joathan.

2-kings-15:38:7.summary: “Ahaz son of Jotham, king of Judah, became king,” the succession stated here.

2-kings-15:15:0.summary: 1 Kings 14:19 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-15:15:0.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-15:15:0.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-15:38:3.summary: 1 Kings 14:20 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-15:38:3.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-15:38:3.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-16:1:1.summary: Phakee son of Romelias’s reign, by which Ahaz’s accession is dated; range truncated.

2-kings-16:1:4.summary: Jotham, Ahaz’s father, began in Phakee’s second year and reigned sixteen years.

2-kings-16:1:0.summary: Isaiah prophesied in the reign of “Achaz,” the same king.

2-kings-16:1:2.summary: Micah prophesied in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah.

2-kings-16:1:3.summary: Chronicles’ parallel opening of Ahaz’s reign: twenty years old, sixteen years, idolatry and fire.

2-kings-16:1:6.summary: Hosea prophesied in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah.

2-kings-16:1:7.summary: “In the days of Achaz, son of Joatham,” Raasson and Phakee attack Jerusalem.

2-kings-16:2:1.summary: Walking “as your father David walked” is the standard Ahaz failed to meet.

2-kings-16:2:2.summary: Jehoshaphat walked in his father’s earlier ways and avoided idols; loose contrast.

2-kings-16:2:3.summary: Josiah walked “in the ways of his father David,” the opposite of Ahaz.

2-kings-16:2:4.summary: Solomon “did not walk after the Lord as David his father did,” the same failure formula.

2-kings-16:2:5.summary: Abijam’s heart was “not whole … like the heart of David his father”; parallel negative verdict.

2-kings-16:2:6.summary: Hezekiah, Ahaz’s son, “did what was right … in accordance with everything his father David had done.”

2-kings-16:2:7.summary: Josiah walked in every way of his father David; general contrast.

2-kings-16:2:8.summary: Condition to walk as David walked; the standard Ahaz did not keep.

2-kings-16:2:9.summary: Amaziah did right “though not like his father David”; partial echo of the David comparison.

2-kings-16:2:10.summary: Hezekiah did right “according to everything David his father had done,” contrasting with his father Ahaz.

2-kings-16:2:11.summary: Azariah did right like his father Amaziah; same formula, no David comparison.

2-kings-16:2:12.summary: Jotham, Ahaz’s father, “did what was right in the Lord’s eyes,” which Ahaz did not.

2-kings-16:3:2.summary: “According to the abominations of the nations whom the Lord removed before the Israelites” repeated for Manasseh.

2-kings-16:3:0.summary: Nations’ abominations: “they burn their sons and their daughters with fire.”

2-kings-16:3:1.summary: Not giving seed “to serve a ruler”; the Greek-based wording obscures the fire/Molech link.

2-kings-16:3:3.summary: Manasseh’s “evil abominations, worse than … the Amorite”; partial echo of nations’ abominations.

2-kings-16:3:4.summary: Israel “sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons,” the practice Ahaz adopted.

2-kings-16:3:5.summary: “They led their sons and daughters through fire,” the same practice listed among Israel’s sins.

2-kings-16:3:6.summary: The Greek-based verse speaks of defiling gifts, without the passing-through-fire wording the label assumes.
2-kings-16:3:6.why: Greek wording drops the fire link.

2-kings-16:3:7.summary: Manasseh “passed his children through fire,” repeating Ahaz’s practice.
2-kings-16:3:7.why: Same sin by a later king.

2-kings-16:3:8.summary: Manasseh “led his sons through fire,” same wording.
2-kings-16:3:8.why: Same sin by a later king.

2-kings-16:3:9.summary: Ahab followed abominations “according to all that the Amorites had done, whom the Lord destroyed before” Israel.

2-kings-16:3:10.summary: Ahaziah “walked in the way of Ahab’s house”; similar Judean king following Israel’s way.

2-kings-16:3:11.summary: Israel “mixed with the nations and learned their works”; general cause of such abominations.

2-kings-16:3:12.summary: Death penalty for giving seed “unto a ruler”; Greek-based wording obscures the Molech-fire link.

2-kings-16:3:13.summary: Judah practiced “the abominations of the nations the Lord had removed before the sons of Israel.”

2-kings-16:3:14.summary: Jerusalem surpasses others in lawless ways; general indictment.

2-kings-16:3:15.summary: Joram “walked in the way of the kings of Israel,” the same charge against a Judean king.

2-kings-16:3:16.summary: Jerusalem “slaughtered your children and gave them over,” describing child sacrifice.

2-kings-16:3:17.summary: Forbids one who “purifies his son or his daughter by fire.”

2-kings-16:3:18.summary: Manasseh followed “all the abominations of the nations whom the Lord had destroyed before the sons of Israel.”

2-kings-16:3:19.summary: They offered sons and daughters to Molech in the Valley of Hinnom, “this abomination.”
2-kings-16:3:19.why: Location and nature of the practice.

2-kings-16:3:20.summary: Ahab walked “in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat” and worse; general parallel.

2-kings-16:3:21.summary: Josiah defiles Tapheth so no man would “lead his son … through fire to Moloch.”

2-kings-16:3:22.summary: Ahaziah walked in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat; general parallel.

2-kings-16:3:24.summary: Jeroboam’s golden heifers, the origin of “the way of Jeroboam” referred to here.

2-kings-16:3:25.summary: God defiles them through gifts when passing every firstborn; loose reference to child offering.

2-kings-16:4:7.summary: “The people still sacrificed and burned incense at the high places”; same wording.

2-kings-16:4:0.summary: Places of the nations’ worship “upon the hills, and under the leafy tree.”

2-kings-16:4:1.summary: High places “on every high hill and under every shady tree,” same idolatrous setting.

2-kings-16:4:2.summary: Pagan rites in gardens; general illicit worship.

2-kings-16:4:3.summary: Defiling rites in tombs; general illicit worship.

2-kings-16:4:4.summary: Idols “beneath leafy trees” and sacrifices on a “high and lofty mountain.”

2-kings-16:4:6.summary: They saw “every high hill and every shady tree” and sacrificed there; Abama (high place).

2-kings-16:5:3.summary: Raasson and Phakee son of Romelias went up against Jerusalem “but they could not” prevail; range truncated.
2-kings-16:5:3.why: Isaiah’s account of the same siege.

2-kings-16:5:1.summary: The nations’ counsel will be scattered because “God is with us”; general assurance in this crisis.

2-kings-16:5:2.summary: A child’s rule upon David’s throne; part of Isaiah’s message in this era, but no direct shared element.

2-kings-16:5:4.summary: The Emmanuel sign was given to Ahaz in this crisis, but the shown verse names no one.
2-kings-16:5:4.why: The sign given during this siege.

2-kings-16:5:5.summary: Names “Raasson and Romelias’s son,” the two attacking kings.

2-kings-16:5:6.summary: Chronicles’ parallel: Syria’s king and Phakee strike Judah; range truncated.

2-kings-16:5:7.summary: For David’s sake God preserves Jerusalem; explains why the attack failed only in general terms.

2-kings-16:5:8.summary: David to have a place in Jerusalem always; general preservation theme.

2-kings-16:6:2.summary: Uzziah “built Ailath; he restored it to Judah,” the town now lost.

2-kings-16:6:1.summary: Israel passed by “Ailon” on the Arabah road near Edom; likely the same area.

2-kings-16:6:3.summary: Ezion-geber “near Elath … in the land of Edom,” the same port town.
2-kings-16:6:3.why: Locates Ailath and its Edom link.

2-kings-16:7:0.summary: Thaglathphellasar king of the Assyrians already invaded Israel’s north.

2-kings-16:7:2.summary: “I am yours” is a similar vassal submission, but to Syria under Ahab, not Assyria.

2-kings-16:7:3.summary: “Assur will certainly not save us” answers Ahaz’s plea to Assyria to “save me.”

2-kings-16:7:4.summary: Ben-Hadad’s men submit as “your servant”; general vassal pleading.

2-kings-16:7:5.summary: “Do not trust in rulers … who have no salvation”; general warning fitting Ahaz’s appeal.

2-kings-16:7:6.summary: Thaglathphalnasar king of Assour, the same Assyrian king, deports the Transjordan tribes.

2-kings-16:7:7.summary: Watching for “a nation that does not save”; general futility of foreign help.

2-kings-16:7:8.summary: Thaglath-phellasar came against Ahaz and struck him; Chronicles’ parallel outcome.

2-kings-16:7:9.summary: Cursed is one who hopes in a human; general warning against Ahaz’s reliance on Assyria.

2-kings-16:8:0.summary: Joash sends gold “found in the treasuries of the Lord’s house and the king’s house” to a foreign king.

2-kings-16:8:7.summary: Asa took gold and silver “from the treasuries of the Lord’s house and the king’s house” and sent them to Syria’s king.

2-kings-16:8:1.summary: Hezekiah gave silver “in the Lord’s house and in the treasuries of the king’s house” to the Assyrian king.

2-kings-16:8:2.summary: Falling into one’s own pit has no specific link to Ahaz sending treasure.

2-kings-16:8:4.summary: The Lord brings the king of the Assyrians over Judea; the consequence of Ahaz’s alliance in general terms.
2-kings-16:8:4.why: Prophetic outcome of reliance on Assyria.

2-kings-16:8:5.summary: God will bring “the king of the Assyrians” on Ahaz’s house; general judgment on the alliance.

2-kings-16:8:6.summary: Ahaz further dismantles temple furnishings “because of the king of the Assyrians.”

2-kings-16:9:0.summary: The Greek-based text says Syrians came “from a pit,” losing the place link the label assumes.
2-kings-16:9:0.why: Greek wording drops the place link.

2-kings-16:9:1.summary: Elamites with quivers and horsemen; no shared name or event in this Greek-based text.

2-kings-16:9:2.summary: Amos foretells God will “shatter Damascus’s bars” and Syria “will be taken captive,” fulfilled here.

2-kings-16:9:3.summary: Syria’s king brings Judean captives to Damascus; background to Ahaz’s appeal, not the capture of Damascus.

2-kings-16:9:4.summary: Ahaz gave to Assour’s king “but it brought him no help,” a contrasting assessment of the same payment.

2-kings-16:9:5.summary: The land of “the two kings” will be forsaken, fulfilled as Damascus falls and Raasson dies.

2-kings-16:9:6.summary: God scatters enemies rising against Zion; general deliverance theme.

2-kings-16:10:14.summary: Thaglathphellasar king of the Assyrians, whom Ahaz goes to meet, had invaded Israel.

2-kings-16:10:0.summary: “Do not be conformed to this age”; general warning fitting Ahaz copying a foreign altar.

2-kings-16:10:1.summary: Desire at the sight of her eyes leads to sending messengers to foreigners; loose image of foreign seduction.

2-kings-16:10:2.summary: Isaiah names “Uriah” as a reliable witness, likely the same priest.

2-kings-16:10:3.summary: Warning not to ask “How do these nations serve their gods? I also will do so,” exactly Ahaz’s act.

2-kings-16:10:4.summary: Defiled by their works and practices; general apostasy.

2-kings-16:10:5.summary: Ransom from futile ancestral conduct has no specific link to the Damascus altar.

2-kings-16:10:6.summary: David gives Solomon “the pattern” from the Lord’s hand, contrasting with Ahaz sending a pattern from Damascus.

2-kings-16:10:7.summary: “Do not learn according to the nations’ ways”; general warning.

2-kings-16:10:8.summary: Ezekiel draws the house’s structure as God commands; loose contrast with a foreign design.

2-kings-16:10:9.summary: Work done “the way the Lord commanded Moses”; loose contrast with a design copied from Damascus.

2-kings-16:10:10.summary: David gives “the pattern of the temple,” contrasting with Ahaz’s altar pattern from Damascus.

2-kings-16:10:11.summary: Worship by “human commandments”; general critique of man-made worship.

2-kings-16:10:12.summary: Kings set their structures beside God’s house and profaned it; loose fit for altering the temple.

2-kings-16:10:13.summary: Nullifying God’s word by tradition; general critique.

2-kings-16:10:15.summary: Moses builds an altar at Sinai; only the altar-building idea is shared.

2-kings-16:10:16.summary: Ahaz seeks “the gods of Damascus” and makes altars everywhere; Chronicles’ parallel.

2-kings-16:11:0.summary: Isaiah’s witness “Uriah,” likely the priest who built Ahaz’s altar.

2-kings-16:11:1.summary: Priests set aside God’s law and profane holy things; general priestly failure.

2-kings-16:11:2.summary: Pleasing humans versus God; general reflection on Uriah’s compliance.

2-kings-16:11:3.summary: Priest and prophet defiled in God’s house; general priestly corruption.

2-kings-16:11:4.summary: Priests turned from the way and corrupted Levi’s covenant; general priestly failure.

2-kings-16:11:5.summary: Elders did “as Jezebel had sent to them”; similar compliance with royal written orders.

2-kings-16:11:6.summary: Azarias the priest “stood against King Uzziah,” unlike Uriah who complied with Ahaz.

2-kings-16:11:7.summary: Ephraim began “to follow worthless things”; general apostasy.

2-kings-16:11:8.summary: Priests forgot God’s law; general priestly failure.

2-kings-16:11:9.summary: All bow to Nebuchadnezzar’s image; general compliance with royal idolatry.

2-kings-16:12:0.summary: Uzziah entered the sanctuary to burn incense on the altar, a king usurping priestly altar service; range truncated.
2-kings-16:12:0.why: Earlier king overstepping at the altar.

2-kings-16:12:1.summary: Priests keep “every matter of the altar”; law behind the king’s approach; range truncated.

2-kings-16:12:2.summary: Jeroboam “stood at the altar to offer sacrifice” at his own illicit altar.

2-kings-16:12:3.summary: Ahaz made high places for foreign gods; related to his altar worship generally.

2-kings-16:12:4.summary: Ahaz sacrifices to “the gods of Damascus,” Chronicles’ account of this worship.

2-kings-16:13:0.summary: Law of the whole burnt offering; only the offering type is shared.

2-kings-16:14:0.summary: Solomon made “the bronze altar,” the same altar Ahaz moved aside.

2-kings-16:14:1.summary: Altar placed by the tent doors; general altar placement.

2-kings-16:14:2.summary: Command to place the altar by the tent doors; general altar placement.

2-kings-16:14:3.summary: “Between the sanctuary and the altar” echoes the space named here, in another event.

2-kings-16:14:4.summary: Uriah built the new altar from Ahaz’s Damascus model, the altar that displaced the bronze one.
2-kings-16:14:4.why: The altar that took its place.

2-kings-16:14:5.summary: “The bronze altar … before the Lord’s tent” of Beseleel; a predecessor altar, not Solomon’s.

2-kings-16:15:0.summary: One lamb “in the morning and … in the evening” with libation, the daily offerings Ahaz reassigns.

2-kings-16:15:1.summary: Solomon offers whole burnt offerings elsewhere because “the bronze altar before the Lord was too small.”
2-kings-16:15:1.why: Precedent for bypassing the bronze altar.

2-kings-16:15:2.summary: Hezekiah destroying the bronze serpent shares only the word bronze.

2-kings-16:15:3.summary: Priests pour sacrificial blood onto the altar; general sacrificial procedure; range truncated.

2-kings-16:15:4.summary: The continual whole burnt offering, one lamb in the morning and one toward evening; range truncated.

2-kings-16:15:5.summary: The sacrifice removed and an abomination set up; loose theme of corrupted worship.

2-kings-16:15:6.summary: Omens filling the land; the Greek-based source has the bronze altar “for the morning,” not for inquiry.
2-kings-16:15:6.why: Greek wording drops the divination link.

2-kings-16:15:7.summary: Defiling the sanctuary and removing the sacrifice; loose theme of corrupted worship.

2-kings-16:15:8.summary: “In the morning, when the sacrifice was going up”; only the morning sacrifice is shared.

2-kings-16:15:9.summary: The ruler’s burnt offerings and a daily morning burnt offering, paralleling the king’s and morning offerings.

2-kings-16:15:10.summary: Number of burnt offerings brought by the assembly; general offering theme.

2-kings-16:15:11.summary: The bronze altar moved to the north side, which Ahaz now reserves for himself.

2-kings-16:15:12.summary: Sacrifice and libation removed; loose theme of disrupted worship.

2-kings-16:15:13.summary: Inquiring by signs and rods; the Greek-based source has no inquiry wording.
2-kings-16:15:13.why: Greek wording drops the inquiry link.

2-kings-16:15:14.summary: Joseph’s divining cup; no divination appears in the Greek-based source.
2-kings-16:15:14.why: Greek wording drops the inquiry link.

2-kings-16:15:15.summary: Solomon offers whole burnt offerings on the altar; general royal sacrifice.

2-kings-16:15:16.summary: The king and all the people sacrificing; loosely parallels the king’s and people’s offerings.

2-kings-16:15:17.summary: David offers whole burnt and peace offerings; general royal sacrifice.

2-kings-16:15:18.summary: “The hour of the evening sacrifice”; only the evening offering is shared.

2-kings-16:15:19.summary: Manasseh’s omens and sorcery; the Greek-based source has no divination element.
2-kings-16:15:19.why: Greek wording drops the inquiry link.

2-kings-16:15:20.summary: Abundant burnt offerings and libations; general offering vocabulary.

2-kings-16:15:21.summary: Sin-offering procedure with blood at the altar; general sacrificial law; range truncated.

2-kings-16:15:22.summary: The ruler’s Sabbath and new-moon burnt offerings; loose royal offering parallel.

2-kings-16:16:0.summary: Uriah the priest acted “in accordance with everything King Ahaz” sent; same compliance.

2-kings-16:16:1.summary: Speaking to please God, not people; contrasts with Uriah’s obedience to the king.

2-kings-16:16:2.summary: Listening to God rather than men; contrasts with Uriah’s compliance.

2-kings-16:16:3.summary: “We must obey God rather than human beings”; general contrast to Uriah.

2-kings-16:16:4.summary: Cain, Balaam and Korah have no specific link to Uriah obeying Ahaz.

2-kings-16:17:0.summary: “The one Sea, and the twelve bronze calves beneath the Sea,” the same furnishing Ahaz moved.

2-kings-16:17:1.summary: Ahaz “removed the articles of the Lord’s house and cut them up”; Chronicles’ parallel.

2-kings-16:17:2.summary: The Chaldeans break “the mechonoth, and the bronze sea,” the same furnishings.
2-kings-16:17:2.why: Later fate of the same objects.

2-kings-16:17:3.summary: Solomon made ten mechonoth with basins and “the one sea and the twelve calves beneath it.”

2-kings-16:17:4.summary: Articles “King Ahaz defiled” are purified and restored under Hezekiah.

2-kings-16:18:0.summary: Solomon’s attendants’ seating shares only a word with the seat Ahaz built.

2-kings-16:18:1.summary: Guards at the king’s house gateway; no specific link to Ahaz’s altered entrance.

2-kings-16:18:2.summary: The ruler enters by the outer gate’s porch; loosely relates to the king’s outer entrance.

2-kings-16:19:0.summary: Same “are these not written” formula for Rehoboam; different king.

2-kings-16:19:1.summary: Azariah’s closing formula in the same series of Judah’s kings, near-identical wording.

2-kings-16:19:3.summary: Jotham’s death and “his son Ahaz became king in his place,” framing Ahaz’s reign.

2-kings-16:19:4.summary: Hezekiah’s closing formula, “are these not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.”

2-kings-16:19:5.summary: Jotham’s identical closing formula, for Ahaz’s father.

2-kings-16:20:7.summary: Genealogy: “Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son.”

2-kings-16:20:0.summary: Isaiah’s vision spans the reigns of Achaz and Hezekiah.

2-kings-16:20:2.summary: Micah prophesied in the days of Ahaz and Hezekiah.

2-kings-16:20:3.summary: “Hezekiah son of Ahaz, king of Judah, became king,” opening the next reign.

2-kings-16:20:4.summary: Hosea prophesied in the days of Ahaz and Hezekiah.

2-kings-16:20:6.summary: Manasseh “lay down with his fathers … His son Amon became king”; same formula, different king.

2-kings-16:20:8.summary: Amon’s burial and “His son Josiah became king in his place”; formula only.

2-kings-16:4:5.summary: Jeremiah 17:2 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-16:4:5.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-16:4:5.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-17:2:0.summary: Jehoahaz “did evil in the Lord’s eyes”; formula without Hoshea’s qualification.

2-kings-17:2:1.summary: Manaem “did evil in the Lord’s eyes”; formula only, showing the kings Hoshea was milder than.

2-kings-17:2:2.summary: Zechariah “did evil in the Lord’s eyes”; formula only.

2-kings-17:2:3.summary: Joash “did evil in the Lord’s eyes”; formula only.

2-kings-17:2:4.summary: Phakeias “did evil in the Lord’s eyes”; formula only.

2-kings-17:2:5.summary: Jehu did not turn from Jeroboam’s sins; general verdict on Israel’s kings.

2-kings-17:2:6.summary: Hezekiah invites Israel’s survivors to Passover; loosely relates to Hoshea’s era; range truncated.

2-kings-17:2:7.summary: Joram “did what was evil … though not as his father and not as his mother”; same qualified-evil formula.

2-kings-17:3:0.summary: “The ruler Salaman” may echo Salamanasar, but the identification is uncertain from the text.

2-kings-17:3:1.summary: The king of the Assyrians demands Judah’s submission; general Assyrian domination.

2-kings-17:3:2.summary: An earlier Assyrian king invades Israel; general Assyrian pressure.

2-kings-17:3:3.summary: “As I did to Samaria” recalls Assyria’s conquest that this campaign begins.

2-kings-17:3:4.summary: “Salamanassar king of the Assyrians went up against Samaria,” the same campaign retold; range truncated.

2-kings-17:3:5.summary: Ephraim’s kingdom will cease; prophecy realized through Assyria in general terms.

2-kings-17:3:6.summary: Assyria as the rod of God’s anger; general theological frame.

2-kings-17:3:7.summary: Ahaz tells the Assyrian king “I am your slave” and sends gifts, as Hoshea “became his slave.”

2-kings-17:3:8.summary: Syria became David’s servants, bringing gifts; general vassal-tribute formula.

2-kings-17:3:9.summary: Moab became David’s servants, bringing gifts; general vassal-tribute formula.

2-kings-17:3:10.summary: Sennacherib’s assassination has no link to Salamanasar subduing Hoshea.

2-kings-17:3:11.summary: Manaem paid Phul “king of the Assyrians” a thousand talents; earlier Israelite tribute to Assyria.

2-kings-17:4:0.summary: Trusting “this broken reed staff, Egypt” is the folly Hoshea committed by appealing to Egypt.

2-kings-17:4:1.summary: “Sedekias broke faith with the king of Babylon,” a parallel vassal revolt with fatal results.

2-kings-17:4:2.summary: Binding kings in fetters; general image matching Hoshea’s imprisonment.

2-kings-17:4:3.summary: “Woe to those going down to Egypt for help”; condemns the reliance on Egypt Hoshea showed.

2-kings-17:4:4.summary: The Assyrian taunt against Hezekiah shares no specific element with Hoshea’s revolt.

2-kings-17:4:5.summary: Hezekiah submits and pays tribute to Assyria; general vassalage, not revolt via Egypt.

2-kings-17:4:6.summary: A vassal king revolts, “sending his messengers to Egypt,” and is punished; close parallel; range truncated.

2-kings-17:4:7.summary: Joakim “became his slave … then turned and broke faith with him”; same vassal-revolt pattern.

2-kings-17:4:8.summary: Sedekias was bound with fetters and taken away, as Hoshea was bound in prison.

2-kings-17:4:9.summary: Woe to those who go down to Egypt “to be helped by Pharaoh”; condemns the policy Hoshea followed.

2-kings-17:5:0.summary: “Samaria will disappear because she opposed her God,” the doom this siege brings.

2-kings-17:5:1.summary: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem for years; a later parallel siege of a capital.

2-kings-17:5:2.summary: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem until Zedekiah’s eleventh year; later parallel siege.

2-kings-17:6:0.summary: Hosea foretells that “Samaria will disappear” and fall by the sword, the judgment fulfilled when the Assyrian king captured Samaria.
2-kings-17:6:0.why: Shows the fall of Samaria as fulfilled prophecy.

2-kings-17:6:1.summary: Chronicles records the Assyrian deportation of Israelite tribes to Chabor and “the River Gozan,” the same destinations as Abor and Gozan here.
2-kings-17:6:1.why: Parallel record of the same Assyrian deportation sites.

2-kings-17:6:2.summary: The covenant curse that the Lord would “scatter you among all the nations” is broadly fulfilled in Israel’s deportation, but no specific event is named.
2-kings-17:6:2.why: Frames the exile as a covenant curse.

2-kings-17:6:3.summary: Amos threatens Israel, “I will deport you beyond Damascus,” the deportation carried out by the king of the Assyrians here.
2-kings-17:6:3.why: Prophetic warning fulfilled in the deportation.

2-kings-17:6:5.summary: Leviticus warns that God will “scatter you among the nations” and desolate the land; a general covenant threat, not this event specifically.
2-kings-17:6:5.why: Background covenant curse behind the exile.

2-kings-17:6:6.summary: Isaiah’s oracle rouses the Medes against Babylon; the only link is the word Medes, used of a different context.

2-kings-17:6:7.summary: Deuteronomy warns the Lord will lead Israel and its rulers “unto a nation” unknown to them; a general exile curse.
2-kings-17:6:7.why: General covenant warning of exile with its king.

2-kings-17:6:8.summary: Isaiah’s vision of Elamites and Persians against Babylon has no real link to the Assyrian deportation of Israel.

2-kings-17:6:9.summary: Deuteronomy says the Lord “removed them from their land” and cast them into another land, a general pattern matching this deportation.
2-kings-17:6:9.why: Covenant explanation for removal from the land.

2-kings-17:6:10.summary: Moses warns that idolatry will lead the Lord to “scatter you among all the nations”; a general warning, judged on the truncated text.

2-kings-17:6:12.summary: Leviticus threatens “you shall perish among the nations,” a general exile curse rather than this specific deportation.

2-kings-17:6:13.summary: Deuteronomy warns Israel will “surely perish” and not remain long on the land; only a general theme of losing the land.
2-kings-17:6:13.why: Covenant warning about losing the land.

2-kings-17:6:14.summary: Rabshakeh’s boast names “Gozan” among nations Assyria destroyed; the same place appears, but in a different context.
2-kings-17:6:14.why: Identifies Gozan as an Assyrian-conquered region.

2-kings-17:6:15.summary: Isaiah’s parallel boast lists “Gozan” among Assyria’s conquests; shared place name only, not the deportation itself.

2-kings-17:6:16.summary: Hosea’s “Not My People” name signals God’s rejection of Israel, loosely anticipating its exile.

2-kings-17:6:17.summary: Hosea’s “Not Shown Mercy” declares no more mercy for “Israel’s house,” loosely foreshadowing the northern kingdom’s fall.
2-kings-17:6:17.why: Prophetic sign of judgment on Israel.

2-kings-17:6:18.summary: Daniel’s interpretation gives Babylon’s kingdom to “the Medes and Persians”; only the word Medes is shared.

2-kings-17:6:19.summary: Sirach recalls that the people did not repent “until they were plundered from their land and scattered,” summarizing this exile of Israel.
2-kings-17:6:19.why: Later reflection on the northern exile.

2-kings-17:7:0.summary: Joshua warns against going to “serve other gods,” the sin named here, but as a general warning only.
2-kings-17:7:0.why: Earlier warning against the same sin.

2-kings-17:7:1.summary: Judges describes Israel prostituting itself “after other gods” and being delivered to plunderers, a similar pattern of sin and judgment.
2-kings-17:7:1.why: Earlier cycle of apostasy and judgment.

2-kings-17:7:3.summary: Jeremiah says “Do not fear” idols, which cannot act, contrasting with Israel which “feared other gods.”
2-kings-17:7:3.why: Exposes the folly of fearing idols.

2-kings-17:7:4.summary: Nehemiah’s prayer recalls Israel withdrawing from God and casting His law behind them; general history of rebellion.

2-kings-17:7:5.summary: The psalm recounts Israel serving carved images and being handed “into nations’ hands,” a general parallel to sin and exile.
2-kings-17:7:5.why: Poetic summary of idolatry and its judgment.

2-kings-17:7:6.summary: Chronicles explains Judah’s fall by breaches of faith and ignored prophets; a similar explanation but for Judah, not Israel.
2-kings-17:7:6.why: Parallel theological explanation for Judah’s fall.

2-kings-17:7:7.summary: Hosea’s charge against Israel’s inhabitants lists their sins generally, without idolatry or the Exodus.

2-kings-17:7:8.summary: Later in the same chapter the covenant command reads “You shall not fear other gods,” the exact sin named here.

2-kings-17:7:9.summary: Jehoiakim’s regnal notice in Judah has no specific link to Israel’s sin of fearing other gods.

2-kings-17:7:10.summary: Solomon’s heart turned “after their gods,” an earlier instance of following other gods.
2-kings-17:7:10.why: Roots of apostasy in Solomon’s reign.

2-kings-17:7:11.summary: Moses foresees the people going after “foreign gods” and breaking the covenant, generally anticipating this apostasy.

2-kings-17:7:12.summary: The Song of Moses describes Israel forsaking God for “foreign gods” and demons; a broad thematic parallel, judged on truncated text.

2-kings-17:7:13.summary: Moses predicts Israel will do “evil before the Lord” and provoke Him; a general forecast of apostasy.

2-kings-17:7:14.summary: The prophet in Judges quotes God: “You shall not fear the gods of the Amorites,” yet Israel disobeyed, matching “they feared other gods.”
2-kings-17:7:14.why: Same charge of fearing other gods.

2-kings-17:7:15.summary: Ahaz’s regnal notice concerns Judah’s king, not Israel’s fear of other gods or the Exodus.

2-kings-17:7:16.summary: The Red Sea crossing narrates deliverance from Pharaoh, the background event the verse recalls, but nothing more is shared.

2-kings-17:7:17.summary: Hosea condemns Samaria’s calf and its turning to the Assyrians, related to Israel’s sin, judged on truncated text.

2-kings-17:7:18.summary: Ezekiel’s allegory names Samaria as Oholah, who prostituted herself from Egypt onward and with the Assyrians, picturing Israel’s apostasy.
2-kings-17:7:18.why: Allegory of Samaria’s faithlessness and fate.

2-kings-17:7:19.summary: Abijam’s heart not being whole with the Lord concerns a Judean king, not Israel’s fear of other gods.

2-kings-17:7:20.summary: Sirach says they sought every wickedness “until vengeance came upon them,” loosely summarizing the north’s sin and judgment.
2-kings-17:7:20.why: Later summary of sin leading to judgment.

2-kings-17:8:1.summary: Ahaz followed “the abominations of the nations whom the Lord removed before the Israelites,” the same formula as here.
2-kings-17:8:1.why: Same formula for adopting Canaanite practices.

2-kings-17:8:11.summary: Manasseh did evil “according to the abominations of the nations whom the Lord removed before the Israelites,” repeating this formula.
2-kings-17:8:11.why: Same formula applied to Judah’s king.

2-kings-17:8:0.summary: Leviticus forbids following Canaan’s practices: “neither shall you walk in their statutes,” the very thing Israel did.

2-kings-17:8:3.summary: Judah “walked in the ordinances Israel had made,” extending this verse’s charge of walking in foreign ordinances.
2-kings-17:8:3.why: Continues the same indictment to Judah.

2-kings-17:8:4.summary: Ahaz copies a Damascus altar, an example of adopting foreign practice, but it concerns Judah, not Israel’s kings.

2-kings-17:8:5.summary: The psalm says Israel “mixed with the nations and learned their works,” the same charge of adopting the nations’ ways.
2-kings-17:8:5.why: Poetic summary of the same sin.

2-kings-17:8:6.summary: Deuteronomy forbids following the nations destroyed before Israel and asking how they serve their gods, the command this verse says Israel broke.

2-kings-17:8:7.summary: Ahab followed the abominations of the Amorites “whom the Lord destroyed before the children of Israel,” an Israelite king matching this charge.
2-kings-17:8:7.why: Example of an Israelite king doing this.

2-kings-17:8:8.summary: Micah condemns keeping “the ordinances of Zambri” and Achaab’s works, matching Israel walking in ordinances set by its kings.
2-kings-17:8:8.why: Prophetic indictment of following Israel’s kings.

2-kings-17:8:9.summary: Leviticus warns against the abominations of the people before Israel and commands keeping God’s ordinances instead.
2-kings-17:8:9.why: Explains why the nations were removed.

2-kings-17:8:10.summary: Jeremiah’s “Do not learn according to the nations’ ways” is a related general warning, not specific to this charge.

2-kings-17:8:12.summary: Jeroboam’s two golden heifers are an example of Israel’s kings introducing false worship, though not the nations’ ordinances directly.
2-kings-17:8:12.why: Origin of the northern kings’ sin.

2-kings-17:8:13.summary: Ahab’s Baal worship illustrates Israel’s kings acting wickedly, but without the verse’s specific wording.
2-kings-17:8:13.why: Example of a king leading Israel astray.

2-kings-17:8:14.summary: Hosea says Ephraim began “to follow worthless things,” a loose parallel to following the nations’ ordinances.

2-kings-17:9:0.summary: The distinctive phrase “from watchtower to fortified city” recurs, here of Hezekiah’s conquests rather than high places.

2-kings-17:9:1.summary: Job’s secret heart-deception assumes the English “secretly”; the Saints verse speaks of words “not so,” giving no real link.
2-kings-17:9:1.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

2-kings-17:9:2.summary: Hosea mocks altars at Gilgal heaped on the field, loosely matching high places multiplied through the land.

2-kings-17:9:3.summary: Ezekiel’s elders worshiping in a “hidden bedchamber” relies on the English idea of secret acts, which the Greek-based verse lacks.
2-kings-17:9:3.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

2-kings-17:9:4.summary: Deuteronomy’s secret enticement to other gods rests on the “secretly” of the English label, not present in the Saints verse.
2-kings-17:9:4.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

2-kings-17:9:5.summary: The curse on an image set “in a secret place” presumes secret worship, absent from the Saints wording about words “not so.”
2-kings-17:9:5.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

2-kings-17:10:0.summary: Judah built “standing stones, and groves on every high hill and under every shady tree,” nearly identical wording.
2-kings-17:10:0.why: Same formula for idolatrous worship sites.

2-kings-17:10:1.summary: Micah’s promise to “cut down your groves” shares the grove image but is a general judgment oracle.
2-kings-17:10:1.why: Judgment on the same cult objects.

2-kings-17:10:2.summary: Ahaz sacrificed at high places, on the hills, and “under every leafy tree,” the same distinctive phrasing.

2-kings-17:10:3.summary: God commanded Israel to “break their pillars, cut down their sacred groves,” the very objects Israel instead set up.

2-kings-17:10:5.summary: Isaiah condemns those who appeal to idols “beneath leafy trees,” echoing the same image of worship sites.
2-kings-17:10:5.why: Prophetic condemnation of the same practice.

2-kings-17:10:6.summary: Deuteronomy forbids planting “a sacred grove,” the cult object Israel set up for itself here.

2-kings-17:10:7.summary: Leviticus forbids that you “set up a pillar for yourselves,” exactly what Israel did with pillars.

2-kings-17:11:0.summary: Manasseh’s evil is described as “provoking Him,” sharing only the provocation motif, not incense at high places.
2-kings-17:11:0.why: Similar language of provoking the Lord.

2-kings-17:11:1.summary: Judah’s refugees vow to “burn incense to the queen of heaven,” a related incense practice in a different setting.
2-kings-17:11:1.why: Another case of incense to false gods.

2-kings-17:11:2.summary: Jeroboam standing at the Bethel altar to sacrifice is a loose link to illicit worship at high places.

2-kings-17:11:3.summary: Ahaz made “high places for burning incense” and “provoked the Lord,” closely matching this verse’s wording.

2-kings-17:11:4.summary: The psalm says Israel “angered Him with their hills” and provoked Him “with their carvings,” matching high places and engraved images.
2-kings-17:11:4.why: Poetic parallel of the same provocation.

2-kings-17:12:0.summary: Leviticus forbids making images or carved images to bow down to, the command the Lord had given against idols.

2-kings-17:12:1.summary: Deuteronomy’s “You shall not do so unto the Lord your God” closely echoes the quoted command here.

2-kings-17:12:2.summary: Moses warns against making a graven likeness “concerning which the Lord your God has given commandment,” the prohibition Israel violated.

2-kings-17:12:3.summary: Deuteronomy forbids making any graven likeness or worshiping heavenly bodies, the ban behind this verse.

2-kings-17:12:5.summary: Exodus forbids bowing “to another god” because the Lord is jealous, the commandment Israel broke by serving idols.
2-kings-17:12:5.why: Grounds the prohibition in God’s jealousy.

2-kings-17:12:6.summary: The Decalogue forbids making an idol or serving them, the very command against serving idols referenced here.

2-kings-17:13:0.summary: Jeremiah recalls God sending “My servants the prophets” saying, “turn from his evil way,” matching this warning closely.

2-kings-17:13:1.summary: Samuel explains that a prophet was formerly called “the seer,” clarifying the term but not the warning itself.

2-kings-17:13:2.summary: Jeremiah’s call “Let each turn from his evil way” echoes the prophetic warning given here.

2-kings-17:13:3.summary: The Song of Moses stands as a witness against Israel, loosely related to God’s warnings.

2-kings-17:13:4.summary: Nehemiah recalls God testifying “through Thy prophets” to turn Israel back to the law, but they did not listen.
2-kings-17:13:4.why: Later confession of the same warnings.

2-kings-17:13:5.summary: Ezekiel’s call to cast away impieties is a general appeal to repent, not specific to this warning.

2-kings-17:13:6.summary: Isaiah’s indictment and call to Judah is a general prophetic warning, judged on truncated text.

2-kings-17:13:7.summary: Samuel’s review of Israel’s history and warnings is a general parallel, judged on truncated text.

2-kings-17:13:8.summary: Jeremiah warns about not walking in God’s ordinances and ignoring “My servants the prophets,” matching this verse.

2-kings-17:13:9.summary: Hosea addresses both Israel and Judah with a warning, a loose parallel to warning both kingdoms.

2-kings-17:13:10.summary: Jeremiah recalls the command to “walk in all My ways,” loosely matching God’s commandments given to the fathers.

2-kings-17:13:11.summary: Deuteronomy warns that serving other gods means Israel “shall surely perish,” a general warning.

2-kings-17:13:12.summary: Jeremiah’s call to “correct your ways” is a general prophetic appeal similar in theme.

2-kings-17:13:13.summary: Hosea’s “Return, Israel, to the Lord your God” is one prophetic call to turn, general in content.
2-kings-17:13:13.why: Example of a prophet’s call to return.

2-kings-17:13:14.summary: God rebukes Israel for forsaking Him and serving other gods despite deliverance; a general parallel.

2-kings-17:13:15.summary: Chronicles says God “sent through prophets” repeatedly but they mocked them, the same pattern of ignored warnings.

2-kings-17:13:16.summary: Zechariah recalls the former prophets saying, “Turn away from your evil ways,” and “My servants the prophets,” closely echoing this verse.

2-kings-17:13:17.summary: The records of Samuel “the seer” share only the word seer, with no link to the warning.

2-kings-17:13:18.summary: Paul’s witness to “repentance toward God” shares only a general call to repentance.

2-kings-17:13:19.summary: Moses calls heaven and earth to witness that Israel will perish from the land; a general covenant warning.

2-kings-17:13:20.summary: Jeremiah’s word to Judah’s survivors not to enter Egypt has no real link to this warning to Israel and Judah.

2-kings-17:13:21.summary: God says “Israel, I testify unto you,” sharing the idea of solemn divine warning.
2-kings-17:13:21.why: Same motif of God testifying to Israel.

2-kings-17:13:22.summary: Jeremiah’s complaint about prophets prophesying unjust things concerns false prophets, not God’s warnings through true prophets.

2-kings-17:13:23.summary: Jeremiah shows Judah ignoring Israel’s fate, related to both kingdoms being warned but not this warning itself.

2-kings-17:13:24.summary: The chapter’s conclusion repeats “through all His servants the prophets,” showing the warnings fulfilled.

2-kings-17:13:25.summary: The psalm has God solemnly testifying to Israel against any foreign god; a general parallel.

2-kings-17:13:26.summary: Joshua warns against transgressing the covenant and serving other gods; a general earlier warning.

2-kings-17:13:27.summary: Peter speaks of God’s patience wanting all to come to repentance, a general theme behind repeated warnings.

2-kings-17:13:28.summary: Isaiah urges the ungodly to “forsake his ways” and return to the Lord, a general call to repent.

2-kings-17:13:30.summary: A prophet in Judges reminds Israel of God’s command they disobeyed, a loose parallel to prophetic warning.

2-kings-17:13:31.summary: Sirach says the people “did not repent or turn away from their sins” until exiled, reflecting the unheeded call here.

2-kings-17:14:0.summary: Moses knows Israel’s “stiff neck” and provocation, a general parallel to their hardening here.

2-kings-17:14:1.summary: Stephen calls Israel “stiff-necked” and says “as your fathers did, so do you,” matching hardening like the fathers.
2-kings-17:14:1.why: New Testament echo of inherited stubbornness.

2-kings-17:14:2.summary: Jeremiah says “they did not hear Me” and “hardened their neck beyond their fathers,” a close verbal parallel.

2-kings-17:14:3.summary: Proverbs warns that a “stiff-necked man” meets sudden ruin; a general proverb on stubbornness.

2-kings-17:14:4.summary: The psalm’s “did not believe His word” relies on unbelief language absent from the Saints verse, which speaks of not listening and hardening.
2-kings-17:14:4.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

2-kings-17:14:5.summary: The psalm’s “did not believe in His wonders” assumes the English “did not believe,” not present in the Saints verse.
2-kings-17:14:5.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

2-kings-17:14:6.summary: Isaiah describes Israel’s neck as “an iron sinew,” a related image of stubbornness.

2-kings-17:14:7.summary: Hebrews warns “do not harden your hearts” as in the wilderness, a general parallel to hardening.

2-kings-17:14:8.summary: Hebrews warns against an “unbelieving heart that turns away,” a general theme of turning from God.

2-kings-17:14:9.summary: Deuteronomy’s “you did not trust the Lord” presumes unbelief wording not carried by the Saints verse.
2-kings-17:14:9.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

2-kings-17:14:10.summary: Paul speaks of “hardness and unrepentant heart” storing up wrath, a general theme of hardening.

2-kings-17:14:11.summary: The psalm’s “did not believe in God” relies on unbelief language absent from the Saints verse.
2-kings-17:14:11.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

2-kings-17:14:12.summary: Zedekiah “hardened his neck” rather than return to the Lord; a similar idiom applied to a different king.

2-kings-17:15:0.summary: Deuteronomy forbids following the nations’ gods and ways, the command Israel broke by following the nations around them.

2-kings-17:15:1.summary: The Song of Moses says Israel provoked God with idols; related to following vain things, but not this wording.

2-kings-17:15:4.summary: The covenant ceremony assumes the English mention of the covenant, which the Saints verse lacks; it speaks of testimonies.
2-kings-17:15:4.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

2-kings-17:15:5.summary: Jeremiah says the wise “rejected the Lord’s word,” a general parallel to rejecting God’s testimonies.

2-kings-17:15:6.summary: “May those who make them become like them” matches Israel following vain things and becoming vain.
2-kings-17:15:6.why: Explains becoming like what one worships.

2-kings-17:15:7.summary: Baasha and Elah provoked the Lord “with their worthless things,” related to following vain things.
2-kings-17:15:7.why: Similar language for idols as worthless.

2-kings-17:15:8.summary: Manasseh led Judah to do evil beyond the nations, a related but different case of following the nations.

2-kings-17:15:9.summary: Nehemiah says God testified to turn Israel back but “they did not listen,” matching the ignored testimonies by which He warned.
2-kings-17:15:9.why: Later confession of the same rebellion.

2-kings-17:15:10.summary: Judah’s refugees did not walk in God’s “law, and testimonies,” sharing the term but in another setting.

2-kings-17:15:11.summary: Samuel warns against turning aside “after things that are nothing,” loosely matching following vain things.

2-kings-17:15:12.summary: Deuteronomy explains exile by forsaking the covenant and serving other gods; the covenant wording is absent from the Saints verse.

2-kings-17:15:13.summary: Earlier in the chapter Israel “walked in the ordinances of the nations,” the same charge as following the nations around them.

2-kings-17:15:14.summary: Jeremiah calls idols “futile, mocked works,” related to the vain things Israel followed.

2-kings-17:15:15.summary: Manasseh followed “the abominations of the nations,” a similar charge applied to Judah’s king.

2-kings-17:15:16.summary: The adjacent verses say they acted “like the nations” and served idols the Lord had forbidden, the same indictment.
2-kings-17:15:16.why: Immediate context of the same charge.

2-kings-17:15:17.summary: The covenant ceremony in Moab relies on the covenant wording of the English verse, absent in the Saints text; judged on truncated text.
2-kings-17:15:17.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

2-kings-17:15:18.summary: Jeremiah says the fathers “did not remain in My covenant,” loosely matching not keeping God’s testimonies.

2-kings-17:15:19.summary: Paul’s “an idol is nothing” loosely relates to following vain things.

2-kings-17:15:20.summary: God sent prophets but they mocked them; related to ignoring warnings, though about Judah.

2-kings-17:15:21.summary: The Song’s contrast of their gods with ours has no specific link to Israel following vain things.

2-kings-17:15:23.summary: Nehemiah recalls Israel casting off the law and killing prophets who “testified among them,” matching the rejected warnings.
2-kings-17:15:23.why: Later confession of the same rebellion.

2-kings-17:15:24.summary: God sent prophets warning against defilement, a general parallel to warnings ignored.

2-kings-17:15:25.summary: Deuteronomy commands keeping “the testimonies and the ordinances,” exactly what Israel failed to keep.

2-kings-17:15:26.summary: The wedding at Cana instruction has no connection with Israel’s apostasy.

2-kings-17:16:8.summary: Manasseh made groves, served Baal, and “bowed down to all heaven’s host,” matching this verse’s list closely.

2-kings-17:16:1.summary: Ahab “served Baal and bowed down to him,” the Baal worship introduced into Israel named here.
2-kings-17:16:1.why: Origin of Baal worship in Israel.

2-kings-17:16:3.summary: Judah built groves on every high hill; shares groves but concerns Judah rather than this list.

2-kings-17:16:4.summary: Deuteronomy warns against bowing to sun, moon and stars, “all the adornment of heaven,” the host Israel worshiped.

2-kings-17:16:5.summary: Judah’s destruction of Baal’s house shares only the Baal cult, in a different kingdom and context.

2-kings-17:16:6.summary: Ahaziah of Israel “served the Baalim, bowed down to them,” an instance of the Baal worship listed.

2-kings-17:16:7.summary: Asa removes his mother’s grove; shares the grove motif but concerns Judah’s reform.

2-kings-17:16:9.summary: “Ahab made a grove” in Samaria, the origin of the groves Israel made.

2-kings-17:16:10.summary: Jehu’s purge of Baal worship relates to Israel’s Baal service, but as a contrasting episode, judged on truncated text.

2-kings-17:16:11.summary: Isaiah mocks idol makers as futile, a general parallel to making a casting.

2-kings-17:16:12.summary: At Sinai they “made themselves a calf” and bowed to it, the model for the cast heifers Israel made.

2-kings-17:16:13.summary: Aaron made “a cast calf,” echoing Israel’s “casting” of two heifers.

2-kings-17:16:14.summary: The same chapter says they set up “pillars and groves,” matching “made groves” here.

2-kings-17:16:15.summary: The psalm recalls the calf at Horeb, related to the heifers but not this event.

2-kings-17:16:16.summary: Jeremiah condemns those who served and bowed down to “all heaven’s host,” the same worship named here.

2-kings-17:17:0.summary: Manasseh “led his sons through fire,” practiced divination, read omens, provoking Him: almost identical wording.

2-kings-17:17:13.summary: Chronicles’ account of Manasseh passing children through fire and seeking omens closely matches this list.

2-kings-17:17:2.summary: Ezekiel says Samaria and Jerusalem made their children “pass through fire,” the same practice.

2-kings-17:17:4.summary: The psalm recalls Israel sacrificing “their sons and their daughters” to idols, matching the sin here.

2-kings-17:17:5.summary: Elijah tells Ahab he was “sold in vain to do evil before the Lord, provoking Him,” the same rare phrase.
2-kings-17:17:5.why: Same idiom of being sold to evil.

2-kings-17:17:6.summary: Ezekiel’s passing through those who open the womb alludes vaguely to child offerings; link is unclear.

2-kings-17:17:7.summary: Micah promises removal of sorceries and oracles, a general parallel to divination.

2-kings-17:17:8.summary: Leviticus forbids giving seed “to serve a ruler,” the Greek rendering of the Molech law, without fire wording.
2-kings-17:17:8.why: Law behind child offerings, obscured in Greek.

2-kings-17:17:9.summary: Leviticus forbids that you “divine by omens,” the practice Israel adopted.

2-kings-17:17:10.summary: Ahab “was sold to do evil before the Lord,” the same rare idiom applied to Israel here.
2-kings-17:17:10.why: Same idiom of being sold to evil.

2-kings-17:17:11.summary: Ahaz “made his children pass through fire,” the same practice of child sacrifice.

2-kings-17:17:12.summary: Ezekiel speaks of defilement through gifts; the shown text does not explicitly mention fire or children.

2-kings-17:17:14.summary: A slave girl with a spirit of divination in Philippi shares only the general word divination.

2-kings-17:17:15.summary: Isaiah says “you were sold because of your sins,” a loose echo of being sold to do evil.

2-kings-17:17:16.summary: Isaiah condemns Babylon’s sorcery and enchanters, a general parallel to divination.

2-kings-17:17:17.summary: Jeremiah warns against diviners and “omens,” a general parallel to practicing divinations.

2-kings-17:17:18.summary: The earlier verse of the same chapter shares only the idea of acting “to provoke the Lord.”

2-kings-17:17:19.summary: Isaiah mocks Babylon’s enchantments and astrologers, a general parallel to divination.

2-kings-17:17:20.summary: Ezekiel says they “slaughtered their children for their idols,” matching the child sacrifice here.

2-kings-17:17:21.summary: Isaiah rejects seeking mediums instead of God, a general parallel to divination.

2-kings-17:17:22.summary: Paul’s warning against provoking one another shares only the word provoking.

2-kings-17:18:0.summary: God promises Solomon’s son “one scepter,” anticipating that only Judah remained when Israel was removed.

2-kings-17:18:1.summary: At the division, “None followed David’s house except Judah’s scepter,” echoing “None remained except the tribe of Judah.”
2-kings-17:18:1.why: Roots Judah’s survival in the division.

2-kings-17:18:2.summary: Hosea contrasts Ephraim and Judah, a loose parallel to Judah alone remaining.

2-kings-17:18:3.summary: God promises Solomon’s line remaining scepters, though the Greek reads “two scepters,” not Judah alone.

2-kings-17:18:4.summary: The promise of “two scepters” for David’s line loosely parallels Judah remaining after Israel’s removal.

2-kings-17:18:5.summary: The Song of Moses describes God’s wrath against idolatry, a general theme of anger, judged on truncated text.

2-kings-17:18:6.summary: Hosea says Ephraim will not dwell in the Lord’s land but eat unclean things “among the Assyrians,” foretelling this removal.

2-kings-17:18:7.summary: God says, “I shall also remove Judah from My presence, as I removed Israel,” directly echoing this verse.

2-kings-17:18:8.summary: Earlier God “did not cast them from His presence” out of covenant mercy, contrasting with their final removal.
2-kings-17:18:8.why: Shows how long God withheld judgment.

2-kings-17:18:9.summary: Joshua warns God will bring harm until He destroys Israel from the land; a general covenant warning.

2-kings-17:18:10.summary: Deuteronomy describes the Lord’s anger and curses against the apostate, a general parallel, judged on truncated text.

2-kings-17:18:11.summary: Joshua warns Israel will “perish from this good land,” a general warning of removal.

2-kings-17:18:12.summary: God tells Jeremiah to send this people away from His presence, a similar theme applied to Judah.

2-kings-17:18:13.summary: Sirach says they sought wickedness “until vengeance came upon them,” a general summary of judgment.

2-kings-17:18:14.summary: Sirach notes the people “were left few in number, with a ruler in David’s house,” reflecting Judah alone remaining.

2-kings-17:19:0.summary: Rehoboam’s Judah built high places and groves; an early instance of Judah’s sin, not following Israel specifically.

2-kings-17:19:2.summary: Jehoram made high places and led Judah astray, a general parallel to Judah’s disobedience.

2-kings-17:19:3.summary: Jehoram “walked in the ways of Israel’s kings,” exactly Judah walking in Israel’s ordinances.
2-kings-17:19:3.why: Specific case of Judah imitating Israel.

2-kings-17:19:4.summary: Ezekiel says Samaria did not sin half of Jerusalem’s sins, showing Judah following and exceeding Israel.

2-kings-17:19:5.summary: Jeremiah says faithless Judah saw Israel’s fate yet “she too went and prostituted herself,” matching Judah following Israel.
2-kings-17:19:5.why: Judah failing to learn from Israel.

2-kings-17:19:6.summary: Ahaziah of Judah “walked in the way of the house of Ahab,” an example of Judah following Israel.
2-kings-17:19:6.why: Specific case of Judah imitating Israel.

2-kings-17:19:7.summary: Ezekiel’s Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem) allegory pictures Judah following Samaria’s unfaithfulness, judged on truncated text.

2-kings-17:19:8.summary: Jehoram “walked in the way of the kings of Israel,” a direct instance of Judah adopting Israel’s practices.
2-kings-17:19:8.why: Specific case of Judah imitating Israel.

2-kings-17:19:9.summary: Ezekiel’s indictment of Jerusalem’s bloodshed and idols is general, not about following Israel, judged on truncated text.

2-kings-17:19:10.summary: Jeremiah says Judah’s gods were as many as its cities, a general parallel to Judah’s disobedience.

2-kings-17:20:0.summary: Thaglathphellasar took Israelite lands and “deported them to the Assyrians,” an instance of Israel given to plunderers.

2-kings-17:20:1.summary: Jeremiah’s “the Lord rejected them” assumes God rejecting Israel, but the Saints verse says Israel rejected the Lord.
2-kings-17:20:1.why: Greek wording reverses the assumed link.

2-kings-17:20:2.summary: The Lord “gave them into the hand of Hazael,” an earlier instance of giving Israel to plunderers.

2-kings-17:20:3.summary: Saul treated the Lord’s word as nothing and was rejected; a loose parallel of rejection and judgment.
2-kings-17:20:3.why: Pattern of rejecting God and being rejected.

2-kings-17:20:4.summary: Deuteronomy’s description of God caring for the land has no specific link to Israel being cast off.

2-kings-17:20:5.summary: Paul insists God “has not rejected His people,” a contrast weakened because the Saints verse has Israel rejecting the Lord.
2-kings-17:20:5.why: Contrasts with notions of final rejection.

2-kings-17:20:6.summary: Syria reduced Jehoahaz’s army “like dust for trampling,” an example of Israel afflicted by plunderers.

2-kings-17:20:7.summary: God’s setting aside of Saul and sending Samuel to Jesse has no specific link to Israel’s exile.

2-kings-17:20:8.summary: Paul speaks of punishment “from the presence of the Lord,” echoing being cast from His presence in general.
2-kings-17:20:8.why: Similar image of separation from God.

2-kings-17:20:9.summary: God promises to discipline Jacob but not destroy him, a loose contrast to Israel being cast out.

2-kings-17:20:10.summary: Saul treated the Lord’s word as nothing and was set aside, a loose parallel of rejection.

2-kings-17:20:11.summary: The psalm’s “offspring of Israel” shares only a phrase with no judgment context.

2-kings-17:20:12.summary: Jonah fleeing “from the presence of the Lord” shares only the phrase, not the exile theme.

2-kings-17:20:13.summary: Isaiah’s promise that Israel’s offspring will be justified shares only the phrase “offspring of Israel.”

2-kings-17:20:14.summary: Two verses earlier the Lord “removed them from His presence,” the same judgment restated here.

2-kings-17:20:15.summary: Jesus’ “Depart from Me” loosely parallels being cast from God’s presence.

2-kings-17:20:17.summary: Israel separating from foreigners and confessing sins has no specific link to being cast off.

2-kings-17:20:19.summary: Judah was delivered into Syria’s and Israel’s hands for abandoning the Lord, a general pattern applied to Judah.

2-kings-17:20:20.summary: Jonah fleeing “from the presence of the Lord” shares only the phrase.

2-kings-17:20:21.summary: Nehemiah recalls God giving Israel “into the hand of those oppressing them” and abandoning them to enemies, the same pattern.

2-kings-17:20:22.summary: Salamanassar besieging Samaria is the same final event in which Israel was cast from God’s presence.
2-kings-17:20:22.why: Narrates the same fall of Samaria.

2-kings-17:20:23.summary: Phul’s invasion and tribute is an earlier Assyrian pressure on Israel, loosely related to plunderers.

2-kings-17:20:24.summary: God says He will not reject Israel’s family; a contrast, though the Saints verse has Israel rejecting the Lord.

2-kings-17:20:25.summary: Sirach says they were “plundered from their land and scattered,” reflecting God giving them to plunderers.

2-kings-17:21:0.summary: God tells Solomon, “I will surely tear your kingdom from your hand,” the origin of Israel’s separation from David’s house.

2-kings-17:21:1.summary: Achia gives Jeroboam ten pieces, as the kingdom is torn from Solomon, the background to Jeroboam’s kingship.

2-kings-17:21:2.summary: Jeroboam’s two golden heifers in Bethel and Dan “became a sin,” the great sin by which he drew Israel away.

2-kings-17:21:3.summary: Isaiah refers to “the day He removed Ephraim from Judah,” the division described here.

2-kings-17:21:5.summary: Rehoboam fortifying cities with supplies has no specific link to Jeroboam’s sin.

2-kings-17:21:6.summary: Jesus’ words to Pilate about “greater sin” share only the word sin.

2-kings-17:21:8.summary: Moses accuses Aaron of bringing “so great a sin” on the people with the calf, like Jeroboam causing a great sin through heifers.
2-kings-17:21:8.why: Leader causing a great calf sin.

2-kings-17:21:9.summary: Eli’s sons’ sin was “very great,” leading people to reject sacrifice; a loose parallel of leaders causing sin.

2-kings-17:21:10.summary: The psalmist’s plea for pardon of great sin shares only the words sin and great.

2-kings-17:21:11.summary: Eli warns his sons’ conduct causes the people not to serve God, loosely like Jeroboam turning Israel away.

2-kings-17:21:12.summary: Chronicles narrates Israel’s break from David’s house: “What share have we in David,” the separation stated here.

2-kings-17:21:13.summary: Abimelech complains Abraham brought “a great sin” on his kingdom; shared phrase but unrelated context.
2-kings-17:21:13.why: Similar phrase of a ruler bringing sin.

2-kings-17:21:15.summary: Jeroboam appointed priests for “the calves Jeroboam had made,” the sin by which he turned Israel away.

2-kings-17:21:16.summary: Sirach recalls Jeroboam “who made Israel sin,” whose sins led to removal from the land, summarizing this verse.

2-kings-17:22:0.summary: Jehu “did not turn away from following the sins of Jeroboam,” the same formula as here.

2-kings-17:22:1.summary: Zechariah “did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat,” the recurring formula.

2-kings-17:22:2.summary: Joash “did not turn away from every sin of Jeroboam” and walked in them, matching this verse.

2-kings-17:22:3.summary: Joram clung to Jeroboam’s sin and “did not turn away from it,” the same formula.

2-kings-17:22:4.summary: Jehu “did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat,” the recurring formula.

2-kings-17:22:5.summary: Israel “did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam’s house” and walked in them, close to this verse.

2-kings-17:22:6.summary: Jehoahaz followed Jeroboam’s sins and “did not turn away from them,” the same formula.

2-kings-17:23:0.summary: The chapter’s opening reports Israel deported “to the Assyrians,” the same exile summarized here.

2-kings-17:23:1.summary: God warned Israel “through all His prophets” and “My servants the prophets,” the warnings now fulfilled.

2-kings-17:23:2.summary: Amos’s “I will deport you beyond Damascus” is one prophetic word fulfilled in Israel’s deportation.

2-kings-17:23:4.summary: The Lord “cast them from His presence,” the same removal restated here.

2-kings-17:23:5.summary: Hosea foretells God will “put an end to the kingdom of Israel’s house,” fulfilled in this deportation.

2-kings-17:23:7.summary: The Lord “removed them from His presence,” the same phrase used here.

2-kings-17:23:8.summary: The prophecy against Bethel’s altar is a prophetic word about the north, but concerns Josiah, not exile.
2-kings-17:23:8.why: Example of prophecy against the north.

2-kings-17:23:9.summary: Micah foretells Samaria’s ruin, a prophetic word fulfilled in Israel’s removal.

2-kings-17:24:0.summary: Rabshakeh names Aimath and Seppharouain and Samaria, the same places whose people were resettled.
2-kings-17:24:0.why: Shows these cities as Assyrian conquests.

2-kings-17:24:1.summary: The Assyrian boast names Aimath, Seppharouain, and Ava, the same cities from which settlers came.

2-kings-17:24:2.summary: Jesus mentions cities of Samaritans, the later population descended partly from this resettlement.

2-kings-17:24:4.summary: The deportation of Israel from Samaria by the king of the Assyrians is the counterpart of resettling foreigners there.
2-kings-17:24:4.why: The other half of Assyria’s policy.

2-kings-17:24:5.summary: Hamath appears only as a border marker in Solomon’s feast, a slight place-name link.

2-kings-17:24:6.summary: The Assyrian offer to Jerusalem hints at the policy of relocating peoples, but the verse shown does not state it.

2-kings-17:24:7.summary: Isaiah’s parallel boast names Aimath and Seppharim, the same cities whose people were resettled.

2-kings-17:24:8.summary: Assyrian commanders bringing Manasseh to Babylon shares only Assyria and Babylon.

2-kings-17:24:9.summary: The Assyrian boasts of taking Babylon’s region and Samaria, loosely linking the places involved.

2-kings-17:24:10.summary: Isaiah’s account names Aimath and Seppharim and Samaria together, matching this verse’s places.

2-kings-17:24:11.summary: The people of the land say Asaraddon king of Assour “brought us here,” describing the same foreign resettlement policy.
2-kings-17:24:11.why: Later descendants of the resettled peoples.

2-kings-17:24:12.summary: Sirach scorns those living on Mount Samaria, later inhabitants of the region.

2-kings-17:25:0.summary: Later in the chapter the settlers’ mixed fearing of the Lord is described, following on from not fearing Him here.

2-kings-17:25:1.summary: “These nations feared the Lord while serving their carved images” concludes the story begun here.

2-kings-17:25:2.summary: The settlers later “feared the Lord” yet installed abominations, developing this verse’s note that they did not fear Him.

2-kings-17:25:3.summary: A lion killed the disobedient man of God, another case of a lion as the Lord’s judgment.
2-kings-17:25:3.why: Lions as instruments of divine judgment.

2-kings-17:25:4.summary: The eastern tribes worry their sons may not “revere the Lord,” sharing only the fear-of-the-Lord idea.

2-kings-17:25:5.summary: Jeremiah names wild beasts among God’s punishments, a general parallel to sending lions.

2-kings-17:25:6.summary: “A lion from the woodland struck them” because of their impieties, the same image of lions as judgment.
2-kings-17:25:6.why: Lions as instruments of divine judgment.

2-kings-17:25:7.summary: Jonah confesses he worships the Lord before pagan sailors, a loose contrast to settlers not fearing the Lord.
2-kings-17:25:7.why: Foreigners learning to fear the Lord.

2-kings-17:25:8.summary: Bears mauling the youths is another wild-animal judgment, a general parallel.

2-kings-17:25:10.summary: Ezekiel mentions God bringing “evil beasts upon the land,” a general parallel.

2-kings-17:25:11.summary: A man who did not listen to the Lord’s voice is struck by a lion, the same lion judgment motif.

2-kings-17:25:12.summary: Ezekiel lists “evil beasts” among God’s four retributions, a general parallel.

2-kings-17:25:13.summary: A deported priest taught the settlers “how to fear the Lord,” the remedy for not fearing Him here.

2-kings-17:25:14.summary: Darius commands all to worship Daniel’s God, a loose parallel of a foreign king promoting Israel’s God.

2-kings-17:26:0.summary: Samuel writing the king’s claim in a scroll has no real link to the settlers not knowing the God of the land’s judgment.

2-kings-17:26:1.summary: The king responds by sending someone to teach “the judgment of the God of the land,” directly continuing this report.

2-kings-17:26:2.summary: Samuel reporting the king’s claim to the people has no specific link to this report to the Assyrian king.

2-kings-17:26:3.summary: Amos condemns oaths by Samaria’s propitiation and Dan’s god, local cults of Samaria loosely related.

2-kings-17:27:0.summary: Jeroboam appointed non-Levite priests at high places, background to the irregular priesthood sent here.

2-kings-17:27:1.summary: The prophecy against the priests of Bethel’s high places loosely relates to the priest sent back.

2-kings-17:27:2.summary: Micah’s hired Levite priest is a loose parallel to a priest installed to teach worship.

2-kings-17:27:3.summary: Jeroboam appointed priests for high places and calves, background to the northern priests.

2-kings-17:28:0.summary: Jeroboam stationed “in Bethel the priests of the high places,” the same Bethel and priesthood from which this priest came.

2-kings-17:28:1.summary: Isaiah’s people “revere Me in vain, teaching human commands,” loosely matching the mixed fear taught here.

2-kings-17:28:2.summary: Jesus’ “blind guides of the blind” loosely parallels an apostate priest teaching the settlers.
