2-kings-17:29:0.summary: Micah says the peoples will walk “each his own way,” a loose parallel to each nation making its own gods.

2-kings-17:29:1.summary: Jeroboam “made houses on high places,” the same houses of the high places the settlers used.

2-kings-17:29:2.summary: Jeremiah mocks the nations’ handmade idols, a general parallel to each nation making gods.

2-kings-17:29:3.summary: The psalm mocks “the idols of the nations” as handmade, a general parallel.

2-kings-17:29:4.summary: Paul describes exchanging God’s glory for images, a general parallel to making gods.

2-kings-17:29:5.summary: Hosea says of Samaria’s calf, “A craftsman made it, and it is no god,” loosely parallel to making gods in Samaria.

2-kings-17:29:6.summary: Isaiah’s satire on idol-making is a general parallel, judged on truncated text.

2-kings-17:29:7.summary: The psalm mocks the nations’ idols as handmade, a general parallel.

2-kings-17:29:8.summary: The prophecy against “the high houses in Samaria” names the same shrines the settlers used.

2-kings-17:30:0.summary: The settlers came from Babylon, Chountha, and Aimath, the same peoples whose gods are named here.

2-kings-17:31:0.summary: The settlers included people from Aia and Seppharouain, the same groups named here.

2-kings-17:31:2.summary: Adramelech here is Sennacherib’s son, sharing only the name with the god of Seppharouain.

2-kings-17:31:3.summary: The law against giving seed “to serve a ruler” relates to child offerings, but the Greek wording obscures the link.

2-kings-17:31:4.summary: Ezra lists Babylonians and other peoples settled in Samaria, a loose link to the resettled peoples.

2-kings-17:31:5.summary: The general command to obey has no specific link to the settlers’ child sacrifices.

2-kings-17:31:6.summary: Deuteronomy notes the nations “burn their sons and their daughters with fire unto their gods,” the practice here.

2-kings-17:32:0.summary: Jeroboam made houses on high places and priests from the people, the same practice the settlers continued.

2-kings-17:32:1.summary: Each nation placed its gods in “the house of the high places” in its city, directly paralleling this verse.
2-kings-17:32:1.why: Immediate parallel in the same passage.

2-kings-17:32:2.summary: Josiah removed “high-place houses in Samaria’s cities,” the same shrines used here.

2-kings-17:32:3.summary: Zephaniah condemns swearing by the Lord and by their king, a general parallel of mixed worship.

2-kings-17:32:4.summary: Jeroboam appointed “priests of high places from some of the people,” as the settlers did.

2-kings-17:32:5.summary: The old prophet’s burial request has no link to the settlers’ priests and high places.

2-kings-17:33:0.summary: “You cannot serve God and mammon” addresses the divided service shown by fearing the Lord while serving other gods.

2-kings-17:33:2.summary: “No one can serve as a slave to two masters” addresses fearing the Lord while serving their own gods.

2-kings-17:33:3.summary: Elijah’s “How long will you limp on both your knees?” rebukes the same wavering between the Lord and other gods.

2-kings-17:33:4.summary: Zephaniah condemns those “swearing by the Lord and those swearing by their king,” the same mixed loyalty.

2-kings-17:33:5.summary: Hosea says “They divided their hearts,” describing the same divided worship.

2-kings-17:34:0.summary: God tells Jacob “Israel shall be your name,” the naming this verse recalls.

2-kings-17:34:2.summary: Isaiah addresses Jacob’s house “called by Israel’s name” who swear by the Lord without truth, like this hollow fear.

2-kings-17:34:3.summary: At first “they did not fear the Lord,” the beginning of the settlers’ story concluded here.

2-kings-17:34:4.summary: The priest taught them “how to fear the Lord” and the God of the land’s judgment, background to this verse.

2-kings-17:34:5.summary: The previous verse says they feared the Lord while serving their own gods, which this verse continues.

2-kings-17:34:6.summary: Elijah’s twelve stones recall the word “Israel will be your name,” the same naming formula.

2-kings-17:34:7.summary: Jacob’s altar to “the God of Israel” loosely relates to Jacob named Israel.

2-kings-17:34:8.summary: Achia’s tearing of the kingdom for Jeroboam has no specific link to the settlers or Jacob’s naming.

2-kings-17:34:9.summary: Obadiah’s reply to Elijah about reporting to his lord has no link to this verse.

2-kings-17:35:3.summary: Both join “covenant” of the Lord he “commanded” with the ban on going to “serve other gods and bow down to them.”
2-kings-17:35:3.why: Shows Joshua's warning fulfilled in Israel's exile.

2-kings-17:35:0.summary: Same command “You shall not fear” other gods, followed by Israel's failure to obey.
2-kings-17:35:0.why: Earlier instance of the same command and disobedience.

2-kings-17:35:1.summary: Warns not to forget “the covenant of the Lord your God, which He made with you” and threatens perishing from the land (shown text).
2-kings-17:35:1.why: Deuteronomic covenant warning behind the exile verdict.

2-kings-17:35:4.summary: Forbids Israel to “bow down to them or serve them” regarding the nations' gods.
2-kings-17:35:4.why: Same prohibition list from Joshua's farewell.

2-kings-17:35:5.summary: Covenant law forbids bowing to another god and sacrificing to the nations' gods (shown text).
2-kings-17:35:5.why: Sinai covenant source of the prohibitions cited.

2-kings-17:35:6.summary: Deuteronomy 13 forbids following anyone urging “serve other gods” and commands fearing the Lord (shown text).

2-kings-17:35:7.summary: Jeremiah says of idols “Do not fear them,” a different sense from cultic fear of other gods.
2-kings-17:35:7.why: Prophetic mockery of idols as powerless.

2-kings-17:35:8.summary: New covenant promised because Israel “did not remain in My covenant” made at the exodus.
2-kings-17:35:8.why: Answers the broken covenant with a promised new one.

2-kings-17:35:9.summary: Same chapter's indictment: Israel followed the nations “concerning whom He had commanded them not to do such things.”
2-kings-17:35:9.why: Context within the same exile explanation.

2-kings-17:35:10.summary: Ratification of “the covenant the Lord has made with you” at Sinai; no mention of other gods.

2-kings-17:35:11.summary: Hebrews cites the broken first covenant and the promised better one (shown text).

2-kings-17:35:12.summary: Israel enters “the covenant of the Lord your God” at Moab (shown text), without the specific prohibitions.

2-kings-17:35:13.summary: Conditional promise for those who “keep My covenant”; no reference to other gods.

2-kings-17:36:0.summary: The Lord brings Israel out of Egypt “with an uplifted arm,” echoing “a raised arm.”

2-kings-17:36:1.summary: “You shall fear the Lord your God, and you shall serve Him” matches the command to fear only the Lord.

2-kings-17:36:2.summary: Threat to strike Pharaoh with plague; only incidental mention of God's hand.

2-kings-17:36:3.summary: Only shared element is the command to “fear your God,” in a law about elders.

2-kings-17:36:4.summary: Universal fear and worship of the Lord alone, broadly echoing fear and bowing to Him.

2-kings-17:36:5.summary: The Lord “brought you forth” from Egypt “with a mighty hand and with an uplifted arm.”

2-kings-17:36:6.summary: Sacrifices brought to the Lord's chosen place; overlap only in sacrificing to the Lord.

2-kings-17:36:7.summary: “You shall fear the Lord your God, and you shall serve Him” parallels the exclusive fear commanded.

2-kings-17:36:8.summary: Sacrifices brought only to the Lord's chosen place; loosely related to sacrificing to Him.

2-kings-17:36:9.summary: Contrasts fearing humans with fearing God; general theme of rightly directed fear.
2-kings-17:36:9.why: NT teaching on whom to fear.

2-kings-17:36:10.summary: Out of Egypt “with a mighty hand, a high arm,” echoing the exodus formula.
2-kings-17:36:10.why: Prophetic use of the same formula.

2-kings-17:36:11.summary: Prayer for healing by God's stretched-out hand; no link to exodus or exclusive fear.

2-kings-17:37:0.summary: Lists “law,” “ordinances,” and “judgments” Moses gave Israel, matching the source's list.

2-kings-17:37:1.summary: “Commandments, and the ordinances, and the judgments” with “take heed to do” them.
2-kings-17:37:1.why: Same command to observe the law carefully.

2-kings-17:37:2.summary: “You shall take heed to do” every word commanded; general observance theme.

2-kings-17:37:3.summary: Keep “all My law and all My ordinances, and do them”; standard formula.

2-kings-17:37:4.summary: God gave “judgments, laws … ordinances and commandments,” the same fourfold list.

2-kings-17:37:5.summary: Moses “wrote the words of this law,” matching law “He wrote for you.”

2-kings-17:37:6.summary: Israel received lands “so that they might keep His ordinances” and law.
2-kings-17:37:6.why: Purpose of the gift of land.

2-kings-17:37:7.summary: Prayer that Solomon will “do Thy commandments, testimonies, and ordinances.”

2-kings-17:37:8.summary: Command to read the law publicly; related only to the law's centrality.

2-kings-17:37:9.summary: Praise of the Lord's ordinances, commandment, and judgments; devotional rather than command.

2-kings-17:38:0.summary: “Lest you forget the covenant of the Lord your God, which He made with you” closely matches.

2-kings-17:38:1.summary: Warning “lest you forget the Lord your God” who brought them from Egypt.

2-kings-17:38:2.summary: Warning not to “forget the Lord your God” amid prosperity (shown text).

2-kings-17:39:0.summary: “Rescued from our enemies’ hand” to serve God, echoing the promised rescue from enemies.

2-kings-17:39:1.summary: “Only fear the Lord and serve Him,” paralleling the exclusive call to fear the Lord.

2-kings-17:39:4.summary: Fear God rather than human threats; general theme of rightly placed fear.

2-kings-17:39:5.summary: Mercy for “those who fear Him”; general blessing on God-fearers.

2-kings-17:39:6.summary: God saved Israel “from the hand of those oppressing them”; rescue theme.

2-kings-17:39:7.summary: Do not fear what the people fear; the Lord “will be your fear.”
2-kings-17:39:7.why: Fear of the Lord replaces other fears.

2-kings-17:39:8.summary: “Salvation from our enemies,” echoing “He will rescue you from all your enemies.”

2-kings-17:40:0.summary: Same chapter: Israel walked in the nations’ ordinances, the practices forbidden here.

2-kings-17:40:1.summary: Same chapter: Israel served idols the Lord had forbidden.

2-kings-17:40:2.summary: Ingrained evil habit cannot change; loosely fits persistent wrong practice.

2-kings-17:40:3.summary: Threat of serving other gods in exile; general idolatry theme.

2-kings-17:40:4.summary: Same passage: they “acted according to their judgment” and ordinances, the very “judgment” referred to.

2-kings-17:41:0.summary: “You cannot serve” two masters, exactly the divided service of fearing the Lord while serving images.

2-kings-17:41:1.summary: Elijah rebukes limping between the Lord and Baal, the same divided allegiance.

2-kings-17:41:2.summary: Those “swearing by the Lord and those swearing by their king,” a mixed worship like the source.

2-kings-17:41:4.summary: “Fear the Lord and serve Him” and “remove the foreign gods”: the choice the nations failed to make.

2-kings-17:41:5.summary: Lukewarm, neither hot nor cold; loosely evokes half-hearted religion.

2-kings-17:41:6.summary: The deported settlers claim to have sacrificed to Israel's God since Asaraddon, the same syncretistic population.

2-kings-18:1:1.summary: Genealogy listing “Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son,” naming Hezekiah son of Ahaz.

2-kings-18:1:6.summary: Records how “Hoshea son of Ela” became king, the reign dating Hezekiah's accession.

2-kings-18:1:0.summary: Chronicles' parallel: Ahaz dies, “His son Hezekiah reigned in his place.”

2-kings-18:1:4.summary: Introduces Ahaz's reign; relevant only as Hezekiah's father.

2-kings-18:1:5.summary: Same synchronism of Hezekiah's reign with “Hoshea son of Ela, king of Israel.”

2-kings-18:3:9.summary: Josiah “did what was right in the Lord’s eyes” and walked as “his father David,” identical formula.

2-kings-18:3:0.summary: Hezekiah himself recalls he “did what was good in Thine eyes.”

2-kings-18:3:1.summary: Job's speaker confesses sin; no link to Hezekiah's righteousness.

2-kings-18:3:2.summary: Solomon's heart not whole “as was the heart of David his father.”
2-kings-18:3:2.why: Contrasting use of David as standard.

2-kings-18:3:4.summary: Asa “did what was right before the Lord, like David his father,” same formula.

2-kings-18:3:5.summary: Jeroboam told to “do what is right before Me” as David did.

2-kings-18:3:6.summary: Chronicles: Hezekiah “did what was good and right before the Lord his God.”

2-kings-18:3:7.summary: Command to do what is “pleasing and good before the Lord”; general.

2-kings-18:3:8.summary: “David did what was right before the Lord,” the standard Hezekiah matched.

2-kings-18:3:10.summary: Solomon told to walk “as your father David walked.”

2-kings-18:3:11.summary: Do “what is pleasing before Him”; general obedience language.

2-kings-18:3:12.summary: Paul calls the law holy and good; no link to Hezekiah's conduct.

2-kings-18:3:13.summary: Psalmist set right toward commandments; generic, no specific link.

2-kings-18:3:14.summary: Children obeying parents “is right”; only the word “right” and “father” loosely.

2-kings-18:3:15.summary: Sirach: Hezekiah “did what was pleasing to the Lord” in “the ways of his father David.”

2-kings-18:4:0.summary: Chronicles' parallel: Israel “shattered the pillars, cut down the sacred groves, and demolished the high places.”

2-kings-18:4:2.summary: Rabshakeh refers to the high places and altars “Hezekiah removed.”

2-kings-18:4:3.summary: Command to “break their pillars, and cut down their sacred groves” and destroy high places.

2-kings-18:4:5.summary: God threatens to destroy pillars and wooden images; similar objects, different agent.

2-kings-18:4:6.summary: Gideon ordered to pull down Baal's altar and “cut down the grove.”
2-kings-18:4:6.why: Earlier reform of the same kind.

2-kings-18:4:7.summary: Under Joash “the high places were not removed,” contrasting Hezekiah who removed them.

2-kings-18:4:8.summary: Baal's altar demolished and grove cut down in Gideon's day.

2-kings-18:4:9.summary: Jehoshaphat did right; the shown text lacks the high-places detail, so no specific link.

2-kings-18:4:10.summary: “Break their pillars, and cut down their sacred groves.”

2-kings-18:4:11.summary: Asa purged cults but “did not remove the high places,” unlike Hezekiah.

2-kings-18:4:12.summary: People “burning incense at the high places” in Solomon's day.

2-kings-18:4:13.summary: Manasseh “rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had pulled down.”

2-kings-18:4:14.summary: Moses “lifted up the snake in the wilderness,” the bronze serpent Hezekiah destroyed.
2-kings-18:4:14.why: Christ's typological use of the serpent.

2-kings-18:4:15.summary: “He did not remove the high places; the people still … burned incense”; Hezekiah did remove them.

2-kings-18:4:16.summary: Israel provoked God with hill shrines and carvings; general idolatry.

2-kings-18:4:17.summary: “He did not remove the high places,” the recurring failure Hezekiah reversed.

2-kings-18:4:18.summary: Jehoshaphat “removed the sacred groves”; similar but separate reform.

2-kings-18:4:19.summary: “He did not remove the high places,” contrasting Hezekiah's removal.

2-kings-18:4:20.summary: Israel sacrificed on every high hill, a place called Abama (high place).

2-kings-18:4:21.summary: Ahaz's altar instructions; no link to destroying high places or the serpent.

2-kings-18:4:22.summary: Josiah burns vessels made for Baal and “the grove,” a parallel purge.

2-kings-18:5:0.summary: Josiah: no king like him before him, “and after him none like him arose,” the same incomparability formula.

2-kings-18:5:1.summary: Sennacherib mocks Hezekiah's God “in whom you trust,” testing his hope.

2-kings-18:5:2.summary: Mockers taunt Jesus: “He trusts in God; let Him rescue Him.”

2-kings-18:5:3.summary: Believers “hoped beforehand in Christ”; only the verb “hoped.”

2-kings-18:5:4.summary: “I have hoped in Thy mercy”; general hope in the Lord.

2-kings-18:5:5.summary: “Whose hope is in the Lord his God”; general blessing on hope.
2-kings-18:5:5.why: Blessing on the one who hopes.

2-kings-18:5:6.summary: Hezekiah urges trust: “with us is the Lord our God, to save.”

2-kings-18:5:7.summary: Job resolves to plead before God; the Greek text lacks the hope sense.
2-kings-18:5:7.why: No real link in this wording.

2-kings-18:5:8.summary: The Lord as protector; enemies fall; general trust theme.

2-kings-18:5:9.summary: “Blessed is the person who hopes in Thee.”

2-kings-18:5:10.summary: Jehoshaphat: “Trust in the Lord your God”; another king's trust.

2-kings-18:5:11.summary: Hezekiah's prayer to the “Lord, Israel’s God” for rescue from Sennacherib.

2-kings-18:5:12.summary: Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahaziah; no link to Hezekiah's hope.

2-kings-18:5:13.summary: Asa rebuked for trusting Syria's king rather than the Lord.

2-kings-18:5:14.summary: Asa: “we trust in Thee”; another king's trust.

2-kings-18:5:15.summary: Blessed is one who trusted in the Lord, “the Lord will be his hope.”

2-kings-18:5:16.summary: God as refuge and strength; general trust.

2-kings-18:5:17.summary: Sirach praises Hezekiah who “stood strong in the ways of his father David.”

2-kings-18:6:1.summary: “Cling to the Lord your God” matches “He clung to the Lord.”

2-kings-18:6:2.summary: “Keep My commandments” as love; general obedience.

2-kings-18:6:3.summary: Exhortation “to remain with the Lord,” loosely like clinging.

2-kings-18:6:4.summary: “That we keep His commandments”; general obedience.

2-kings-18:6:5.summary: Friendship through obedience; only generic commandment language.

2-kings-18:6:6.summary: Prophets urged Israel to “keep My commandments” and the law; Israel refused, unlike Hezekiah.

2-kings-18:6:7.summary: “Do everything I command you” given at the exodus; general obedience.

2-kings-18:6:8.summary: Israel “abandoned the commandments,” directly contrasting Hezekiah who kept them.

2-kings-18:6:9.summary: The one who keeps commandments loves Christ; general.

2-kings-18:6:10.summary: “Judah also did not keep the commandments,” contrasting Hezekiah's faithfulness.

2-kings-18:6:11.summary: Keeping commandments and remaining in love; general.

2-kings-18:7:0.summary: “If God is for us,” loosely echoing “The Lord was with him.”

2-kings-18:7:1.summary: Ahaz declared himself the Assyrian king's slave; Hezekiah refused to serve him.

2-kings-18:7:2.summary: “The Lord was with Joseph” and prospered whatever he did, the same formula.

2-kings-18:7:3.summary: Through God we will do mighty deeds against afflicters; general.

2-kings-18:7:4.summary: Chronicles: Hezekiah in every work “acted, and prospered.”

2-kings-18:7:5.summary: David “showed understanding in all his ways, and the Lord was with him.”

2-kings-18:7:7.summary: “I am with you all the days”; divine presence theme.

2-kings-18:7:8.summary: The righteous man prospers in “everything he does.”

2-kings-18:7:9.summary: “The Lord of powers is with us.”

2-kings-18:7:10.summary: Emmanuel, “God with us”; presence theme only.

2-kings-18:7:11.summary: “The Lord is with you while you are with Him,” principle illustrated by Hezekiah.

2-kings-18:7:14.summary: “God is with you in all that you do,” said of Abraham.

2-kings-18:7:15.summary: “God was with him” and gave Joseph wisdom.

2-kings-18:7:16.summary: The Lord gave David victory wherever he went.

2-kings-18:7:17.summary: The Lord gave David victory wherever he went.

2-kings-18:8:0.summary: Oracle to the “foreigners” (Philistines) that the one striking them comes, fitting Hezekiah's campaign.

2-kings-18:8:1.summary: Identical phrase “from watchtower to fortified city.”

2-kings-18:8:3.summary: Simeonites struck peoples “in the days of Hezekiah”; a different campaign.

2-kings-18:8:4.summary: Uzziah built towers for herds; only the tower word.

2-kings-18:8:5.summary: Vineyard parable's tower; no connection to Hezekiah's campaign.

2-kings-18:9:0.summary: Greek reads ruler “Salaman” destroying walled places, possibly echoing Salamanassar; uncertain.

2-kings-18:9:1.summary: Same synchronism: Hezekiah's reign dated by “Hoshea son of Ela, king of Israel.”

2-kings-18:10:0.summary: “Samaria will disappear because she opposed her God,” prophesying its fall.

2-kings-18:10:1.summary: Judgment for following Achaab's house; obliteration threatened.

2-kings-18:10:2.summary: Amos: no one fleeing will escape, captivity before enemies (shown text).

2-kings-18:10:3.summary: Land obliterated for its practices; general.

2-kings-18:10:4.summary: Israel's leaders will be captives, Ephraim stripped.

2-kings-18:10:5.summary: “I will make Samaria” a ruin, her stones pulled down.

2-kings-18:10:6.summary: Sons of Israel “who dwell in Samaria will be snatched out” (shown text).

2-kings-18:11:0.summary: Assyrian deportation to “Chalach, Chabor, and the River Gozan,” same places.

2-kings-18:11:3.summary: Amos: “I will deport you beyond Damascus.”

2-kings-18:11:5.summary: Ephraim “among the Assyrians” will eat unclean things.

2-kings-18:11:6.summary: Assyria as the rod of God's anger.

2-kings-18:11:7.summary: Oracle against Ephraim and “those settled in Samaria” (shown text).

2-kings-18:11:8.summary: Warning lest Joseph's house be consumed.

2-kings-18:11:9.summary: “Ephraim’s kingdom will cease from being a people.”
2-kings-18:11:9.why: Prophecy of the end of Israel.

2-kings-18:11:11.summary: Stephen cites “I will deport you beyond Babylon.”

2-kings-18:11:12.summary: What the kings of the Assyrians did to all lands.

2-kings-18:11:13.summary: “Samaria’s spoils before the king of the Assyrians.”

2-kings-18:11:14.summary: “Israel was swallowed up … among the nations”; went to the Assyrians.

2-kings-18:11:15.summary: People did not repent “until they were plundered from their land and scattered.”

2-kings-18:12:0.summary: Daniel confesses Israel “have not listened” and transgressed God's law (shown text).

2-kings-18:12:1.summary: Vengeance on those who “do not obey”; general.

2-kings-18:12:2.summary: Warning if they do not keep commandments “which Moses set before you” and serve other gods.

2-kings-18:12:3.summary: Moses called “My servant,” matching “Moses the Lord’s servant.”

2-kings-18:12:4.summary: Israel sent away for adultery; Judah did not fear.

2-kings-18:12:5.summary: Stumbling by disobeying the word; generic.

2-kings-18:12:6.summary: “If you are willing and listen to Me,” you will eat the land's good.

2-kings-18:12:7.summary: God will not listen to those acting wickedly.

2-kings-18:12:8.summary: “Hear My voice … walk in all My ways that I command you,” the command Israel disobeyed.
2-kings-18:12:8.why: The command they failed to keep.

2-kings-18:12:9.summary: God will forsake the people; evils find them.

2-kings-18:12:10.summary: Curses “if you do not hearken unto the commandments of the Lord your God.”

2-kings-18:12:11.summary: Perish “because you did not hearken unto the voice of the Lord your God.”

2-kings-18:12:12.summary: “They refused to listen” in the wilderness.

2-kings-18:12:13.summary: Judgment beginning with God's house; generic disobedience theme.

2-kings-18:12:14.summary: Only shared element is Moses as servant/attendant.

2-kings-18:12:16.summary: Moses “faithful in all His house as an attendant.”

2-kings-18:12:17.summary: People humbled “because of their lawless deeds”; general sin-and-consequence theme.

2-kings-18:12:18.summary: Nations explain the land's ruin: “they forsook the covenant of the Lord” and served other gods, so He removed them.

2-kings-18:12:19.summary: Israel “cast Thy law behind their bodies” and was handed to oppressors.
2-kings-18:12:19.why: Later confession of the same disobedience.

2-kings-18:12:20.summary: Moses called “the household servant of the Lord.”

2-kings-18:12:21.summary: Instruction on how a “slave of the Lord” behaves; only the servant title overlaps.

2-kings-18:13:5.summary: Chronicles: “Sennacherib king of the Assyrians came … against Judah” and its walled cities.

2-kings-18:13:1.summary: Isaiah foretells “the king of the Assyrians” flooding into Judea.

2-kings-18:13:2.summary: Ephraim's covenant with Assyria and a case against Judah; no link to Sennacherib's invasion.

2-kings-18:13:3.summary: Assyria as “the rod of My anger.”

2-kings-18:13:4.summary: God will bring “the king of the Assyrians” upon Judah (shown text).

2-kings-18:13:6.summary: “In his days Sennacherib came up” against Zion.

2-kings-18:14:0.summary: Hezekiah had “broke with the king of the Assyrians,” which this submission reverses.

2-kings-18:14:1.summary: Ahab submits: “I am yours, and so is everything of mine”; similar capitulation.

2-kings-18:14:2.summary: Weaker king sends a delegation for peace terms.

2-kings-18:14:3.summary: Fear of people trips one up; trusting the Lord saves.

2-kings-18:15:0.summary: Ahaz took the silver “found in the treasuries of the Lord’s house and the king’s house” for Assyria.

2-kings-18:15:1.summary: Asa took silver and gold “found in the treasuries of the king’s house” to buy off a king.

2-kings-18:15:2.summary: Joash sent gold “found in the treasuries of the Lord’s house and the king’s house” to Hazael.

2-kings-18:15:3.summary: Asa took gold and silver “from the treasuries of the Lord’s house and the king’s house.”

2-kings-18:15:4.summary: Asa brought silver and gold into the Lord's house; origin of treasures.

2-kings-18:16:0.summary: Solomon's temple doors “covered … with gold”; the kind of gilded doors stripped.

2-kings-18:16:1.summary: Hezekiah “opened the doors of the Lord’s house and repaired them,” the same doors later stripped.
2-kings-18:16:1.why: Contrast of early piety and later stripping.

2-kings-18:17:1.summary: Same site: the pool of “the upper road of the fuller’s field.”
2-kings-18:17:1.why: Same location as Isaiah's meeting with Ahaz.

2-kings-18:17:5.summary: Sennacherib, “at Lachish,” sent servants against Jerusalem to Hezekiah.

2-kings-18:17:0.summary: “Tanathan” sent by the Assyrian king, possibly the same office as Tharthan.

2-kings-18:17:2.summary: Hezekiah's “fountain and aqueduct”; the aqueduct theme, though not the same pool.

2-kings-18:17:4.summary: Jerusalem's water diverted from “the old pool” during siege preparation.

2-kings-18:18:0.summary: “Eliakim the steward, Somnas the scribe” sent to Isaiah.

2-kings-18:18:2.summary: Oracle against “Somnas the treasurer” and his stewardship (shown text).

2-kings-18:18:3.summary: “Eliakim the steward, Somnas the scribe” sent to Isaiah.

2-kings-18:18:7.summary: “Eliakim son of Chelkias, the steward, Somnas … and Joach son of Asaph,” same three officials.

2-kings-18:18:1.summary: Solomon's scribes and recorder; same offices, different people.

2-kings-18:18:4.summary: Josiah's recorder Joah; same office, different person.

2-kings-18:18:5.summary: David's recorder and scribe; same offices.

2-kings-18:19:5.summary: “On what have you placed your trust,” Sennacherib's parallel taunt.

2-kings-18:19:1.summary: Second Assyrian message: “your God, in whom you trust.”

2-kings-18:19:2.summary: Isaiah gives the Assyrian ruler's boast over conquered lands, including Samaria.

2-kings-18:19:3.summary: Same speech continues, challenging Hezekiah's assurance of rescue.

2-kings-18:19:4.summary: “Your God, on whom you rely,” the Assyrian taunt on trust.

2-kings-18:19:6.summary: Isaiah's parallel speech: “We trust the Lord our God.”

2-kings-18:19:7.summary: Nebuchadnezzar's boast of his might; similar imperial arrogance.

2-kings-18:19:8.summary: Psalmist rebukes love of vanity; no link to the Assyrian taunt.

2-kings-18:19:9.summary: Hezekiah's “with us is the Lord our God,” the very confidence mocked.

2-kings-18:19:10.summary: Same speech: “We trust the Lord God.”

2-kings-18:19:11.summary: Chronicles' parallel taunt: “do not let Hezekiah deceive you or make you confident.”

2-kings-18:19:12.summary: Assyrian boast listing defeated kings, from a later speech.

2-kings-18:20:0.summary: “Counsel” and war-readiness avail nothing; help is from the Lord.

2-kings-18:21:0.summary: Egypt's help is “futile and empty,” as the broken staff image says.

2-kings-18:21:1.summary: Egypt as “a reed staff” that breaks when leaned on.

2-kings-18:21:2.summary: Trusting in Pharaoh's shelter becomes shame for “those trusting in Egypt.”

2-kings-18:21:3.summary: Woe to those trusting Egypt for help; “an Egyptian human being and not God.”

2-kings-18:21:5.summary: Pharaoh mocked with a derisive name; Egypt's unreliability.

2-kings-18:21:6.summary: Hoshea sent to the king of Egypt and was destroyed by Assyria.

2-kings-18:22:0.summary: Chronicles: high places and altars demolished, the removal Rabshakeh cites.

2-kings-18:22:3.summary: Nebuchadnezzar: “What god will rescue you from my hands?”

2-kings-18:22:4.summary: Mockery of trust in God: “He trusts in God.”

2-kings-18:22:5.summary: Isaiah's parallel: “We trust the Lord our God.”

2-kings-18:22:6.summary: Records Hezekiah's removal of high places and his hope in the Lord.

2-kings-18:23:1.summary: Goliath's taunting offer to David; similar contemptuous challenge.

2-kings-18:23:3.summary: Ben-hadad's battle order; no meaningful link.

2-kings-18:23:5.summary: Assyrian king's boast “By strength I will act,” the arrogance of the taunt.

2-kings-18:23:6.summary: Sanballat mocks the Jews' strength; similar ridicule.

2-kings-18:23:7.summary: Prayer against contempt of the proud.

2-kings-18:24:0.summary: Assyrian claim to sole rule; general arrogance.

2-kings-18:24:1.summary: Nebuchadnezzar's tree dream; no specific link.

2-kings-18:24:2.summary: Same speech: trusting the “broken reed staff, Egypt.”
2-kings-18:24:2.why: Immediate context of hope in Egypt.

2-kings-18:24:3.summary: King forbidden to “return unto Egypt” to multiply horses.
2-kings-18:24:3.why: Law against relying on Egypt's horses.

2-kings-18:24:5.summary: Revolt by “sending his messengers to Egypt to give him horses,” and failure.

2-kings-18:24:6.summary: Egyptian horses are “flesh, with no help.”

2-kings-18:24:7.summary: Pharaoh will not help in war.

2-kings-18:24:8.summary: “These rely on chariots, and those on horses,” but we on the Lord.
2-kings-18:24:8.why: Contrasts chariots with trust in God.

2-kings-18:24:11.summary: Warning against seeking safety in Egypt (shown text).

2-kings-18:24:12.summary: Isaiah's parallel: “this broken reed staff, Egypt.”

2-kings-18:24:13.summary: Pharaoh's army returns without helping Judah.

2-kings-18:24:14.summary: Woe to those going to Egypt, trusting “horses and chariots.”

2-kings-18:25:0.summary: Isaiah replies to the Assyrian “young servants” who blasphemed.

2-kings-18:25:1.summary: Neco claims God told him to hurry; foreign king's divine claim.

2-kings-18:25:2.summary: Prophet falsely claims the Lord's word; deceptive divine claim.

2-kings-18:25:3.summary: Calamity a city suffers is done by the Lord.

2-kings-18:25:4.summary: God sends Assyria as His rod against “a lawless nation.”

2-kings-18:25:5.summary: Authority “given you from above” to Pilate.

2-kings-18:25:6.summary: God answers the Assyrian who reproached Israel's Holy One (shown text).

2-kings-18:26:3.summary: Introduces the same “Eliakim son of Chelkias … Somnas … Joash.”

2-kings-18:27:0.summary: Siege sign with dung-baked bread; siege deprivation.

2-kings-18:27:1.summary: Israel will eat unclean things; siege-sign context.

2-kings-18:27:2.summary: The wealthy wrapped in dung heaps after siege.

2-kings-18:27:3.summary: Siege famine where “pigeons’ dung” was sold.

2-kings-18:27:4.summary: Wicked speak arrogantly against the height.

2-kings-18:27:5.summary: Curse of eating one's own children in siege “distress.”

2-kings-18:28:1.summary: He “shouted in a loud voice in the Judean language” to those on the wall.

2-kings-18:28:2.summary: “The great king, the king of the Assyrians,” same title in the same speech.

2-kings-18:28:3.summary: The Lord is “a great King over all the earth,” contrasting the Assyrian “great king.”
2-kings-18:28:3.why: Who is truly the great king.

2-kings-18:28:4.summary: Persian “king of kings” title; imperial title.

2-kings-18:28:6.summary: Assyria as a towering cedar (shown text), Assyrian greatness.

2-kings-18:28:7.summary: Heavenly praise of God's reign; only loud voice overlap.

2-kings-18:28:8.summary: Assyrian boast of conquests and judgment on his “great mind.”

2-kings-18:29:0.summary: “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you … cannot save … from my hand.”

2-kings-18:29:1.summary: Pilate's claim of power over Jesus; power claim.

2-kings-18:29:2.summary: “Is Hezekiah not deceiving you … ‘The Lord our God will save us.’”
2-kings-18:29:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-18:29:3.summary: “What god will rescue you from my hands?” answered by trust that God will rescue.

2-kings-18:29:4.summary: “Your God … will rescue you,” in different spirit.

2-kings-18:29:5.summary: Lawless one destroyed by Christ; no specific link.

2-kings-18:29:6.summary: One exalting himself above every god; arrogance theme.

2-kings-18:29:7.summary: They set their mouth against heaven; arrogant speech.

2-kings-18:30:0.summary: “Jerusalem will certainly not be handed into the hands of the king of the Assyrians.”

2-kings-18:30:2.summary: God answers: “Whom have you reproached and blasphemed?”

2-kings-18:30:3.summary: Those trusting the Lord are like Zion; Jerusalem will never be shaken.

2-kings-18:30:4.summary: Plea not to be forsaken in old age; no link.

2-kings-18:30:5.summary: Enemies say “there is no rescuer”; similar taunt.

2-kings-18:30:6.summary: God promises the Assyrian “shall not enter this city.”

2-kings-18:30:7.summary: “He hoped in the Lord; let Him rescue him,” same taunt.

2-kings-18:30:8.summary: “In the Lord I have trusted” against pressure to flee.

2-kings-18:30:9.summary: Rulers mock Jesus: “let Him save Himself.”

2-kings-18:30:10.summary: “He trusts in God; let Him rescue Him,” same mockery.

2-kings-18:31:0.summary: “Each beneath his vine and beneath his fig tree,” the same peace image.

2-kings-18:31:1.summary: Judah and Israel “eating, drinking”; prosperity theme.

2-kings-18:31:2.summary: “Beneath a vine and beneath a fig tree,” the same image.

2-kings-18:31:4.summary: Jacob's gifts to appease Esau; the Greek “blessing” sense differs.

2-kings-18:31:5.summary: “Take my blessings” meaning gifts, same idiom for a peace gift.

2-kings-18:32:0.summary: “A land of olive oil and honey,” vines, and bread; same description.

2-kings-18:32:1.summary: Good land with milk and honey; promised land.

2-kings-18:32:2.summary: God cares for the land; no specific link.

2-kings-18:32:4.summary: “A land flowing with milk and honey.”

2-kings-18:32:5.summary: Samaria's deportation shows what “take you to a land” meant.

2-kings-18:32:6.summary: Babylon's deportation of Jerusalem; later exile.

2-kings-18:32:7.summary: Israel deported to the Assyrians, the fate offered.

2-kings-18:32:9.summary: Spies report land with milk and honey.

2-kings-18:33:0.summary: Assyria boasts: “as I did to Samaria … so I will also do to Jerusalem.”

2-kings-18:33:1.summary: Hezekiah answers: the Assyrian kings destroyed the nations' gods, “for they are not gods.”

2-kings-18:33:2.summary: “Did the gods of the nations … rescue them?”

2-kings-18:33:3.summary: Spoke against Jerusalem's God as against the peoples' gods.

2-kings-18:33:4.summary: “Who among all the gods of these nations … were they able to save?”

2-kings-18:34:0.summary: Both record an Assyrian king boasting of conquered cities, including Samaria, as proof no power can resist him.
2-kings-18:34:0.why: Shows the Assyrian conquest boast as a recurring motif.

2-kings-18:34:1.summary: Mentions the king of Hamath, the same city as “Aimath”, but in an unrelated David narrative.
2-kings-18:34:1.why: Identifies the city named in the boast.

2-kings-18:34:2.summary: Isaiah’s parallel of the Assyrian message asks whether “the gods of the nations” rescued them, matching this boast.
2-kings-18:34:2.why: Parallel version of the same Assyrian taunt.

2-kings-18:34:4.summary: Names “Hamath and Arpad” together, the same city pair as “Aimath and Arphad”, in an oracle on Damascus.
2-kings-18:34:4.why: Shows these cities’ fate elsewhere in prophecy.

2-kings-18:34:5.summary: Hezekiah’s answer in Isaiah: the Assyrians burned the nations’ idols because “they were not gods”, explaining why those gods failed.
2-kings-18:34:5.why: Gives the faithful answer to the Assyrian question.

2-kings-18:34:6.summary: Assyria resettled people from “Aimath, and Seppharouain” in Samaria, the same places named in the boast.
2-kings-18:34:6.why: Shows the cities Assyria already conquered and deported.

2-kings-18:34:7.summary: The repeated taunt asks “Where are the king of Aimath and the king of Arphad?” and names Seppharouain again.
2-kings-18:34:7.why: Repetition of the same boast in Sennacherib’s letter.

2-kings-18:34:8.summary: The Greek-based “Ephaath” does not carry the Hamath link, and the spies’ survey has no connection to the boast.
2-kings-18:34:8.why: No meaningful link in the Saints text.

2-kings-18:34:9.summary: Records the Assyrian capture of Samaria, the event behind the taunt “have they rescued Samaria from my hand?”
2-kings-18:34:9.why: Explains the Samaria reference in the boast.

2-kings-18:35:0.summary: Nebuchadnezzar asks “What god will rescue you from my hands?”, echoing the Assyrian challenge to God’s power to rescue.
2-kings-18:35:0.why: Another pagan king defying God’s power to save.

2-kings-18:35:1.summary: Pharaoh’s “Who is He…? I do not know the Lord” parallels the Assyrian dismissal of the Lord’s power.
2-kings-18:35:1.why: Classic pattern of a proud king defying the Lord.

2-kings-18:35:2.summary: Kings of the earth set themselves “against the Lord”, a general parallel to the Assyrian defiance.
2-kings-18:35:2.why: Places the boast within rebellion against God.

2-kings-18:35:3.summary: Describes a man who “raised his hands against the Lord” in insolence, only generally like the boast.
2-kings-18:35:3.why: General picture of arrogant defiance of God.

2-kings-18:35:4.summary: The Lord’s reply asks “Whom did you reproach and provoke?”, answering the Assyrian boast directly.
2-kings-18:35:4.why: God’s own answer to this blasphemous challenge.

2-kings-18:35:5.summary: Hezekiah concedes “the kings of the Assyrians have devastated the nations”, granting the fact behind the boast.
2-kings-18:35:5.why: Shows the prayer responding to the boast.

2-kings-18:35:6.summary: The ax boasting against its wielder images arrogance, but the shown verse does not name Assyria.
2-kings-18:35:6.why: Illustrates the folly of the conqueror’s pride.

2-kings-18:35:7.summary: Chronicles’ parallel: no god of any nation could save “from my hand”, so “your God” will not save you.
2-kings-18:35:7.why: Parallel account of the same Assyrian speech.

2-kings-18:36:0.summary: Warns that rebuking the impious brings dishonor, loosely fitting the decision not to answer Rhapsakes.

2-kings-18:36:1.summary: The psalmist is like one “who does not open his mouth” before enemies, a general parallel to the silence.

2-kings-18:36:2.summary: The psalmist guards his mouth “when the sinner stood against me”, loosely matching the silence before Rhapsakes.
2-kings-18:36:2.why: Restraint of speech before an adversary.

2-kings-18:36:3.summary: The understanding person “will be silent” in an evil time, a general principle only.
2-kings-18:36:3.why: General wisdom on silence in crisis.

2-kings-18:36:4.summary: “Do not answer a fool” matches the king’s command, “Do not answer him.”
2-kings-18:36:4.why: Proverb behind the strategic refusal to reply.

2-kings-18:36:5.summary: Not giving holy things to dogs is only loosely related to refusing to answer a mocker.
2-kings-18:36:5.why: Loose principle of withholding from scoffers.

2-kings-18:37:1.summary: Names the same three officials, Eliakim son of Chelkias, Somnas and Joash, speaking with Rhapsakes.
2-kings-18:37:1.why: Same delegation earlier in the scene.

2-kings-18:37:0.summary: Josiah “tore his garments” on hearing words, a shared mourning gesture in another event.
2-kings-18:37:0.why: Common sign of distress at grave words.

2-kings-18:37:2.summary: Josiah is commended for rending his garments on hearing the Lord’s words; only the gesture is shared.
2-kings-18:37:2.why: Torn garments as humility before God.

2-kings-18:37:3.summary: A king of Israel tears his garments in a siege crisis, sharing only the mourning gesture.

2-kings-18:37:4.summary: Reuben “tore his garments”; only the common mourning gesture is shared.

2-kings-18:37:5.summary: Messengers come “weeping bitterly” seeking peace, loosely like the distressed officials returning.

2-kings-18:37:6.summary: Jehoiakim and his servants heard grave words yet did not tear “their garments”, opposite to these officials.
2-kings-18:37:6.why: Contrasts proper and improper responses to warning.

2-kings-18:37:8.summary: Job “tore his garments” in grief; only the gesture links the passages.

2-kings-18:37:9.summary: The high priest tears his garments over “blasphemy”; the shared gesture relates loosely to Rhapsakes’s blasphemous words.
2-kings-18:37:9.why: Torn garments as response to blasphemy.

2-kings-18:37:10.summary: A king tears his garments after reading a threatening letter; only the gesture is shared.

2-kings-18:37:11.summary: Jacob “tore his garments” in mourning; only the gesture is shared.

2-kings-18:7:13.summary: 1 Samuel 18:5 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-18:7:13.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-18:7:13.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-19:1:0.summary: The officials come “with torn garments” and report Rhapsakes’s words, which Hezekiah then hears.

2-kings-19:1:1.summary: Ahab “tore his tunic” and put on sackcloth, the same pairing of torn garments and sackcloth.

2-kings-19:1:2.summary: Jacob “tore his garments, and put sackcloth” on, the same pairing of mourning acts.
2-kings-19:1:2.why: Shows the standard pairing of mourning acts.

2-kings-19:1:3.summary: Chronicles’ account of the same crisis: Hezekiah and Isaiah pray and the Lord defeats the Assyrian camp.
2-kings-19:1:3.why: Parallel account and outcome of this crisis.

2-kings-19:1:4.summary: Job tore his garments and “bowed in worship”, loosely like Hezekiah tearing garments and entering the Lord’s house.

2-kings-19:1:6.summary: The psalmist “put on sackcloth” and prayed; only the sackcloth and prayer are shared.

2-kings-19:1:7.summary: God promises attention to prayer in “this house”, loosely relevant to Hezekiah entering the Lord’s house.
2-kings-19:1:7.why: Background for seeking God at the temple.

2-kings-19:1:8.summary: Mentions repentance “in sackcloth and ashes”, sharing only sackcloth.
2-kings-19:1:8.why: Sackcloth as a sign of repentance.

2-kings-19:1:9.summary: A king of Israel “tore his garments” over a letter; only the gesture is shared.

2-kings-19:1:10.summary: Jehoiakim did not tear his garments on hearing warnings, the opposite of Hezekiah’s response.
2-kings-19:1:10.why: Contrasts a king who refused humility.

2-kings-19:1:11.summary: A messenger arrives “with his garments torn”; only the mourning sign is shared.

2-kings-19:1:12.summary: Nineveh puts on sackcloth and cries to God; shared sackcloth and appeal to God.

2-kings-19:1:13.summary: God notes Ahab’s humbling and delays harm, loosely relating to a king’s humbling before God.
2-kings-19:1:13.why: Shows God’s response to royal humility.

2-kings-19:1:14.summary: A king “tore his garments” and wore “sackcloth” during a siege, the same pairing in a siege crisis.
2-kings-19:1:14.why: Parallel royal response to siege distress.

2-kings-19:1:15.summary: Mordecai “tore his clothes, put on sackcloth” facing a threat to his people (judged on the shown text).
2-kings-19:1:15.why: Same mourning acts at a national threat.

2-kings-19:1:16.summary: Ezra “tore my garments” on hearing a report; only the gesture is shared.

2-kings-19:1:17.summary: The high priest “tore his garments”; only the gesture is shared.

2-kings-19:1:18.summary: Mattathias and his sons “tore their garments, put on sackcloth”, the same pair of acts in national crisis.
2-kings-19:1:18.why: Same mourning acts at foreign oppression.

2-kings-19:1:19.summary: Israel “put on sackcloth” and “tore their garments” before battle with a foreign power.
2-kings-19:1:19.why: Same mourning acts seeking God’s help.

2-kings-19:2:3.summary: Names “Eliakim son of Chelkias the steward, Somnas the scribe”, the same officials sent here.

2-kings-19:2:0.summary: Introduces “Isaiah son of Amos”, prophet during Hezekiah’s reign, the prophet consulted here.

2-kings-19:2:1.summary: Names “Isaiah son of Amos” as receiving the Lord’s word, the same prophet.

2-kings-19:2:4.summary: Refers to “Isaiah the prophet”, the same person, but in an unrelated fulfillment formula.

2-kings-19:2:5.summary: The Saints text names “Jessias the prophet”, so the Isaiah link is not explicit in this wording.

2-kings-19:2:6.summary: Josiah likewise sends officials, including a priest, to consult a prophet in crisis.
2-kings-19:2:6.why: Parallel pattern of a king seeking a prophet.

2-kings-19:2:7.summary: Cites “Isaiah the prophet”; only the prophet’s name is shared.

2-kings-19:3:0.summary: Mentions “the woman who gives birth”, but in a different sense from the image of failed delivery.

2-kings-19:3:1.summary: Describes a fearful, “narrow time” with birth-pain imagery, loosely like Hezekiah’s day of affliction.
2-kings-19:3:1.why: Birth pangs for a national crisis.

2-kings-19:3:2.summary: Shares only the word “provocation”, used of Israel’s wilderness rebellion rather than an enemy’s insult.

2-kings-19:3:3.summary: A woman in labor nearing childbirth images distress, but the Greek here ends in salvation, not failed delivery.

2-kings-19:3:4.summary: “Pangs like those of a woman giving birth” and children not enduring match the image of failed delivery.
2-kings-19:3:4.why: Same image of labor without deliverance.

2-kings-19:3:5.summary: Part of Rhapsakes’s taunt, the rebuke Hezekiah calls a day of “rebuke, and provocation”.
2-kings-19:3:5.why: Shows the insult behind Hezekiah’s words.

2-kings-19:3:6.summary: Shares only the word “provocation”, referring to Israel testing God in the wilderness.

2-kings-19:3:7.summary: Israel seeks God “in their affliction”, a general parallel to Hezekiah’s day of affliction.

2-kings-19:3:8.summary: Shares only the word “rebukes”, here God’s discipline for lawlessness, not an enemy’s insult.

2-kings-19:3:9.summary: A plea for mercy when filled with “contempt” and “reproach” from the proud, loosely like Hezekiah’s day of rebuke.
2-kings-19:3:9.why: Prayer under the scorn of the proud.

2-kings-19:3:10.summary: Sirach’s account of Hezekiah’s time recalls people suffering “pangs like women giving birth”.
2-kings-19:3:10.why: Sirach recalls this crisis with the birth image.

2-kings-19:4:0.summary: “Perhaps the Lord will look” on David and repay an enemy’s curse, like hoping the Lord will hear Rhapsakes’s words.
2-kings-19:4:0.why: Same hope that God will answer insults.

2-kings-19:4:1.summary: Encourages intercessory prayer, generally like the request for Isaiah to pray.

2-kings-19:4:2.summary: Caleb’s hopeful “If the Lord is with me” against fortified cities loosely resembles this tentative hope.
2-kings-19:4:2.why: Confidence in God against strong foes.

2-kings-19:4:3.summary: God being sought by Israel to multiply them has no clear link to the remnant prayer or Rhapsakes’s blasphemy.

2-kings-19:4:4.summary: Paul cites Isaiah that “the remnant will be saved”, sharing the remnant theme.

2-kings-19:4:5.summary: Isaiah says the Lord “left us seed”, a general remnant parallel.

2-kings-19:4:6.summary: The naming of a place “The Lord Has Seen” has no real link to Rhapsakes or the remnant prayer.

2-kings-19:4:7.summary: The Lord sees His people “weakened” and is moved for them, a general hope behind this request.
2-kings-19:4:7.why: God’s compassion for His weakened people.

2-kings-19:4:8.summary: Jonathan’s “Perhaps the Lord will do something for us” echoes the tentative hope here.

2-kings-19:4:9.summary: David faces a foreigner who has defied the battle line of “the Lord Sabaoth, God of Israel”, as Rhapsakes reproached the living God.
2-kings-19:4:9.why: Parallel of a heathen defying Israel’s God.

2-kings-19:4:10.summary: God promises to answer those who cry to Him, a general basis for the requested prayer.

2-kings-19:4:11.summary: Sets the scene: Sennacherib king of the Assyrians attacks Judah, the master who sent Rhapsakes.

2-kings-19:4:12.summary: “An enemy reproached the Lord” matches Rhapsakes sent “to reproach the living God”.

2-kings-19:4:13.summary: Chronicles records Hezekiah and Isaiah praying about the Assyrian threat, the prayer requested here.
2-kings-19:4:13.why: Parallel record of the requested prayer.

2-kings-19:4:14.summary: Ahaz’s defeats by Syria and Israel have no specific link to Rhapsakes’s blasphemy or the remnant prayer.

2-kings-19:4:15.summary: God asks whom the Assyrian has “reproached and blasphemed”, answering this hope that the Lord heard.

2-kings-19:4:16.summary: Isaiah foretells “the king of the Assyrians” flooding Judea, the invasion that left only a remnant.

2-kings-19:4:17.summary: “Call on Me in the day of affliction; I will rescue you” generally supports the plea for prayer.

2-kings-19:4:18.summary: Contains Rhapsakes’s speech for the king of the Assyrians, the very words referred to here.
2-kings-19:4:18.why: The words Hezekiah asks God to hear.

2-kings-19:4:19.summary: God sends an invader against a lawless nation; the shown verse does not name Assyria.

2-kings-19:4:20.summary: Assyria’s capture of Samaria shows why only a “remnant” of God’s people remained.

2-kings-19:4:21.summary: God says “I kept silent” but will rebuke, loosely like the hope that God heard and will act.

2-kings-19:6:0.summary: Shows the king of the Assyrians sending Rhapsakes and others, the servants whose words are meant.

2-kings-19:6:2.summary: Rhapsakes’s claim that the Lord cannot rescue Jerusalem is the blasphemy Isaiah tells them not to fear.

2-kings-19:6:3.summary: “Thus says the Lord… Do not fear” before a great army, the same prophetic reassurance.

2-kings-19:6:4.summary: The Lord says “Do not fear them” and promises deliverance from enemies, the same assurance form.

2-kings-19:6:5.summary: The beast opens its mouth “to blaspheme” God, a general parallel to blasphemous enemies.

2-kings-19:6:6.summary: “Do not fear or be terrified” and see the Lord’s salvation for Judah and Jerusalem, matching this assurance.

2-kings-19:6:7.summary: Moses tells Israel “fear not” for God fights for them, a general parallel.
2-kings-19:6:7.why: General basis for not fearing enemies.

2-kings-19:6:8.summary: Israel shall “not fear” a stronger enemy because the Lord is with them; general parallel.
2-kings-19:6:8.why: General basis for not fearing enemies.

2-kings-19:6:9.summary: Rhapsakes denies “The Lord will surely rescue us”, among the words Isaiah says not to fear.

2-kings-19:6:10.summary: “Do not fear people’s reproach” matches not fearing the blasphemous words of men.
2-kings-19:6:10.why: Same command not to fear human scorn.

2-kings-19:6:11.summary: God says “do not fear” and promises that “the people who insult you” will perish, matching this reassurance.
2-kings-19:6:11.why: Same divine command not to fear insulting foes.

2-kings-19:6:12.summary: Promises enemies falling before Israel, only a general assurance of victory.

2-kings-19:6:13.summary: Moses urges the people to “behold the salvation from God” before a threatening army; general parallel.
2-kings-19:6:13.why: Trusting God before a superior enemy.

2-kings-19:6:14.summary: Elisha says “Do not be afraid” to a servant facing a besieging army, a prophet’s reassurance like Isaiah’s.

2-kings-19:6:15.summary: “An enemy reproached the Lord” matches the Assyrian servants’ blasphemy addressed here.

2-kings-19:6:16.summary: Contains Rhapsakes’s words, including the claim the Lord sent him, part of the blasphemy Isaiah addresses.

2-kings-19:6:17.summary: The “arrogance of those hating Thee” rising to God loosely fits the blasphemy here.

2-kings-19:6:18.summary: God asks why His people feared “a mortal person” and “your oppressor’s anger”, matching “Do not fear the words”.
2-kings-19:6:18.why: Explains why human threats need not be feared.

2-kings-19:7:0.summary: The Lord made Syria’s camp hear a sound and flee, like God sending a report to turn back the Assyrian.
2-kings-19:7:0.why: God routing enemies by a report.

2-kings-19:7:1.summary: God scatters enemies by “the blast of the spirit of Thine anger”, loosely like the spirit put in the king.

2-kings-19:7:2.summary: God sends dishonor and fire against a proud foe; the shown verses do not name Assyria.

2-kings-19:7:3.summary: The ungodly slain “with breath through his lips”, a general picture of God overthrowing the wicked.

2-kings-19:7:4.summary: The king “returned to his land” and was “struck… down with the sword”, fulfilling this prophecy.

2-kings-19:7:5.summary: Shares only the word “report”, here a summons of nations against Edom.

2-kings-19:7:6.summary: God appearing with fire and tempest has no specific link to the spirit, report, or sword here.

2-kings-19:7:7.summary: Fire and storm on sinners has no specific link to this prophecy of a report and sword.

2-kings-19:7:8.summary: The wicked perish “by the breath of His anger”, generally like God’s judgment on the king.

2-kings-19:7:9.summary: “His fear is in his ears” and sudden overthrow loosely match the king hearing a report and falling.
2-kings-19:7:9.why: Alarm and sudden downfall of the wicked.

2-kings-19:7:10.summary: Shares only “report”, used of a call to nations against Edom.

2-kings-19:7:11.summary: Sennacherib returns to Nineveh and his sons strike him “with the sword”, fulfilling this word.

2-kings-19:7:12.summary: God rouses a destroying wind against Babylon, loosely like God acting against a foreign king.

2-kings-19:8:0.summary: The king of the Assyrians at Lachish, the place he had departed from.

2-kings-19:8:1.summary: Joshua besieges “Libnah”; the Saints source spells it “Lomna”, so the same-place link is not explicit.
2-kings-19:8:1.why: Possible identification of the besieged town.

2-kings-19:8:3.summary: A list naming the king of “Libnah”; place link only, and the spelling differs from “Lomna”.

2-kings-19:8:4.summary: Lists “Libnah” in Judah’s towns; the Saints source reads “Lomna”.

2-kings-19:8:5.summary: Lists “Lachish” among Judah’s towns; place mention only.

2-kings-19:8:6.summary: Names “the king of Lachish” in a conquest list; place mention only.

2-kings-19:8:7.summary: Prophecy against “Lachish” with chariots and horsemen, same place, different context.

2-kings-19:8:8.summary: “Lobena” revolts from Judah; possibly the same town, but spelling differs from “Lomna”.

2-kings-19:9:0.summary: A report of an attack elsewhere makes Saul break off, like the report about Tharaka diverting the Assyrian.
2-kings-19:9:0.why: Enemy diverted by a timely report.

2-kings-19:9:1.summary: The king of the Assyrians earlier sent envoys to Hezekiah; here he sends messengers again.
2-kings-19:9:1.why: Earlier embassy in the same campaign.

2-kings-19:10:0.summary: Hezekiah “hoped in the Lord”, the very trust the Assyrian now mocks.

2-kings-19:10:1.summary: Same taunt: Do not let Hezekiah lift you up; the city “will certainly not be handed into the hand of the king of the Assyrians”.
2-kings-19:10:1.why: Earlier form of the same taunt.

2-kings-19:10:3.summary: Chronicles’ parallel of the letter: “your God certainly will not save you from my hand” (judged on shown text).
2-kings-19:10:3.why: Parallel account of the same message.

2-kings-19:11:0.summary: Hezekiah answers that “the kings of the Assyrians have devastated the nations”, conceding the fact but not the conclusion.

2-kings-19:11:1.summary: Assyria’s conquest of Samaria shows what “the kings of the Assyrians did” to lands (judged on shown text).

2-kings-19:11:2.summary: Chronicles’ parallel: “Will you not learn what I and my fathers did to all the peoples”, and could their gods save?
2-kings-19:11:2.why: Parallel account of the same boast.

2-kings-19:11:3.summary: Assyria boasts that as it did to Samaria, “so I will also do to Jerusalem”, the same threat.
2-kings-19:11:3.why: Isaiah’s report of the same boast.

2-kings-19:12:0.summary: Assyria deported Israel to “rivers of Gozan”, a place named in the boast.

2-kings-19:12:1.summary: Terah settles in “Harran”, likely the same city as “Charran”, but in an unrelated patriarchal story.

2-kings-19:12:2.summary: “Haran” appears as a trading partner of Tyre; place mention only.

2-kings-19:12:4.summary: The garden “in Eden” is not the “sons of Edem in Thaesthen”; the names only look alike.

2-kings-19:12:5.summary: Herdsmen say they are “from Harran”; place mention only.

2-kings-19:12:6.summary: Same boast: have “the gods of the nations ever rescued” their countries from the king of the Assyrians?
2-kings-19:12:6.why: Earlier form of the same taunt.

2-kings-19:12:7.summary: Assyrian kings deported Israelites to “the River Gozan”, a place named in the boast.

2-kings-19:12:8.summary: Abraham lived in “Haran”; place mention only.

2-kings-19:13:0.summary: Same taunt naming “Aimath and Arphad” and “Seppharouain”.
2-kings-19:13:0.why: Earlier form of the same taunt.

2-kings-19:13:2.summary: Mentions “Hamath” as a border point; the Saints source spells it “Aimath”.

2-kings-19:13:3.summary: The Greek-based “Ephaath” does not clearly carry the Hamath link, and the context is unrelated.
2-kings-19:13:3.why: No meaningful link in the Saints text.

2-kings-19:13:4.summary: Mentions “Emath”, likely Hamath, in an oracle against nations; place mention only.

2-kings-19:13:5.summary: Assyria brought people from “Aimath, and Seppharouain”, cities named in the taunt.
2-kings-19:13:5.why: Shows these cities under Assyrian control.

2-kings-19:13:7.summary: “Hamath and Arpad” appear together in an oracle; same city pair, different event.
2-kings-19:13:7.why: Prophetic fate of the same cities.

2-kings-19:13:8.summary: The Saints text lists no Hamath or other named city from the taunt; only Assyria is shared.

2-kings-19:14:1.summary: Taking refuge in God loosely fits Hezekiah bringing the letters before the Lord.

2-kings-19:14:2.summary: Eyes turned to the Lord amid “contempt” of the proud, loosely like spreading the letters before Him.

2-kings-19:14:3.summary: Solomon asks God to hear prayer made toward “this house”, where Hezekiah brings his crisis.
2-kings-19:14:3.why: Basis for praying at the temple.

2-kings-19:14:4.summary: “How long… will the enemy reproach?” fits the reproachful letters only generally.

2-kings-19:14:5.summary: Ezra spreads his hands toward the Lord in distress, generally like Hezekiah presenting the letters.

2-kings-19:15:0.summary: Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges “the God of heaven”, only a general parallel to this confession.
2-kings-19:15:0.why: A king acknowledging the true God.

2-kings-19:15:1.summary: God asks whether “there is a God apart from Me”, matching “Thou alone art God”.

2-kings-19:15:2.summary: God speaks “from between the two cherubim”, the basis for “seated upon the cherubim”.

2-kings-19:15:3.summary: “Truly the Lord is God!” confesses the Lord as God, like Hezekiah’s confession.
2-kings-19:15:3.why: Shared confession of the Lord’s sole deity.

2-kings-19:15:4.summary: Naaman confesses “no God in all the earth except in Israel”, matching God alone among the kingdoms.
2-kings-19:15:4.why: A foreigner’s confession of God’s uniqueness.

2-kings-19:15:5.summary: “Apart from Me there is no God” matches “Thou alone art God”.

2-kings-19:15:6.summary: Daniel’s prayer opens by praising “the great, strong, and fearsome God”, a general parallel.

2-kings-19:15:7.summary: Gods “who did not make heaven and earth” perish, while the Lord made them, matching this prayer.

2-kings-19:15:8.summary: All things came into being through the Word, a general creation link.
2-kings-19:15:8.why: God as source of all creation.

2-kings-19:15:9.summary: David prays “there is none like Thee and no God” besides, as Hezekiah confesses (judged on shown text).

2-kings-19:15:10.summary: “Before Me no other god came to be”, matching God alone over all kingdoms.

2-kings-19:15:11.summary: “I am God, and there is no other”, addressed to the earth’s extremity, matching this confession.

2-kings-19:15:12.summary: The Lord founded the earth and the heavens, generally matching “Thou madest heaven and earth”.

2-kings-19:15:13.summary: “God made heaven and earth” matches “Thou madest heaven and earth”.

2-kings-19:15:14.summary: Solomon’s prayer opens “Lord, the God of Israel, there is no God like Thee”, like Hezekiah’s address.

2-kings-19:15:15.summary: “God made heaven and earth” matches Hezekiah’s confession of the Creator.

2-kings-19:15:16.summary: Jehoshaphat prays “Thou rulest over all the kingdoms of the nations” before an invasion.

2-kings-19:15:17.summary: Asa prays to the Lord against “this great multitude”, a parallel royal prayer against invaders.

2-kings-19:15:18.summary: God “who made heaven and earth” matches this confession.

2-kings-19:15:19.summary: The Lord “who is seated upon the cherubim” uses the same title.

2-kings-19:15:20.summary: “Thou who sittest upon the cherubim” is the same title in a plea for help.

2-kings-19:15:21.summary: Shares only the phrase “God of Israel” in Jacob’s altar naming.

2-kings-19:15:22.summary: Chronicles notes that Hezekiah prayed and cried to heaven, the prayer recorded here.

2-kings-19:15:23.summary: “The God of Israel” promises to listen to the needy, generally relevant to this prayer.

2-kings-19:15:24.summary: Describes the cherubim over the ark, background to the cherubim title.

2-kings-19:15:25.summary: God spoke and creation came to be, a general parallel to God as maker.

2-kings-19:15:26.summary: Igabes calls on “the God of Israel” and is answered; a general prayer parallel.

2-kings-19:15:27.summary: The Lord as King who “sits upon the cherubim” over raging peoples, matching this address.
2-kings-19:15:27.why: Same title with God ruling nations.

2-kings-19:15:28.summary: Jacob’s renaming to Israel has no specific link to this prayer.

2-kings-19:15:29.summary: Sirach recalls the people calling on the Lord in Hezekiah’s day and being redeemed “by Isaiah’s hand”.
2-kings-19:15:29.why: Later retelling of this prayer’s answer.

2-kings-19:16:1.summary: Both speak of hearing words sent “to reproach the living God”.
2-kings-19:16:1.why: Same request that God hear the blasphemy.

2-kings-19:16:8.summary: Isaiah’s parallel: words sent “to reproach the living God”, which may the Lord hear.
2-kings-19:16:8.why: Parallel account of the same plea.

2-kings-19:16:2.summary: Opens with the same plea, “Incline Thine ear”, asking God to save.

2-kings-19:16:3.summary: Asks God’s “eyes be open” and “ears attentive”, matching Hezekiah’s plea.
2-kings-19:16:3.why: Same appeal to God’s attentive eyes and ears.

2-kings-19:16:4.summary: “Attend with Thine ear, Lord, and hear… Open Thine eyes and see” closely matches Hezekiah’s words.

2-kings-19:16:5.summary: Asks that “Thine eyes may be open” to hear prayer at the temple, echoing this plea.

2-kings-19:16:6.summary: Asks God to repay the “insult with which they insulted Thee”, as Hezekiah asks God to hear Sennacherib’s reproach.
2-kings-19:16:6.why: Plea for God to answer insults to Him.

2-kings-19:16:7.summary: Moses bearing “the reproach of Christ” has no real link to Sennacherib’s reproach of God.

2-kings-19:16:9.summary: A prayer pointing God to the nations gathered “to destroy us”, generally like Hezekiah’s plea.

2-kings-19:17:0.summary: Shares only the word “truly”; the context is worship in church.

2-kings-19:17:1.summary: Deserted houses heard by the Lord have no specific link to the Assyrian devastation here.

2-kings-19:17:2.summary: Shares only “Truly”, in Nebuchadnezzar’s praise of Daniel’s God.

2-kings-19:17:3.summary: Assyrian kings deported Israel’s tribes, an example of “the kings of the Assyrians” devastating nations.

2-kings-19:17:4.summary: Shares only the word “truly”; Jeremiah’s defense is unrelated.

2-kings-19:17:5.summary: Isaiah warns God will bring “the king of the Assyrians” on Judah, background to Assyrian power.

2-kings-19:17:6.summary: A prayer beginning “For truly” about rulers gathered against God’s Anointed; only loosely parallel.

2-kings-19:17:7.summary: The king of the Assyrians captured and deported Damascus, one of the nations devastated.

2-kings-19:17:8.summary: The Assyrians moved peoples from conquered cities into Samaria, showing their devastation of nations.

2-kings-19:17:9.summary: Shares only “Truly”, in Peter’s denial scene.

2-kings-19:17:10.summary: The king of the Assyrians captured Samaria and deported Israel, an instance of this devastation.

2-kings-19:17:11.summary: The Assyrian boasts of taking Damascus, Samaria and more, the conquests Hezekiah admits.
2-kings-19:17:11.why: Assyria’s own claim of these conquests.

2-kings-19:17:12.summary: Shares only “Truly”; Job’s question about righteousness is unrelated.

2-kings-19:17:13.summary: Shares only “Truly”, in a confession of Jesus as God’s Son.

2-kings-19:18:0.summary: The divine is not like “stone, an image formed by human art”, matching gods that are works of human hands.
2-kings-19:18:0.why: NT echo of idols as human products.

2-kings-19:18:1.summary: Idols are “wood” and “a carpenter’s work”, artisans’ works that cannot act, matching this verse.
2-kings-19:18:1.why: Develops idols as wood and handiwork.

2-kings-19:18:2.summary: Craftsmen fashion a god from “wood”, a useless thing (judged on shown text), matching gods made by hands.

2-kings-19:18:3.summary: Philistines abandon “their gods” to David, showing captured idols, but no burning is shown.

2-kings-19:18:4.summary: Carved idols are “futile, mocked works” that “will perish”, matching gods that were destroyed.

2-kings-19:18:6.summary: Bel and Dagon’s images “cannot be saved from war”, like the nations’ gods destroyed by Assyria.

2-kings-19:18:7.summary: Idols are “works of human hands”, the same phrase used here.

2-kings-19:19:0.summary: “Let them know… Thou alone art Most High over all the earth” matches all kingdoms knowing God alone.
2-kings-19:19:0.why: Same aim of God’s universal recognition.

2-kings-19:19:1.summary: Solomon asks God to answer so “all the peoples may know Thy name”, as Hezekiah asks.
2-kings-19:19:1.why: Prayer for nations to know God.

2-kings-19:19:2.summary: Asks that God’s “salvation” be known “among all nations”, like deliverance making God known.
2-kings-19:19:2.why: Salvation revealing God to the nations.

2-kings-19:19:3.summary: Joshua appeals to God’s “great name” before the nations, a general parallel.

2-kings-19:19:4.summary: Victory over the defiant foreigner so “all the earth will know that there is a God in Israel”, matching this aim.

2-kings-19:19:5.summary: A foreign king comes to praise the “God of gods”, generally like nations knowing God.

2-kings-19:19:6.summary: God acts “that My name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth”, matching this purpose.

2-kings-19:19:7.summary: Elijah prays “let this people know that Thou art the Lord God”, matching Hezekiah’s petition.
2-kings-19:19:7.why: Parallel prayer for God to reveal Himself.

2-kings-19:19:8.summary: Because Syria belittled the Lord, God gives victory so “you will know that I am the Lord”.
2-kings-19:19:8.why: God vindicates His name after insult.

2-kings-19:19:9.summary: Opens this prayer: “Thou alone art God among all the kingdoms of the earth”, repeated here.

2-kings-19:19:10.summary: “All the nations will know” that One saves Israel, matching the hoped result of deliverance.
2-kings-19:19:10.why: Same hope in a later crisis.

2-kings-19:19:11.summary: “Let them know… there is no God except Thee, Lord”, matching “Thou art the Lord, God alone”.
2-kings-19:19:11.why: Same prayer for nations to know God.

2-kings-19:20:0.summary: Through Isaiah, the Lord tells Hezekiah “I have heard your prayer”, the same assurance.

2-kings-19:20:1.summary: Chronicles records Hezekiah and Isaiah praying and the Lord striking the Assyrian camp.
2-kings-19:20:1.why: Parallel account of the prayer’s answer.

2-kings-19:20:2.summary: God promises to hear before His people cry out, a general parallel to answered prayer.

2-kings-19:20:3.summary: Confidence that God “hears us”, a general teaching on answered prayer.

2-kings-19:20:4.summary: “Cry out to Me and I will answer you” is a general promise of answered prayer.

2-kings-19:20:5.summary: Cornelius is told “your prayer has been heard”, a general parallel.

2-kings-19:20:6.summary: Cornelius’s prayers “ascended as a memorial before God”, a general parallel.

2-kings-19:20:7.summary: Jesus says “Thou always hearest Me”, a general statement on heard prayer.

2-kings-19:20:8.summary: David prays against an enemy’s counsel, loosely like Hezekiah’s prayer against Sennacherib.

2-kings-19:20:9.summary: Daniel’s prayer is answered by a messenger at once, a general parallel.
2-kings-19:20:9.why: Prayer met by a divine reply.

2-kings-19:20:10.summary: Ahithophel’s suicide has no specific link to God hearing Hezekiah’s prayer.

2-kings-19:20:11.summary: “When you pray to Him, He will hear you” is a general promise.

2-kings-19:20:12.summary: “You will cry, and God will hear you” is a general promise.

2-kings-19:20:13.summary: “Call on Me in the day of affliction; I will rescue you” generally fits this answered prayer.

2-kings-19:20:14.summary: “Hear my prayer” is a general plea, loosely matching God hearing Hezekiah.

2-kings-19:21:0.summary: Uses the same titles “Daughter Jerusalem” and “virgin Daughter Zion”, though here Zion is crushed.

2-kings-19:21:1.summary: Job speaks of shaking his head against someone; only the mocking gesture is shared.

2-kings-19:21:2.summary: Passers-by revile Jesus, “shaking their heads”; only the gesture is shared.

2-kings-19:21:3.summary: Laments “the daughter of My people” crushed; only daughter imagery is shared.

2-kings-19:21:4.summary: Passers-by “shook their heads at Daughter Jerusalem”, the reverse of Jerusalem shaking her head at Assyria.

2-kings-19:21:6.summary: Enemies “shook their heads” at the psalmist; only the gesture is shared.

2-kings-19:21:7.summary: Mockers “sneered” and “shook their heads” at one who hoped in the Lord, the same scorn gestures turned here.
2-kings-19:21:7.why: Mockery of trust in God reversed.

2-kings-19:21:8.summary: “Daughter Zion” left “like a besieged city”, loosely relevant to Jerusalem under siege.

2-kings-19:21:9.summary: Addresses “daughter of Zion” and “daughter of Jerusalem”; titles only.

2-kings-19:21:10.summary: Addresses “virgin Israel” with restoration; only the title form is shared.

2-kings-19:21:11.summary: Uses “virgin Daughter Judah”, a similar title in lament.

2-kings-19:21:12.summary: Praise in “daughter Zion” exulting in salvation, loosely matching Zion’s triumph.

2-kings-19:21:13.summary: “Daughter Babylon” shares only a title pattern with Zion.

2-kings-19:21:14.summary: “Daughter of Idumea” shares only a title pattern.

2-kings-19:21:15.summary: “Virgin Israel has fallen” shares only the title form, with the opposite situation.

2-kings-19:21:16.summary: “Daughter of the Chaldeans” shares only a title pattern.

2-kings-19:21:17.summary: “Sidon’s daughter” shares only a title pattern.

2-kings-19:21:18.summary: “Daughter Zion” and “daughter Jerusalem” are paired, here in rejoicing over salvation.

2-kings-19:21:19.summary: Tyre’s shipping oracle has no shared element with Zion’s scorn of Assyria.

2-kings-19:21:20.summary: Shares only “virgin Israel”, in a charge of Israel’s sins.

2-kings-19:21:21.summary: “Virgin daughter Babylon” uses the same title form, here for a humbled enemy.
2-kings-19:21:21.why: Same title form for a city.

2-kings-19:21:22.summary: “Virgin daughter Egypt” uses the same title form in an unrelated oracle.
2-kings-19:21:22.why: Same title form for a nation.

2-kings-19:22:0.summary: People “provoked the utterance of the Holy One of Israel”, sharing the title and offense against Him.

2-kings-19:22:1.summary: Shares only the title “Holy One of Israel”, in praise.

2-kings-19:22:2.summary: The Greek-based text speaks of “Israel’s holy ones”, not the divine title, and has no link to blasphemy.
2-kings-19:22:2.why: Wording does not carry the link.

2-kings-19:22:3.summary: Shares the title “Israel’s Holy One”, in a call to repent.

2-kings-19:22:4.summary: One “exalts himself above everything called god”, a general picture of arrogance against God.

2-kings-19:22:5.summary: Shares the title “Israel’s Holy One”, rejected by His own people.

2-kings-19:22:6.summary: “Every lofty thing raised against the knowledge of God” loosely matches the Assyrian raising his voice.

2-kings-19:22:7.summary: The arrogant “set their mouth toward heaven”, loosely like speech raised against God.

2-kings-19:22:8.summary: “Lofty eyes” of the proud loosely echo “lifted your eyes on high”.

2-kings-19:22:9.summary: Rhapsakes’s speech for the king of the Assyrians contains the words God now calls blasphemy.

2-kings-19:22:10.summary: Pharaoh’s “Who is He…? I do not know the Lord” parallels the Assyrian contempt for the Lord.
2-kings-19:22:10.why: Classic proud king defying the Lord.

2-kings-19:22:11.summary: A king says “I will be like the Most High”, a general picture of arrogance on high.

2-kings-19:22:12.summary: God rebukes Pharaoh for acting “against My people”; only loosely like this rebuke.

2-kings-19:22:13.summary: Tyre’s ruler “said, ‘I am a god’” with an exalted heart, a general parallel to royal pride.
2-kings-19:22:13.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-19:22:14.summary: Rhapsakes was sent “to reproach the living God and to blaspheme”, matching “reproached and blasphemed”.

2-kings-19:22:15.summary: Belshazzar praised idols and did not bless the living God, a general parallel to royal arrogance.

2-kings-19:22:16.summary: “The reproaches against Thee” and the “arrogance of those hating Thee” match this charge.

2-kings-19:22:17.summary: The boasting ax images a proud instrument; the shown verse does not name Assyria.

2-kings-19:22:18.summary: Isaiah refers to words with which the Assyrian servants “blasphemed”, the same offense.
2-kings-19:22:18.why: Earlier word on the same blasphemy.

2-kings-19:22:19.summary: Sirach recalls Sennacherib sending Rabshakeh, who “boasted greatly in his arrogance” against Zion.

2-kings-19:23:0.summary: “These rely on chariots” while we trust the Lord’s name, contrasting the boast of “my chariots”.
2-kings-19:23:0.why: Contrasts trust in chariots with trust in God.

2-kings-19:23:1.summary: The king sent Rhapsakes and others to Jerusalem, the “messengers” through whom he reproached the Lord.

2-kings-19:23:2.summary: Mountains and forests consumed in judgment, loosely answering the boast of conquering forests.

2-kings-19:23:3.summary: He wrote “to reproach the Lord God of Israel”, the same reproach sent through messengers.

2-kings-19:23:4.summary: Assyria is pictured as “a cypress in Lebanon” (judged on shown text), echoing the Lebanon cedars and cypresses here.
2-kings-19:23:4.why: Same Lebanon tree imagery for Assyria.

2-kings-19:23:6.summary: Uzziah’s vinedressers in “Carmel” share only a place name.

2-kings-19:23:7.summary: The earlier boast of conquering nations whose gods could not rescue them, part of the same reproach.
2-kings-19:23:7.why: Earlier form of the arrogant boast.

2-kings-19:23:8.summary: The Assyrian boasts he will “seize the whole inhabited world” with none to resist, like this boast.
2-kings-19:23:8.why: Isaiah’s picture of the same arrogance.

2-kings-19:23:9.summary: Rhapsakes mocks Judah’s lack of horsemen, loosely related to boasting of chariots.

2-kings-19:23:10.summary: The Assyrian king’s boast of taking cities and doing the same to Jerusalem matches this boasting.
2-kings-19:23:10.why: Isaiah’s report of the same boast.

2-kings-19:24:0.summary: Rivers and canals “dry up” in an oracle on Egypt, loosely like drying up rivers.

2-kings-19:24:1.summary: A boast of dragging a city to the torrent, a general parallel to military boasting.

2-kings-19:24:2.summary: Ben-hadad’s boast about his “foot soldiers” overwhelming Samaria loosely parallels this boast.

2-kings-19:24:3.summary: Nebuchadnezzar boasts of his might, a general parallel to royal arrogance.

2-kings-19:24:4.summary: The enemy’s string of “I will” boasts loosely matches this self-exalting speech.

2-kings-19:25:0.summary: God says “I fashioned” and “create calamities”, matching His claim “I formed it; now I brought it”.

2-kings-19:25:1.summary: Assyria is God’s “rod of My anger” to reduce cities to dust, as here God brought the ruin.

2-kings-19:25:3.summary: “I spoke and brought it about… I brought him” matches God planning and bringing events.
2-kings-19:25:3.why: Same claim of God’s planned acts.

2-kings-19:25:4.summary: The ax cannot boast against its wielder, as Assyria’s victories were God’s doing.
2-kings-19:25:4.why: Exposes the conqueror as a tool.

2-kings-19:25:5.summary: Enemies did what God’s purpose “determined beforehand”, a general parallel.

2-kings-19:25:6.summary: “The Lord’s counsel remains for ever” generally supports God’s long-planned acts.

2-kings-19:25:7.summary: God speaks of creating and of destruction, loosely like God forming events.

2-kings-19:25:8.summary: The Greek-based wording, human thought acknowledging God, only loosely relates to God directing events.

2-kings-19:26:0.summary: “I dried up like grass” shares only the grass image.

2-kings-19:26:1.summary: Sinners “spring up like grass” to be destroyed; only the grass image is shared.

2-kings-19:26:2.summary: God guarding a city has no specific link to weakened inhabitants likened to grass.

2-kings-19:26:3.summary: Shares only the word “hand”, of the Lord’s power, not weakened inhabitants.

2-kings-19:26:4.summary: Warriors “disabled” and becoming “like women”, a general picture of defenders losing strength.

2-kings-19:26:5.summary: Calling enemies “food for us” has no specific link to the conquered inhabitants here.

2-kings-19:26:6.summary: Kings “troubled and shaken” with trembling, generally like inhabitants cowering.

2-kings-19:26:7.summary: “All flesh is grass”, sharing the grass image for human frailty.

2-kings-19:26:8.summary: Babylon’s warriors’ power crushed, generally like inhabitants growing weak.

2-kings-19:26:9.summary: The sun “dried the grass”; only the withering grass image is shared.

2-kings-19:26:10.summary: “All flesh is like grass… The grass withered”, sharing only the grass image.

2-kings-19:26:11.summary: Babylon’s burned crossings have no specific link to grass-like inhabitants.
