2-kings-19:26:12.summary: Wounded Chaldeans burning the city has no specific link to this verse.

2-kings-19:26:13.summary: “Grass on roofs, which dried up” matches “rooftop grass” as an image of withering.

2-kings-19:27:1.summary: God sees those who hide and fills heaven and earth, a general parallel to God knowing the king.

2-kings-19:27:2.summary: Shares “come in” and “go out”, here as blessing.

2-kings-19:27:3.summary: “Thou knewest my sitting and my rising” matches “I know your sitting, your going out”.
2-kings-19:27:3.why: Same picture of God’s full knowledge.

2-kings-19:27:4.summary: Shares “coming in” and “going out”, here as God’s protection.

2-kings-19:27:5.summary: Shares “go out” and “come in”, here as curse.

2-kings-19:28:0.summary: God puts “traps in your jaws” to drag Pharaoh out, like hooks in the Assyrian’s nostrils.
2-kings-19:28:0.why: Same image of God hooking a proud king.

2-kings-19:28:1.summary: The Greek-based Saints text has no hooks or bridle, only gathering an army.
2-kings-19:28:1.why: Wording does not carry the link.

2-kings-19:28:2.summary: “By the road on which he came he shall return” repeats this promise.

2-kings-19:28:3.summary: The Greek-based text speaks of weapons and cauldrons, not hooks, so the expected link is missing.
2-kings-19:28:3.why: Wording does not carry the link.

2-kings-19:28:4.summary: The Saints text has no bridle in the jaws, only delusion seizing nations.
2-kings-19:28:4.why: Wording does not carry the link.

2-kings-19:28:5.summary: A ring in the “nostril” and a band through the “lip”, the same image of mastering a beast.

2-kings-19:28:6.summary: Rivers lifting up their voices has no specific link to God’s hook and bridle.

2-kings-19:28:7.summary: Shares only the idea of anger, aimed at Jesus.

2-kings-19:28:8.summary: Horse and mule restrained with “bridle”, sharing only the bridle image.

2-kings-19:28:9.summary: “The arrogance of those hating Thee ascended” matches “your arrogance rose to My ears”.
2-kings-19:28:9.why: Same picture of arrogance reaching God.

2-kings-19:28:10.summary: The ungodly provoke God, but He sees “trouble and anger”, a general parallel.

2-kings-19:28:11.summary: Sennacherib “returned” to Nineveh, fulfilling the threat to turn him back.

2-kings-19:28:12.summary: The world hating Jesus has no specific link to the Assyrian’s anger against God.

2-kings-19:28:13.summary: A king led captive in “a muzzle” loosely resembles the bridle image.

2-kings-19:28:14.summary: Troubled seas and nations have no specific link to this verse.

2-kings-19:28:15.summary: God’s enemies “made an uproar” and lifted their head, generally like the Assyrian’s arrogance.

2-kings-19:28:16.summary: Israel resisting the Spirit has no specific link to the Assyrian’s rage.

2-kings-19:28:17.summary: Hatred of Jesus and the Father is unrelated to this oracle.

2-kings-19:28:18.summary: Nations disturbed until God gives His voice, a general parallel to God subduing a king.

2-kings-19:28:19.summary: A plea for the Lord to rise against enemies, only generally related.

2-kings-19:28:20.summary: Those hating God “boasted”, generally like the Assyrian arrogance.

2-kings-19:28:21.summary: Raging kings against the Lord are answered in His anger, a general parallel.

2-kings-19:29:0.summary: God provides food when no sowing occurs and sowing resumes later, like this three-year sign.

2-kings-19:29:1.summary: “This shall be the sign to you” is a later-confirming sign, the same form as here.

2-kings-19:29:2.summary: Isaiah gives Hezekiah another “sign from the Lord”, a second sign to the same king.

2-kings-19:29:4.summary: “This is the sign for you” shares only the formula.

2-kings-19:29:5.summary: “The things growing of themselves” in a no-sowing year match “what grows by itself”.
2-kings-19:29:5.why: Same idea of eating self-sown growth.

2-kings-19:29:6.summary: Isaiah offers a sign from the Lord to the house of David, as here to Hezekiah.

2-kings-19:29:7.summary: “This will be the sign for you” shares only the formula.

2-kings-19:29:8.summary: The promised remnant and protection of the city are what this sign confirms.

2-kings-19:29:9.summary: Opens the same oracle against the Assyrian of which this sign is part.

2-kings-19:30:0.summary: Hezekiah asks prayer “for the remnant that remains”, the remnant promised to take root.

2-kings-19:30:1.summary: Israel “will sprout and flower” and fill the world with “fruit”, like the remnant bearing fruit.
2-kings-19:30:1.why: Same image of Israel’s renewed growth.

2-kings-19:30:2.summary: The Lord saved Hezekiah and Jerusalem from Sennacherib, the rescue that preserved this remnant.

2-kings-19:30:3.summary: “Jacob’s survivors” and “their remnant will be saved” match the rescued remnant of Judah.

2-kings-19:30:5.summary: The Lord “left us seed”, a general remnant parallel.

2-kings-19:30:6.summary: God planted Israel’s “roots”, sharing the rooting image.

2-kings-19:31:0.summary: “The zeal of the Lord Sabaoth will do these things” matches “The zeal of the Lord of hosts shall do this”.

2-kings-19:31:1.summary: Paul speaks of “a remnant” by grace, a general remnant parallel.

2-kings-19:31:2.summary: “Israel’s remainder” and “Jacob’s survivors” trusting God match the escaping remnant here.

2-kings-19:31:3.summary: Quotes Isaiah that “the remnant will be saved”, a general parallel.

2-kings-19:31:4.summary: Shares only the word “zeal”, used of Jesus and the temple.

2-kings-19:31:5.summary: God acts “in My jealousy”, but in judgment, not rescue.

2-kings-19:31:6.summary: The Saints text lacks “zeal”; God’s armor of righteousness has no specific link to the remnant.
2-kings-19:31:6.why: Wording does not carry the link.

2-kings-19:31:7.summary: God acts so His name is not profaned before nations, loosely like acting for His own sake.

2-kings-19:31:8.summary: Judah’s “remainder” and “those rescued” appear, but in judgment on Egypt’s refugees.

2-kings-19:31:9.summary: “Where are Thy zeal and strength?” appeals to the zeal promised here.

2-kings-19:31:10.summary: The Lord is “jealous for Jerusalem and Zion”, the zeal that preserves Zion’s remnant.

2-kings-19:31:11.summary: Hezekiah’s prayer “for the remnant that remains” is answered by this promise of a remnant.

2-kings-19:32:0.summary: Joab’s men heap “a siege mound” against Abel, sharing only the general siege-ramp image with the promise that none will be raised against Jerusalem.
2-kings-19:32:0.why: Illustrates the siege method the promise rules out.

2-kings-19:32:1.summary: Isaiah foretells “the king of the Assyrians” flooding Judea yet declares “God is with us” and that the Lord will scatter the nations’ counsel.
2-kings-19:32:1.why: Prophetic background to Assyria being stopped short of Jerusalem.

2-kings-19:32:2.summary: An invader’s march toward Daughter Zion and Jerusalem’s hills is traced, but the shown Greek text does not name Assyria or say he is halted.
2-kings-19:32:2.why: Pictures an advance that stops at Zion.

2-kings-19:32:4.summary: Ezekiel’s oracle has a mound cast up and siege set against Jerusalem’s gates, the opposite of the promise that no siege ramp will come.
2-kings-19:32:4.why: Contrasts later judgment with this deliverance.

2-kings-19:32:5.summary: Jesus foretells enemies building “a siege barrier” around Jerusalem, contrasting with the city spared from siege here.
2-kings-19:32:5.why: Shows a later siege the city does not escape.

2-kings-19:32:6.summary: The Lord tells His people in Zion, “Do not fear the Assyrians,” for His wrath will soon cease.

2-kings-19:33:0.summary: The Lord vows to “turn you back by the road on which you came,” the same phrase as “by the road on which he came he shall return.”
2-kings-19:33:0.why: Same oracle’s earlier statement of the promise.

2-kings-19:33:1.summary: Sennacherib “departed, went away, returned” to Nineveh, fulfilling the word that he would return by his road.

2-kings-19:34:0.summary: God spares part of the kingdom “because of David My servant and because of Jerusalem,” the same motive named here.
2-kings-19:34:0.why: Shows the recurring “for David’s sake” protection.
2-kings-19:34:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-19:34:2.summary: “For David’s sake” the Lord preserved Jerusalem, matching the shielding of the city for David’s sake.
2-kings-19:34:2.why: Another instance of Jerusalem kept for David.

2-kings-19:34:3.summary: “The Lord will shield Jerusalem” like flying birds, echoing “I shall shield this city.”
2-kings-19:34:3.why: Isaiah’s image of the same protection.

2-kings-19:34:5.summary: God promises Hezekiah rescue from “the king of the Assyrians’ hand” and says “I will shield this city.”

2-kings-19:34:6.summary: A righteous rising for David will save Judah, a broad Davidic-promise theme rather than this specific protection.
2-kings-19:34:6.why: Links David’s sake to the messianic hope.

2-kings-19:34:8.summary: “For My sake I will act” shares God’s self-motivated action, but concerns exile and His name, not Jerusalem’s siege.
2-kings-19:34:8.why: Highlights God acting for His own sake.

2-kings-19:34:9.summary: The Greek-based text speaks of wiping out lawless acts and lacks any “for My own sake” phrase linking it to this verse.
2-kings-19:34:9.why: No shared element in the Saints wording.

2-kings-19:34:10.summary: Praise of God’s glorious grace in the Beloved has no real link to shielding Jerusalem for David’s sake.

2-kings-19:34:11.summary: God restrains judgment lest adversaries boast “Our hand is exalted,” loosely like God acting for His own honor.
2-kings-19:34:11.why: God’s concern for His reputation before enemies.

2-kings-19:34:12.summary: The throne of David upheld by “the zeal of the Lord Sabaoth” relates generally to God acting for David’s line.
2-kings-19:34:12.why: Connects Davidic promise to divine zeal.

2-kings-19:34:13.summary: “For My name’s sake” God restrains destruction, a similar motive but in a different setting.
2-kings-19:34:13.why: Shows God sparing for His own name.

2-kings-19:34:14.summary: The Spirit as pledge of inheritance “to the praise of His glory” has no specific link to this promise.

2-kings-19:34:15.summary: God acts “not for you” but for His holy name, a general parallel to acting for His own sake.
2-kings-19:34:15.why: Develops the theme of God’s self-motivated deliverance.
2-kings-19:34:15.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-19:34:16.summary: Kings gathered against “the city of the great King” but were troubled and shaken; God supports and founds her for ever.
2-kings-19:34:16.why: Psalm celebrating Zion’s defense from assembled kings.

2-kings-19:34:17.summary: “God is in her midst; she will not be shaken; God will help her toward morning” while nations are disturbed.
2-kings-19:34:17.why: Psalm of the city God protects, deliverance by morning.

2-kings-19:35:1.summary: “The Lord’s angel” destroys people until restrained beside Jerusalem, the same figure of a destroying angel.
2-kings-19:35:1.why: Another mass judgment by the Lord’s angel.

2-kings-19:35:2.summary: At midnight the Lord struck Egypt’s firstborn and there was no house without someone dead.
2-kings-19:35:2.why: Paradigm night-time slaughter of an oppressor.

2-kings-19:35:4.summary: Men “slept their sleep” and horsemen grew drowsy at God’s rebuke, picturing an army struck silent.
2-kings-19:35:4.why: Psalm imagery of a defeated host lying still.

2-kings-19:35:5.summary: “Sudden destruction” coming like a thief in the night shares only a general night-judgment theme.

2-kings-19:35:6.summary: “An angel of the Lord struck him” for not giving glory to God, echoing the angel striking the boastful Assyrians.
2-kings-19:35:6.why: Angelic judgment on a proud ruler.

2-kings-19:35:7.summary: The Greek-based text only says kingship passed to the Medes; it has no night death or angel to link it.
2-kings-19:35:7.why: No shared element in this wording.

2-kings-19:35:8.summary: God will save Judah “by the Lord their God” and not by bow or horses, fitting but not naming this event.
2-kings-19:35:8.why: Frames deliverance as God’s act alone.

2-kings-19:35:9.summary: The Lord Sabaoth shatters “those lofty in insolence,” a general picture of humbling a proud invader.

2-kings-19:35:10.summary: The Lord sends burning against the proud host so that “those left” are so few “a child will write them down.”
2-kings-19:35:10.why: Prophesies the sudden destruction of the invading army.

2-kings-19:35:11.summary: David sees “the Lord’s angel” with drawn sword over Jerusalem, sharing the destroying-angel figure only.
2-kings-19:35:11.why: Another appearance of the destroying angel.

2-kings-19:35:12.summary: Choice of plagues includes “the Lord’s angel destroying,” a shared image but a different judgment.
2-kings-19:35:12.why: Background on the angel of destruction.

2-kings-19:35:13.summary: “At the Lord’s voice the Assyrians will be defeated by the blow with which He strikes them.”
2-kings-19:35:13.why: Isaiah foretells God’s direct blow on Assyria.

2-kings-19:35:14.summary: Human thought acknowledging God follows His wrath in the psalm, only loosely tied to this defeat.
2-kings-19:35:14.why: Response of praise after God’s judgment.

2-kings-19:35:15.summary: Prayer for “an angel of the Lord” to drive and pursue enemies shares the avenging-angel idea.
2-kings-19:35:15.why: Angel acting against enemies of God’s people.

2-kings-19:35:16.summary: The Lord passes through “to strike the Egyptians” by night through the destroyer, a close parallel of divine night-striking.
2-kings-19:35:16.why: Passover precedent for the destroying angel.

2-kings-19:35:17.summary: Judas recalls: “Thine angel went out and struck a hundred and eighty-five thousand,” citing this very event.

2-kings-19:35:18.summary: Judas recounts what happened “under Sennacherib, how one hundred eighty-five thousand perished.”

2-kings-19:35:19.summary: Prayer recalls the angel sent “in the time of Hezekiah” who killed “one hundred eighty-five thousand in Sennacherib’s camp.”
2-kings-19:35:19.why: Later prayer explicitly citing this event.

2-kings-19:35:20.summary: Sirach recalls that God “struck the Assyrians’ camp, and His angel destroyed them.”
2-kings-19:35:20.why: Wisdom retelling of the same event.

2-kings-19:36:0.summary: Nineveh, where Sennacherib retired, is the city Jonah is sent to; only the place is shared.

2-kings-19:36:1.summary: The prophecy “by the road on which he came he shall return” is fulfilled by Sennacherib’s return.

2-kings-19:36:2.summary: God foretold the king would “return to his land” after hearing a report, as he now does.

2-kings-19:36:3.summary: God vows to “turn you back by the road on which you came,” fulfilled in Sennacherib’s retreat.

2-kings-19:36:4.summary: Nahum pictures Nineveh’s people fleeing; only the city Nineveh is shared.

2-kings-19:36:5.summary: Jonah’s preaching in Nineveh, “the great city,” shares only the place name.

2-kings-19:36:6.summary: Asshur built Nineveh, explaining the origin of the Assyrian city named here.

2-kings-19:36:7.summary: Nahum’s oracle “concerning Nineveh” shares only the city.

2-kings-19:36:8.summary: The men of Nineveh judging Jesus’ generation share only the city name, with no link to Sennacherib’s return.

2-kings-19:37:0.summary: “Asaraddon king of Assour” is the same Assyrian king as Asordan who succeeded Sennacherib.
2-kings-19:37:0.why: Identifies the successor in later history.

2-kings-19:37:1.summary: The ark rested on “the mountains of Ararat,” sharing only the place the assassins fled to.

2-kings-19:37:2.summary: God said “I shall bring him down by the sword in his land,” fulfilled when his sons strike him.

2-kings-19:37:3.summary: “Ararat’s kingdoms” are summoned against Babylon; only the region is shared.

2-kings-19:37:4.summary: Sennacherib mocked trust in Israel’s God, yet he dies in his own god’s house, an implied irony.
2-kings-19:37:4.why: Sets his boast against his end.

2-kings-19:37:5.summary: Hezekiah “hoped in the Lord,” loosely contrasted with Sennacherib slain while worshiping his god.
2-kings-19:37:5.why: Contrast of trusting the Lord and idols.

2-kings-19:37:6.summary: Sennacherib spoke of Jerusalem’s God like gods of “human hands,” yet his own god could not protect him.

2-kings-19:37:8.summary: “Their gods are not as our God” fits the outcome only as a general principle.

2-kings-19:37:9.summary: The taunt that the Lord would not rescue the city contrasts with the king’s own death.
2-kings-19:37:9.why: Shows the reversal of the boast.

2-kings-19:37:10.summary: He asked which gods could save their people, yet his own god could not save him.

2-kings-19:37:11.summary: Chronicles records the king entering “the house of his god” where his own offspring “struck him down with the sword.”

2-kings-19:7:13.summary: Jeremiah 51:46 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-19:7:13.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-19:7:13.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-19:13:6.summary: Jeremiah 39:5 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-19:13:6.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-19:13:6.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-19:34:4.summary: Jeremiah 33:26 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-19:34:4.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-19:34:4.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-19:34:7.summary: Jeremiah 33:21 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-19:34:7.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-19:34:7.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-20:1:1.summary: “In those days Hezekiah became ill to the point of death,” Chronicles’ account of the same illness.

2-kings-20:1:2.summary: Epaphroditus “was sick, near death; but God had mercy,” a general parallel.

2-kings-20:1:3.summary: A prophetic doom on Nineveh is averted by repentance, a general parallel of an announced death reversed.

2-kings-20:1:4.summary: “Isaiah son of Amos” sends God’s word to Hezekiah in another episode.

2-kings-20:1:5.summary: Ahithophel “gave instructions to his household” before dying, echoing “Give instructions for your house.”
2-kings-20:1:5.why: Setting one’s house in order before death.

2-kings-20:1:6.summary: God may “change My mind” about announced judgment, explaining a reversible prophecy generally.

2-kings-20:1:7.summary: Epaphroditus came near to death, a general parallel.

2-kings-20:1:8.summary: Lazarus’ illness is “not for death,” a general mortal-illness parallel.

2-kings-20:1:9.summary: Hezekiah sends to “Isaiah the prophet, son of Amos,” sharing the same persons.

2-kings-20:1:10.summary: The Saints Sirach text on excelling in works has no link to setting one’s house in order.

2-kings-20:2:0.summary: “Call on Me in the day of affliction; I will rescue you” fits Hezekiah’s prayer generally.

2-kings-20:2:1.summary: Solomon asks God to hear supplication, a general prayer theme.

2-kings-20:2:2.summary: Private prayer behind a shut door loosely parallels turning to the wall.

2-kings-20:2:4.summary: “Do not be negligent in your illness, but pray to the Lord, and He Himself will heal you.”

2-kings-20:3:0.summary: Nehemiah asks “remember me, O God” for his faithful acts, as Hezekiah asks the Lord to remember his walk.
2-kings-20:3:0.why: Plea for God to remember faithfulness.

2-kings-20:3:1.summary: “Remember me, O God, in this,” pleading his kindness, like Hezekiah’s plea.
2-kings-20:3:1.why: Plea for God to remember faithfulness.

2-kings-20:3:2.summary: Hezekiah “did what was right in the Lord’s eyes” and clung to the Lord, the record he appeals to.

2-kings-20:3:3.summary: “Remember me for good, God, for everything I have done,” a parallel plea.
2-kings-20:3:3.why: Plea for God to remember faithfulness.

2-kings-20:3:4.summary: Confidence in asking because we do what is pleasing loosely parallels Hezekiah’s appeal.

2-kings-20:3:5.summary: “Remember me, our God, for goodness,” another plea based on faithful service.
2-kings-20:3:5.why: Plea for God to remember faithfulness.

2-kings-20:3:6.summary: Walking blamelessly in the Lord’s commandments is a general piety parallel.

2-kings-20:3:7.summary: David wept hoping the Lord would have mercy and the child live, a general weeping-prayer parallel.

2-kings-20:3:8.summary: Hezekiah’s psalm of this illness: he cries out and his eyes look toward the Lord who rescued him.
2-kings-20:3:8.why: Hezekiah’s own account of this crisis.

2-kings-20:3:9.summary: The Lord is near to those who call on Him “in truth,” a general echo.

2-kings-20:3:10.summary: “Let our hearts be complete toward the Lord,” similar to “with a full heart.”

2-kings-20:3:11.summary: God tells Abram to be pleasing and blameless, a general parallel.

2-kings-20:3:12.summary: God strengthens every heart “whole toward Him,” a general echo.

2-kings-20:3:13.summary: Solomon’s heart “was not whole” with the Lord, contrasting Hezekiah’s full heart.

2-kings-20:3:14.summary: David “walked before Thee in truth,” the same phrasing Hezekiah uses.

2-kings-20:3:15.summary: Hezekiah “did what was good and right before the Lord” and sought God with his whole soul.

2-kings-20:3:16.summary: Enoch “pleased God,” a general piety parallel.

2-kings-20:3:17.summary: Asa’s heart “was whole with the Lord,” a general echo.

2-kings-20:3:18.summary: “Remember Thy word to Thy servant” shares the plea “remember.”

2-kings-20:3:19.summary: Mixing drink with weeping loosely parallels Hezekiah’s bitter weeping.

2-kings-20:3:20.summary: Job described as blameless and true, a general piety parallel.

2-kings-20:3:21.summary: Blessing on the forgiven without deceit has no specific link.

2-kings-20:3:22.summary: Enoch “pleased God,” a general parallel to doing what was good in God’s eyes.

2-kings-20:3:23.summary: Nathanael without deceit has no specific link to Hezekiah’s prayer.

2-kings-20:3:24.summary: The psalmist wets his bed with tears, a general weeping-in-distress parallel.

2-kings-20:3:25.summary: “Walking before Me in truth with all their heart” matches Hezekiah’s “walked before Thee in truth and with a full heart.”

2-kings-20:3:26.summary: “God remembered Noah” shares only the idea of divine remembering.

2-kings-20:3:27.summary: “Remember what my existence is” is a general plea about life’s brevity.

2-kings-20:3:28.summary: “Remember me Thyself” for mercy’s sake shares the plea to remember.

2-kings-20:3:29.summary: “Remember, Lord, the reproach of Thy servants” shares only the plea form.

2-kings-20:3:30.summary: Job was “true, blameless, righteous,” a general parallel.

2-kings-20:3:31.summary: Paul’s conscience testifies to sincere conduct, loosely like Hezekiah’s appeal to his conduct.

2-kings-20:3:32.summary: Swearing “The Lord lives” with truth shares only the word truth.

2-kings-20:3:33.summary: Remembering days of old in Isaiah has no specific tie to Hezekiah’s plea.

2-kings-20:3:34.summary: Christ offered supplications “with loud crying and tears” to the One able to save from death, and was heard.

2-kings-20:4:0.summary: Olda living in “the masena” has no link to Isaiah in the middle courtyard in the Saints wording.
2-kings-20:4:0.why: Link depends on Hebrew place term.

2-kings-20:4:1.summary: A palace court description shares only the word court.

2-kings-20:5:0.summary: The psalmist says God “heard” his petition and did not turn away his prayer, as God tells Hezekiah “I have heard your prayer.”
2-kings-20:5:0.why: General witness that God hears prayer.

2-kings-20:5:2.summary: Both speak of God's people and their cry reaching Him, but Saul's anointing is a separate situation.
2-kings-20:5:2.why: Echo of God noticing His people's need.

2-kings-20:5:3.summary: Isaiah earlier tells Hezekiah, “What you did pray to Me … I have heard,” the same divine assurance to the same king.
2-kings-20:5:3.why: Shows God answering Hezekiah's prayers twice through Isaiah.

2-kings-20:5:4.summary: The psalmist asks God to “hear my prayer” and not be silent “at my tears,” the very pair God answers for Hezekiah.
2-kings-20:5:4.why: Same pairing of prayer and tears before God.

2-kings-20:5:5.summary: Only the motif of tears turning to joy links this to God seeing Hezekiah's tears.

2-kings-20:5:6.summary: God “heals” the brokenhearted, a general statement echoing “I shall heal you.”
2-kings-20:5:6.why: General picture of God as healer.

2-kings-20:5:7.summary: Prayer over the sick leading to the Lord raising them up loosely parallels Hezekiah's prayer and healing.
2-kings-20:5:7.why: New Testament practice of prayer for the sick.

2-kings-20:5:8.summary: God set the psalmist's “tears” before Him, a general echo of “seen your tears.”

2-kings-20:5:9.summary: God wiping every tear is an eschatological image only loosely tied to God seeing Hezekiah's tears.

2-kings-20:5:10.summary: Zechariah's “petition has been heard” echoes answered prayer, but the situations differ.

2-kings-20:5:11.summary: “I will not die, but live” and entering the gates to give thanks fit Hezekiah's recovery only thematically.
2-kings-20:5:11.why: Voice of one spared from death.

2-kings-20:5:12.summary: Only the phrase “God of” the fathers is shared; the teaching on resurrection has no link to Hezekiah's healing.

2-kings-20:5:13.summary: God declares “I am the Lord who heals you,” a general parallel to “I shall heal you.”

2-kings-20:5:14.summary: Joshua's encounter with the “chief captain” shares no real element with God's message to Hezekiah as “leader of My people.”

2-kings-20:5:15.summary: Saul is anointed “ruler over His people,” a title loosely echoing “leader of My people.”

2-kings-20:5:16.summary: A sufferer near death is restored when he turns to the Lord, loosely like Hezekiah (truncated range).

2-kings-20:5:17.summary: A healed man is found in the temple, loosely like Hezekiah going up to the Lord's house after healing.

2-kings-20:5:18.summary: Isaiah's account has Hezekiah ask for the sign that he “will go up to the house of the Lord,” the same promise.
2-kings-20:5:18.why: Parallel account of the same healing.

2-kings-20:5:19.summary: David is called “ruler over Israel” and shepherd of “My people,” only echoing the royal title.

2-kings-20:5:20.summary: Perfecting the pioneer of salvation through sufferings has no specific link to Hezekiah's healing.

2-kings-20:5:21.summary: God sends Nathan to “say to David” with “Thus says the Lord,” a similar prophetic commission formula.

2-kings-20:5:22.summary: God says “I will smite, and I will heal,” a general statement of His power to heal.
2-kings-20:5:22.why: God's sovereignty over life and healing.

2-kings-20:5:23.summary: The “sure blessings of David” loosely relate to God acting as “the God of your father David.”

2-kings-20:5:24.summary: Repaying the Lord with thanksgiving loosely fits a healed person's response.

2-kings-20:5:25.summary: The next verses show the fig remedy and Hezekiah asking for the sign he will go up to the Lord's house “on the third day.”
2-kings-20:5:25.why: Continuation of the same healing narrative.

2-kings-20:5:26.summary: “Hear my prayer” is a general plea echoing God hearing Hezekiah's prayer.

2-kings-20:5:27.summary: God sends Nathan: “Go and say to My servant David, ‘Thus says the Lord,’” a similar commissioning formula.
2-kings-20:5:27.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-20:5:28.summary: Abijah's battle speech mentioning “our fathers' God” shares only an incidental divine title.

2-kings-20:5:29.summary: Josiah seeks “the God of his father David,” the same title used for God here.

2-kings-20:5:30.summary: Entering God's house to pay vows made “in my affliction” loosely fits Hezekiah's promised visit to the temple.

2-kings-20:6:0.summary: Nearly identical promise: “I shall shield this city for My own sake and for the sake of David My servant.”

2-kings-20:6:1.summary: God tells Zion's people not to fear the Assyrians, a general parallel to deliverance from Assyria.

2-kings-20:6:2.summary: God's assurance to Paul at sea has no specific link to Hezekiah's added years or Jerusalem's protection.

2-kings-20:6:3.summary: The preciousness of saints' death has no real link to God adding fifteen years to Hezekiah's life.

2-kings-20:6:4.summary: Chronicles says the Lord “saved Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem from the hand of Sennacherib king of Assyria.”
2-kings-20:6:4.why: Records the fulfillment of the promise.

2-kings-20:6:5.summary: Sirach recalls that in Hezekiah's days “He added life to the king,” referring to these added years.

2-kings-20:7:1.summary: Elisha uses flour to make a harmful pot safe, a loose parallel to a physical means of healing.
2-kings-20:7:1.why: Prophet using ordinary material to heal.

2-kings-20:7:2.summary: Elisha uses salt to heal waters, another prophetic remedy through a simple substance.
2-kings-20:7:2.why: Similar prophetic healing by material means.

2-kings-20:7:3.summary: Sirach says God “healed and removed the sufferer's pain” through medicines, loosely like the fig poultice.

2-kings-20:8:0.summary: Gideon asks for “a sign” confirming God's word, a general parallel to Hezekiah requesting one.
2-kings-20:8:0.why: Another request for a confirming sign.

2-kings-20:8:1.summary: Isaiah invites Ahaz to ask a sign from the Lord, a general parallel within Isaiah's ministry.
2-kings-20:8:1.why: Isaiah offering signs to Judah's kings.

2-kings-20:8:2.summary: Restoring “to health” and rising “on the third day” loosely echo Hezekiah's healing and third-day promise.

2-kings-20:8:3.summary: Isaiah earlier gives Hezekiah another sign: “This shall be the sign for you,” mentioning a third year.
2-kings-20:8:3.why: Another sign given to the same king.

2-kings-20:8:4.summary: This is the promise Hezekiah asks about: “I shall heal you; on the third day you shall go up to the Lord's house.”
2-kings-20:8:4.why: Directly preceding promise behind the request.

2-kings-20:8:6.summary: The Lord Himself gives Ahaz a sign through Isaiah, only generally similar.
2-kings-20:8:6.why: Another Isaianic sign to a king.

2-kings-20:8:7.summary: Gideon tests God with the fleece, a loose parallel to asking for a confirming sign.

2-kings-20:9:0.summary: Isaiah's account gives the same sign: the shadow on the steps turned back “ten steps.”
2-kings-20:9:0.why: Parallel account of the same sign.

2-kings-20:9:1.summary: Jesus refuses a sign to those testing Him, contrasting with God granting Hezekiah's sign.
2-kings-20:9:1.why: Contrast in how signs are sought.

2-kings-20:9:2.summary: Jesus refuses a sign except Jonah's, only loosely contrasting with the sign given Hezekiah.

2-kings-20:9:3.summary: Jesus declares no sign will be given this generation, a loose contrast with Hezekiah's sign.

2-kings-20:10:0.summary: “A light thing in the eyes of the Lord” loosely echoes Hezekiah calling one sign “easy.”
2-kings-20:10:0.why: Similar language of easy and hard signs.

2-kings-20:10:1.summary: Elijah calls Elisha's request “difficult,” a loose parallel to Hezekiah choosing the harder sign.
2-kings-20:10:1.why: Similar motif of a difficult request.

2-kings-20:10:2.summary: The servant's calling as light to nations shares nothing specific with the shadow sign.

2-kings-20:10:3.summary: Casting out a demon by prayer has no specific link to the shadow returning.

2-kings-20:10:4.summary: Believers doing greater works has no specific link to Hezekiah's request for a harder sign.

2-kings-20:10:5.summary: Sirach recalls that “the sun went backward” in Hezekiah's days, the very sign requested here.

2-kings-20:11:1.summary: Joshua prays and the sun stands still, another distinctive miracle of the sun at a human's prayer.

2-kings-20:11:2.summary: Chronicles says Hezekiah prayed when ill and the Lord “gave him a sign.”
2-kings-20:11:2.why: Parallel summary of the same sign.

2-kings-20:11:3.summary: Elijah cries out to the Lord for a miracle, a general parallel to Isaiah crying to the Lord.

2-kings-20:11:4.summary: Peter prays and a miracle follows, only loosely similar to Isaiah's cry.

2-kings-20:11:5.summary: Chronicles mentions Babylon's envoys coming to learn about “the wonder that had happened upon the land,” this sign.

2-kings-20:11:6.summary: Moses is said to “cry” to the Lord, a general echo of Isaiah crying to the Lord.

2-kings-20:11:7.summary: Elijah cries to heaven and God answers with fire, a general parallel of prophetic prayer and miracle.
2-kings-20:11:7.why: Prophetic prayer answered by a sign.

2-kings-20:12:0.summary: Chronicles recounts the “ambassadors of the rulers from Babylon sent to him,” the same embassy.

2-kings-20:12:2.summary: A lament against “Babylon's king” shares only the figure of Babylon's ruler.

2-kings-20:12:3.summary: Isaiah's vision “against Babylon” shares Babylon and the prophet, but not the embassy.

2-kings-20:12:4.summary: Babylon's future ruin shares only the city named here.

2-kings-20:12:5.summary: Toi sends his son with gifts to David after a victory, loosely like a king sending gifts and greetings.

2-kings-20:12:6.summary: David sends servants to comfort a ruler, a loose parallel to an envoy sent after news.

2-kings-20:12:7.summary: The Greek-based text names the place “Confusion,” not Babylon, so the Babylon link does not carry.
2-kings-20:12:7.why: Link depends on a name not in this reading.

2-kings-20:12:8.summary: Babylon's early mention as Nimrod's kingdom shares only the place name.

2-kings-20:13:0.summary: The queen of Sheba brings spices and gold to Solomon, loosely echoing displayed treasures.

2-kings-20:13:1.summary: Gifts of gold vessels and spices to Solomon share only the wealth items.

2-kings-20:13:2.summary: Gold and “very many spices” given to Solomon only loosely echo Hezekiah's treasury.

2-kings-20:13:4.summary: Chronicles describes Hezekiah's treasuries “for silver, gold, precious stones, and spices” and his heart “lifted up.”

2-kings-20:13:5.summary: Riches flying away like an eagle loosely anticipate the loss of Hezekiah's displayed treasures.

2-kings-20:13:6.summary: No righteous person does good without sin, a general comment fitting even Hezekiah's misstep.

2-kings-20:13:7.summary: Solomon's tribute and merchants share nothing specific with Hezekiah showing his treasuries.

2-kings-20:14:0.summary: Isaiah's oracle on Babylon speaks of coming “from a distant land,” Hezekiah's exact words about the Babylonians.

2-kings-20:14:1.summary: Nathan confronts David over sin, a general pattern of prophet confronting king (truncated range).

2-kings-20:14:2.summary: A prophet rebukes Asa for trusting a foreign king, loosely like Isaiah questioning the Babylonian contact.

2-kings-20:14:3.summary: The Gibeonites claim to come “from a very distant land,” sharing only the phrase.

2-kings-20:14:4.summary: Elisha asks Gehazi “From where?” to expose his act, loosely like Isaiah's probing question.
2-kings-20:14:4.why: Prophet questioning to expose a fault.

2-kings-20:14:5.summary: Amaziah's dismissal of Amos shares nothing specific with Isaiah questioning Hezekiah.

2-kings-20:14:6.summary: Envoys tell Joshua “We have come from a distant land,” sharing only the phrase.

2-kings-20:14:7.summary: Accepting a righteous man's correction has no specific link to Isaiah's question to Hezekiah.

2-kings-20:14:8.summary: John rebukes Herod, a general pattern of a prophet confronting a ruler.

2-kings-20:14:9.summary: A nation “from afar” brought in judgment loosely foreshadows Babylon from a distant land.
2-kings-20:14:9.why: Covenant threat of a distant nation.

2-kings-20:14:10.summary: A man of God warns Amaziah against relying on foreign troops, a general prophetic warning to a king.

2-kings-20:14:11.summary: Hezekiah heeded Micah's prophecy of Jerusalem's ruin, another prophetic threat to the same king.

2-kings-20:14:12.summary: A prophet rebukes Amaziah and is silenced, a general pattern of prophet confronting king.

2-kings-20:14:13.summary: A wise word into a receptive ear loosely fits a prophet's counsel to a king.

2-kings-20:15:0.summary: The previous verse narrates the same act: “There was nothing in his house … that Hezekiah did not show them.”

2-kings-20:15:1.summary: Job's denial of hiding sin shares nothing specific with Hezekiah's candid answer about his treasures.

2-kings-20:15:2.summary: Confessing sin in 1 John has no specific link to Hezekiah reporting what he showed.

2-kings-20:15:3.summary: Covering impiety versus explaining reproofs is not specifically tied to this exchange.

2-kings-20:15:4.summary: Joshua asks Achar to tell what he has done and hide nothing, loosely like Isaiah's probing questions.

2-kings-20:16:0.summary: Elisha opens with the same prophetic formula, “Hear the word of the Lord.”

2-kings-20:16:1.summary: Amos uses the same formula, “Now hear the Lord's word,” before pronouncing judgment.

2-kings-20:16:2.summary: Micaiah says “Hear the Lord's word” before announcing judgment on a king.

2-kings-20:16:3.summary: Isaiah himself uses “Hear the Lord's word” to open an oracle.

2-kings-20:17:0.summary: Fulfillment: all the treasures of the king's house are taken “according to the Lord's word.”

2-kings-20:17:1.summary: Nebuchadnezzar brings the king into Babylon “with the desirable vessels of the Lord's house.”
2-kings-20:17:1.why: Fulfillment of treasures taken to Babylon.

2-kings-20:17:2.summary: The Chaldeans carry the temple bronze “to Babylon,” part of the predicted plundering.

2-kings-20:17:3.summary: The shown text says only “they will go into Babylon,” a brief echo of things taken there.
2-kings-20:17:3.why: Brief echo of exile to Babylon.

2-kings-20:17:4.summary: The Chaldeans carry the temple's bronze and gold and silver vessels “to Babylon.”

2-kings-20:17:5.summary: Shattering pride and making heaven iron shares nothing specific with treasures taken to Babylon.

2-kings-20:17:6.summary: All the treasures, including “all the treasures of the king,” are brought “into Babylon.”

2-kings-20:18:0.summary: Hezekiah's own son Manasseh is brought in fetters “to Babylon.”

2-kings-20:18:1.summary: Joakim, Hezekiah's descendant, surrenders with his “eunuchs” to the king of Babylon.

2-kings-20:18:2.summary: Babylon's chief eunuch takes youths “of the royal family” of Israel into service.
2-kings-20:18:2.why: Fulfillment of royal sons serving in Babylon's court.

2-kings-20:18:3.summary: A later Davidic king is brought to the king of Babylon, a general fulfillment of the threat.

2-kings-20:19:0.summary: Eli accepts announced judgment saying the Lord “will do what is good before Him,” closely like Hezekiah.
2-kings-20:19:0.why: Similar acceptance of a judgment oracle.

2-kings-20:19:1.summary: Aaron's silent acceptance after God's word only loosely parallels Hezekiah's response.

2-kings-20:19:2.summary: The angel's good news of joy shares only the idea of something good.

2-kings-20:19:3.summary: God promising healing and peace for Jerusalem shares only the word “peace.”

2-kings-20:19:4.summary: Not grumbling over one's sin loosely relates to accepting God's word of judgment.

2-kings-20:19:5.summary: Job blesses the Lord who gave and took away, a general model of accepting loss.

2-kings-20:19:6.summary: The angels' song shares only the word “peace.”

2-kings-20:19:7.summary: Fasts becoming joy with a call to “love truth and peace” shares only the word “peace.”

2-kings-20:19:10.summary: The psalmist falls silent before God, loosely like Hezekiah's submissive reply.

2-kings-20:20:1.summary: Hezekiah blocks the springs' waters against Assyria, part of the same water works.
2-kings-20:20:1.why: Chronicles detail on Hezekiah's water projects.

2-kings-20:20:4.summary: Isaiah describes the old pool's water diverted “into the city” and water provided between the walls.
2-kings-20:20:4.why: Prophetic comment on the same water works.

2-kings-20:20:6.summary: Same regnal formula: “The rest of … acts … are these not written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Judah?”
2-kings-20:20:6.why: Standard closing formula of Judah's kings.

2-kings-20:20:7.summary: Same regnal formula for Ahaz, Hezekiah's father, citing the chronicles of the kings of Judah.

2-kings-20:20:8.summary: Same formula, including “all the power,” for Asa in the Annals of the Kings of Judah.

2-kings-20:20:9.summary: Same closing formula for an Israelite king, citing the chronicles of the kings of Israel.

2-kings-20:20:10.summary: Same closing formula for Joram, citing the records for the kings of Judah.

2-kings-20:20:11.summary: Same closing formula for Azariah, citing the chronicles of the kings of Judah.

2-kings-20:20:12.summary: 1 Maccabees uses a similar formula: “The rest of John's deeds … the building of the walls.”
2-kings-20:20:12.why: Later imitation of the regnal formula.

2-kings-20:20:13.summary: Sirach says Hezekiah “brought water into its midst” and dug through rock, the same water project.
2-kings-20:20:13.why: Later praise of the same achievement.

2-kings-20:21:1.summary: Same death-and-succession formula: slept with his fathers, buried in the City of David, son reigned in his place.

2-kings-20:21:2.summary: The next verse begins Manasseh's reign, continuing the succession noted here.

2-kings-20:21:3.summary: Same burial-and-succession formula for Uzziah, “His son Jotham reigned in his place.”

2-kings-20:21:4.summary: Same formula for Solomon, buried in the City of David, his son reigning in his place.

2-kings-20:21:5.summary: David “lay down with his fathers and was buried in the City of David,” the same wording.

2-kings-20:21:6.summary: Manasseh's own burial uses the same formula, closing the reign that begins here.

2-kings-21:1:0.summary: The link relies on the Hebrew meaning of Hephzibah; here the name is “Opsiba” and Isaiah reads “My Desire.”
2-kings-21:1:0.why: Wordplay not carried in this reading.

2-kings-21:1:1.summary: The proverb about a beloved wife has no link to Manasseh's mother in this reading.

2-kings-21:1:3.summary: The preceding verse records Manasseh becoming king in Hezekiah's place.

2-kings-21:1:4.summary: Matthew's genealogy lists “Hezekiah begot Manasseh,” the same king.

2-kings-21:1:5.summary: The Davidic genealogy lists “Hezekiah his son, Manasseh his son.”

2-kings-21:2:9.summary: Ahaz acted “according to the abominations of the nations whom the Lord removed before the Israelites,” identical wording.
2-kings-21:2:9.why: Same verdict formula for an evil king.

2-kings-21:2:1.summary: Judah's leaders multiplied “the nations' abominations” and defiled the Lord's house.
2-kings-21:2:1.why: Same sin pattern leading to exile.

2-kings-21:2:2.summary: Jerusalem's sin exceeding Samaria's loosely parallels Manasseh's excessive evil.

2-kings-21:2:3.summary: Manasseh places the grove's image in the Lord's house, detailing his evil.

2-kings-21:2:4.summary: Manasseh caused Judah “to do evil in the Lord's eyes” and shed innocent blood.

2-kings-21:2:5.summary: God's wrath for burning incense to other gods states the consequence of such sins.

2-kings-21:2:6.summary: Jeremiah names “Manasseh son of Hezekiah” and what he did in Jerusalem as cause of judgment.

2-kings-21:2:7.summary: Moses forbids the “abominations” the nations did to their gods.

2-kings-21:2:8.summary: The people before Israel did “these abominations” and the land expelled them (truncated range).
2-kings-21:2:8.why: Background for nations removed for abominations.

2-kings-21:3:0.summary: Israel “made groves, bowed down to all heaven's host, and served Baal,” the same sins.
2-kings-21:3:0.why: Same sins that doomed the northern kingdom.

2-kings-21:3:1.summary: Hezekiah “removed the high places” and destroyed the groves that Manasseh rebuilt.

2-kings-21:3:2.summary: The law forbids serving and bowing to “the array of heaven.”

2-kings-21:3:3.summary: Ahab set up “an altar for Baal” and made a grove, the model Manasseh followed.
2-kings-21:3:3.why: Ahab's precedent named in the verse.

2-kings-21:3:4.summary: Moses warns against bowing down to and serving the sun, moon, stars, and heavenly adornment.

2-kings-21:3:5.summary: Joram walked “as the house of Ahab had done,” a general Ahab-like comparison.

2-kings-21:3:6.summary: Job's disavowal of revering sun and moon loosely contrasts with worshipping heaven's host.

2-kings-21:3:7.summary: Elijah's challenge between the Lord and Baal shares only the Baal theme.

2-kings-21:3:8.summary: Ahaziah walked in the way of Ahab's house, a general Ahab comparison.

2-kings-21:3:9.summary: Baal's prophets on their altar share only the Baal altar theme.

2-kings-21:3:10.summary: Judah kept “all the works of Achaab's house,” a general echo of following Ahab.

2-kings-21:3:11.summary: Hezekiah “removed His altars and His high places,” the reforms Manasseh undid.

2-kings-21:3:13.summary: Josiah cleanses Judah of high places and groves, later reversing such sins.

2-kings-21:3:14.summary: Jehu's ruse against Baal worshippers shares only the Baal theme.

2-kings-21:3:15.summary: Josiah removes vessels for Baal, the grove, and “all heaven's host,” undoing these very cults.

2-kings-21:3:16.summary: Rabshakeh mentions the high places and altars Hezekiah removed.

2-kings-21:4:0.summary: Solomon prays toward the house where God said “My name shall be there.”

2-kings-21:4:1.summary: David's son will build “a house for My name,” a general background to the temple.
2-kings-21:4:1.why: Origin of the temple for God's name.

2-kings-21:4:2.summary: They set pollutions “in the house over which My name is invoked,” the same desecration.

2-kings-21:4:3.summary: God consecrated the house “to put My name there for ever,” the promise Manasseh profaned.
2-kings-21:4:3.why: Promise behind the quoted divine word.

2-kings-21:4:4.summary: God chooses a place “to set His name there,” the principle cited in this verse.
2-kings-21:4:4.why: Law of the chosen place for God's name.

2-kings-21:4:5.summary: Ahaz built a foreign-style altar in the Lord's house (truncated range), a precedent for Manasseh's altar.
2-kings-21:4:5.why: Earlier king's altar in the temple.

2-kings-21:4:6.summary: God chose Mount Zion and built His sanctuary there, general background for Jerusalem.

2-kings-21:4:7.summary: The Lord chose Zion as His dwelling, general background to the name promise.

2-kings-21:4:8.summary: Altars belong where God “names My name,” loosely tied to the name language.
2-kings-21:4:8.why: Early altar law about God's name.
2-kings-21:4:8.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-21:5:1.summary: Josiah removes from the sanctuary vessels made “for all heaven's host,” undoing this cult.

2-kings-21:5:0.summary: Describes Solomon's “great court,” giving only general background on the temple courts named here.

2-kings-21:5:2.summary: Solomon built the “innermost court,” background for the two courts Manasseh defiled.

2-kings-21:5:3.summary: Josiah tears down “the altars Manasseh had made in the two courts of the Lord's house.”
2-kings-21:5:3.why: Records the removal of these altars.

2-kings-21:5:4.summary: Ezekiel's rule on priestly robes in the outer court shares only the word “court.”

2-kings-21:5:5.summary: Manasseh himself later removes the altars he had built on the mountain of the Lord's house.

2-kings-21:5:6.summary: Ezekiel sees the inner court filled with the Lord's glory, a loose contrast with idolatrous altars there.

2-kings-21:5:8.summary: Architectural details of Ezekiel's visionary temple share only the word “court.”

2-kings-21:5:9.summary: A measured gate in Ezekiel's vision has no specific link to Manasseh's altars.

2-kings-21:5:10.summary: Measuring the inner courtyard gate in Ezekiel's vision shares only the courtyard setting.

2-kings-21:5:11.summary: Measuring the court and altar in Ezekiel's vision has no specific link to the altar for heaven's host.

2-kings-21:5:12.summary: Porches facing the outer courtyard in Ezekiel's vision share only the court setting.

2-kings-21:5:13.summary: Josiah removes the grove from the Lord's house, a related cleansing but not the altar for heaven's host.

2-kings-21:6:0.summary: Israel “led their sons and daughters through fire, practiced divinations, read omens … provoking Him,” nearly identical.

2-kings-21:6:1.summary: The law forbids following spirit mediums and enchanters, the practices Manasseh adopted.

2-kings-21:6:2.summary: The Greek-based text forbids giving seed “to serve a ruler,” only obliquely referring to child offering.
2-kings-21:6:2.why: Law on offering children, obscured in wording.

2-kings-21:6:3.summary: The law forbids divining “by omens,” one of Manasseh's practices.

2-kings-21:6:4.summary: Ahaz “led his son through fire,” the same act.

2-kings-21:6:6.summary: Moses forbids passing children through fire, divination, omens, mediums, and charms, matching Manasseh's list.

2-kings-21:6:7.summary: Sodom's general wickedness shares nothing specific with Manasseh's occult practices.

2-kings-21:6:8.summary: Saul died for consulting a spirit medium, loosely like Manasseh's appointing mediums.

2-kings-21:6:9.summary: The Greek-based text punishes giving seed “to a ruler,” only obliquely about child offering.
2-kings-21:6:9.why: Law on offering children, obscured in wording.

2-kings-21:6:10.summary: Egyptians consulting those speaking from the earth and belly-speakers loosely parallels Manasseh's mediums.

2-kings-21:6:11.summary: Offering one's firstborn for sin loosely relates to passing sons through fire.

2-kings-21:6:12.summary: A slave girl with a spirit of divination shares only the practice of divination.
2-kings-21:6:12.why: Divination in a New Testament setting.

2-kings-21:6:13.summary: Judah's fall is attributed to “Manasseh's sins, according to everything he had done.”
2-kings-21:6:13.why: Shows the consequence of these sins.

2-kings-21:6:14.summary: Ahaz “made his children pass through fire, according to the abominations of the nations.”
2-kings-21:6:14.why: Same sin by an earlier king.

2-kings-21:6:15.summary: Isaiah rebukes seeking belly-speakers and the dead, loosely related to Manasseh's mediums.

2-kings-21:7:0.summary: God chose and sanctified the house “for My name to be there for ever,” the promise cited here.

2-kings-21:7:1.summary: Solomon's prayer recalls God saying “My name shall be there” of this house.

2-kings-21:7:2.summary: God tells Solomon He has “chosen this place for Myself as a house of sacrifice.”

2-kings-21:7:3.summary: God consecrated the house “to put My name there for ever,” matching the cited promise.

2-kings-21:7:4.summary: David's son will build “a house for My name,” general background to the promise.
2-kings-21:7:4.why: Origin of the temple for God's name.

2-kings-21:7:5.summary: Josiah brings “the grove out of the Lord's house” and burns it, removing this image.
2-kings-21:7:5.why: Josiah's removal of the same grove.

2-kings-21:7:7.summary: Pollutions are set “in the house over which My name is invoked,” the same desecration.
2-kings-21:7:7.why: Prophetic charge of the same defilement.

2-kings-21:7:8.summary: The Lord chose Zion as His dwelling, general background for the chosen place.

2-kings-21:7:9.summary: Manasseh built an altar in the Lord's house, where God said “In Jerusalem I shall place My name.”
2-kings-21:7:9.why: Same act and promise in context.

2-kings-21:7:10.summary: God will reject “this city which I chose, Jerusalem, and the house of which I said, ‘My name shall be there.’”

2-kings-21:7:11.summary: The law forbids planting a sacred grove beside the Lord's altar, exactly what Manasseh did.

2-kings-21:7:12.summary: Manasseh later removes “the carved object from the Lord's house,” this image.

2-kings-21:7:13.summary: God warns He will turn away “this house that I sanctified for My name” if Israel serves other gods.

2-kings-21:7:14.summary: “The place I chose for My name to dwell” echoes the promise, but in a return context.

2-kings-21:7:15.summary: Solomon speaks of “the city Thou didst choose and the house I built for Thy name.”

2-kings-21:7:16.summary: God chose Judah and Mount Zion and built His sanctuary, general background.

2-kings-21:7:17.summary: God warns He will cast away “this house I consecrated for My name” if Israel turns to other gods.

2-kings-21:7:18.summary: Mount Zion as God's dwelling and inheritance gives only general background.

2-kings-21:8:0.summary: God promises to plant Israel in a place where they will “worry no more,” the secure settlement promised here.
2-kings-21:8:0.why: Promise of secure dwelling in the land.

2-kings-21:8:1.summary: Blessings in the land depend on keeping “all His commandments,” the same condition (truncated range).

2-kings-21:8:2.summary: Obedience leading to eating the land's good things is a general parallel.
2-kings-21:8:2.why: Obedience and life in the land.

2-kings-21:8:3.summary: God will plant Israel so they “no longer be anxious,” the promise of secure settlement.

2-kings-21:8:5.summary: God will settle them “in the land I gave your fathers” if they amend their ways.

2-kings-21:8:6.summary: Conditional blessing for Sabbath keeping is a general parallel (truncated range).

2-kings-21:8:7.summary: Walking in all God's commanded ways so it may be well loosely parallels the condition.

2-kings-21:8:8.summary: Settling in the land through trust is a general theme.

2-kings-21:8:9.summary: Joshua warns Israel may perish from the good land God gave if they turn away.

2-kings-21:8:10.summary: God wishes Israel would keep His commandments so it would be well, a general parallel.

2-kings-21:8:11.summary: God laments Israel did not listen, else He would have subdued enemies, a general parallel.

2-kings-21:8:12.summary: The land made desolate for abominations is the negative side of this conditional promise.
2-kings-21:8:12.why: Loss of the land for sin.

2-kings-21:8:13.summary: Jerusalem's bloodshed and defilement are judged, a general parallel (truncated range).

2-kings-21:8:14.summary: Samaria was deported for not keeping “everything Moses the Lord's servant commanded.”
2-kings-21:8:14.why: Shows the condition already applied to Israel.

2-kings-21:8:15.summary: Keeping God's commandments leads to dwelling “securely in your land” (truncated range).

2-kings-21:9:0.summary: A king's ill choices corrupting his subjects loosely fits Manasseh leading Judah astray.

2-kings-21:9:1.summary: Israel did not listen to the Lord's voice and the law of Moses, a general parallel.

2-kings-21:9:2.summary: The people mocked God's messengers until there was no healing, a general parallel.

2-kings-21:9:3.summary: Jesus' saying about having no excuse for sin shares nothing specific with Manasseh's misleading.

2-kings-21:9:4.summary: Ephraim following worthless things shares nothing specific with this verse.

2-kings-21:9:6.summary: Jerusalem sinning more than Samaria loosely echoes doing evil “beyond the nations.”

2-kings-21:9:7.summary: Israel “did not listen” to God's warnings through the prophets, a general echo.

2-kings-21:9:8.summary: Not listening to the prophets speaking to kings is a general parallel.

2-kings-21:9:9.summary: Israel cast God's law behind them and committed great provocations, a general parallel.

2-kings-21:9:11.summary: Jezebel deceives God's servants into idolatry, loosely like Manasseh leading Judah astray.

2-kings-21:9:12.summary: Knowing good and not doing it is a general ethic with no specific link.

2-kings-21:9:13.summary: Jerusalem killing prophets shares nothing specific with this verse's not listening.

2-kings-21:9:14.summary: Abandoning the commandments amid the nations' repulsive practices loosely parallels this verse.

2-kings-21:9:15.summary: The ungodly walking around has no specific link to Manasseh's misleading of Judah.

2-kings-21:9:16.summary: God's reminder of the exodus and offer to fill Israel's mouth has no specific link.

2-kings-21:9:17.summary: Jerusalem soon surpassing others in lawlessness loosely echoes doing evil beyond the nations.

2-kings-21:9:18.summary: Sirach notes a ruler in David's house while others “multiplied sins,” a general parallel.

2-kings-21:10:0.summary: God testified “through Thy prophets” but they did not give ear, echoing God speaking through His prophets.

2-kings-21:10:1.summary: Chronicles says “The Lord spoke against Manasseh and his people, but they did not listen.”

2-kings-21:10:2.summary: God “sent through prophets” because He spared His people, the same prophetic warning pattern.
2-kings-21:10:2.why: Same divine practice of warning through prophets.

2-kings-21:10:3.summary: Israel killed the prophets who testified to them, a general parallel.

2-kings-21:10:4.summary: Jesus sends prophets whom Jerusalem kills, a general parallel to God sending prophets.

2-kings-21:11:0.summary: Ahab acted abominably “according to all that the Amorites had done,” the same comparison.
2-kings-21:11:0.why: Same Amorite comparison used for Ahab.

2-kings-21:11:1.summary: Judah was removed “because of Manasseh's sins, according to everything he had done.”

2-kings-21:11:3.summary: Jeremiah names Manasseh and all he did in Jerusalem as cause of disaster.

2-kings-21:11:4.summary: Jeroboam “caused Israel to sin,” the same formula used of Manasseh causing Judah to sin.

2-kings-21:11:5.summary: God's wrath burned against Judah “because of the provocations with which Manasseh had provoked Him.”

2-kings-21:11:7.summary: Amon served “the idols his father had served,” Manasseh's idols.

2-kings-21:11:8.summary: Jerusalem's father was “an Amorite,” loosely echoing the Amorite comparison.

2-kings-21:11:9.summary: Manasseh “caused Judah to do evil in the Lord's eyes,” the same charge.

2-kings-21:11:10.summary: Jerusalem's father “an Amorite” loosely echoes the comparison with the Amorites.

2-kings-21:11:11.summary: The Amorites' sins filling up explains their removal, loosely background to Manasseh surpassing them.

2-kings-21:11:12.summary: Manasseh did evil “according to the abominations of the nations,” the same charge.
2-kings-21:11:12.why: Earlier statement of the same verdict.

2-kings-21:11:13.summary: An Israelite king walking in Jeroboam's sins “as he caused Israel to sin” shares a formula only.

2-kings-21:12:0.summary: Jeremiah: “Behold, I am bringing evils upon this place, so that both ears of everyone hearing them will ring.”

2-kings-21:12:2.summary: Huldah: “Behold, I am bringing disasters on this place and its inhabitants.”

2-kings-21:12:3.summary: Jerusalem's coming ruin is a general parallel to disaster upon Jerusalem.

2-kings-21:12:4.summary: God's judgment on His chosen people is a general parallel.

2-kings-21:12:5.summary: God brought “great calamities” on Jerusalem such as had never occurred, fulfilling this threat.

2-kings-21:12:6.summary: Unprecedented affliction is a general parallel to shocking disaster.

2-kings-21:12:7.summary: The precious cornerstone in Zion is a promise of salvation, not judgment.

2-kings-21:12:8.summary: End-time terror before the Lamb shares nothing specific with this oracle.

2-kings-21:12:9.summary: Jesus warns Jerusalem's daughters of coming days of disaster, a general parallel.

2-kings-21:13:0.summary: God sets “adamant” among Israel and will not pass them by; the Greek wording loses the measuring-line image.

2-kings-21:13:1.summary: The Lord “stretched out a measure” to destroy Zion's wall, the same image fulfilled.

2-kings-21:13:2.summary: “A measuring cord for deserted land” is cast over a doomed city, the same judgment image.

2-kings-21:13:3.summary: Jehu destroys Ahab's house leaving no remnant, the fate meant by “the weight of Ahab's house.”

2-kings-21:13:5.summary: A saved remnant from Israel's multitude shares nothing specific with this oracle.

2-kings-21:13:6.summary: Jerusalem must drink “your sister Samaria's cup,” sharing Samaria's fate as here.

2-kings-21:13:7.summary: God will bring the northern clan to lay the land waste, a general parallel.
2-kings-21:13:7.why: Later announcement of the same judgment.

2-kings-21:13:8.summary: God's sweeping destruction of Jeroboam's house loosely parallels judgment on royal houses.

2-kings-21:13:9.summary: Samaria is captured and deported, the fate “Samaria's measure” applies to Jerusalem.

2-kings-21:13:10.summary: Babylon's desolation shares no specific image with this verse in the shown wording.

2-kings-21:13:11.summary: Babylon thrown like a millstone shares nothing specific with this oracle.

2-kings-21:13:12.summary: “A measure will again be extended over Jerusalem” for rebuilding reverses this measuring for destruction.

2-kings-21:13:13.summary: Jerusalem as a pot scorched to remove its rust loosely parallels wiping out the city.

2-kings-21:14:0.summary: God will “dash you down,” a general image of rejecting His people.

2-kings-21:14:1.summary: Hezekiah asks prayer for “the remnant that remains,” sharing only the remnant idea.

2-kings-21:14:2.summary: God “didst reject” His anointed; all plundered him and his enemies were gladdened (truncated range).

2-kings-21:14:3.summary: God gave Israel “into the hand of those oppressing them” and abandoned them to enemies (truncated range).

2-kings-21:14:4.summary: Spoils and plunder are commanded against a lawless nation, sharing only the plunder image.

2-kings-21:14:5.summary: God says He “let go My inheritance” and gave His beloved “into her enemies' hands.”

2-kings-21:14:6.summary: God delivered Israel “into the hand of plunderers” and “of their enemies.”
2-kings-21:14:6.why: Same pattern of handing over to plunderers.

2-kings-21:14:7.summary: God will forsake His people and many evils will find them, a general covenant warning.

2-kings-21:14:8.summary: God sends raiders against Judah “according to the Lord's word … through His servants the prophets.”

2-kings-21:14:9.summary: A remnant from Jerusalem will take root, contrasting with God rejecting the remnant.

2-kings-21:14:10.summary: Israel's fall with none to raise her is a general image of national ruin.

2-kings-21:14:11.summary: Those who remain perish in enemies' lands, a general covenant curse.

2-kings-21:14:12.summary: Israel given to slaughter before enemies is a general covenant curse.

2-kings-21:14:13.summary: The oppressor seizes Zion's desired things, a general fulfillment of plunder.

2-kings-21:14:14.summary: Perishing from the land and scattering among nations is a general covenant threat.

2-kings-21:14:15.summary: A personal plea for rescue shares nothing specific with this judgment, beyond a captivity heading.

2-kings-21:14:16.summary: Serving enemies sent by the Lord is a general covenant curse.

2-kings-21:14:17.summary: Zion's enemies prosper and her infants go into captivity, a general fulfillment.

2-kings-21:14:18.summary: God brought the Chaldeans and “handed everything into their hands,” fulfilling this threat.

2-kings-21:14:19.summary: “If you forsake Him, He will forsake you” states the principle behind this judgment.
2-kings-21:14:19.why: Principle of forsaking and being forsaken.

2-kings-21:14:20.summary: Falling before enemies is a general covenant curse.

2-kings-21:14:21.summary: God not abandoning His holy ones is a general contrast with no specific link.

2-kings-21:14:22.summary: Possessions given to enemies is a general covenant curse.

2-kings-21:14:23.summary: God “abhorred His inheritance” and “handed them over into nations' hands.”

2-kings-21:14:24.summary: The lament asks why God forsakes His people, a general response to this judgment.

2-kings-21:15:0.summary: The golden calf exemplifies Israel's sin from the exodus onward, a loose parallel.

2-kings-21:15:1.summary: Israel served images, sacrificed children, and shed innocent blood until God was angry, the same history.

2-kings-21:15:2.summary: Israel rebelled in the wilderness, a general parallel to provocation since Egypt.

2-kings-21:15:3.summary: Testifying to the fathers' lawlessness is a general parallel.

2-kings-21:15:4.summary: Daniel confesses the people's long sin and the resulting shame (truncated range).

2-kings-21:15:5.summary: Israel's unfaithfulness from Egypt in its youth loosely parallels sin since the exodus.

2-kings-21:15:6.summary: The next generation also embittered God in the wilderness, a general parallel.

2-kings-21:15:7.summary: Moses foretells they will do “evil before the Lord, to provoke Him to anger.”

2-kings-21:15:8.summary: Moses says Israel had been provoking God from the start, as here.

2-kings-21:15:9.summary: Israel “did evil before the Lord” and “provoked the Lord” who brought them out of Egypt.

2-kings-21:15:10.summary: Ezekiel's allegory of unfaithfulness since Egypt is a general parallel (truncated range).

2-kings-21:15:11.summary: Jerusalem's idolatrous unfaithfulness is a general parallel (truncated range).

2-kings-21:15:12.summary: Defilement in the fathers' lawlessness is a general parallel.

2-kings-21:16:0.summary: Shed blood pollutes the land, general background to filling Jerusalem with blood.

2-kings-21:16:1.summary: Chronicles says Manasseh “led Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray, to do evil.”

2-kings-21:16:2.summary: Manasseh “caused Judah to sin,” the same charge.

2-kings-21:16:3.summary: Jeremiah warns not to “shed innocent blood in this place,” a general echo.

2-kings-21:16:4.summary: Jerusalem killing prophets loosely parallels innocent blood shed in Jerusalem.

2-kings-21:16:5.summary: The “price of blood” for Judas' coins has no specific link.

2-kings-21:16:6.summary: “Judah's kings filled this place with innocent blood,” the same charge.

2-kings-21:16:8.summary: Descendants of those who murdered the prophets loosely relate to Jerusalem's bloodshed.

2-kings-21:16:10.summary: Aaron brought great sin on the people, loosely like Manasseh causing Judah to sin.

2-kings-21:16:11.summary: Martyrs “sawn apart” may recall prophets killed, but no one is named.

2-kings-21:16:12.summary: Jeremiah names Manasseh and all he did in Jerusalem as cause of judgment.

2-kings-21:16:13.summary: Manasseh set the grove's image in the Lord's house, another of his sins.

2-kings-21:16:14.summary: The law provides atonement for innocent blood, general background to bloodguilt.

2-kings-21:16:15.summary: The blood of innocent lives on Judah's hands is a general echo.

2-kings-21:16:16.summary: They “poured out innocent blood around the sanctuary,” a later echo of the phrase.

2-kings-21:17:1.summary: Hezekiah’s closing notice uses the same “are these not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah” formula and names Manasseh as successor.
2-kings-21:17:1.why: Shows the standard regnal closing formula across father and son.

2-kings-21:18:1.summary: Amon is likewise buried in “Oza’s garden,” the same burial place as his father Manasseh.
2-kings-21:18:1.why: Links the two kings buried outside David’s city.

2-kings-21:18:2.summary: Jehoiada is honored with burial “in David’s city with the kings,” unlike Manasseh’s garden burial; only a general burial-honor contrast.
2-kings-21:18:2.why: Illustrates how burial place reflected a person’s record.

2-kings-21:18:3.summary: Jehoram is buried in David’s city “but not in the tombs of the kings”; a different king and only a loose burial-place parallel.
2-kings-21:18:3.why: Another king denied the royal tombs.

2-kings-21:18:4.summary: Hezekiah, Manasseh’s father, is buried with honor among David’s sons, contrasting Manasseh’s garden burial; link is only the burial notice.
2-kings-21:18:4.why: Contrasts father’s honored burial with son’s.

2-kings-21:18:5.summary: Ahaz was not brought “into the tombs of Israel’s kings”; a different king with a similar non-royal burial.
2-kings-21:18:5.why: Pattern of wicked kings excluded from royal tombs.

2-kings-21:18:6.summary: Joash is buried in David’s city “but not in the tomb of the kings”; only a general burial-place parallel.
2-kings-21:18:6.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-21:18:7.summary: Jehoiakim’s “donkey’s burial” outside Jerusalem shares only the topic of burial, not Manasseh’s garden tomb.

2-kings-21:19:1.summary: Nadab of Israel also reigned “two years,” an incidental numerical coincidence with Amon.

2-kings-21:19:2.summary: The Chronicles genealogy lists “Amon his son, Josiah his son,” the same king and succession.
2-kings-21:19:2.why: Places Amon in David’s royal line.

2-kings-21:19:3.summary: Elah of Israel reigned “two years” in Tirzah; only the reign length coincides.

2-kings-21:19:4.summary: Phakeias of Israel ruled “for two years”; a coincidental reign length with no other connection.

2-kings-21:19:5.summary: Matthew’s genealogy “Manasseh begot Amos; Amos begot Josiah” names Amon (as Amos) in Christ’s line.

2-kings-21:19:6.summary: Ahaziah of Israel “reigned in Israel two years”; only the reign length matches.

2-kings-21:20:0.summary: Details Manasseh’s evil “in the Lord’s eyes”—altars, high places, child sacrifice—which Amon is said to have repeated.
2-kings-21:20:0.why: Specifies what Amon’s imitation of his father involved.

2-kings-21:20:1.summary: God condemns Manasseh’s “evil abominations,” the father’s conduct that Amon followed.
2-kings-21:20:1.why: Shows the gravity of the sins Amon copied.

2-kings-21:20:3.summary: Stephen’s “as your fathers did, so do you” echoes sons repeating fathers’ sins, but only as a general theme.

2-kings-21:20:4.summary: “Fill up the measure of your fathers” shares the idea of sons continuing fathers’ sin; general link.

2-kings-21:20:5.summary: Moses rebukes a generation that “risen in your fathers’ place” to add sin; loosely parallels Amon following Manasseh.
2-kings-21:20:5.why: General theme of sons repeating fathers’ sin.

2-kings-21:22:0.summary: Solomon “abandoned Me” and “did not walk in My ways,” the same twofold charge laid against Amon.
2-kings-21:22:0.why: Same Deuteronomistic verdict formula on a king.

2-kings-21:22:1.summary: Huldah’s oracle says the people “abandoned Me,” the same verdict as Amon’s, explaining coming wrath.
2-kings-21:22:1.why: Connects Amon’s apostasy to the announced judgment.

2-kings-21:22:2.summary: David warns Solomon to know “the God of your fathers” lest he “forsake Him”; general warning against abandoning God.
2-kings-21:22:2.why: Warning that Amon failed to heed.

2-kings-21:22:3.summary: Jacob “forsook God who made him”; shares the general theme of abandoning God.

2-kings-21:22:4.summary: Those who guard vain things “abandoned their mercy”; only a loose link through abandoning God for idols.

2-kings-21:22:5.summary: God’s people “abandoned Me, a spring of water of life”; shares the verb and theme of forsaking God.

2-kings-21:23:0.summary: Joash’s “slaves” formed “a conspiracy” and struck him, as Amon’s servants did; a parallel palace assassination.
2-kings-21:23:0.why: Another Judean king killed by his own servants.

2-kings-21:23:1.summary: Amaziah’s subjects formed “a conspiracy against him” and “put him to death,” paralleling Amon’s murder.
2-kings-21:23:1.why: Parallel conspiracy against a Judean king.

2-kings-21:23:3.summary: Baasha strikes down Nadab while besieging Gibbethon; a royal assassination but no conspiracy by servants shown.
2-kings-21:23:3.why: Loose parallel of a king being killed.

2-kings-21:23:4.summary: Zimri, Elah’s officer, “conspired against him” while he was in a house; a close parallel to servants killing Amon.

2-kings-21:23:5.summary: Phakee, an officer, “conspired against him” and struck the king near the king’s house, as with Amon.

2-kings-21:23:6.summary: Hoshea “formed a conspiracy” against Phakee and “put him to death,” the same pattern of regicide.

2-kings-21:24:0.summary: Amaziah strikes down the servants who killed his father, paralleling the punishment of Amon’s assassins.
2-kings-21:24:0.why: Another case of avenging a murdered king.

2-kings-21:24:1.summary: Israel calls an assembly and makes Jeroboam king; only a general picture of the people installing a king.

2-kings-21:24:2.summary: Jehoiada’s covenant between king and people follows a coup, but shares only a loose royal-succession setting.
2-kings-21:24:2.why: Loose parallel of restoring the Davidic line.

2-kings-21:24:3.summary: “All the people of Judah” made Azariah king “in place of his father” after Amaziah’s assassination, as with Josiah.
2-kings-21:24:3.why: Same pattern of the people enthroning the heir after a murder.

2-kings-21:24:4.summary: “All the people of the land” took Uzziah and made him king after his father’s killing, matching the source’s phrase.
2-kings-21:24:4.why: Same role of “the people of the land” in succession.

2-kings-21:24:5.summary: Israel’s elders anoint David king at Hebron; a general picture of the people making a king.

2-kings-21:24:7.summary: All the people make Saul king at Gilgal; only a general parallel of popular coronation.

2-kings-21:24:8.summary: Jerusalem’s inhabitants made Ahaziah “king in his place” after a crisis; similar formula but different circumstances.
2-kings-21:24:8.why: Another popular installation of an heir.

2-kings-21:24:9.summary: All Israel gathers at Shechem to make Rehoboam king; only a loose popular-coronation link.

2-kings-21:25:0.summary: Manasseh’s closing notice uses the identical “rest of … deeds … are these not written” formula as Amon’s.
2-kings-21:25:0.why: Same regnal formula for father and son.

2-kings-21:25:1.summary: Hezekiah’s closing notice uses the same “book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah” formula.
2-kings-21:25:1.why: Shows the standard regnal closing formula.

2-kings-21:26:0.summary: Manasseh was also buried “in Oza’s garden,” the same place as Amon.
2-kings-21:26:0.why: Father and son share the same burial site.

2-kings-21:26:1.summary: Matthew’s “Amos begot Josiah” records the same succession from Amon to Josiah.
2-kings-21:26:1.why: Shows the succession in Jesus’ genealogy.

2-kings-21:26:2.summary: The splitting of the Bethel altar has no shared element with Amon’s burial and Josiah’s accession in the texts shown.

2-kings-21:9:10.summary: 1 Kings 14:16 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-21:9:10.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-21:9:10.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-21:11:6.summary: 1 Kings 14:16 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-21:11:6.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-21:11:6.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-21:16:7.summary: 1 Kings 14:15–16 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-21:16:7.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-21:16:7.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-22:1:7.summary: Manasseh’s accession notice uses the same age-reign-mother formula, but concerns a different king.
2-kings-22:1:7.why: Compares the regnal formula of grandfather and grandson.

2-kings-22:1:0.summary: Joshua’s town list near Lachish includes “Basedoth,” probably Josiah’s mother’s hometown, though the source spells it “Basouroth.”
2-kings-22:1:0.why: Locates the queen mother’s town, if the forms match.

2-kings-22:1:2.summary: Jeremiah’s ministry is dated “in the days of Josiah,” the same king.
2-kings-22:1:2.why: Shows Jeremiah prophesied during Josiah’s reign.

2-kings-22:1:3.summary: Zephaniah prophesied “in the days of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah,” the same king.

2-kings-22:1:4.summary: Matthew’s “Amos begot Josiah” includes Josiah in the messianic genealogy.

2-kings-22:1:5.summary: “Woe to you, city, whose king is young” contrasts with the boy-king Josiah’s righteous reign; only a general theme.
2-kings-22:1:5.why: Shows a young king need not bring woe.

2-kings-22:1:6.summary: Praise “from the mouth of infants” has no specific link to Josiah becoming king at eight.

2-kings-22:1:8.summary: Joash “was seven years old when he became king,” another child king of Judah; a general parallel.

2-kings-22:1:9.summary: The man of God foretells “a son … Josiah by name” born to David’s house, naming this very king.
2-kings-22:1:9.why: Shows Josiah’s reign was prophesied long before.

2-kings-22:1:10.summary: Isaiah’s threat of “young men as their rulers” is a judgment oracle, not a link to Josiah’s accession.

2-kings-22:2:2.summary: Hezekiah also “did what was right in the Lord’s eyes” according to “his father David,” the same commendation.
2-kings-22:2:2.why: Places Josiah beside Hezekiah as a model king.

2-kings-22:2:0.summary: Deuteronomy commands “turn neither to the right nor to the left,” the phrase used of Josiah.

2-kings-22:2:1.summary: Joshua is told not to turn “to the right or to the left” from Moses’ commands, the same idiom as Josiah’s praise.
2-kings-22:2:1.why: Links Josiah’s fidelity to Joshua’s charge.

2-kings-22:2:3.summary: Solomon praises David who “walked before Thee in truth”; a general picture of David’s way that Josiah followed.

2-kings-22:2:4.summary: The Greek-based proverb about one “fettered in his practices” and a straight way has no clear link to Josiah.
2-kings-22:2:4.why: Saints wording does not carry the link.

2-kings-22:2:5.summary: “Do not turn to the right or the left” shares the idiom but is general wisdom, not about kings or David.

2-kings-22:2:6.summary: Ahaz “did not … do what was right … as his father David had done,” the exact opposite of Josiah’s verdict.
2-kings-22:2:6.why: Contrasts Josiah with an unfaithful king.

2-kings-22:2:7.summary: Hezekiah “did what was right before the Lord, according to everything David his father had done,” matching Josiah’s praise.
2-kings-22:2:7.why: Same commendation for another reforming king.

2-kings-22:2:8.summary: Jeroboam is told to “walk in My ways, and do what is right … as David” did; similar wording but a conditional promise.
2-kings-22:2:8.why: Shows the Davidic standard set for kings.

2-kings-22:2:9.summary: David “did what was right” and “did not turn aside” all his life, the very standard Josiah is said to match.
2-kings-22:2:9.why: Defines the Davidic standard Josiah followed.

2-kings-22:2:10.summary: Jehoshaphat “walked in his father’s earlier ways”; a similar commendation but not the same wording or person.
2-kings-22:2:10.why: Another king praised for following a godly father.
