2-kings-22:2:11.summary: Ezekiel’s son who sees his father’s sins and does not follow them parallels Josiah’s break from Amon, but only thematically.
2-kings-22:2:11.why: Illustrates a righteous son of a wicked father.

2-kings-22:2:12.summary: Sirach’s praise of Josiah (named in the surrounding verses) says he “directed his heart toward the Lord” amid lawless days.
2-kings-22:2:12.why: Later tradition’s tribute to Josiah’s piety.

2-kings-22:4:4.summary: Chronicles parallels the delivery of temple silver to “Hilkiah the high priest,” gathered by Levites “guarding the gate.”
2-kings-22:4:4.why: Parallel account of Josiah’s temple repair funding.

2-kings-22:4:0.summary: Joash ordered “all the silver … brought into the Lord’s house” collected for repairs, the precedent for Josiah’s procedure.
2-kings-22:4:0.why: Shows the earlier temple-repair funding model.

2-kings-22:4:2.summary: Solomon stations “gatekeepers in their divisions at each gate”; only a general link to the doorkeepers in the source.

2-kings-22:4:3.summary: Korite Levites served “guarding the entrance”; general background for those guarding the temple doorpost.

2-kings-22:4:5.summary: Lists “Azaria son of Chelkia” in the high-priestly line, naming the same high priest Chelkias.
2-kings-22:4:5.why: Places Hilkiah in the priestly genealogy.

2-kings-22:4:6.summary: “Salom begot Chelkias” names the high priest Chelkias of the source in the priestly genealogy.

2-kings-22:4:7.summary: Jesus watches money put into the temple treasury; a general link to people’s gifts brought to the Lord’s house.

2-kings-22:4:8.summary: Lots are cast for the temple gates and guards; general background for the doorkeepers who collected silver.

2-kings-22:4:9.summary: The Greek-based psalm says “cast aside in the house of God,” not doorkeeper, so the gatekeeper link is lost.
2-kings-22:4:9.why: Saints wording does not carry the link.

2-kings-22:4:10.summary: Lists post-exilic “gatekeepers” by name; only general background on temple door-guards.

2-kings-22:4:11.summary: Joash’s collection box at the temple gate, emptied by the high priest’s overseer, parallels the silver collected by doorkeepers.
2-kings-22:4:11.why: Earlier model for gathering repair funds.

2-kings-22:5:0.summary: Under Joash silver was given to those doing the work “to make firm the bedek of the Lord’s house,” the same rare term.
2-kings-22:5:0.why: Same procedure and term for temple repair.

2-kings-22:5:1.summary: Joash’s order to “strengthen the bedek of the house” uses the same distinctive repair term.
2-kings-22:5:1.why: Shared technical term for temple breaches.

2-kings-22:5:2.summary: Notes on Joash’s sons and successor share nothing with paying temple workers.

2-kings-22:5:3.summary: Joash and Jehoiada “gave it to those doing the work” to repair and strengthen the Lord’s house, paralleling Josiah’s order.

2-kings-22:5:4.summary: Athaliah’s sons “pulled down God’s house,” explaining earlier damage; only background to temple repairs.
2-kings-22:5:4.why: Explains why repairs were needed earlier.

2-kings-22:5:5.summary: Returned exiles “gave silver to the stonecutters and craftsmen” for the temple; a general parallel of funding builders.

2-kings-22:7:1.summary: “What is required of stewards is that each be found faithful” matches the workers trusted because they “act faithfully.”
2-kings-22:7:1.why: Applies faithful stewardship to handling funds.

2-kings-22:7:2.summary: Nehemiah entrusts Jerusalem to a “truthful man”; general theme of trusting reliable people.

2-kings-22:7:3.summary: Under Joash the remaining silver was brought back to the king, an accounting that contrasts loosely with no account being demanded.

2-kings-22:7:4.summary: Jesus’ teaching that one “faithful in the least is faithful also in much” shares the faithful-handling theme only generally.

2-kings-22:7:5.summary: Paul takes care to be honorable in administering a gift; a general link on handling money with integrity.

2-kings-22:7:6.summary: “A trustworthy man will be greatly blessed”; general wisdom on trustworthiness.

2-kings-22:7:7.summary: Paul entrusts teaching “to faithful people”; only the general idea of entrusting to the faithful.
2-kings-22:7:7.why: Loose theme of entrusting to faithful people.

2-kings-22:7:8.summary: The people bring more than needed for the sanctuary work; general theme of generous, honest provision for God’s house.

2-kings-22:7:9.summary: “You act faithfully” shares the phrase, but concerns hospitality, not handling funds.

2-kings-22:8:0.summary: Moses has “this book of the law” laid beside the ark in the sanctuary, the likely origin of the book Chelkias found.
2-kings-22:8:0.why: Explains why a law book was in the temple.

2-kings-22:9:0.summary: Names “Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan,” the grandson of the scribe Sapphan in the source.
2-kings-22:9:0.why: Traces Shaphan’s family into Jeremiah’s time.

2-kings-22:9:1.summary: “Elasah son of Shaphan” may belong to the same scribal family, but the text does not identify him with the scribe.

2-kings-22:9:2.summary: “Gemariah son of Shaphan the scribe” and his son appear when Baruch’s scroll is read, linking to the scribe Sapphan.
2-kings-22:9:2.why: Shaphan’s family again involved with a read scroll.

2-kings-22:9:3.summary: Josiah sends “Sapphan … the scribe of the Lord’s house,” setting up the report in the source.
2-kings-22:9:3.why: Immediate narrative context of the same mission.

2-kings-22:9:4.summary: Gedaliah son of Ahikam is appointed over Judah; Shaphan is not named here, so the family link is indirect.

2-kings-22:9:5.summary: Ishmael kills Gedaliah; Shaphan is not named in this verse, so the connection is indirect.

2-kings-22:9:6.summary: “Ahikam son of Shaphan” protects Jeremiah, naming the scribe’s son.

2-kings-22:9:7.summary: “Godolias son of Achikam son of Saphan” is made governor, naming the scribe’s grandson.
2-kings-22:9:7.why: Traces Shaphan’s family after the fall.

2-kings-22:9:8.summary: Hezekiah’s officials include a scribe and “Eliakim son of Chelkias,” a different Chelkias; only a court-official parallel.

2-kings-22:9:9.summary: Josiah commands “Chelkias the priest … Sapphan the scribe,” the same officials in the continuing narrative.
2-kings-22:9:9.why: Same officials in the next scene.

2-kings-22:9:10.summary: “Jaazaniah son of Shaphan” stands among idolatrous elders; possibly a different Shaphan, and the text does not say.

2-kings-22:10:0.summary: Jehudi reads Jeremiah’s roll “to the king,” a parallel royal reading with Jehoiakim’s opposite response.
2-kings-22:10:0.why: Contrasts two kings hearing God’s written word.

2-kings-22:10:1.summary: Baruch is told to “read from this roll” in the temple; general theme of reading God’s word aloud.

2-kings-22:10:2.summary: The king is to have a copy of the law and “read therein all the days of his life,” the duty Josiah now meets.
2-kings-22:10:2.why: Shows the law’s requirement for kings.

2-kings-22:10:3.summary: Returned exiles “found written in the law” a forgotten command; a general parallel of rediscovering the law.

2-kings-22:10:4.summary: A call to the king to “humble yourselves”; only a loose link to the king’s response to the book.

2-kings-22:10:5.summary: Moses commands reading the law “before all Israel”; relevant to public reading but not to Sapphan reading to the king.
2-kings-22:10:5.why: Background on reading the law aloud.

2-kings-22:10:6.summary: A reading “from a book of Moses” reveals a forgotten rule; a general parallel to reading the found book.

2-kings-22:10:8.summary: Esdras reads the book of the law to the assembly; a general parallel of reading the law aloud.

2-kings-22:10:9.summary: Esdras reads “from a book of God’s law” daily; only a general reading-of-the-law theme.
2-kings-22:10:9.why: General theme of reading the law.

2-kings-22:10:10.summary: Officials ask Baruch to read the scroll and he “read it”; general theme of reading God’s word to officials.
2-kings-22:10:10.why: Loose parallel of reading to leaders.

2-kings-22:10:11.summary: Jeremiah is sent to speak to the king of Judah; no reading of a book or other specific shared element.

2-kings-22:11:4.summary: Jehoiakim and his servants heard the words yet did not tear “their garments,” the opposite of Josiah’s response.
2-kings-22:11:4.why: Sharp contrast between two kings hearing God’s word.

2-kings-22:11:1.summary: “Tear your hearts, not your garments” shares the image of torn garments as repentance, but generally.
2-kings-22:11:1.why: Shows the inner repentance the gesture should express.

2-kings-22:11:2.summary: When the word reached the king of Nineveh he put off his robe and wore sackcloth, a parallel royal repentance on hearing God’s word.
2-kings-22:11:2.why: Another king’s humble response to a warning.

2-kings-22:11:3.summary: Joshua “tore his clothes” before the Lord after defeat; shares the gesture but not the setting.

2-kings-22:12:5.summary: Chronicles gives the same command to Hilkiah, “Ahikam son of Shaphan,” “Shaphan the scribe” and Asaias.
2-kings-22:12:5.why: Parallel account of the same delegation.

2-kings-22:12:0.summary: “Ahikam son of Shaphan,” one of the delegation, later protects Jeremiah.
2-kings-22:12:0.why: Shows the later role of a delegation member.

2-kings-22:12:1.summary: “Godolias son of Achikam son of Saphan” names Achikam of the delegation as father of the later governor.

2-kings-22:12:2.summary: Hezekiah sends his steward, scribe and elder priests to Isaiah the prophet, a parallel royal embassy to inquire of a prophet.
2-kings-22:12:2.why: Parallel royal delegation to a prophet.

2-kings-22:12:3.summary: The preceding report to Josiah about the silver is the same narrative, but the shown verse does not name the officials.

2-kings-22:12:4.summary: Hezekiah “tore his garments” and sent his steward, scribe and elder priests to Isaiah, closely paralleling Josiah’s delegation.
2-kings-22:12:4.why: Parallel royal response and embassy to a prophet.

2-kings-22:12:6.summary: The king sending men to Egypt shares no named person or element in the Saints text shown.

2-kings-22:13:0.summary: The people read “a book of the law” and confessed; a general parallel of response to the law.
2-kings-22:13:0.why: Parallel confession upon reading the law.

2-kings-22:13:1.summary: God visits “the sins of fathers upon children”; general link to wrath falling because “our fathers did not listen.”

2-kings-22:13:2.summary: James urges being doers of the word, not hearers only; a general link to failing “to do everything written.”
2-kings-22:13:2.why: General theme of obeying the written word.

2-kings-22:13:3.summary: Moses warns of perishing for provoking God by idols; general background to the anger the book announces.
2-kings-22:13:3.why: Shows the law’s warnings about anger.

2-kings-22:13:4.summary: God foretells being “kindled in wrath” against a faithless people; general link to the burning anger in the source.

2-kings-22:13:5.summary: Nations ask about “this great heat of anger” because Israel forsook the fathers’ covenant—close to Josiah’s “great is the Lord’s anger.”
2-kings-22:13:5.why: Shows the book’s own explanation of the wrath.

2-kings-22:13:6.summary: Zedekiah secretly asks Jeremiah for “a word from the Lord”; a general parallel of a king inquiring of a prophet.
2-kings-22:13:6.why: Another king seeking a prophetic word.

2-kings-22:13:7.summary: “Who will stand before His anger?” shares only the general theme of God’s wrath.

2-kings-22:13:8.summary: The people acted worse “than your fathers” and did not obey; a general link to the fathers’ disobedience.

2-kings-22:13:9.summary: The people boast of idolatry practiced by “our fathers, our kings”; loosely parallels the fathers’ failure.

2-kings-22:13:11.summary: The eschatological “great day of Their wrath” shares only the word wrath.

2-kings-22:13:12.summary: God revealing His discipline to the prophets has no specific link to Josiah’s inquiry.

2-kings-22:13:13.summary: “Through law comes knowledge of sin” loosely fits Josiah recognizing guilt through the book.
2-kings-22:13:13.why: Theological reflection on the law exposing sin.

2-kings-22:13:14.summary: Zedekiah sends named men, including a priest, to Jeremiah to “Ask the Lord about us,” a parallel royal inquiry.
2-kings-22:13:14.why: Parallel royal inquiry through a prophet.

2-kings-22:13:15.summary: “Our fathers sinned … we bore their lawless acts” shares the theme of suffering for fathers’ sins.
2-kings-22:13:15.why: Later lament on the same theme.

2-kings-22:13:16.summary: Jehoshaphat asks for a prophet “so we may inquire of the Lord”; a general inquiry parallel.
2-kings-22:13:16.why: Another king seeking the Lord through a prophet.

2-kings-22:13:17.summary: Hezekiah confesses “our fathers departed and did what was evil,” the same admission of the fathers’ guilt leading to wrath.
2-kings-22:13:17.why: Parallel royal confession of ancestral sin.

2-kings-22:13:18.summary: Paul’s personal account of sin reviving through the commandment has no specific link to the found book.

2-kings-22:13:19.summary: “Who will withstand Thee? … Thy wrath” shares only the general theme of God’s anger.

2-kings-22:13:20.summary: Elders come to question the Lord and are refused an answer, a loose contrast with Josiah’s inquiry.

2-kings-22:13:21.summary: “We sinned with our fathers” shares the general confession of ancestral sin.

2-kings-22:13:22.summary: Daniel confesses “we … have not listened” to the prophets, with shame to “our kings, rulers, and fathers,” echoing the fathers’ disobedience.

2-kings-22:13:23.summary: Jehoshaphat asks for a prophet “through whom we may inquire of the Lord”; a general inquiry parallel.
2-kings-22:13:23.why: Another king inquiring of the Lord.

2-kings-22:13:24.summary: Saul “did not seek the Lord” but consulted a medium, contrasting with Josiah seeking the Lord.

2-kings-22:13:25.summary: The people weep “as they heard the words of the law”; a general parallel of response to the law.
2-kings-22:13:25.why: Similar response to hearing the law.

2-kings-22:13:26.summary: The Lord as stronghold of those who fear Him has no specific link to the inquiry about the book.

2-kings-22:13:27.summary: “The law brings wrath” loosely matches the book revealing God’s anger.
2-kings-22:13:27.why: Theological reflection on law and wrath.

2-kings-22:13:28.summary: God refuses to answer idolaters who inquire of a prophet, loosely contrasting Josiah’s sincere inquiry.

2-kings-22:13:29.summary: Daniel confesses Israel “have not listened to the voice of the Lord” and His law; general parallel to the fathers’ failure.

2-kings-22:13:30.summary: Acknowledging wisdom in all ways has no specific connection to Josiah’s inquiry.

2-kings-22:14:1.summary: Chronicles parallels the visit to “Huldah the prophetess, wife of Sellem,” keeper of the robes in Jerusalem’s Masana.
2-kings-22:14:1.why: Parallel account of the same visit.

2-kings-22:14:0.summary: “Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth” is another named prophetess, a general parallel.

2-kings-22:14:2.summary: Elizabeth and Mary’s meeting (truncated) does not mention a prophetess or any element of the source.

2-kings-22:14:3.summary: “Miriam the prophetess” is another prophetess; only a general parallel.

2-kings-22:14:4.summary: A “dresser” over garments in Baal’s house loosely parallels Sellem as “keeper of the garments.”

2-kings-22:14:5.summary: Zephaniah’s “second quarter” matches the Hebrew district, but the source’s Greek-based “masena” does not carry that link.
2-kings-22:14:5.why: Saints wording does not carry the link.

2-kings-22:14:6.summary: “A prophetess, Anna” is another woman prophet; only a general parallel.

2-kings-22:14:7.summary: Philip’s daughters “prophesied”; a general parallel of women prophesying.

2-kings-22:14:8.summary: A list of gifts including priests’ garments shares only incidental vocabulary with the keeper of the garments.

2-kings-22:14:9.summary: Miriam is named as sent before Israel but not called a prophetess here; no real link to Olda.

2-kings-22:14:10.summary: Mentions a woman who “prophesies”; only a general theme of women prophesying.

2-kings-22:15:0.summary: The one with God’s word should “tell My word in truth”; general link to Olda speaking the Lord’s word.

2-kings-22:15:1.summary: Elijah answers a king who sent messengers to inquire with “Thus says the Lord”; a loose parallel.
2-kings-22:15:1.why: Similar prophetic response to a king’s inquiry.

2-kings-22:15:2.summary: “Return to the king who sent you and tell him, Thus says the Lord” closely matches Olda’s “Tell the man who sent you.”
2-kings-22:15:2.why: Same prophetic reply formula to royal envoys.

2-kings-22:16:6.summary: “Behold, I am bringing disasters upon Jerusalem and Judah” uses the same wording as Huldah’s oracle.
2-kings-22:16:6.why: Links Huldah’s word to the earlier judgment on Manasseh’s sin.

2-kings-22:16:0.summary: Daniel confesses that the curse “written in the law of Moses” brought calamities on Jerusalem, fulfilling what the book announced.

2-kings-22:16:1.summary: Joshua warns the Lord “shall bring upon you all the harmful words,” matching the disasters “of the book.”
2-kings-22:16:1.why: Shows the covenant warning now enacted.

2-kings-22:16:2.summary: The Song of Moses (truncated) recounts Israel’s apostasy and God’s jealous response; general background to the judgment.

2-kings-22:16:4.summary: Speaks of the Lord’s anger and “all the curses of this covenant which are written in this” book, as in the source (truncated).
2-kings-22:16:4.why: Identifies the written curses being invoked.

2-kings-22:16:5.summary: Isaiah’s word that all in Hezekiah’s house will go to Babylon is a parallel announcement of coming disaster on Judah.
2-kings-22:16:5.why: Earlier prophecy of the same coming judgment.

2-kings-22:16:7.summary: God foretells that “many evils and afflictions” will find the faithless people; general background to the disasters.

2-kings-22:16:8.summary: Moses warns that turning to other gods means “you shall surely perish”; a general covenant warning.

2-kings-22:16:9.summary: Joshua warns Israel may “perish from this good land”; a general covenant-threat link.

2-kings-22:16:10.summary: The covenant curses (truncated) “shall come upon you” for disobedience—the written disasters Huldah confirms.
2-kings-22:16:10.why: Shows the curses the book contained.

2-kings-22:16:11.summary: The Lord brings “all the curses which are written in this book of the law,” matching “all the words of the book.”
2-kings-22:16:11.why: Direct link between book and judgment.

2-kings-22:16:12.summary: Nabouchodonosor’s siege and breach of Jerusalem record the fulfillment of the disasters Huldah announced.

2-kings-22:16:13.summary: Leviticus’ covenant curses (truncated) parallel the threatened disasters, but only as general background.

2-kings-22:17:0.summary: Amon “abandoned the Lord, the God of his fathers,” the same charge “they abandoned Me.”
2-kings-22:17:0.why: Shows the recent royal apostasy behind the verdict.

2-kings-22:17:1.summary: Fire in Jerusalem’s gates that will “not be extinguished” echoes unquenchable wrath, but for Sabbath-breaking.

2-kings-22:17:2.summary: Israel “abandoned the Lord” for foreign gods and He was angered; the general judges-cycle pattern.
2-kings-22:17:2.why: Same pattern of apostasy and anger.

2-kings-22:17:3.summary: Isaiah mocks gods made by human hands; general link to “the works of their hands.”

2-kings-22:17:4.summary: “The day of the Lord’s wrath” and consuming fire share only the general judgment theme.

2-kings-22:17:5.summary: Isaiah’s satire of carved gods relates loosely to provoking God “with the works of their hands.”

2-kings-22:17:6.summary: Israel “forsook God” and “provoked Me with foreign gods,” the same charge of abandonment and provocation.
2-kings-22:17:6.why: Shows the Song of Moses’ charge realized.

2-kings-22:17:7.summary: Idols are “works of human hands”; a general link to provoking God with works of their hands.

2-kings-22:17:8.summary: The Lord’s anger rose “until there was no healing,” matching wrath that “shall not be quenched.”

2-kings-22:17:9.summary: “A fire has been kindled out of My wrath” shares the image of God’s burning wrath.
2-kings-22:17:9.why: Same image of wrath as fire.

2-kings-22:17:10.summary: God tells Israel “you have forsaken Me and served other gods”; a general parallel of the same charge.
2-kings-22:17:10.why: Same charge in an earlier era.

2-kings-22:17:11.summary: “They abandoned Me, a spring of water of life” shares the verb but in a broader prophetic indictment.

2-kings-22:17:12.summary: Israel withdrew from God and “committed great provocations”; general link to provoking God.

2-kings-22:17:13.summary: “Wrath has overtaken them to the end” shares only the general theme of final wrath.

2-kings-22:17:14.summary: Israel “forsook the Lord,” followed other gods, “provoked the Lord,” and He was angered—the same sequence.

2-kings-22:17:15.summary: Israel “forsook the covenant” and “served other gods,” so the Lord “was kindled in wrath against that land.”
2-kings-22:17:15.why: Shows the book’s threat now applied.

2-kings-22:17:16.summary: “I will bring their sin upon them” is a general statement of deferred judgment.

2-kings-22:17:17.summary: Judah’s many gods and turning their backs to God parallel idolatry only generally.

2-kings-22:17:18.summary: Israel “forgot the Lord” and served Baalim, and He was angered; general pattern parallel.

2-kings-22:17:19.summary: The psalm recounts Israel serving carved images and the Lord’s wrath; general historical parallel.

2-kings-22:17:20.summary: “My wrath and fury are poured upon this place … it will burn and not be extinguished” closely echoes the source.

2-kings-22:17:21.summary: God will end bowing down “to the works of your hands”; shares the phrase in a different context.

2-kings-22:17:22.summary: Trembling of the ungodly and burning fire share only vague imagery with the source.

2-kings-22:17:23.summary: God warns that serving “other gods” and abandoning the Lord will bring ruin on land and house, the judgment now pronounced.

2-kings-22:17:24.summary: The land bowed to “the works of their hands”; shares the idol phrase in a general oracle.

2-kings-22:17:25.summary: God kindles a fire that “will not be quenched,” the same image as the wrath that “shall not be quenched.”

2-kings-22:18:0.summary: Chronicles repeats Huldah’s word to “the king of Judah who sent you to seek the Lord … The words which you have heard.”
2-kings-22:18:0.why: Parallel account of the same oracle.

2-kings-22:18:1.summary: A plot to bind the righteous has no specific link to Huldah’s message to the king.

2-kings-22:18:2.summary: The Lord “listened” to those who feared Him; a general link to God hearing the humble king.
2-kings-22:18:2.why: General theme of God heeding the God-fearing.

2-kings-22:19:0.summary: “A broken and humbled heart God will not despise” matches God hearing Josiah’s softened heart.

2-kings-22:19:1.summary: Because Ahab humbled himself, harm is deferred to “his son’s days,” the same deferral granted Josiah.
2-kings-22:19:1.why: Parallel case of judgment postponed for humility.

2-kings-22:19:2.summary: God gives life “to the brokenhearted”; a general theme of God favoring the contrite.

2-kings-22:19:3.summary: Pharaoh’s refusal to “reverence” God lacks the humbling language the link assumes in the Greek-based wording.
2-kings-22:19:3.why: Saints wording does not carry the link.

2-kings-22:19:4.summary: David’s heart “struck him” after cutting Saul’s cloak; a loose link to a tender conscience.
2-kings-22:19:4.why: Loose theme of a sensitive heart.

2-kings-22:19:5.summary: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God” shares the general theme of humility rewarded.

2-kings-22:19:6.summary: What the Lord seeks—justice, mercy, walking with God—relates only generally to Josiah’s response.

2-kings-22:19:7.summary: Jesus wept over the doomed city; a general parallel to weeping over coming judgment.

2-kings-22:19:8.summary: The land became “a desolation … and a curse,” echoing the source’s “obliteration and a curse.”

2-kings-22:19:9.summary: Addressed to “you who tremble at His word”; a general link to Josiah’s fear on hearing God’s word.
2-kings-22:19:9.why: General theme of trembling at God’s word.

2-kings-22:19:10.summary: James calls to mourn, weep and humble oneself before the Lord; a general theme of humility.

2-kings-22:19:11.summary: God looks to “the humble and quiet one who trembles at My words,” describing Josiah’s response.
2-kings-22:19:11.why: Shows why God regards such humility.

2-kings-22:19:12.summary: God will “make the city a curse,” the same fate announced for “this place.”

2-kings-22:19:13.summary: Manasseh “humbled himself greatly” in affliction; a general parallel of royal humility.

2-kings-22:19:14.summary: Notes how God listened to Manasseh’s prayer; general theme of God hearing a repentant king.

2-kings-22:19:15.summary: God tells Hezekiah “I have heard your prayer and seen your tears,” matching “did weep before Me, I also have heard.”
2-kings-22:19:15.why: Parallel divine response to a king’s tears.

2-kings-22:19:16.summary: The threat to make cities “desolate” relates generally to the place becoming an obliteration.

2-kings-22:19:17.summary: Amon “did not humble himself before the Lord,” contrasting directly with his son Josiah.

2-kings-22:19:18.summary: “When I heard these words, I sat down and wept”; a general parallel of weeping on hearing bad news.

2-kings-22:19:19.summary: Israel “wept before the Lord” at Bethel; a general parallel of weeping before God.
2-kings-22:19:19.why: General theme of weeping before God.

2-kings-22:19:20.summary: God answers Hezekiah, “What you did pray to Me … I have heard,” the same reply formula as to Josiah.
2-kings-22:19:20.why: Same divine reply to a godly king.

2-kings-22:19:21.summary: Esdras prays “weeping … before the house of God”; a general parallel of penitent weeping.

2-kings-22:19:22.summary: The land overthrown “in wrath and anger” illustrates the obliteration threatened, but only generally.

2-kings-22:19:23.summary: The people “raised their voice and wept” at the Lord’s rebuke; a general parallel.

2-kings-22:19:24.summary: Records that Josiah “tore his garments” on hearing the book, the act God cites here.

2-kings-22:19:25.summary: Leviticus foresees confession when “their uncircumcised heart will feel shame,” echoing Josiah’s heart that did “feel shame.”
2-kings-22:19:25.why: Shows the covenant’s path of penitence.

2-kings-22:19:26.summary: The people weeping at the Tent during the Midianite incident shares only the word weeping.

2-kings-22:19:27.summary: Jeremiah longs to weep day and night for his people; a general theme of weeping over judgment.

2-kings-22:19:28.summary: The prophet’s soul “will weep in secret” if the people do not hear; general weeping theme.

2-kings-22:19:29.summary: “I feared Thy judgments” shares the general theme of fear before God’s word.
2-kings-22:19:29.why: General theme of fearing God’s judgments.

2-kings-22:19:30.summary: Paul’s anguish over his kinsmen shares only a general grief for one’s people.
2-kings-22:19:30.why: Loose theme of grieving for one’s people.

2-kings-22:19:31.summary: Jehoiakim and his servants did not tear “their garments” on hearing God’s words, the opposite of Josiah.

2-kings-22:19:32.summary: A call to those who have “lost heart” shares no specific element with Josiah’s softened heart.

2-kings-22:19:33.summary: “Hardness and unrepentant heart” contrasts with Josiah’s softened heart, but only as general teaching.

2-kings-22:19:34.summary: Those who “sigh deeply and grieve” over Jerusalem’s lawlessness are spared; a general parallel to Josiah being spared.
2-kings-22:19:34.why: God sparing those who grieve over sin.

2-kings-22:19:35.summary: Tears flowing “since they did not keep Thy law” match Josiah weeping over the book’s unkept words.

2-kings-22:19:36.summary: Esdras “tore my garments” on hearing of covenant-breaking, a close parallel to Josiah’s reaction.

2-kings-22:19:37.summary: A call to bring down tears day and night for the crushed people; general weeping theme.

2-kings-22:19:38.summary: “All the people were weeping as they heard the words of the law,” paralleling Josiah weeping at the book.
2-kings-22:19:38.why: Same response to hearing the law.

2-kings-22:19:39.summary: Jehoiakim burned the roll and is judged because “they did not listen” (truncated); a loose contrast to Josiah.
2-kings-22:19:39.why: Contrasts a king who rejected the word.

2-kings-22:20:0.summary: “A peaceful person has a remnant” relates only generally to being gathered “in peace.”
2-kings-22:20:0.why: Loose theme of peace for the upright.

2-kings-22:20:1.summary: The righteous man “was taken from the presence of injustice” and his “burial will be in peace,” mirroring Josiah’s promise.
2-kings-22:20:1.why: Righteous spared coming evil through death.

2-kings-22:20:2.summary: “You sleep with your fathers” uses a similar death idiom, but concerns David’s succession.

2-kings-22:20:3.summary: Abraham died in old age and “was added to his people,” matching “I am adding you to your fathers.”
2-kings-22:20:3.why: Same idiom of being gathered to one’s ancestors.

2-kings-22:20:4.summary: The Greek-based text addresses one provoked “in Ahaz your father,” obscuring the Hebrew reference to Josiah’s righteousness.
2-kings-22:20:4.why: Saints wording does not carry the link.

2-kings-22:20:5.summary: “Do not weep for the dead” may allude to Josiah’s death, but he is not named in the shown text.

2-kings-22:20:6.summary: Records Josiah’s death at Mageddo and burial in his grave, the fulfillment (and tension) of being gathered “in peace.”
2-kings-22:20:6.why: Shows how the promise was fulfilled.

2-kings-22:20:8.summary: “You shall sleep with your fathers” is a similar death idiom, said of Moses before Israel’s apostasy.

2-kings-22:20:9.summary: The righteous one “was snatched away, lest evil change his understanding,” paralleling Josiah removed before the disasters.
2-kings-22:20:9.why: Righteous taken away before evil comes.

2-kings-23:1:1.summary: Hezekiah takes counsel with rulers and the assembly; a general parallel of a king convening leaders.

2-kings-23:1:2.summary: Hezekiah “gathered the city’s rulers, and went up to the Lord’s house,” paralleling Josiah gathering elders and going up.

2-kings-23:1:3.summary: Moses says “Gather unto me … your elders” to speak the law’s words in their hearing, as Josiah does.

2-kings-23:1:4.summary: David “gathered” Israel’s young men for the ark; only a general royal-gathering parallel.

2-kings-23:2:0.summary: The “book of the law in the Lord’s house” found by Chelkias is the same book Josiah reads.

2-kings-23:2:1.summary: Moses commands reading the law “before all Israel in their hearing,” men, women and children, as Josiah does.
2-kings-23:2:1.why: Josiah fulfills the Mosaic reading command.

2-kings-23:2:2.summary: The judgment scene shares only “the great and the small” and opened scrolls, incidental to the covenant reading.

2-kings-23:2:3.summary: The people “read from a book of the law” and confessed; a general parallel of public reading.

2-kings-23:2:4.summary: The ark holds “the tablets of the covenant”; general background to the covenant book.

2-kings-23:2:5.summary: “The small together with the great” is only an incidental phrase match.

2-kings-23:2:6.summary: The plague on Gath’s men “small and great” shares only the phrase.

2-kings-23:2:7.summary: Jehoshaphat’s envoys taught Judah with “a book of the Lord’s law”; a general parallel of teaching the law.

2-kings-23:2:8.summary: Asa’s covenant assembly includes all “from younger to older”; a loose parallel of a covenant gathering.

2-kings-23:2:9.summary: Paul testifying “to small and great” shares only the phrase.

2-kings-23:2:10.summary: “A reading was made from a book of Moses in the hearing of the people”; a general parallel.

2-kings-23:2:11.summary: Captives taken “from small to great” at Ziklag shares only the phrase.

2-kings-23:2:12.summary: “This book of the law” laid beside the ark relates generally to the book found in the Lord’s house.

2-kings-23:2:13.summary: A Persian king’s feast for the city has no real link to the covenant reading.

2-kings-23:2:14.summary: All the people gather to hear “the book of the law of Moses” read aloud, a close parallel to Josiah’s public reading.

2-kings-23:2:15.summary: Sodom’s men struck blind “from small to great” shares only the phrase.

2-kings-23:2:16.summary: “Small and great are there” in the grave shares only the phrase.

2-kings-23:3:0.summary: Joash stands “by the pillar according to the ordinance,” the same royal station where Josiah makes the covenant.
2-kings-23:3:0.why: Shows the king’s customary place by the pillar.

2-kings-23:3:1.summary: Jehoiada “made a covenant between the Lord, the king, and the people,” a parallel covenant renewal.

2-kings-23:3:2.summary: “You shall walk after the Lord … and keep His commandments” matches the covenant terms Josiah pledges.

2-kings-23:3:3.summary: Serving God “with all your heart and with all your soul” matches “whole heart and whole soul.”
2-kings-23:3:3.why: Deuteronomic source of the pledge’s wording.

2-kings-23:3:4.summary: The “eternal covenant” in Christ’s blood shares only the word covenant.

2-kings-23:3:5.summary: Loving God “with all your heart, with all your soul” echoes the pledge, but as general teaching.

2-kings-23:3:6.summary: “The commandments, and the ordinances” shares legal vocabulary only generally.

2-kings-23:3:7.summary: Warning against going after other gods is general covenant background.

2-kings-23:3:8.summary: The promised new covenant contrasts with failed old covenants; only a general covenant theme.

2-kings-23:3:9.summary: Hezekiah resolves “to establish a covenant of the Lord” to turn away wrath, a parallel royal covenant renewal.

2-kings-23:3:10.summary: All Israel stands “before the Lord” to “enter into the covenant,” as the people stood in Josiah’s covenant.

2-kings-23:3:12.summary: Jesus as mediator of a new covenant shares only the word covenant.

2-kings-23:3:13.summary: Leaders establish and seal a written pledge, a parallel covenant renewal after reading the law.

2-kings-23:3:14.summary: “The testimonies, and the ordinances, and the judgments” match the triad in Josiah’s pledge.
2-kings-23:3:14.why: Deuteronomic source of the legal terms.

2-kings-23:3:16.summary: Moses relates God’s words and “all the people answered,” agreeing to obey—parallel to the people standing in the covenant.

2-kings-23:3:17.summary: Asa’s people enter “a covenant to seek the Lord … with all the heart and all the soul,” matching Josiah’s covenant.

2-kings-23:3:18.summary: Joash stands “at his station” at the temple, paralleling the king’s place, though the pillar is not named here.
2-kings-23:3:18.why: Parallel royal station in the temple.

2-kings-23:3:19.summary: The people enter “a curse and an oath to walk in the law” and keep the commandments, a parallel covenant pledge (truncated).

2-kings-23:3:20.summary: The psalm praises the Lord’s law, testimony, ordinances and commandment; shared vocabulary, general theme.

2-kings-23:3:21.summary: Advice about the king’s mouth and an oath shares no real link to the covenant.

2-kings-23:3:22.summary: Joshua “made a covenant with the people” after they pledged to serve the Lord, a parallel covenant renewal.

2-kings-23:3:23.summary: Returning exiles seek “an everlasting covenant”; only a general covenant theme.

2-kings-23:3:24.summary: To “walk in all His ways … with all your heart and with all your soul” closely matches Josiah’s pledge.

2-kings-23:3:25.summary: Moses “took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people,” who agreed to obey—the model for Josiah.
2-kings-23:3:25.why: Sinai precedent for reading the covenant book.

2-kings-23:3:26.summary: Swearing “The Lord lives” in truth has no specific link to Josiah’s covenant.

2-kings-23:3:27.summary: Moses reminds Israel of the Horeb covenant made “with you”; general covenant background.

2-kings-23:3:28.summary: “Let us make a covenant with our God” to act by the law is a general covenant-renewal parallel.

2-kings-23:3:29.summary: “The words of the covenant” Moses established in Moab correspond to “the words of this covenant” Josiah upholds.

2-kings-23:3:30.summary: Jehoiada “made a covenant between himself, the people, and the king,” a parallel royal covenant renewal.

2-kings-23:4:1.summary: Manasseh placed the carved image of the “grove” in the Lord’s house; Josiah brings the grove vessels out of that sanctuary.
2-kings-23:4:1.why: Shows the origin of the grove objects Josiah removes.

2-kings-23:4:2.summary: Manasseh made sacred groves, pillars for the Baals, and served “the army of heaven”—the very cults whose vessels Josiah burns.
2-kings-23:4:2.why: Explains which cults Josiah's reform undoes.

2-kings-23:4:3.summary: The same temple offices recur: the first priest, the priest “of the second rank,” and the “doorpost guards.”
2-kings-23:4:3.why: Clarifies the priestly ranks named in Josiah's command.

2-kings-23:4:4.summary: Parallel list of first priest, second priest and guards at the exile, but wording here lacks “doorpost” and second rank.

2-kings-23:4:5.summary: Chelkias the high priest and those guarding the doorpost appear in the same Josiah narrative.
2-kings-23:4:5.why: Identifies Chelkias and the doorkeepers earlier in the reform.

2-kings-23:4:6.summary: Shown text describes priestly divisions under David, loosely background for the “priests of the second rank”; truncated range.

2-kings-23:4:7.summary: Jeroboam set a calf in Bethel; Josiah carries the idolatrous dust to Bethel, defiling that shrine.
2-kings-23:4:7.why: Explains Bethel's significance as an idolatrous center.

2-kings-23:4:8.summary: Jeremiah condemns burning incense to Baal, a general Baal-worship theme.
2-kings-23:4:8.why: Prophetic indictment of the Baal cult.

2-kings-23:4:9.summary: Israel served Baal and the Astartes; general Baal-worship theme.
2-kings-23:4:9.why: Shows the long history of Baal worship.

2-kings-23:4:10.summary: Altar stones crushed “like fine dust” and idols cut down echo Josiah reducing cult objects to dust.
2-kings-23:4:10.why: Prophetic picture of idolatry ground to dust.

2-kings-23:4:11.summary: Israel made groves, bowed to “all heaven’s host,” and served Baal—the same three cults listed in Josiah's purge.
2-kings-23:4:11.why: Same triad of Baal, grove and heaven's host.

2-kings-23:4:12.summary: Faithful remnant who did not bow to Baal; only general Baal theme.

2-kings-23:4:13.summary: Jesus crosses the “winter-stream Kidron”; only the place is shared.
2-kings-23:4:13.why: Geographic link to the Kidron valley.

2-kings-23:4:14.summary: Only the term “high priest” is shared; Caiaphas's council has no link to Josiah's purge.

2-kings-23:4:15.summary: Ahab served Baal and bowed to him, origin of Baal worship in Israel; general theme.

2-kings-23:4:16.summary: David crosses the “Kidron torrent”; shared location only.

2-kings-23:4:17.summary: Hosea warns against the “house of On” (Bethel) as idolatrous; Bethel link is indirect in this wording.

2-kings-23:4:18.summary: Josiah later tears down Bethel's altar, reduces it to dust and burns the grove—same reform and place.

2-kings-23:4:19.summary: Baal's prophets call on Baal at Carmel; general Baal theme.

2-kings-23:4:20.summary: Chief priests plot against Jesus; no link beyond the word priests.

2-kings-23:4:21.summary: Gatekeeper divisions under David give background for the “doorpost guards”; shown text is only names, truncated.

2-kings-23:4:22.summary: Chronicles' account of Josiah cleansing Judah of groves and Baal altars, pulverizing the cast objects.
2-kings-23:4:22.why: Parallel account of the same reform.

2-kings-23:4:23.summary: Manasseh set the carved image in God’s house, which Josiah's purge of the sanctuary undoes.
2-kings-23:4:23.why: Shows how idols entered the temple.

2-kings-23:4:24.summary: Elijah destroys Baal's prophets at a wadi; loosely parallel purge of Baal worship.

2-kings-23:4:25.summary: Amos condemns lawlessness at Bethel; Bethel as idolatrous site.

2-kings-23:4:26.summary: Prophets of Baal (“shame”) and “prophets of the groves” at Jezebel's table; same cults, different event.
2-kings-23:4:26.why: Shows Baal and grove cults together.

2-kings-23:4:27.summary: Sirach praises Josiah who “removed the abominations of lawlessness,” summarizing this reform.

2-kings-23:5:3.summary: Bones exposed before the sun, moon and “all heaven’s host” which Judah served—the same astral cult Josiah ends.

2-kings-23:5:0.summary: Burning incense to the queen of heaven “in Judah’s cities and outside Jerusalem” as kings did echoes Josiah's purge.

2-kings-23:5:1.summary: Manasseh rebuilt high places, an altar for Baal, and served “all heaven’s host”—the practices Josiah stops.
2-kings-23:5:1.why: Origin of the cults Josiah abolishes.

2-kings-23:5:2.summary: Hosea mentions the calf of the house of On and its mourning priests; general idolatrous priesthood theme.

2-kings-23:5:4.summary: Wisdom critiques treating “the lights of heaven” as gods, general theme of astral worship.
2-kings-23:5:4.why: Reflection on worship of heavenly bodies.

2-kings-23:6:1.summary: At Bethel Josiah likewise “reduced it to dust” and “burned the grove.”
2-kings-23:6:1.why: Same reform and same destruction method.

2-kings-23:6:0.summary: Chronicles' Josiah cuts down groves, pulverizes them and scatters them “over the graves” of worshippers.
2-kings-23:6:0.why: Parallel to dust thrown on graves.

2-kings-23:6:3.summary: Israel served the Baalim and “the groves”; general idolatry theme.

2-kings-23:6:5.summary: Moses burned the calf and ground it fine, like Josiah burning and grinding the grove to dust.
2-kings-23:6:5.why: Precedent for destroying idols to dust.

2-kings-23:6:6.summary: Jehu tears down Baal's pillars and house, defiling it; similar purge, different object.

2-kings-23:6:7.summary: Ahab “made a grove”; general background on the grove cult.

2-kings-23:6:8.summary: Moses burned the calf, ground it “as dust,” and cast it into “the torrent”—closely echoing the Kidron torrent.

2-kings-23:6:9.summary: The law commands burning graven images “with fire,” which Josiah carries out on the grove.

2-kings-23:6:10.summary: Judah built high places, standing stones and groves; general background.

2-kings-23:7:0.summary: Asa removed the “initiatory rites” from the land, an earlier purge of the same cultic personnel.

2-kings-23:7:1.summary: Garments made into sewn idols loosely echoes women weaving for the grove.

2-kings-23:7:2.summary: Abominations of the nations practiced in Judah; general link, Greek wording lacks a specific cult term.

2-kings-23:7:3.summary: Skilled women spun for the tabernacle, contrasting with women weaving for the grove.
2-kings-23:7:3.why: Contrast of holy and idolatrous weaving.

2-kings-23:7:4.summary: Sodom's assault has no textual link to the kadesim house as shown.
2-kings-23:7:4.why: Link depends on English label assumptions.

2-kings-23:7:5.summary: Chronicles summarizes Josiah removing “all the abominations” from the land—the same reform.

2-kings-23:7:6.summary: Paul on unnatural passions has no shared wording with the kadesim house or grove weaving.
2-kings-23:7:6.why: Thematic leap not carried by the texts.

2-kings-23:7:7.summary: Israel adorned herself for the Baalim; general idolatry imagery.

2-kings-23:7:8.summary: Jehoshaphat removed the remaining cultic “unions” from Asa's days, an earlier purge of similar practices.
2-kings-23:7:8.why: Earlier removal of the same practice.

2-kings-23:7:9.summary: Women lamenting Tammuz at the Lord’s house parallel women in the temple serving a pagan cult.

2-kings-23:8:0.summary: Asa builds the hill of Benjamin (Gaba region); only a place link to “Gabaa.”

2-kings-23:8:1.summary: Benjamin's Levitical cities list; Gabaa not clearly named in this Greek wording.

2-kings-23:8:2.summary: Isaiah's route names Rama; Gabaa only implied, not in the shown text.

2-kings-23:8:3.summary: “Gabee” appears among Benjamin's priestly cities—the northern limit Gabaa.
2-kings-23:8:3.why: Identifies Gabaa as a priestly city.

2-kings-23:8:4.summary: Naming of the “Well of Swearing” (Beersheba); place link only.

2-kings-23:8:5.summary: “From Gabe to Remmon” is a similar north-south span of Judah's land.

2-kings-23:8:6.summary: Elijah comes to Beer-sheba in Judah; place link only.

2-kings-23:8:7.summary: Isaac goes to the Well of the Oath (Beersheba); place link only.

2-kings-23:8:8.summary: “From Dan to Beersheba” is the parallel north-south formula to “from Gabaa to Beersheba.”

2-kings-23:9:0.summary: Levites who served idols may serve the house but not draw near as priests—like high-place priests barred from the altar.

2-kings-23:9:1.summary: Priests' food portions loosely relate to high-place priests eating among brothers.

2-kings-23:9:2.summary: Corrupt priests are degraded; general theme of priestly failure.

2-kings-23:9:3.summary: Demoted priests seeking a priestly office “so I may eat bread” parallels excluded priests eating among brothers.

2-kings-23:10:0.summary: A burning ravine prepared for judgment; LXX wording lacks Topheth, so only imagery is shared.

2-kings-23:10:1.summary: The “Burial Ground of the Son of Hinnom” renamed for slaughter—same valley.
2-kings-23:10:1.why: Prophetic judgment on the Hinnom valley.

2-kings-23:10:2.summary: Topheth’s altar in the ravine of the son of Hinnom, where sons and daughters were burned in fire.
2-kings-23:10:2.why: Describes the Topheth cult Josiah defiled.

2-kings-23:10:3.summary: Law forbids giving seed to serve “a ruler” (Molech in Hebrew); Greek wording weakens the explicit Moloch link.

2-kings-23:10:4.summary: Altars in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom to offer sons and daughters “to Molech.”

2-kings-23:10:5.summary: The “ravine of Onom” beside Jerusalem is the valley of the son of Ennom.

2-kings-23:10:7.summary: Jerusalem to be like a defiled “collapsing place” (Topheth); place link is indirect in this wording.

2-kings-23:10:8.summary: Ahaz “led his son through fire,” the exact practice Josiah stops.

2-kings-23:10:9.summary: Children made to “pass through fire” for idols, defiling the sanctuary.

2-kings-23:10:10.summary: Children slaughtered for averting rites; general child-sacrifice theme without fire wording.

2-kings-23:10:11.summary: Defilement through gifts of the firstborn alludes obliquely to child offerings.

2-kings-23:10:12.summary: Israel “led their sons and daughters through fire,” same wording as the rite Josiah ends.

2-kings-23:10:13.summary: “Gehenna of fire” derives from the valley of Ennom, but the link is not explicit in the texts.

2-kings-23:10:14.summary: Ahaz sacrificed in Gaibenenom (valley of the son of Ennom) and passed children through fire.

2-kings-23:10:15.summary: Manasseh “led his sons through fire,” the practice Josiah ended.
2-kings-23:10:15.why: Shows Manasseh's role in the cult.

2-kings-23:10:16.summary: Solomon's high places for Ammon's idol; Moloch not named in this wording.
2-kings-23:10:16.why: Origin of foreign cults near Jerusalem.

2-kings-23:10:17.summary: Defilement through “gifts” and “separations” alludes to child offerings, but this Greek wording lacks the fire rite.
2-kings-23:10:17.why: Oblique prophetic indictment of the practice.

2-kings-23:10:18.summary: Manasseh passed children through fire in “Gai-banai-ennom,” the same valley.

2-kings-23:10:19.summary: The burial ground near the Charsith Gate is the Hinnom area, though the name is obscured here.

2-kings-23:11:0.summary: Men bowing to the sun “at the entrance of the Lord’s temple,” the same sun cult at the temple entrance.
2-kings-23:11:0.why: Shows sun worship at the temple itself.

2-kings-23:11:1.summary: Asa removed altars and idols from Judah’s cities; general reform theme.

2-kings-23:11:2.summary: Law forbids worshipping “the sun, and the moon, and the stars,” the sun cult Josiah abolishes.

2-kings-23:11:3.summary: Chronicles' Josiah reform generally, but shown text does not mention sun horses or chariot.
2-kings-23:11:3.why: Broader account of the same reform.

2-kings-23:12:0.summary: Those worshipping “the army of heaven on rooftops” match the rooftop altars Josiah pulls down.

2-kings-23:12:1.summary: Houses of “Judah’s kings” where incense burned “upon their roofs” to heaven’s host—the kings' rooftop altars.

2-kings-23:12:3.summary: Manasseh built altars “in the two courtyards of the Lord’s house,” the very altars Josiah tears down.

2-kings-23:12:4.summary: Amon served his father's idols; general continuation of Manasseh's idolatry.

2-kings-23:12:5.summary: Same reform: Josiah burns cult vessels at the Kidron and disposes of their dust.

2-kings-23:12:6.summary: Manasseh removed the altars he built on the temple mount—the same altars Josiah later destroys.

2-kings-23:12:7.summary: Roof parapet law shares only the word “roof” with the rooftop altars.

2-kings-23:12:8.summary: Josiah likewise reduces the grove to dust and throws it into the “Kidron torrent.”

2-kings-23:13:0.summary: Solomon built high places for Chemosh, Ammon's idol, and Astarte “the abomination of the Sidonians.”

2-kings-23:13:1.summary: Same passage: Solomon's high places for Chemosh, Ammon's idol, and Astarte.

2-kings-23:13:2.summary: Moab as “people of Chemosh”; names the god only.

2-kings-23:13:3.summary: Israel served the Astaroth and the gods of Sidon, Moab and Ammon—the same trio of national cults.

2-kings-23:13:4.summary: Nehemiah recalls Solomon king of Israel led astray by foreign wives, the cause of these shrines.
2-kings-23:13:4.why: Explains why Solomon built the shrines.

2-kings-23:13:5.summary: Jephthah names Chemosh as Ammon/Moab's god; name only.

2-kings-23:13:6.summary: Israel served Baal and the Astartes; general Astarte worship.

2-kings-23:13:7.summary: Israel repents of serving the Baalim and groves; general idolatry.

2-kings-23:13:8.summary: Astarte “the abomination of the Sidonians,” Chemosh of Moab, and the offense of Ammon—same list and labels.

2-kings-23:13:9.summary: Chemosh goes into deportation; name shared only.

2-kings-23:13:10.summary: Moab's coming calamity; no mention of Chemosh or the shrine.

2-kings-23:13:11.summary: Israel removed the Baalim and “groves of Astaroth”; general reform theme.

2-kings-23:13:12.summary: Moab ashamed of Chemosh; name shared only.

2-kings-23:13:13.summary: Swearing “by their king” may allude to Milcom/Molchol, but the Greek wording obscures it.

2-kings-23:14:0.summary: Command to “utterly shatter their pillars,” which Josiah fulfils.

2-kings-23:14:2.summary: Josiah takes bones from tombs to defile Bethel's altar—same tactic of defiling with human bones.
2-kings-23:14:2.why: Same reform using bones to defile.

2-kings-23:14:3.summary: Command to destroy cast idols and “remove all their pillars.”

2-kings-23:14:4.summary: Human bones and land cleansing; bones here are buried to cleanse rather than defile.

2-kings-23:14:5.summary: Touching “a human bone” makes one unclean, explaining why bones defile the sites.

2-kings-23:14:6.summary: Burn graven images and abhor abominations; general law against idols.

2-kings-23:14:7.summary: Bones taken from tombs and exposed; shares bone imagery with idolatry judgment.

2-kings-23:14:8.summary: Tombs full of “dead people’s bones and all uncleanness”; bones as uncleanness image only.

2-kings-23:14:9.summary: Purification for one who touched “the human bone”; supports bones as defiling.

2-kings-23:14:10.summary: Chronicles' Josiah cuts down sacred groves and scatters the remains over graves.
2-kings-23:14:10.why: Parallel account of the same reform.

2-kings-23:14:11.summary: God will cut up carved images and obliterate idols; general idol destruction.

2-kings-23:15:1.summary: Josiah also “reduced it to dust” and burned the grove at Kidron.

2-kings-23:15:2.summary: Jeroboam “caused Israel to sin,” the same formula describing him.

2-kings-23:15:3.summary: “Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin”—same formula.

2-kings-23:15:5.summary: Jeroboam son of Nebat and causing Israel to sin, but about Ahab's house, not Bethel.

2-kings-23:16:1.summary: The prophet affirms the word “against the altar in Bethel” will surely come to pass—fulfilled here.

2-kings-23:16:2.summary: Scripture “cannot be broken,” general theme of the word's reliability.

2-kings-23:16:3.summary: Christ's words never pass away; general theme of fulfilled prophecy.

2-kings-23:17:1.summary: The old prophet buried with the man of God, asking his bones be placed beside his—the same tomb.

2-kings-23:18:1.summary: The man of God from Judah prophesied Josiah would burn human bones on Bethel's altar.
2-kings-23:18:1.why: Original prophecy and story of the tomb.

2-kings-23:19:0.summary: Chronicles' Josiah extends the purge to northern cities, destroying groves, altars and high places.
2-kings-23:19:0.why: Parallel account of the northern reform.

2-kings-23:19:1.summary: Israel provoked God with hills and carvings; general high-place provocation.

2-kings-23:19:2.summary: Walking in the way of Israel's kings; general apostasy.

2-kings-23:19:3.summary: Israel's high-place sins “provoking Him,” for which Samaria was removed.

2-kings-23:19:4.summary: Israelites built high places “in all their cities”—the shrines Josiah removes.

2-kings-23:19:5.summary: Hezekiah invites northern Israel to return; loose link to reform reaching north.

2-kings-23:19:6.summary: Ahab made a grove and committed provocations; general provocation theme.

2-kings-23:19:7.summary: Manasseh provoking the Lord; general provocation, not Samaria.

2-kings-23:19:9.summary: Earlier purge reaching Ephraim and Manasse, demolishing high places and altars.

2-kings-23:19:10.summary: Cults that “provoke Me to anger”; general provocation theme.

2-kings-23:19:11.summary: Jeroboam made “houses on high places,” the high-place houses Josiah removes.

2-kings-23:19:12.summary: Works of Ahab's house condemned; general northern apostasy.

2-kings-23:19:13.summary: Judah's lawlessness in the temple; no specific link to Samaria's high places.

2-kings-23:20:1.summary: Chronicles: Josiah “burned priests’ bones upon the altars.”
2-kings-23:20:1.why: Parallel account of the same act.

2-kings-23:20:0.summary: Mattan, Baal’s priest, killed “before the altars”—similar execution of idolatrous priests.

2-kings-23:20:2.summary: One who sacrifices to other gods “shall surely be destroyed,” the law Josiah enforces.

2-kings-23:20:3.summary: Jehu kills Baal worshippers after a burnt offering; similar purge.

2-kings-23:20:4.summary: Elijah slaughters Baal's prophets; similar purge of idolatrous clergy.

2-kings-23:20:6.summary: The Lord's sacrifice in Edom is a judgment image unrelated to high-place priests.

2-kings-23:20:7.summary: Removing idols and false prophets from the land; general purge theme.

2-kings-23:20:8.summary: The seducing prophet “shall die”; legal background for executing false clergy.

2-kings-23:21:0.summary: Deuteronomy's command to “observe the Passover” at the chosen place—the covenant book's law Josiah follows.

2-kings-23:21:1.summary: Israel told to observe the Passover at its time; general Passover law.

2-kings-23:21:2.summary: Passover offerings regulations; general Passover law.

2-kings-23:21:3.summary: Chronicles' extended account of Josiah's Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month.

2-kings-23:21:5.summary: Passover and Unleavened Bread calendar law; general background.

2-kings-23:22:0.summary: Hezekiah's irregular second-month Passover, a lesser precedent to the unrivalled Josiah Passover.

2-kings-23:22:2.summary: Hezekiah's Passover delayed to the second month; comparison with Josiah's.

2-kings-23:24:0.summary: Law against following spirit mediums and enchanters, the charmers and knowing ones Josiah removes.

2-kings-23:24:1.summary: Rachel stole her father's household idols; teraphim not named in this wording.

2-kings-23:24:2.summary: Manasseh appointed “a charmer and knowing ones,” the very figures Josiah removes.

2-kings-23:24:4.summary: Law sentences any “spirit-medium or an enchanter” to death—the law behind removing them.

2-kings-23:24:5.summary: Isaiah rebukes consulting belly-speakers rather than God's law; general necromancy theme.

2-kings-23:24:6.summary: Micah's shrine held “the teraphim” alongside carved and cast images—the same objects Josiah removes.

2-kings-23:24:7.summary: Sorcerers and idolaters excluded from the city; general condemnation.

2-kings-23:24:8.summary: Manasseh's idolatry generally, without the mediums or teraphim named.

2-kings-23:24:9.summary: Chronicles: Hilkiah the priest “found a book” of the Lord’s law in the Lord’s house.
2-kings-23:24:9.why: Parallel account of the book's finding.

2-kings-23:24:10.summary: Amon served his father's idols; general background.

2-kings-23:24:11.summary: Saul “removed the mediums and the knowers from the land,” an earlier parallel removal.

2-kings-23:24:12.summary: Israel without priesthood or “manifestations” (teraphim in Hebrew); Greek wording obscures the link.

2-kings-23:24:13.summary: Manasseh's abominations and idols; general background to the removed offensive things.

2-kings-23:24:14.summary: Paul's teaching on law and justification has no link to Josiah's purge.
2-kings-23:24:14.why: Only the word law is shared.

2-kings-23:24:15.summary: Paul expels a spirit of divination; general theme of removing divination.

2-kings-23:24:17.summary: Micah made “an ephod and teraphim,” the household idols named in Josiah's purge.

2-kings-23:24:18.summary: James on doing the law of freedom shares only the idea of keeping law.

2-kings-23:24:19.summary: Chelkias the high priest found “a book of the law in the Lord’s house”—the book Josiah upholds.

2-kings-23:24:20.summary: Sirach: Josiah “removed the abominations of lawlessness,” summarizing this purge.

2-kings-23:25:0.summary: Hezekiah likewise had “none like him” among Judah's kings before or after—a parallel incomparability formula.

2-kings-23:25:1.summary: Seeking God “with your whole heart”; general wholehearted devotion.

2-kings-23:25:2.summary: The Law given through Moses; only the Mosaic law phrase is shared.

2-kings-23:25:3.summary: Josiah's covenant to keep the commandments “with the whole heart and whole soul.”

2-kings-23:25:4.summary: Solomon's prayer for those who “return to Thee with all their heart and all their soul.”

2-kings-23:25:6.summary: Jesus says none keeps Moses' law; only the Moses-law phrase overlaps.

2-kings-23:25:7.summary: Call to remember “the law of Moses”; general Mosaic law theme.

2-kings-23:25:8.summary: Seek the Lord “with all your heart and with all your soul,” the Deuteronomic language Josiah fulfils.

2-kings-23:25:9.summary: Oath to walk in “the law of God given through Moses”; general covenant theme.

2-kings-23:25:10.summary: David did what was right all his days; general royal faithfulness.

2-kings-23:25:11.summary: Walking before God “with all their heart and all their soul”—the royal ideal Josiah meets.

2-kings-23:25:12.summary: Sirach praises “the remembrance of Josiah” as sweet incense.

2-kings-23:26:0.summary: Manasseh's innocent blood and the Lord “unwilling to be propitiated,” explaining the unturned wrath.

2-kings-23:26:1.summary: God pronounces disaster on Judah because of Manasseh's abominations.

2-kings-23:26:2.summary: The Lord’s anger rose “until there was no healing”; general irreversible wrath.

2-kings-23:26:3.summary: “Provoking Me”—“My wrath shall burn… and shall not be quenched,” matching the unturned burning wrath.

2-kings-23:26:4.summary: Raiders sent against Judah per the prophets' word; the wrath's outworking.

2-kings-23:26:5.summary: Judah handed over to distresses “because of Manasseh,” even Moses and Samuel could not avert it.

2-kings-23:26:6.summary: Judah did not return with whole heart but in falsehood; general unfaithfulness.

2-kings-23:26:7.summary: All Judah's kings but David, Hezekiah, Josiah offended and came to an end.

2-kings-23:27:0.summary: “Samaria’s measure” over Jerusalem—Judah treated as Israel was.
2-kings-23:27:0.why: Earlier announcement of the same judgment.

2-kings-23:27:1.summary: Samaria's deportation by Assyria—the removal of Israel to which Judah's is compared.

2-kings-23:27:3.summary: “In Jerusalem I shall place My name” is the promise now revoked.

2-kings-23:27:4.summary: God cast Israel “from His presence,” the same fate now announced for Judah.

2-kings-23:27:5.summary: The Lord “removed them from His presence,” leaving Judah alone—now Judah too.

2-kings-23:27:6.summary: “The Lord rejected His altar and shook off His sanctuary”—the rejection fulfilled.

2-kings-23:27:7.summary: The Lord “removed them from their land in wrath”—covenant curse being enacted.

2-kings-23:27:8.summary: God promises not to reject Israel's family, tempering the threatened rejection.

2-kings-23:27:9.summary: God consecrated the house “to put My name there for ever”—the house now rejected.

2-kings-23:27:10.summary: Prayer not to be cast from God’s face; general removal-from-presence language.

2-kings-23:27:11.summary: Nebuzaradan removes the remaining people—the fulfilment of Judah's removal.

2-kings-23:27:12.summary: Solomon prays toward the place where “My name shall be there”—the same quoted promise.

2-kings-23:27:13.summary: “In this house and in Jerusalem, which I chose… I shall place My name”—the same chosen city and house.

2-kings-23:27:14.summary: Judah must drink “your sister Samaria’s cup”—sharing Israel's fate.

2-kings-23:27:15.summary: Judgment came “to remove it from His presence because of Manasseh’s sins.”

2-kings-23:28:0.summary: Same closing formula: the rest of the king's deeds “are these not written in the book of the chronicles”.

2-kings-23:29:0.summary: Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt “beside the Euphrates River”—same campaign context.

2-kings-23:29:2.summary: Greek wording speaks of a pomegranate grove cut down “in a plain,” losing the Megiddo mourning link.
2-kings-23:29:2.why: Hebrew Megiddo reference absent in Greek.

2-kings-23:29:3.summary: Kings fought “by Megiddo’s water”; place link only.

2-kings-23:29:4.summary: One event comes to righteous and ungodly alike—reflection on a righteous king's death.

2-kings-23:29:5.summary: Megiddo in Solomon's district list; place only.

2-kings-23:29:6.summary: Another Judean king, Ahaziah, died at Megiddo; place link.

2-kings-23:29:7.summary: Amaziah faces the king of Israel after ill-advised challenge; loose parallel of rash confrontation.

2-kings-23:29:8.summary: The righteous man taken “from the presence of injustice”; general reflection on righteous death.

2-kings-23:29:9.summary: Huldah's promise that Josiah would be gathered to his grave before the disasters.

2-kings-23:29:10.summary: Doxology on God's unsearchable judgments has no specific link to Josiah's death.

2-kings-23:29:11.summary: Righteous people receive what the ungodly deserve; general reflection.

2-kings-23:29:12.summary: Pharaoh Nechao's subsequent control of Judah after killing Josiah.

2-kings-23:29:13.summary: “Harmagedon” draws on the name of Mageddo, the battlefield; name link only.

2-kings-23:29:14.summary: Megiddo allotted to Manasseh; place only.

2-kings-23:29:16.summary: Egypt's power reaching the Euphrates ends—the outcome of Nechao's Euphrates campaign.

2-kings-23:29:17.summary: Amaziah's challenge “let us face one another”; loose parallel to going to meet a foe.

2-kings-23:30:3.summary: Chronicles: servants bring Josiah by chariot to Jerusalem where he is buried.

2-kings-23:30:0.summary: Ahaziah, killed near Megiddo, also brought “to Jerusalem” and buried “in the city of David.”

2-kings-23:30:2.summary: Ahab mortally wounded in battle and brought back; loose parallel of a king dying in battle.

2-kings-23:30:4.summary: The people of Judah “took” the king's son and made him king in his father's place.

2-kings-23:30:5.summary: “The people of the land” made Josiah king—same group now enthrones his son.
2-kings-23:30:5.why: Role of the people of the land.

2-kings-23:31:2.summary: Sedekias's mother is also “Amital daughter of Jeremiah,” making him Joachas's full brother.

2-kings-23:31:0.summary: Lists Josiah's sons, including Salloum, the other name of Joachas.

2-kings-23:31:1.summary: Shallum son of Josiah “who reigned in place of his father” and went out never to return—Joachas.

2-kings-23:32:0.summary: Manasseh “did evil in the Lord’s eyes”; Joachas follows his fathers' pattern.
2-kings-23:32:0.why: Defines the evil of his fathers.

2-kings-23:32:1.summary: Amon walked in his father's ways; similar formula of following ancestral evil.

2-kings-23:33:0.summary: Zedekiah likewise brought to the foreign king “at Deblatha” for judgment.

2-kings-23:33:1.summary: “The entrance of Hamath” names the same region as Emath’s land; place only.

2-kings-23:33:2.summary: Zedekiah also brought to the king “at Deblatha” for judgment.
2-kings-23:33:2.why: Deblatha as site of royal judgment.

2-kings-23:33:4.summary: Captives struck “at Deblatha in Aimath’s land”—same place formula.

2-kings-23:33:5.summary: Proverb about an evil man's penalties shares only the idea of penalty.

2-kings-23:33:6.summary: Ezekiel's lion cub caught and led “to Egypt’s land” allegorizes Joachas's removal.

2-kings-23:33:7.summary: Spies' route toward Ephaath (Hamath region); place link only and obscured in Greek.

2-kings-23:33:9.summary: Pharaoh Nechao, who killed Josiah, now deposes his son.

2-kings-23:33:10.summary: Assyria “imposed” talents of silver and gold on Hezekiah—same kind of tribute penalty.

2-kings-23:33:11.summary: Law fining a man who harms a pregnant woman shares only fine wording.

2-kings-23:33:12.summary: Greek boundary list reads Arbela, not Deblatha; the Riblah link is lost.
2-kings-23:33:12.why: Hebrew place link absent in Greek.

2-kings-23:34:0.summary: The lion cub caught and led “to Egypt’s land” pictures Joachas taken into Egypt.

2-kings-23:34:1.summary: A foreign king makes a Judean prince king and changes his name—Maththanias to Sedekias.

2-kings-23:34:2.summary: Joakim listed among Josiah's sons, with Salloum (Joachas).

2-kings-23:34:3.summary: Shallum son of Josiah will die where deported, never returning—Joachas's death in Egypt.

2-kings-23:34:4.summary: Foreign official renames captive Judeans; parallel renaming custom.

2-kings-23:34:6.summary: Pharaoh renames Joseph; a Pharaoh renaming theme only.

2-kings-23:34:7.summary: Boundary of Beth-arabah has no link to Joakim's enthronement.

2-kings-23:35:0.summary: The penalty of silver and gold Nechao imposed, which Joakim now pays.

2-kings-23:35:1.summary: Manaem exacted silver from the people to pay a foreign king—same taxation for tribute.

2-kings-23:36:0.summary: Chronicles: Jehoiakim twenty-five, reigned eleven years in Jerusalem; mother's name differs in this Greek text.

2-kings-23:36:1.summary: Joakim is listed as Josiah's second son.

2-kings-23:36:2.summary: Jeremiah's ministry spans the days of “Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah.”

2-kings-23:36:3.summary: A word dated to the beginning of King Jehoiakim's reign.

2-kings-23:37:0.summary: Manasseh's evils exemplify what “his fathers had done.”

2-kings-23:37:1.summary: Second lion cub caught and brought to Babylon's king; allegory of a later Judean king, possibly Joakim.

2-kings-23:37:2.summary: Ahaz's idolatry is one of the fathers' evils; general background.

2-kings-23:37:3.summary: King Jehoiakim had the prophet Uriah hunted and killed—concrete evil of this king.

2-kings-23:37:4.summary: God will bring calamities on the king who did not listen (Jehoiakim).

2-kings-23:37:6.summary: Jeremiah condemns the king building his house without righteousness—Jehoiakim's injustice; partial range.

2-kings-23:37:7.summary: Amon “did what was evil before the Lord, as his father” did—parallel formula.

2-kings-23:37:8.summary: The king burns Jeremiah's roll and seeks to arrest the prophets—Jehoiakim's evil.
2-kings-23:37:8.why: Shows Joakim's contempt for God's word.

2-kings-23:6:2.summary: Jeremiah 17:2 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-23:6:2.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-23:6:2.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-23:15:0.summary: 1 Kings 14:16 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-23:15:0.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-23:15:0.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-23:27:2.summary: Jeremiah 33:24 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-23:27:2.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-23:27:2.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-23:33:3.summary: Jeremiah 39:5–6 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-23:33:3.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-23:33:3.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-24:1:0.summary: Dated to Jehoiakim's fourth year; time context only.

2-kings-24:1:1.summary: Nebuchadnezzar comes against Jerusalem in King Joakim's reign.

2-kings-24:1:2.summary: God sends the northern clan against the land; general prophecy.

2-kings-24:1:3.summary: Assyria's three-year siege of Samaria shares only “three years.”

2-kings-24:1:4.summary: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon defeats Neco in Jehoiakim's fourth year—the rise preceding this subjection.

2-kings-24:1:5.summary: Chronicles: Nebuchadnezzar came up against Jehoiakim and bound him.

2-kings-24:2:0.summary: Rechabites flee to Jerusalem from Nebuchadnezzar's Chaldean and “Assyrian” (Syrian) forces.

2-kings-24:2:1.summary: God's decree to remove Judah, now carried out by the raiders.

2-kings-24:2:3.summary: City handed to Babylon's king; general prophecy of conquest.

2-kings-24:2:4.summary: God sends the clan from the north against the land—prophetic word behind the raids.

2-kings-24:2:5.summary: Nations “from the surrounding countries set themselves against him,” like the surrounding raiders.

2-kings-24:2:6.summary: Syria’s “lightly equipped troops”—same raider term, different event.

2-kings-24:2:7.summary: Isaiah's word that all would be taken to Babylon—“the Lord’s word… through His servants.”

2-kings-24:2:8.summary: Covenant curse of a nation from afar; general judgment theme.

2-kings-24:2:9.summary: Moab’s “lightly equipped raiders”—same term for Moabite raiders.

2-kings-24:2:10.summary: God's armed fighters from a distant land; general divine-army theme.

2-kings-24:2:11.summary: God brings a foreign king against Judah; general judgment theme.

2-kings-24:2:12.summary: Threat to make the house like Shiloh; general prophetic judgment.

2-kings-24:2:13.summary: Uriah prophesied against the land; one of the prophets whose word is fulfilled.

2-kings-24:2:14.summary: Chaldean raiders against Job's camels; Greek text says “horsemen,” no real link.
2-kings-24:2:14.why: Link lost in the Greek wording.

2-kings-24:2:15.summary: Cities laid waste and people removed; general judgment prophecy.

2-kings-24:2:16.summary: The Lord brought foreign commanders against Manasseh; parallel divine sending of armies.

2-kings-24:2:17.summary: Zion plowed like a field; general prophecy of Jerusalem's ruin.

2-kings-24:3:0.summary: Same decree: wrath for Manasseh's provocations and removal of Judah “from My presence.”

2-kings-24:3:1.summary: Rabshakeh claims the Lord sent him to destroy; theme of God-sent invasion.

2-kings-24:3:3.summary: “The Lord removed them from their land in wrath”—the covenant curse enacted.

2-kings-24:3:4.summary: God creates calamities; general divine sovereignty.

2-kings-24:3:5.summary: God's counsel will stand; general sovereignty theme.

2-kings-24:3:6.summary: No calamity in a city that the Lord has not done; general sovereignty.

2-kings-24:3:7.summary: Rise and go because of uncleanness; general exile theme.

2-kings-24:3:8.summary: God repays fathers' sins upon children; general link to Manasseh's sins punished later.

2-kings-24:3:9.summary: Warning of perishing from the land and scattering; general covenant threat.

2-kings-24:3:10.summary: God gave Judah to a small Syrian army for abandoning Him; parallel judgment by raiders.
2-kings-24:3:10.why: Precedent of divine judgment by Syria.

2-kings-24:3:11.summary: The Lord will bring harmful words until He destroys them from the land; general covenant theme.

2-kings-24:3:12.summary: “You shall be removed from the land”; general covenant curse.

2-kings-24:3:13.summary: Scattering among nations and desolate land; general covenant curse.

2-kings-24:3:14.summary: Judah handed over to distresses “because of Manasseh,” beyond intercession.

2-kings-24:3:15.summary: Assyria as rod of God's anger; general divine use of nations.

2-kings-24:3:16.summary: God has purposed to destroy a disobedient king; general theme.

2-kings-24:3:17.summary: Joseph's providence speech has no specific link to judgment for Manasseh.

2-kings-24:3:18.summary: Judah's kings offended and came to an end; general summary.

2-kings-24:4:4.summary: “Shed innocent blood” of children sacrificed, the land “murdered with blood.”

2-kings-24:4:1.summary: Blood stains the land and “atonement shall not be made” for it—why the Lord would not be propitiated.

2-kings-24:4:2.summary: “The blood of innocent lives” found on Judah's hands.

2-kings-24:4:3.summary: Only an introductory formula is shown; no content linking to innocent blood.

2-kings-24:4:5.summary: Law that “innocent blood may not be shed in your land.”

2-kings-24:4:6.summary: Even Moses and Samuel could not turn God; general unwillingness to relent.

2-kings-24:4:7.summary: “Thou wast not propitiated”—the same refusal of propitiation.

2-kings-24:4:8.summary: Judah's kings “filled this place with innocent blood.”
2-kings-24:4:8.why: Same charge in nearly same words.

2-kings-24:5:0.summary: Both close Joakim/Jehoiakim’s reign with the same formula pointing to the written chronicles of Judah’s kings.
2-kings-24:5:0.why: Shows the Chronicler’s parallel to the Kings notice.

2-kings-24:5:1.summary: Jeremiah’s temple sermon is dated to the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign; shown text gives prophetic background, not his acts.
2-kings-24:5:1.why: Gives prophetic context for this king’s reign.

2-kings-24:5:2.summary: Woe on a king building his house unjustly is traditionally aimed at Jehoiakim, but the shown text does not name him.
2-kings-24:5:2.why: Adds a prophetic verdict on the king’s deeds.

2-kings-24:6:0.summary: Jeremiah foretells Jehoiakim son of Josiah unmourned and given “a donkey’s burial,” set against the Kings note of his death.
2-kings-24:6:0.why: Shows the prophetic judgment on this king’s end.

2-kings-24:6:1.summary: Jehoiakim will have no one on David’s throne and his carcass thrown out, contrasting with his son reigning in his place.
2-kings-24:6:1.why: Pairs the death notice with Jeremiah’s judgment.

2-kings-24:6:2.summary: Chronicles describes Nebuchadnezzar binding Jehoiakim and taking him to Babylon, the parallel account of this king’s end.
2-kings-24:6:2.why: Supplies the Chronicler’s differing version of his end.

2-kings-24:6:3.summary: Chronicles likewise says Jehoiakim lay down with his fathers and his son Jechonias reigned in his place.
2-kings-24:6:3.why: Direct parallel to the succession notice.

2-kings-24:7:0.summary: Nebuchadnezzar struck Pharaoh Neco’s force beside the Euphrates, explaining why Egypt’s king no longer left his land.
2-kings-24:7:0.why: Names the battle behind Egypt’s loss of territory.

2-kings-24:7:1.summary: Pharaoh’s force later comes out of Egypt and returns, touching Egypt’s weakness but under a later king.
2-kings-24:7:1.why: Shows Egypt’s ineffective help in a later crisis.

2-kings-24:7:2.summary: Both define territory from Egypt’s river to “the river Euphrates.”
2-kings-24:7:2.why: Echoes the promised land’s ideal boundaries.

2-kings-24:7:3.summary: The Wadi of Egypt marks the land’s boundary, the same southern limit as “Egypt’s torrent.”

2-kings-24:7:4.summary: Solomon ruled “from the River” to “Egypt’s borders,” the same span now held by Babylon’s king.
2-kings-24:7:4.why: Contrasts Solomon’s realm with Babylon’s domination.

2-kings-24:7:5.summary: Judah’s boundary passes to “the ravine of Egypt,” the same landmark as Egypt’s torrent.

2-kings-24:7:6.summary: The span from the River to Rhinocorura matches the Euphrates-to-Egypt boundary, but the Greek place name obscures the link.
2-kings-24:7:6.why: Shows the same boundary in prophecy.

2-kings-24:8:0.summary: Jechonias was eighteen and reigned three months (and ten days) in Jerusalem, the Chronicles parallel.

2-kings-24:8:1.summary: The genealogy lists Jechonias as son of Joakim, identifying this young king.
2-kings-24:8:1.why: Places the king in the royal genealogy.

2-kings-24:8:2.summary: Jeremiah’s oracle against Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim concerns this same king.
2-kings-24:8:2.why: Adds the prophetic word against him.

2-kings-24:8:3.summary: Jeconiah dishonored and cast into an unknown land refers to the same king.
2-kings-24:8:3.why: Shows the prophetic lament over his fate.

2-kings-24:8:4.summary: Zedekiah reigning in place of Jehoiakim implies the end of the predecessor’s reign but does not describe this king.
2-kings-24:8:4.why: Links to the succession that followed.

2-kings-24:8:5.summary: Nebuchadnezzar deported Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, the same king, to Babylon.
2-kings-24:8:5.why: Ties the vision of figs to this king’s exile.

2-kings-24:8:6.summary: Matthew’s genealogy names Jechoniah at the deportation to Babylon.
2-kings-24:8:6.why: Places this king in Jesus’ lineage.

2-kings-24:10:0.summary: Both mention the city under siege, but 25:2 concerns the later siege under Sedekias.
2-kings-24:10:0.why: Contrasts the first and final sieges.

2-kings-24:10:1.summary: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it, though Daniel dates this to Joakim’s third year.
2-kings-24:10:1.why: Compares Daniel’s siege account with Kings.

2-kings-24:12:0.summary: Nebuchadnezzar deported Jeconiah with “the rulers” from Jerusalem, matching the king and rulers going out.

2-kings-24:12:2.summary: Chronicles reports Nebuchadnezzar bringing the king into Babylon at the turn of the year.
2-kings-24:12:2.why: Parallel account of the same capture.

2-kings-24:12:3.summary: Joakim king of Judah, deported here, is released from prison in the thirty-seventh year.
2-kings-24:12:3.why: Shows the outcome of this captivity.

2-kings-24:12:4.summary: King Jeconiah, the queen, and the eunuchs left Jerusalem, matching the king, his mother, and eunuchs.

2-kings-24:12:5.summary: The fourth-year dating of Jehoiakim gives no link to this surrender; the Greek lacks the synchronism with Nebuchadnezzar.
