2-kings-24:12:5.why: No shared event in the shown text.

2-kings-24:12:6.summary: Babylon’s king will “take her king and her rulers” to Babylon, interpreting this surrender.

2-kings-24:12:7.summary: Ioakim king of Judah, deported here, is released from guard in the thirty-seventh year.
2-kings-24:12:7.why: Shows the later fate of the captive king.

2-kings-24:12:8.summary: Jeremiah urges Zedekiah to “go out” to Babylon’s king’s commanders, echoing surrender but under a later king.

2-kings-24:12:9.summary: Jeconiah and “your mother who bore you” are handed to the Chaldeans, matching the king and his mother taken.

2-kings-24:13:0.summary: Isaiah foretells that what the fathers gathered will reach Babylon, fulfilled in the treasures carried off.

2-kings-24:13:1.summary: “All the treasures of Judah’s king” will be brought to Babylon, as happens here.

2-kings-24:13:2.summary: Everything stored up in the king’s house shall be taken to Babylon, fulfilled “according to the Lord’s word.”
2-kings-24:13:2.why: Links fulfillment to Isaiah’s word to Hezekiah.

2-kings-24:13:3.summary: Solomon placed gold utensils in the Lord’s house, the very gold vessels now cut apart.

2-kings-24:13:4.summary: The gold and silver vessels Nebuchadnezzar brought from Jerusalem are used at Belshazzar’s feast.
2-kings-24:13:4.why: Traces the plundered vessels’ later fate.

2-kings-24:13:5.summary: The Chaldeans break up and carry off the temple’s bronze and gold utensils in the final plunder.
2-kings-24:13:5.why: Shows the completed despoiling of the temple.

2-kings-24:13:6.summary: False promise to return “the vessels of the Lord’s house” and Jeconiah, taken in this deportation.
2-kings-24:13:6.why: Shows the dispute over the plundered vessels.

2-kings-24:13:7.summary: Prophets claim the Lord’s house’s vessels will return, mentioning vessels left when Jeconiah was deported.
2-kings-24:13:7.why: Connects the plunder to Jeremiah’s warnings.

2-kings-24:13:8.summary: Jeremiah wishes the vessels of the Lord’s house and deportees would return from Babylon.

2-kings-24:13:9.summary: Solomon’s golden lampstands and bowls made for the temple are the gold vessels later cut apart.

2-kings-24:13:10.summary: Cyrus returns the vessels of the Lord’s house that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem.

2-kings-24:13:11.summary: A later king takes silver, gold, and precious vessels, a similar temple plunder but different event.

2-kings-24:14:1.summary: Some of “the land’s poor” are left behind, the same phrase as in this deportation.
2-kings-24:14:1.why: Shows the pattern of leaving the poor.

2-kings-24:14:3.summary: Chronicles parallels Jechonias’s brief reign and his removal to Babylon.

2-kings-24:14:5.summary: Ezekiel dates his visions from the king’s captivity among the captives, this deportation.

2-kings-24:14:6.summary: People not deported remain under Gedaliah, a later remnant similar to those left behind.
2-kings-24:14:6.why: Shows the remnant left in the land.

2-kings-24:14:7.summary: The remaining people are left as vinedressers, echoing the poor left behind, but in the later deportation.
2-kings-24:14:7.why: Parallel pattern of leaving a remnant.

2-kings-24:14:8.summary: Every craftsman and prisoner left Jerusalem with King Jeconiah, matching this deportation list.

2-kings-24:14:9.summary: Ezekiel’s allegory says the kingdom was made weak, the result of removing its mighty men.

2-kings-24:14:10.summary: Ziphites betraying David share only the incidental word “shut,” with no link to the deportation.

2-kings-24:14:11.summary: Nebuchadnezzar deported Jeconiah, the rulers, craftsmen, and prisoners from Jerusalem, matching this list.

2-kings-24:15:0.summary: Mordecai was a captive taken from Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar; the Greek omits the link to Jeconiah.

2-kings-24:15:1.summary: Jeconiah and his mother are cast into another land, fulfilled in the king and his mother deported.

2-kings-24:15:2.summary: Nebuchadnezzar brought the king into Babylon, the Chronicles parallel.

2-kings-24:15:3.summary: Names the king’s mother Nestha, the same queen mother deported with him.

2-kings-24:15:4.summary: Babylon’s king takes her king and rulers to Babylon, interpreting this deportation.

2-kings-24:16:2.summary: Every craftsman left Jerusalem with King Jeconiah, matching the craftsmen deported.

2-kings-24:17:0.summary: Nebuchadnezzar made Zedekiah king over Judah, the same installation.

2-kings-24:17:1.summary: Pharaoh Neco installed Eliakim and changed his name, the same overlord practice as renaming Maththanias.
2-kings-24:17:1.why: Shows the pattern of vassal renaming.

2-kings-24:17:2.summary: Pharaoh Nechao made Eliakim king and changed his name to Joakim, parallel to renaming Sedekias.

2-kings-24:17:3.summary: Zedekiah’s accession notice follows directly on his installation, same king.

2-kings-24:17:4.summary: The genealogy lists Sedekias among Josiah’s sons, clarifying his relation to the king he replaced.

2-kings-24:17:5.summary: Nebuchadnezzar made Zedekiah king over Judah and Jerusalem, the Chronicles parallel.

2-kings-24:18:0.summary: Joachas’s mother is also “Amital daughter of Jeremiah,” making the two kings full brothers.
2-kings-24:18:0.why: Shows Joachas and Sedekias shared a mother.

2-kings-24:18:3.summary: Zedekiah was twenty-one and reigned eleven years in Jerusalem, identical notice.

2-kings-24:18:2.summary: Zedekiah son of Josiah reigned by Nebuchadnezzar’s appointment, same king.

2-kings-24:19:0.summary: Same evaluation formula: did evil before the Lord “according to everything” predecessors had done.

2-kings-24:19:1.summary: A “profane, lawless leader of Israel” is traditionally Zedekiah, but the shown text does not name him.
2-kings-24:19:1.why: Adds prophetic judgment on the king.

2-kings-24:19:2.summary: Chronicles likewise says he did evil before the Lord, adding his disregard of Jeremiah.

2-kings-24:19:3.summary: Zedekiah and his servants did not obey the Lord’s words through Jeremiah, illustrating his evil.

2-kings-24:19:4.summary: Zedekiah king of Judah is likened to bad figs to be handed over, God’s verdict on him.

2-kings-24:20:1.summary: God sending delusion before the lawless one’s coming has no specific link to Judah’s exile or Zedekiah’s rebellion.
2-kings-24:20:1.why: Only a loose idea of divine judgment.

2-kings-24:20:2.summary: The Lord hardened Sihon so he would be delivered up, a loose parallel to rebellion leading to ruin.

2-kings-24:20:3.summary: Jeremiah tells Zedekiah to serve Babylon’s king, the submission he later broke.

2-kings-24:20:4.summary: God making worldly wisdom foolish has no link to Jerusalem’s fall or Zedekiah’s rebellion.

2-kings-24:20:5.summary: The Lord was kindled in wrath against the land, echoing the Lord’s anger that brings exile.
2-kings-24:20:5.why: Shows the covenant curse being fulfilled.

2-kings-24:20:6.summary: Egypt’s foolish counselors led astray share no specific link with Jerusalem or Zedekiah.

2-kings-24:20:7.summary: Ezekiel’s king “will revolt from him” and transgress the sworn covenant, describing Zedekiah’s rebellion.

2-kings-24:20:8.summary: Pharaoh preserved to display God’s power has no specific link to Zedekiah or Jerusalem.

2-kings-24:20:9.summary: Jeremiah urges Zedekiah to surrender to Babylon’s commanders, the course he refused.

2-kings-24:20:10.summary: The Lord’s wrath will burn against this place unquenched, the anger now bringing Judah’s fall.
2-kings-24:20:10.why: Links the fall to Huldah’s prophecy.

2-kings-24:20:11.summary: Judah’s kings gave their glory to a foreign nation, a general summary of the downfall.

2-kings-24:12:1.summary: Jeremiah 52:28 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-24:12:1.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-24:12:1.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-24:14:0.summary: Jeremiah 52:28 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-24:14:0.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-24:14:0.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-24:14:4.summary: Jeremiah 39:10 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-24:14:4.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-24:14:4.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-24:16:0.summary: Jeremiah 52:28 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-kings-24:16:0.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-kings-24:16:0.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-kings-25:1:1.summary: Nebuchadnezzar and his whole army fight Jerusalem, with the city to be handed over and burned.

2-kings-25:1:2.summary: Josadak went into deportation by Nabouchodonosor’s hand, a result of this campaign.
2-kings-25:1:2.why: Notes the high priestly line’s exile.

2-kings-25:1:3.summary: Nebuchadnezzar setting his throne in Egypt concerns a different campaign, not the siege of Jerusalem.
2-kings-25:1:3.why: Only the king’s name is shared.

2-kings-25:1:4.summary: God sets a palisade and towers around the city, a siege image akin to the enclosing wall.

2-kings-25:1:5.summary: In Zedekiah’s ninth year, tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar and his whole force besieged Jerusalem.
2-kings-25:1:5.why: Direct parallel account of the siege.

2-kings-25:1:6.summary: The city will be handed over to Babylon’s king, a general prophecy of this siege’s outcome.

2-kings-25:1:7.summary: Chronicles narrates the Chaldean king’s assault, burning, and deportation, the same fall of Jerusalem.

2-kings-25:1:8.summary: An earlier coming up of Nabouchodonosor against Joakim, not this siege.

2-kings-25:1:9.summary: The oracle against Jerusalem foresees siege stakes, a mound, and missile stations, matching the siege works.

2-kings-25:1:10.summary: Nebuchadnezzar’s dream and proclamation share only his name, not the siege.

2-kings-25:1:11.summary: Ezekiel enacts the siege of Jerusalem with palisade and camps all around, prefiguring this siege.

2-kings-25:1:12.summary: Ezekiel records the same date, ninth year, tenth month, when Babylon’s king pressed against Jerusalem.

2-kings-25:1:13.summary: A multitude has reached the city to seize it, a general reference to the Chaldean siege.
2-kings-25:1:13.why: Describes the siege from Jeremiah’s prayer.

2-kings-25:1:14.summary: Nabouchodonosor came up to Jerusalem and besieged it, but this is the earlier siege.

2-kings-25:1:15.summary: Jesus foretells enemies building a siege barrier around Jerusalem, echoing this siege in a later one.
2-kings-25:1:15.why: Shows the pattern of judgment repeated.

2-kings-25:1:16.summary: Nations refusing Babylon’s yoke will be punished, a general warning behind the siege.

2-kings-25:1:17.summary: Nebuchadnezzar devoured and seized Jerusalem, a lament over his conquest in general.
2-kings-25:1:17.why: Gives the city’s perspective on conquest.

2-kings-25:1:18.summary: Nebuchadnezzar is brought against Tyre, not Jerusalem; only his name links them.

2-kings-25:3:12.summary: “On the ninth day of the fourth month” the city was breached, the same date.
2-kings-25:3:12.why: Supplies the month of the famine.

2-kings-25:3:0.summary: Ezekiel foretells many perishing by famine within the city, generally fulfilled here.

2-kings-25:3:1.summary: Those remaining in the city die by sword and famine, generally anticipating this famine.

2-kings-25:3:2.summary: Famine and death will consume those in the city, a general prophecy of siege famine.

2-kings-25:3:4.summary: Famine is one of four judgments sent against Jerusalem, a general link.

2-kings-25:3:5.summary: Infants asked for bread with none to give, describing Jerusalem’s siege famine vividly.

2-kings-25:3:6.summary: Covenant curse of bread scarcity, generally fulfilled when no loaves remained.

2-kings-25:3:7.summary: Covenant curse of siege distress in the cities, generally fulfilled in Jerusalem’s famine.

2-kings-25:3:8.summary: Ezekiel’s rationed loaves enact scarcity, a sign of siege famine; shown text is truncated.

2-kings-25:3:9.summary: Extreme siege famine leading to cannibalism is threatened, generally linked to this famine.
2-kings-25:3:9.why: Shows the severity of siege famine.

2-kings-25:3:10.summary: The fourth-month fast likely commemorates the breach, but the source names only “the ninth of the month.”

2-kings-25:3:11.summary: Jeremiah receives a loaf daily “until the city’s loaves ran out,” the same famine.
2-kings-25:3:11.why: Shows the famine from Jeremiah’s cell.

2-kings-25:4:0.summary: A survivor reports to Ezekiel that the city has been captured, news of this fall.
2-kings-25:4:0.why: Shows the news reaching the exiles.

2-kings-25:4:2.summary: In Zedekiah’s eleventh year “the city was breached” and Babylon’s commanders entered.
2-kings-25:4:2.why: Direct parallel account of the breach.

2-kings-25:4:3.summary: The next verse continues the flight: the Chaldeans overtake the king in Araboth Jericho.

2-kings-25:4:4.summary: A command to tear down her battlements loosely anticipates the city’s breach.

2-kings-25:4:5.summary: Nehemiah’s wall near “the king’s shearing” may correspond to the king’s garden area, but the Greek obscures it.
2-kings-25:4:5.why: Possible location near the escape gate.

2-kings-25:4:6.summary: Covenant curse of hunger and sword shares no specific detail with the night flight from the breached city.

2-kings-25:4:7.summary: Covenant curse of fleeing as from war, loosely matching the warriors’ flight.

2-kings-25:4:8.summary: Ezekiel foresees the ruler going out through the wall concealed, fulfilled in the night escape.
2-kings-25:4:8.why: Prophetic sign of the king’s flight.

2-kings-25:4:9.summary: Defeat because the Lord delivered them up, a general explanation of Judah’s rout.

2-kings-25:4:10.summary: Fleeing before enemies and being scattered, a general curse matching the rout.

2-kings-25:4:11.summary: Falling before enemies and fleeing, a general curse loosely matching the flight.

2-kings-25:5:0.summary: Even the swift and mighty cannot escape, a general image matching the overtaken king.

2-kings-25:5:3.summary: God will hand over Zedekiah king of Judah, generally fulfilled in his capture; he is unnamed in the source.

2-kings-25:5:4.summary: Those who flee will be overtaken by swift pursuers, loosely matching the chase.

2-kings-25:6:0.summary: Deblatha is where Pharaoh Nechao also removed a king of Judah, the same place.
2-kings-25:6:0.why: Same site of two kings’ fall.

2-kings-25:6:1.summary: God will hand Zedekiah king of Judea over to his enemies, fulfilled in his seizure.

2-kings-25:6:2.summary: “He will be caught” in God’s net, Ezekiel’s image of Zedekiah’s capture.

2-kings-25:6:3.summary: “Babylon’s king will seize you,” fulfilled when they seized the king.

2-kings-25:6:4.summary: God will give Zedekiah king of Judah into enemies’ hands, fulfilled here.

2-kings-25:6:6.summary: “The Lord’s anointed was seized” after pursuers lay in wait, lamenting the king’s capture.
2-kings-25:6:6.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-25:6:7.summary: Manasseh was seized and brought to Babylon, a parallel fate of a Judean king.

2-kings-25:6:8.summary: The lawless leader’s day of end has arrived and crown removed, a general prophecy of the king’s fall.

2-kings-25:6:9.summary: Zedekiah handed to Babylon’s king, “his eyes will see his eyes,” fulfilled in this face-to-face judgment.

2-kings-25:7:1.summary: Jehoiakim was “bound with bronze fetters” and taken to Babylon, the same treatment.
2-kings-25:7:1.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-25:7:2.summary: Manasseh was bound “in fetters, and brought to Babylon,” matching Sedekias’s fate.
2-kings-25:7:2.why: Parallel fate of a Judean king.
2-kings-25:7:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-25:7:0.summary: Zedekiah will see Babylon’s king eye to eye and “enter Babylon,” fulfilled here.

2-kings-25:7:3.summary: Samson’s eyes were dug out and he was “bound with bronze fetters,” a striking parallel.
2-kings-25:7:3.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-kings-25:7:4.summary: Judah’s plea not to see his father’s grief shares only the idea of seeing evil.

2-kings-25:7:5.summary: Hagar not wanting to see her child die shares only the theme of seeing a child’s death.

2-kings-25:7:6.summary: Binding “kings in fetters” shares wording but is a general psalm of judgment.

2-kings-25:7:9.summary: Covenant curse of madness from what “your eyes” see, loosely matching sons slain before his eyes.

2-kings-25:7:10.summary: No offspring will sit on David’s throne, said of Jeconiah, loosely linked to Sedekias’s sons slain.
2-kings-25:7:10.why: End of the Davidic line in Judah.

2-kings-25:7:11.summary: Those fettered in iron for spurning God’s counsel generally resemble the bound king.

2-kings-25:7:12.summary: A ruler clothed in devastation and judged by his ways, generally fitting Sedekias.

2-kings-25:7:13.summary: “I will bring him to Babylon … and he will not see it,” fulfilled when the blinded king was taken there.
2-kings-25:7:13.why: Explains the paradox by the blinding.

2-kings-25:7:14.summary: The oath-breaking king will die in the midst of Babylon, fulfilled as Sedekias is taken there.

2-kings-25:7:15.summary: Zedekiah will be captured, see Babylon’s king, and “enter Babylon,” fulfilled here.

2-kings-25:8:0.summary: In the fifth month Nebuzaradan, who stood before the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem; day differs (tenth vs seventh).

2-kings-25:8:1.summary: Jeremiah released and handed to Gedaliah after the fall; the commander is not named in shown text.

2-kings-25:8:2.summary: Another dated Babylonian event in the same chapter, sharing only a chronological formula.

2-kings-25:8:3.summary: No one believed the enemy would enter Jerusalem’s gates, generally reflecting the city’s fall.

2-kings-25:8:4.summary: Both date events by the Babylonian king’s regnal year, but concern different deportations.

2-kings-25:8:5.summary: Nebuzaradan the chief guard appears again releasing Jeremiah, the same official.

2-kings-25:8:6.summary: The “fifth fast” commemorates the fifth-month destruction of Jerusalem, turned to joy.
2-kings-25:8:6.why: Shows how the date was remembered.

2-kings-25:9:0.summary: God will send fire upon Judah to devour Jerusalem, fulfilled in the burning.

2-kings-25:9:1.summary: “They burned Thy sanctuary with fire,” lamenting the temple’s burning.

2-kings-25:9:2.summary: He burned the Lord’s house and Jerusalem’s citadels with fire, the Chronicles parallel.

2-kings-25:9:3.summary: Zion plowed and the house’s mountain made a forest, a general prophecy of ruin.

2-kings-25:9:4.summary: Passersby astonished at this lofty house, Solomon’s warning of the temple’s ruin.

2-kings-25:9:5.summary: Nations defiled God’s holy temple and made Jerusalem a “fruit-watchman’s hut,” lamenting this destruction.

2-kings-25:9:6.summary: The Chaldeans will “seize it, and burn it with fire,” fulfilled in the burning.

2-kings-25:9:7.summary: “The house, our holy place … became fire-burned,” lamenting the temple’s burning.

2-kings-25:9:9.summary: Charges that Jesus will destroy “this holy place” recall the temple’s destruction only loosely.

2-kings-25:9:10.summary: The Chaldeans will take the city “and burn it with fire,” fulfilled here.

2-kings-25:9:11.summary: Even wounded Chaldeans would “burn this city with fire,” fulfilled in the burning.

2-kings-25:9:12.summary: Jesus foretells the temple torn down, echoing this destruction in a later one.
2-kings-25:9:12.why: Shows the pattern of temple judgment.

2-kings-25:9:13.summary: God will do to “this house” as He did to Shiloh, foretelling the temple’s ruin.

2-kings-25:9:14.summary: Jeremiah prophesied this house would be like Shiloh, generally fulfilled; context is his trial.

2-kings-25:9:16.summary: The Lord rejected His sanctuary and shattered its citadels in the enemy’s hand, lamenting this event.

2-kings-25:9:17.summary: Nations entering the sanctuary to seize desired things, generally reflecting the temple’s fall.

2-kings-25:9:18.summary: Judah’s kings gave their glory to a foreign nation, a general summary of the fall.

2-kings-25:9:19.summary: “They burned the chosen city of the sanctuary,” recalling this burning of Jerusalem.

2-kings-25:10:0.summary: Jerusalem’s pulled-down walls fit the full verse, but the shown source is only the fragment “the chief cook.”

2-kings-25:10:1.summary: Tearing down battlements has no link to the shown source fragment “the chief cook.”

2-kings-25:10:3.summary: The Chaldean force “with the chief guard” pulled down Jerusalem’s wall, the parallel to this fragmentary verse.

2-kings-25:11:0.summary: God will scatter them among nations and spare a few, a general prophecy of the deportation.

2-kings-25:11:1.summary: Nebuzaradan, the chief guard, came to Jerusalem, the same official who removes the people.

2-kings-25:11:2.summary: God will scatter them among the nations, a general prophecy of exile.

2-kings-25:11:4.summary: “As many for captivity, to captivity” generally anticipates this deportation.

2-kings-25:11:5.summary: Ezekiel’s sign of a quarter scattered after the siege loosely anticipates this deportation.

2-kings-25:11:6.summary: He deported the survivors to Babylon, the Chronicles parallel.

2-kings-25:12:0.summary: Only “the land’s poor” remained, the same group left behind again here.

2-kings-25:12:1.summary: People not deported were entrusted to Gedaliah, broadly the remnant left in the land.

2-kings-25:12:4.summary: Those dwelling in the devastated land claim it, the remnant left behind.

2-kings-25:13:0.summary: All the vessels of God’s house were brought into Babylon, parallel to the bronze carried off.

2-kings-25:13:1.summary: Isaiah foretold everything in the house would be taken to Babylon, fulfilled here.

2-kings-25:13:2.summary: Solomon cast the two bronze pillars for the porch, the very pillars now shattered.

2-kings-25:13:3.summary: The oppressor seized her desired things in the sanctuary, generally reflecting the plunder.

2-kings-25:13:5.summary: Bronze altar utensils in the tabernacle share only the bronze theme with the pillars and sea.

2-kings-25:13:6.summary: Solomon made the Sea and bronze stands, the same objects the Chaldeans shattered.

2-kings-25:13:7.summary: Solomon’s cast sea is the bronze sea later shattered and carried off.

2-kings-25:13:8.summary: The remaining vessels not taken with Jeconiah “will go into Babylon,” fulfilled here.

2-kings-25:13:9.summary: The two pillars, ten mechonoth, and the sea made for Solomon are the objects destroyed.

2-kings-25:14:0.summary: Bowls and “all its utensils of bronze” for the altar match the bronze utensils taken.
2-kings-25:14:0.why: Shows the cultic use of the items.

2-kings-25:14:1.summary: Solomon’s abundant bronze works, bowls, and dishes are the temple utensils taken.

2-kings-25:14:2.summary: The altar’s firepan, bowls, and bronze meat forks parallel the bronze ministering utensils.

2-kings-25:14:3.summary: Gold bowls and incense cups of the temple are related, though the source lists bronze utensils.

2-kings-25:14:4.summary: Articles for temple service and incense vessels made under Jehoiada, generally similar items.

2-kings-25:15:0.summary: The gold and silver vessels Nebuchadnezzar brought from Jerusalem appear at Belshazzar’s feast.

2-kings-25:15:1.summary: Golden and silver incense vessels made for the temple are similar items, a general link.

2-kings-25:15:2.summary: Solomon’s gold bowls and censers in the Lord’s house are among the vessels taken.

2-kings-25:15:3.summary: Silver bowls and a gold incense vessel offered at the tabernacle are similar items only.

2-kings-25:15:4.summary: Gold tongs and trays for the lampstand share only the gold-vessel theme.

2-kings-25:15:5.summary: “All the gold and silver vessels” return from Babylon, the vessels taken here.

2-kings-25:16:0.summary: “There was no measured weight of the bronze,” the same note about Solomon’s bronze.

2-kings-25:17:0.summary: Jeremiah describes the same pillars, bronze cornice, net, and pomegranates, with differing height.

2-kings-25:17:1.summary: Solomon’s pillar “eighteen cubits high” with bronze capitals, nets, and pomegranates matches exactly.

2-kings-25:18:4.summary: The chief guard took the first priest, the second priest, and three guards, the parallel list.

2-kings-25:18:0.summary: Saraias the high priest begot Josadak, identifying the first priest taken.
2-kings-25:18:0.why: Places Saraias in the priestly line.

2-kings-25:18:1.summary: Esdras is son (descendant) of Saraias son of Azarias, linking Ezra to this priest.

2-kings-25:18:2.summary: Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest is the Sophonias of second rank taken here.

2-kings-25:18:3.summary: Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest, same priest later taken by the chief cook.

2-kings-25:18:5.summary: Zephaniah reads Jeremiah’s letter, the same priest later seized.

2-kings-25:18:6.summary: Gedaliah’s oath and murder share no specific link with the seizure of the priests.

2-kings-25:19:0.summary: Persian rulers “nearest the king” loosely resemble men who saw the king’s face, a courtly idiom.

2-kings-25:20:0.summary: Nebuzaradan took them to the king of Babylon at Deblatha, an exact parallel.

2-kings-25:20:1.summary: No respect shown to priests or elders loosely reflects the execution of priests.

2-kings-25:20:2.summary: Deblatha in Emath’s land is where Pharaoh also removed a king, the same place.

2-kings-25:21:0.summary: The Lord said He would remove Judah from His presence, fulfilled as Judah is deported.

2-kings-25:21:1.summary: Covenant curse of scattering among nations, generally fulfilled in Judah’s exile.

2-kings-25:21:2.summary: The land becomes a ruin and they “serve among the nations for seventy years,” fulfilled in the deportation.

2-kings-25:21:3.summary: God’s word will not be delayed, generally fulfilled in Judah’s fall.

2-kings-25:21:4.summary: Moses warns they will perish from the land, generally fulfilled in exile.

2-kings-25:21:5.summary: The Lord will lead “you, and your rulers” to a foreign nation, fulfilled as king and people are deported.

2-kings-25:21:6.summary: Scattering among nations and the land’s desolate Sabbaths generally fit the exile.

2-kings-25:21:7.summary: Israel was cast from His presence into plunderers’ hands, the same fate now befalling Judah.

2-kings-25:21:8.summary: The Lord will act without mercy and judge by their ways, a general link.

2-kings-25:21:9.summary: Scattering into kingdoms until they disappear from the land generally fits the exile.

2-kings-25:21:10.summary: Deportation beyond Damascus concerns Israel, a general parallel to Judah’s exile.

2-kings-25:22:0.summary: Names Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan, the same governor.

2-kings-25:22:1.summary: Ahikam son of Shaphan, Gedaliah’s father, protected Jeremiah.

2-kings-25:22:2.summary: Gedaliah, “whom Babylon’s king had appointed over the land,” is struck by Ishmael.

2-kings-25:22:3.summary: Achikam son of Sapphan served King Josiah, Gedaliah’s father.

2-kings-25:22:4.summary: Ahikam son of Shaphan, Gedaliah’s father, appears in Josiah’s court.

2-kings-25:22:5.summary: Ishmael strikes Godolias at Massephath, the same appointed governor.

2-kings-25:22:6.summary: Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan, “whom Babylon’s king appointed in Judah’s land,” the parallel account.

2-kings-25:23:0.summary: The same commanders, Ishmael, Johanan, Seraiah, Jezaniah, come to Gedaliah at Mizpah.

2-kings-25:23:1.summary: Scattered Judeans heard Babylon’s king appointed Gedaliah and came to him at Mizpah.

2-kings-25:23:2.summary: “Massema” in a Benjamin town list may be Mizpah/Massephath, but the spelling obscures the link.

2-kings-25:24:0.summary: David swearing to Shimei shares only the act of swearing an oath.

2-kings-25:24:1.summary: Gedaliah swore to them: do not be afraid, live in the land and work for Babylon’s king.

2-kings-25:24:2.summary: The people Nebuzaradan left with Gedaliah are later taken to Egypt, a related aftermath.

2-kings-25:24:3.summary: Those in the devastated land trust they will keep it, loosely related to settling the land.

2-kings-25:24:4.summary: David’s oath to the Tekoite woman shares only an oath of safety.

2-kings-25:25:2.summary: In the seventh month Ishmael son of Nethaniah, of the king’s family, came with ten men and struck Gedaliah.

2-kings-25:25:0.summary: The “seventh fast” matches the seventh month of Gedaliah’s murder, a mourning later turned to joy.
2-kings-25:25:0.why: Shows how the event was remembered.

2-kings-25:25:1.summary: Fasting at the “fifth or seventh” observances recalls the fifth-month fall and seventh-month murder.

2-kings-25:25:3.summary: Athaliah destroyed “all the royal offspring,” echoing Ishmael being of the kings’ offspring.

2-kings-25:26:0.summary: Johanan, the commanders, and all the people entered Egypt, the parallel account.

2-kings-25:26:1.summary: The commanders took the people intending to go to Egypt because they feared the Chaldeans.

2-kings-25:26:2.summary: The Lord warns that those who enter Egypt will perish by the sword they fear.
2-kings-25:26:2.why: Shows the flight defied God’s word.

2-kings-25:27:1.summary: Pharaoh remembers his imprisoned servants at a feast; the Greek lacks the “lifted the head” idiom.

2-kings-25:27:2.summary: Joakim king of Judah went out to the king of Babylon, the start of this captivity.

2-kings-25:27:3.summary: Pharaoh restoring the cupbearer resembles the release, but the Greek lacks the head-lifting phrase.

2-kings-25:27:4.summary: A king’s heart in God’s hand loosely explains Euilmarodach’s favor.
2-kings-25:27:4.why: Suggests divine hand in the release.

2-kings-25:27:5.summary: He deported Joakim to Babylon, the deportation from which this year is counted.

2-kings-25:27:6.summary: God promises good to Judah’s deportees, loosely foreshadowed by the king’s release.

2-kings-25:27:7.summary: Rulers brought low and the unsuspected raised illustrates reversals of fortune generally.

2-kings-25:28:0.summary: God gave the earth to Babylon’s king, generally explaining his supremacy over kings.

2-kings-25:28:1.summary: Nebuchadnezzar as “king of kings” loosely parallels thrones of kings in Babylon.

2-kings-25:29:0.summary: Mephibosheth will “eat bread at my table continually,” the same royal favor.
2-kings-25:29:0.why: Parallel royal kindness to a survivor.

2-kings-25:29:1.summary: A robe of glory replacing despondency loosely parallels changed prison garments.

2-kings-25:29:2.summary: Pharaoh clothes Joseph in fine linen, a general parallel to a prisoner honored.

2-kings-25:29:3.summary: Joakim’s surrender begins the imprisonment that ends here, a background link.

2-kings-25:29:4.summary: Esther sends clothes to replace Mordecai’s sackcloth, a loose garment-change parallel.

2-kings-25:29:5.summary: Joshua’s filthy garments are removed and replaced, a loose image of restoration.

2-kings-25:29:6.summary: The prodigal is clothed in the best robe, a loose parallel to restored dignity.

2-kings-25:29:7.summary: Mordecai goes out in royal robes, a loose parallel to elevated status.

2-kings-25:29:8.summary: Joseph was brought out of the fortress and “changed his garments,” a close parallel.
2-kings-25:29:8.why: Parallel release and change of clothes.

2-kings-25:30:0.summary: “Day by day our daily bread” loosely echoes the daily portion.

2-kings-25:30:1.summary: Prayer for daily bread loosely echoes the daily royal portion.

2-kings-25:30:2.summary: Only “the king’s command” is shown; the Greek lacks the daily provision link.

2-kings-25:30:3.summary: A ration “from the king’s house each day” from the royal table, closely parallel.

2-kings-25:30:4.summary: Portions given “each day’s requirement on its day,” the same allotment formula.

2-kings-25:30:5.summary: God who nourished Jacob all his life loosely parallels lifelong provision.

2-kings-25:30:6.summary: Daily service to widows loosely echoes a daily allowance.
